title: SimpleWikiSearch: A Clean Offline Wikipedia Environment for Agentic Search
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agentic search systems are often evaluated as if the underlying LLM were the only component that matters, yet their measured performance also depends on the surrounding search environment: the Wikipedia snapshot, preprocessing pipeline, chunking policy, retrieval backend, tool schema, observation format, and answer submission rule. These details are frequently under-specified, making it difficult to compare results or reproduce reported baselines. We present SimpleWikiSearch, whose corpus construction, retrieval stack, tool contract, and evaluation protocol are explicit and runnable. The environment starts from a full English Wikipedia dump, cleans and chunks the corpus, builds keyword and dense retrieval indexes, and exposes a minimal tool interface consisting of \texttt{search}, \texttt{open\_url}, and \texttt{submit\_answer}. We report baseline results on six QA datasets using open-source LLMs and provide a random-300 subset for comparisons with closed-source commercial models. SimpleWikiSearch provides a domain-specific agent harness and a controlled offline environment for reproducible agentic-search evaluation. Its contribution is this specified reference setup, rather than a new agent algorithm. Code and data will be available at: https://github.com/JimXiongGM/simple_wiki_search.

AI.tldr: SimpleWikiSearch provides a fully specified, reproducible evaluation environment for LLM-based agentic search systems, addressing the problem of under-specified search pipeline details that hinder fair comparison of results.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agentic search systems are typically evaluated treating the LLM as the sole variable, but performance heavily depends on the surrounding search infrastructure (corpus construction, chunking, retrieval backend, tool schemas, etc.). These details are often under-specified, making cross-paper comparisons and reproducibility difficult.
AI.method: The authors build SimpleWikiSearch from a full English Wikipedia dump, applying explicit corpus construction (cleaning + chunking), building keyword and dense retrieval indexes, and exposing a minimal tool interface (search, open_url, submit_answer). They evaluate on six QA datasets using open-source LLMs and provide a random-300 subset for closed-source model comparisons.
AI.result: Baseline results are reported on six QA datasets with open-source LLMs. A random-300 subset enables comparisons with closed-source commercial models. The primary contribution is the reference setup itself rather than novel algorithmic performance.
AI.conclusion: SimpleWikiSearch serves as a domain-specific agent harness and controlled offline environment for reproducible agentic-search evaluation. Its contribution is a fully specified reference setup — covering corpus, retrieval stack, tool contract, and evaluation protocol — rather than a new agent algorithm.

title: GuidedRAG: Semantic Steering of Retrieval-Augmented Generation
comment: 8 pages + 5 pages of references and appendix. 8 figures and 6 tables
summary: In this work, we propose GuidedRAG, a novel extension to traditional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) that introduces a dedicated selection stage and semantic steering during retrieval. In contrast to current state-of-the-art RAG approaches, which depend on increasingly complex retrieval and knowledge structures, GuidedRAG constrains the knowledge base using semantics before retrieval, aligning the retrieval space with user intent while substantially reducing the search space. Our evaluation shows that GuidedRAG improves retrieval relevance by 14.0-15.8%, mitigates a 19.7-27.4% loss in retrieval precision, and reduces retrieval overhead by orders of magnitude. Moreover, relevant chunks are consistently retrieved earlier in the ranking process, while alignment with user intent improves by 31.8-36.8%. We further show that GuidedRAG achieves full coverage across 15 diverse RAG variants, demonstrating generalizability across the literature. Together, these findings establish semantic steering and selections as a powerful and generalizable paradigm for improving the current state-of-the-art in RAG.

AI.tldr: GuidedRAG extends traditional RAG by adding a semantic selection stage before retrieval, constraining the knowledge base to align with user intent. This improves retrieval relevance by ~15%, reduces precision loss by ~20-27%, cuts retrieval overhead drastically, and achieves earlier ranking of relevant chunks with ~32-37% better intent alignment. It generalizes across 15 RAG variants.
AI.motivation: Current state-of-the-art RAG approaches rely on increasingly complex retrieval architectures and knowledge structures, yet they still suffer from retrieval precision loss and misalignment with user intent. There is a need for a simpler, more efficient paradigm that constrains the search space semantically before retrieval rather than adding complexity post-hoc.
AI.method: GuidedRAG introduces two key innovations: (1) a dedicated semantic selection stage that constrains the knowledge base before retrieval, and (2) semantic steering during the retrieval process itself. These mechanisms align the retrieval space with user intent and substantially reduce the search space, without requiring complex retrieval or knowledge structures.
AI.result: GuidedRAG yields: (a) 14.0–15.8% improvement in retrieval relevance, (b) mitigation of 19.7–27.4% loss in retrieval precision, (c) orders-of-magnitude reduction in retrieval overhead, (d) consistent early ranking of relevant chunks, (e) 31.8–36.8% improvement in user intent alignment, and (f) full coverage/generalizability across 15 diverse RAG variants.
AI.conclusion: Semantic steering and selection constitute a powerful and generalizable paradigm for advancing RAG, offering significant gains in relevance, precision, efficiency, and intent alignment without the complexity of current SOTA approaches.

title: IFCMemoryBench: Evaluating Long-Term Memory of LLM-Based Agents in BIM Information Retrieval
comment: KDD 2026 Workshop on Evaluation and Trustworthiness of Agentic AI
summary: Long-term memory is becoming a core capability of LLM-based agents, but existing evaluations largely test conversational recall in open-domain or persona-grounded settings. We argue that a stronger test is whether an agent can reuse information from prior sessions while acting over a live, structured, domain-specific environment. We study this problem in Building Information Modelling (BIM), a professional engineering workflow where agents must query large IFC models while also relying on project specifications, client decisions, and engineering conventions often discussed in conversation but absent from the model. We introduce IFCMemoryBench, a benchmark for evaluating long-term memory in LLM-based BIM information retrieval. IFCMemoryBench contains 143 multi-session tasks across 19 projects and 4,016 prior sessions, derived from incomplete-information questions in IFC-Bench v2. Each task seeds missing project context across earlier conversations and later asks a probe question that can be answered only by combining remembered context with live IFC queries. Our evaluation framework decomposes memory performance into ingestion, retrieval, and utilization, and measures both answer quality and memory quality with expert-validated LLM judges. We evaluate representative vector-, graph-, and file-based memory systems. The strongest system achieves only 32.4% answer accuracy under a deployment-realistic ingestion scope, and remains below 60% under oracle-filtered ingestion or a stronger probe agent. Analysis shows that current general-purpose memory systems often retrieve topically relevant context but store project knowledge as incomplete or fragmented facts. These results reveal a domain-transfer gap in agent memory and suggest that reliable professional agents require domain-aware memory representations linking conversations, project knowledge, and structured model entities.

AI.tldr: IFCMemoryBench introduces a benchmark evaluating long-term memory in LLM agents for BIM (Building Information Modelling). Spanning 143 multi-session tasks across 19 projects with 4,016 prior sessions, it tests whether agents can recall missing project context from earlier conversations to answer probe questions requiring combined memory and live IFC queries. The strongest system achieves only 32.4% accuracy, revealing a domain-transfer gap: general-purpose memory systems store fragmented facts rather than structured, linked project knowledge.
AI.motivation: Existing long-term memory evaluations for LLM agents focus on conversational recall in open-domain or persona-grounded settings. The authors argue this is insufficient for professional, domain-specific environments where agents must reuse information across sessions while interacting with live, structured data. BIM workflows exemplify this challenge: agents must query IFC models while relying on project specifications, client decisions, and engineering conventions discussed conversationally but absent from the model itself.
AI.method: The authors construct IFCMemoryBench from incomplete-information questions in IFC-Bench v2, yielding 143 multi-session tasks across 19 BIM projects and 4,016 prior sessions. Each task seeds missing project context across earlier conversations, then poses a probe question answerable only by combining remembered context with live IFC queries. Their evaluation framework decomposes memory performance into ingestion, retrieval, and utilization, measuring both answer quality and memory quality via expert-validated LLM judges. Representative vector-, graph-, and file-based memory systems are evaluated.
AI.result: The strongest memory system achieves only 32.4% answer accuracy under deployment-realistic ingestion scope, remaining below 60% even with oracle-filtered ingestion or a stronger probe agent. Analysis reveals that general-purpose memory systems retrieve topically relevant context but store project knowledge as incomplete or fragmented facts, failing to link conversations, project knowledge, and structured model entities coherently.
AI.conclusion: Current general-purpose memory systems exhibit a domain-transfer gap when applied to professional BIM workflows. Reliable professional agents require domain-aware memory representations that explicitly link conversations, project knowledge, and structured model entities, rather than treating memory as flat fact storage.

title: Guess Where You Go: Generative Next Point-of-Interest Recommendation in Amap
summary: Generative retrieval enables recommender systems to retrieve items by generating compact item identifiers, but scaling it to industrial scenarios remains challenging due to redundant or colliding token assignments and insufficient integration of heterogeneous item signals. These challenges are particularly critical for next Point-of-Interest (POI) recommendation, where models must represent structured spatial entities, capture sequential mobility patterns, and produce predictions consistent with real user behavior. We propose Gwhere, an end-to-end industrial framework that integrates semantic identifier (SID) generation with LLM-based generative next POI recommendation. Gwhere first learns discriminative POI SIDs through a contrastive residual-quantization tokenizer that aligns textual, visual, spatial, and collaborative signals. Based on these SIDs, Gwhere adapts LLMs to mobility scenarios via continued pretraining on enriched spatio-temporal corpora, supervised fine-tuning, and Exposure-Aware Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (EAKTO), a reinforcement learning objective for behavioral preference alignment. Experiments on public datasets and Amap's large-scale industrial dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of Gwhere. The system has been deployed in Amap's homepage service under high-concurrency and low-latency constraints. Long-term online A/B tests show improvements of 5.83% in P-CTR and 6.20% in U-CTR over the production baseline. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/alibaba/SimCIT.

AI.tldr: Gwhere is an end-to-end industrial framework for next POI recommendation that combines semantic identifier generation with LLM-based generative retrieval, achieving significant CTR improvements in production deployment at Amap.
AI.motivation: Scaling generative retrieval to industrial scenarios is challenging due to redundant/colliding token assignments and insufficient integration of heterogeneous item signals. These issues are exacerbated in next POI recommendation, which requires modeling structured spatial entities, sequential mobility patterns, and behaviorally consistent predictions.
AI.method: Gwhere employs: (1) a contrastive residual-quantization tokenizer that learns discriminative POI semantic identifiers (SIDs) by aligning textual, visual, spatial, and collaborative signals; (2) continued pretraining of LLMs on enriched spatio-temporal corpora followed by supervised fine-tuning; and (3) Exposure-Aware Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (EAKTO), a reinforcement learning objective for behavioral preference alignment.
AI.result: On public datasets and Amap's large-scale industrial dataset, Gwhere demonstrates effectiveness. Deployed in Amap's homepage under high-concurrency, low-latency constraints, long-term online A/B tests show improvements of 5.83% in P-CTR and 6.20% in U-CTR over the production baseline.
AI.conclusion: Gwhere successfully bridges the gap between generative retrieval research and industrial deployment for POI recommendation, validated by both offline experiments and online A/B testing in a high-traffic production environment. Code is publicly available.

title: Probing the Origins of Reasoning Performance: Representational Quality for Mathematical Problem-Solving in RL vs. SFT Fine-Tuned Models
summary: Large reasoning models trained via reinforcement learning (RL) have been increasingly shown to outperform their supervised fine-tuned (SFT) counterparts on mathematical reasoning tasks; Yet the mechanistic basis for this advantage remains unclear. We therefore ask, what internal representational differences enable RL models' superior performance? Our work presents two converging lines of evidence: First, linear probes trained on layer-wise hidden states reveal that RL models tend to achieve higher accuracy in predicting answer correctness compared to SFT models, indicating more linearly separable and structured representations. Second, mean ablation studies show that RL models develop a hierarchical architecture where deeper layers become progressively more critical, whereas SFT models distribute importance uniformly across layers. Together, these findings demonstrate that RL training fundamentally restructures how models represent and process reasoning problems. Finally, we analyze token-count variability under repeated sampling across problems to assess adaptive compute allocation. While we observe higher variability in some RL-tuned models than in their SFT counterparts, we see strong consistency in others, suggesting that token allocation may depend more on the overall training pipeline than on RL versus SFT alone. We believe this token-allocation variability reveals the spread of plausible on-policy reasoning, highlighting which models exhibit stable policies versus those that are under-determined, potentially non-identifiable solution behaviour.

AI.tldr: RL-trained reasoning models outperform SFT models on math tasks; this paper shows RL models develop more linearly separable hidden representations, a hierarchical layer-wise importance structure, and variable token allocation patterns depending on the training pipeline.
AI.motivation: Despite the empirical success of RL-trained models over SFT models on mathematical reasoning, the mechanistic basis — specifically, what internal representational differences drive this advantage — remains poorly understood.
AI.method: Two-pronged approach: (1) linear probing on layer-wise hidden states to assess how accurately answer correctness can be decoded (measuring representational separability), and (2) mean ablation studies to quantify the causal importance of each layer. Additionally, token-count variability under repeated sampling is analyzed to study adaptive compute allocation.
AI.result: RL models exhibit (a) higher linear probe accuracy for predicting answer correctness, indicating more structured/linearly separable representations; (b) a hierarchical architecture where deeper layers are progressively more critical (vs. SFT's uniform importance distribution); and (c) mixed token-allocation variability — some RL models show high variability, others strong consistency, suggesting dependence on the overall training pipeline rather than RL vs. SFT alone.
AI.conclusion: RL training fundamentally restructures internal representations and layer-wise processing hierarchies. Token-allocation variability may signal the spread of plausible on-policy reasoning, distinguishing models with stable policies from those exhibiting under-determined, potentially non-identifiable solution behavior.

title: Framework Implementation Maturity in Blockchain-Based Third-Party Compliance Assessment
summary: Cybersecurity and privacy frameworks such as NIST SP~800--53, ISO/IEC~27001, GDPR, and HIPAA are widely used to guide organizational security posture and regulatory compliance. In practice, however, framework adoption is often assessed through point-in-time audits, self-attestations, and fragmented evidence reviews, providing limited assurance that controls are consistently implemented, independently validated, and sustained over time, particularly in environments that rely on third-party vendors. These limitations are amplified in multi-vendor ecosystems, such as healthcare remote patient monitoring (RPM), where compliance obligations span organizational boundaries and assessments are conducted by multiple independent assessors. This paper investigates how permissioned blockchain systems can support framework implementation maturity measurement rather than static compliance verification. We propose a blockchain-based Third-Party Risk Assessment (TPRA) framework that operationalizes assessment workflows, enforces multi-party governance, and preserves longitudinal assessment state using programmable smart contracts. Building on this framework, we introduce a set of evaluation metrics and a qualitative maturity model designed to assess whether compliance controls are verifiably implemented, governed, and sustained across repeated assessment cycles.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a permissioned blockchain-based Third-Party Risk Assessment (TPRA) framework that shifts compliance evaluation from static point-in-time audits to continuous, verifiable maturity measurement of cybersecurity controls, particularly in multi-vendor ecosystems like healthcare remote patient monitoring.
AI.motivation: Current cybersecurity and privacy frameworks (NIST SP 800-53, ISO/IEC 27001, GDPR, HIPAA) rely on point-in-time audits and self-attestations, which fail to provide assurance that controls are consistently implemented and sustained over time. This problem is exacerbated in multi-vendor environments (e.g., healthcare RPM) where compliance spans organizational boundaries and involves multiple independent assessors, making fragmented evidence review insufficient for meaningful assurance.
AI.method: The authors design a permissioned blockchain-based TPRA framework that (1) operationalizes assessment workflows, (2) enforces multi-party governance, and (3) preserves longitudinal assessment state via programmable smart contracts. They further introduce a set of evaluation metrics and a qualitative maturity model to assess whether compliance controls are verifiably implemented, governed, and sustained across repeated assessment cycles.
AI.result: The paper presents a conceptual framework and maturity model rather than empirical experimental results. The key contribution is the architectural design demonstrating how blockchain can enable continuous, multi-party assessment state tracking and governance, moving beyond binary compliance verification toward graded maturity measurement.
AI.conclusion: Permissioned blockchain systems can serve as a foundation for shifting cybersecurity compliance from static verification to continuous maturity measurement. The proposed TPRA framework and maturity model provide a mechanism for verifiable, sustained, and independently governed control assessment across organizational boundaries, particularly relevant for complex third-party risk ecosystems.

title: A Persona-based Rate Action Index
summary: We propose an index for predicting the U.S.\ Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) decision to hike/hold/cut the current federal funds target rate based on how a collection of personas responds to current market conditions. To construct the index, we collected a new dataset consisting of nearly $25{,}000$ retrievable chunks from publicly available data. We partition the data into per-member corpora and use each as the retrieval database of a generative system we refer to throughout as a ``persona''. We first evaluate the personas across two complementary components of likeness: identifiability and detectability. Each persona's behavior is highly attributable (average member-conditional recall is $ 8\times $ chance) and generated content is nearly indistinguishable from held-out real content ($\hatτ_{\mathrm{det}} = 0.23$ against a $0.15$ floor). We then present evidence that query-conditioned representations of the personas capture members' monetary-policy stance relative to a known hawk--dove reputational ordering (Kendall's $τ= 0.63$, $p < 0.001$), substantially outperforming retrieval-only representations. These representations vary with time and current market conditions and form the basis of our proposed persona-based rate action index. For the $2022$--$2025$ period the index tracks the rate cycle (Kendall's $τ= 0.68$, $p < 10^{-6}$) and can be used to construct a simple classifier that predicts per-meeting outcomes at non-trivial accuracy ($0.69$ versus a $0.47$ base rate). Importantly, the index outperforms informative baselines and leads the federal funds target rate by roughly three quarters. As far as we are aware, our results are the first to demonstrate the ability to capture time-varying group behavior via a collection of digital personas.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a persona-based index for predicting FOMC rate decisions (hike/hold/cut) by modeling individual FOMC members as retrieval-augmented generative "personas." These personas exhibit high identifiability and detectability, and their query-conditioned representations capture members' hawk-dove stances, enabling a composite index that tracks and leads the federal funds rate by ~3 quarters with significant predictive accuracy.
AI.motivation: Predicting FOMC monetary policy decisions is challenging due to the complexity of individual members' evolving stances and the committee's collective dynamics. Existing approaches typically rely on aggregate market data or static hawk-dove scores, failing to capture time-varying, member-specific policy preferences in response to changing market conditions.
AI.method: The authors collect ~25,000 retrievable text chunks from publicly available FOMC member communications and partition them into per-member corpora. Each member's corpus serves as the retrieval database for a generative system (a "persona"). They evaluate personas on two dimensions: identifiability (member-conditional recall) and detectability (distinguishability from real content). Policy stance is extracted via query-conditioned representations, validated against known hawk-dove rankings. These time-varying representations are aggregated into a composite "persona-based rate action index" used to predict hike/hold/cut decisions.
AI.result: Personas achieve 8× chance identifiability and near-indistinguishable generated content (τ̂_det = 0.23 vs. 0.15 floor). Query-conditioned representations correlate strongly with hawk-dove reputations (Kendall's τ = 0.63, p < 0.001), substantially outperforming retrieval-only baselines. The resulting index tracks the 2022–2025 rate cycle (τ = 0.68, p < 10⁻⁶), predicts per-meeting outcomes at 0.69 accuracy (vs. 0.47 base rate), outperforms informative baselines, and leads the federal funds target rate by roughly three quarters.
AI.conclusion: This is the first demonstration of capturing time-varying group behavior via digital personas. The persona-based index not only tracks but leads FOMC rate decisions, suggesting that per-member generative models conditioned on historical communications can surface latent policy stances that evolve with market conditions, offering a novel tool for monetary policy forecasting.

title: Emergent Sparsity in Frozen Random CNN Feature Extractors for Deep Reinforcement Learning
summary: We report a striking phenomenon: deep reinforcement learning agents trained with frozen, randomly initialized CNN feature extractors spontaneously develop extremely sparse fully-connected representations, without any sparsity-inducing objective. In the first fully-connected layer (FC1, $3{,}136 \to 64$), agents compress task-relevant information through as few as 1-3 neurons out of 64 for deterministic Pong (5-11 for stochastic Pong), while trainable CNNs activate 55-64 neurons under matched conditions. We establish four principal findings. First, FC1 sparsity scales with task complexity: 1-11 for Pong, 19-26 for Breakout, and $\sim$42 for Space Invaders. Width-scaling confirms this reflects task structure rather than a fixed capacity fraction. Second, within-game scaling emerges: three identical Pong seeds produce 5, 7, and 11 active neurons. The 5-neuron seed plateaus at $+14$ reward, while the others reach expert performance ($+18.4$, $+18.7$), suggesting the random projection's usable dimensionality bounds achievable performance. Third, ablation confirms necessity: removing these active neurons crashes performance across two PPO implementations and four games. Fourth, the information bottleneck commits early: a sweep shows the active set locks by 15-30M steps, while reward turns positive 35-105M steps later. A complementary finding in Breakout shows frozen and trainable CNNs reach competitive rewards via structurally different bottlenecks: frozen agents use 17-25 active neurons (participation ratio $\sim$10-14), while trainable agents use 51 (participation ratio $\sim$3.6). Finally, wherever input dimensionality dwarfs intrinsic task dimensionality, gradient descent on a frozen random projection may reveal the effective rank of the underlying problem without explicit sparsity machinery.

AI.tldr: Deep RL agents with frozen random CNN features spontaneously develop ultra-sparse fully-connected representations (1–3 neurons for deterministic Pong), with sparsity scaling predictably with task complexity. This emergent sparsity reveals task intrinsic dimensionality without any sparsity-inducing regularization.
AI.motivation: Investigate the unexpected emergence of extreme sparsity in deep RL when using frozen, randomly initialized CNN feature extractors, and understand whether this sparsity reflects intrinsic task structure rather than optimization artifacts.
AI.method: Train PPO agents on Atari games (Pong, Breakout, Space Invaders) using frozen random CNNs followed by trainable fully-connected layers. Analyze FC1 neuron activations, conduct ablation studies on active neurons, sweep width-scaling, and compare against standard trainable CNN baselines.
AI.result: (1) FC1 sparsity scales with task complexity: 1–11 neurons for Pong, 19–26 for Breakout, ~42 for Space Invaders. (2) Within-game seeds produce different active neuron counts (5, 7, 11) with corresponding performance ceilings. (3) Ablating active neurons crashes performance across implementations and games. (4) Active neuron set locks by 15–30M steps, long before reward turns positive. Frozen and trainable CNNs achieve competitive rewards via structurally different bottlenecks.
AI.conclusion: When input dimensionality far exceeds intrinsic task dimensionality, gradient descent on frozen random projections reveals the effective rank of the learning problem, offering a principled diagnostic for task complexity without explicit sparsity machinery.

title: Reproducibility in Recommender Systems: A Survey
comment: Accepted at ACM Transactions on Recommender Systems
summary:
Reproducibility has become a cornerstone of credible recommender systems research, driven by growing concerns about the reliability and generalizability of experimental results. In response, the ACM RecSys conference introduced a dedicated Reproducibility Track in 2020 to encourage rigorous, transparent, and repeatable research. This paper presents a structured analysis of the track from 2020 to 2025, covering 51 accepted papers. We classify contributions by type and analyze common patterns in datasets, algorithms, frameworks, and evaluation practices, with the goal of understanding how reproducibility is operationalized in practice within the community.
  Our findings reveal three main trends. First, the track has expanded in scope, evolving from a focus on reproduction and replication to include benchmarking, resources, and methodological contributions. Second, reproducibility papers exhibit a consistent methodological profile, relying on a limited set of datasets, algorithms, and evaluation protocols. Third, reproducibility in practice often involves extending prior experiments rather than strictly replicating them, with studies frequently introducing additional models or evaluation criteria. Overall, reproducibility work has improved transparency and documentation, but has had limited impact on methodological diversity, highlighting a gap between the conceptual definition of reproducibility and its implementation.

AI.tldr: A structured analysis of 51 papers from the ACM RecSys Reproducibility Track (2020–2025) reveals that reproducibility work has expanded in scope but relies on a narrow set of datasets and methods, often extending rather than strictly replicating prior work, highlighting a gap between the conceptual ideal and practical implementation of reproducibility.
AI.motivation: Growing concerns about the reliability and generalizability of experimental results in recommender systems research, coupled with the establishment of the ACM RecSys Reproducibility Track in 2020, motivate a systematic examination of how reproducibility is actually operationalized within the community.
AI.method: The authors conduct a structured analysis of all 51 papers accepted to the RecSys Reproducibility Track from 2020 to 2025, classifying contributions by type and analyzing patterns in datasets, algorithms, frameworks, and evaluation practices.
AI.result: Three main trends emerged: (1) the track's scope broadened from reproduction/replication to include benchmarking, resources, and methodology; (2) reproducibility papers converge on a limited set of datasets, algorithms, and evaluation protocols; (3) studies frequently extend prior experiments with additional models or criteria rather than strictly replicating them. While transparency and documentation have improved, methodological diversity remains limited.
AI.conclusion: The Reproducibility Track has successfully improved transparency and documentation in recommender systems research, but its impact on methodological diversity is limited, revealing a gap between the conceptual definition of reproducibility and how it is implemented in practice.

title: Even More Deception: Objective Misalignment in Mixed-Motive LLM Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs)-powered multi-agent systems are increasingly deployed in mixed-motive environments, where agents operate under asymmetric information and strategic deception due to conflicting or hidden objectives. In these settings, misalignment with collective goals becomes a central concern. We propose a novel framework for evaluating objective misalignment using the social deduction game Werewolf, modifying the objective of a single agent while preserving its assigned role. Across LLMs from four different model families and sizes, four player roles, and three objective formulations, we introduce a dual analysis of the agents' internal reasoning and their public cheap-talk behavior (i.e costless, non-binding communication that does not directly affect the agents' utilities), complemented by an analysis of game outcomes. Our results show that objective misalignment undermines outcomes in inherently adversarial environments, an effect exacerbated by asymmetric information and specialized roles. While compromised agents consistently develop distinct objective-dependent reasoning strategies, these adaptations remain largely invisible in their public behavior. More broadly, our findings suggest that even subtle objective misalignment can profoundly affect collective decision-making, highlighting the need for effective mitigation strategies for LLM-based multi-agent systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a framework for evaluating objective misalignment in LLM-based multi-agent systems using the Werewolf social deduction game. By altering a single agent's objective while keeping its role unchanged, the authors analyze internal reasoning and public communication across multiple LLM families, roles, and objective types. Results reveal that misalignment degrades outcomes in adversarial settings, with compromised agents developing hidden reasoning strategies that remain undetectable in their public behavior.
AI.motivation: As LLM-powered multi-agent systems are increasingly deployed in mixed-motive environments with asymmetric information and strategic deception, misalignment with collective goals poses a critical risk. Existing work lacks robust evaluation frameworks for detecting and understanding how subtle objective misalignment manifests in agent reasoning and behavior, motivating this study.
AI.method: The authors use the social deduction game Werewolf as a testbed, modifying a single agent's objective while preserving its assigned role. They conduct a dual analysis across four LLM model families/sizes, four player roles, and three objective formulations: (1) internal reasoning analysis of compromised agents, (2) analysis of public cheap-talk communication, and (3) game outcome analysis.
AI.result: Objective misalignment significantly undermines outcomes in adversarial environments, with effects amplified by asymmetric information and specialized roles. Compromised agents consistently develop distinct objective-dependent reasoning strategies, but these adaptations remain largely invisible in their public cheap-talk behavior, making detection difficult from surface-level communication alone.
AI.conclusion: Even subtle objective misalignment can profoundly affect collective decision-making in LLM-based multi-agent systems. The disconnect between internal reasoning and public behavior highlights the urgent need for effective mitigation strategies and detection mechanisms that go beyond surface-level communication monitoring.

title: Lilith: Backdoor Generalization under Training-Inference Trigger Shift
summary: Machine-learning services increasingly rely on public data, third-party providers, and outsourced training, creating opportunities for data-poisoning attacks that implant persistent malicious behavior while preserving benign utility. However, existing backdoor studies largely evaluate exact trigger reuse, training-exposed trigger diversity, or variations along predefined transformation axes. They therefore leave a critical blind spot: whether a backdoor learned from one training-time trigger can generalize to an inference-time trigger family absent from victim training. We formulate this problem as backdoor generalization under training--inference trigger shift and introduce Lilith, a black-box anchor-to-family framework. Using only disjoint surrogate resources, Lilith first induces a compact target-side vulnerability with a single training anchor, then constructs a bounded inference-only family that preserves the anchor-induced representation geometry. We characterize this mechanism through anchor clearance and family reach, deriving sufficient conditions for family-wise target preservation under local regularity and bounded surrogate--victim discrepancy. Experiments across datasets, architectures, poisoning rates, and defenses show that Lilith achieves high family-wise attack success with limited utility degradation and a small trigger generalization gap. Additional analyses show that family activation depends on representation alignment rather than the proposal mechanism, exposing a broader threat overlooked by exact-trigger evaluation.

AI.tldr: Lilith introduces a black-box backdoor attack where a single training-time anchor trigger generalizes to a family of inference-time triggers never seen during training, exposing a critical blind spot in existing backdoor defenses that only evaluate exact trigger reuse or predefined variations.
AI.motivation: Current backdoor defenses assume attackers reuse the same trigger at inference or only vary triggers along known axes. The authors identify a gap: a backdoor learned from one trigger could generalize to an entire unseen trigger family, making detection and mitigation far harder.
AI.method: Lilith uses disjoint surrogate resources to (1) induce a compact target-side vulnerability with a single anchor trigger during training, then (2) construct a bounded inference-only trigger family that preserves the anchor's representation geometry. The approach is characterized via anchor clearance and family reach, with sufficient conditions derived for family-wise target preservation under local regularity and bounded surrogate-victim discrepancy.
AI.result: Across multiple datasets, architectures, poisoning rates, and defenses, Lilith achieves high family-wise attack success with minimal utility degradation and a small trigger generalization gap. Family activation depends on representation alignment rather than the specific proposal mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Backdoor generalization across unseen trigger families represents a serious, underexplored threat. Evaluation limited to exact-trigger reuse or predefined variations is insufficient; the community must consider representation-level vulnerabilities that enable broad trigger generalization.

title: One Run Is Not an Idea: The Implementation Lottery in Automated Research
summary: Automated research systems use experimental scores both to deliver artifacts and to decide which ideas to retain, transfer, and pursue. Yet one run scores one implementation of an idea. Crediting that realization-level score as evidence about the parent mechanism creates the \emph{implementation lottery}, in which an idea-level conclusion depends on which plausible implementation was sampled. The mismatch is structural whenever one run updates beliefs about a mechanism. We estimate its magnitude. The \emph{Idea Reliability Audit} measures \emph{idea reliability} by validating and freezing candidate cards, sampling fresh-session implementations, using outcome-blind fidelity labels, and rerunning saved artifacts. It reports idea ICC and leave-one-implementation-out (LOO) winner reversal. Prior work generally repeats the task; we repeat the idea. Across 312 assignments on 13 tabular tasks and two coding-agent setups, implementation variance was more than five and ten times same-artifact rerun variance, respectively, and the winner from one implementation draw differed from the winner under the other-two mean in 25.6\% and 43.6\% of decisions. Reversal survives card-level filtering under two outcome-blind review rules. An exploratory diagnostic on three materials-regression workflows with a deterministic evaluator also finds implementation variation dominating the decomposition. These findings distinguish idea reliability from best-of-$N$ artifact utility. Before a score guides idea-level branching, transfer, or research memory, evidence should cover multiple implementations.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and quantifies the "implementation lottery" — a structural mismatch where a single implementation's score is wrongly credited as evidence about the parent idea. The authors introduce the Idea Reliability Audit, which measures idea-level reliability by sampling multiple implementations per idea. Across 312 assignments, implementation variance dominated rerun variance by 5–10×, and winner reversals occurred in 25.6–43.6% of decisions.
AI.motivation: Automated research systems (e.g., AutoML, LLM-agent pipelines) use experimental scores to decide which ideas to retain, transfer, or pursue. However, any single run scores only one implementation of an idea, not the idea itself. This creates an "implementation lottery": conclusions about an idea's merit depend on which plausible implementation was sampled. The problem is structural — it arises whenever one run updates beliefs about a mechanism — yet its magnitude has not been systematically estimated.
AI.method: The authors propose the **Idea Reliability Audit**, a protocol that: (1) validates and freezes candidate idea "cards" (specifications), (2) samples multiple fresh-session implementations per idea, (3) uses outcome-blind fidelity labels to verify implementations faithfully instantiate the idea, and (4) reruns saved artifacts. Key metrics are **Idea ICC** (intraclass correlation measuring the fraction of variance attributable to ideas vs. implementations) and **LOO winner reversal** (whether the winning idea changes when evaluated under the mean of the other implementations). The audit is applied across 312 assignments on 13 tabular tasks and two coding-agent setups, plus an exploratory diagnostic on three materials-regression workflows with a deterministic evaluator.
AI.result: Implementation variance exceeded same-artifact rerun variance by more than 5× (tabular) and 10× (coding-agent). The winner under one implementation draw differed from the winner under the mean of the other two implementations in 25.6% (tabular) and 43.6% (coding-agent) of decisions. These reversals persisted even under card-level filtering with two outcome-blind review rules. The exploratory diagnostic on materials-regression workflows likewise found implementation variation dominating the variance decomposition.
AI.conclusion: Idea reliability is distinct from best-of-N artifact utility. Before using a score to guide idea-level branching, transfer, or research memory, evidence should cover multiple implementations. The Idea Reliability Audit provides a concrete methodology for distinguishing signal about a mechanism from noise arising from its particular instantiation.

title: Sim2Win: A Team-Agnostic, Event-Based Pre-Match Outcome Prediction and Tactical Profiling System for Football
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures. Code available at https://github.com/Mouad-Ze/SIM2WIN
summary:
Pre-match tactical decision-making in professional football relies heavily on subjective expert analysis and identity-based scouting systems that cannot generalize to unseen teams. This paper presents Sim2Win, a team-agnostic, event-based pre-match tactical recommendation framework that reframes match outcome prediction as a tactical decision-support problem. Using StatsBomb open event data from eleven competitions spanning 178 teams and 1,411 team-match records, Sim2Win constructs five-match rolling tactical profiles, engineers four interpretable tactical feature ratios, clusters team behaviors into eight playstyles via K-Means, and trains thirteen classifiers to estimate win, draw, and loss probabilities from tactical matchup representations.
  The system operates without team names or identity features, enabling generalization to teams never seen during training. A rigorous Leave-One-Competition-Out (LOCO) evaluation demonstrates that Sim2Win achieves a mean ROC-AUC of 0.704 and mean accuracy of 55.4% on completely unseen teams, outperforming ELO, Pi-Rating, and GAP baselines on all 21 ROC-AUC comparisons and 19 of 21 accuracy comparisons. Among all evaluated models, CatBoost achieved the strongest in-distribution performance with 60.90% accuracy.
  These findings suggest that behavioral tactical representations provide transferable predictive signal under distribution shift and offer a viable alternative to identity-dependent football prediction systems.

AI.tldr: Sim2Win is a team-agnostic pre-match tactical recommendation framework that predicts match outcomes (win/draw/loss) using only behavioral tactical features, without team identity. It clusters team playstyles via K-Means, trains classifiers on tactical matchup representations, and generalizes to unseen teams, outperforming ELO, Pi-Rating, and GAP baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing pre-match tactical decision-making in professional football depends on subjective expert analysis and identity-based scouting systems that fail to generalize to unseen teams. There is a need for an objective, transferable approach that leverages behavioral tactics rather than team identity.
AI.method: Using StatsBomb open event data (11 competitions, 178 teams, 1,411 team-match records), Sim2Win: (1) constructs five-match rolling tactical profiles, (2) engineers four interpretable tactical feature ratios, (3) clusters team behaviors into eight playstyles via K-Means, and (4) trains thirteen classifiers to estimate win/draw/loss probabilities from tactical matchup representations. Evaluation uses Leave-One-Competition-Out (LOCO) to test generalization on entirely unseen teams.
AI.result: Sim2Win achieves a mean ROC-AUC of 0.704 and mean accuracy of 55.4% on completely unseen teams under LOCO evaluation. It outperforms ELO, Pi-Rating, and GAP baselines on all 21 ROC-AUC comparisons and 19 of 21 accuracy comparisons. CatBoost achieves the strongest in-distribution accuracy at 60.90%.
AI.conclusion: Behavioral tactical representations provide transferable predictive signal under distribution shift and offer a viable, identity-independent alternative to traditional football prediction systems, enabling generalization to previously unseen teams.

title: IDP AutoOpt: Agent-Driven Optimization of Document Processing Pipeline Configurations
summary: We present IDP AutoOpt, an autonomous LLM agent that discovers high-performing configurations for intelligent document processing (IDP) pipelines. Tuning IDP prompts, models, OCR settings, and schemas jointly currently costs domain specialists 20 to 80+ person-hours per document type and does not scale as enterprises add document classes. IDP AutoOpt runs a closed loop: it scores a configuration on a small labeled set, diagnoses field-level errors, generates targeted edits, and re-evaluates, guided by human-authored domain skills that encode production expertise. Across extraction, classification, and packet-splitting tasks deployed in healthcare, marketing-intelligence, and financial-services settings, IDP AutoOpt matches or exceeds human-expert accuracy at equal or lower cost (on an extraction benchmark, 90.2% vs 81.6% at 4.6 x lower per-page cost), cutting configuration time from weeks to under two hours. We further show that agent LLM capability has a hard threshold below which optimization fails, and that curated domain skills outperform raw source-code access, which can degrade performance when provided without structure. We also share practical lessons on context management and variance mitigation. Requiring only a configurable pipeline, a scoring function, and a small labeled set, the approach extends beyond IDP to other enterprise AI systems, such as RAG and multi-agent workflows, where configuration bottlenecks deployment.

AI.tldr: IDP AutoOpt is an autonomous LLM agent that discovers optimal configurations for intelligent document processing pipelines, matching or surpassing human experts while reducing configuration time from weeks to under two hours and cutting per-page costs significantly.
AI.motivation: Tuning IDP pipelines (prompts, models, OCR settings, schemas) requires 20–80+ person-hours per document type from domain specialists, creating a scalability bottleneck as enterprises handle growing numbers of document classes. Automating this configuration process addresses both cost and deployment velocity.
AI.method: A closed-loop autonomous LLM agent that: (1) scores pipeline configurations on a small labeled dataset, (2) diagnoses field-level errors, (3) generates targeted edits guided by human-authored domain skills encoding production expertise, and (4) re-evaluates iteratively. The agent operates over a configurable pipeline with a scoring function and uses curated domain skills rather than raw source-code access.
AI.result: On extraction benchmarks across healthcare, marketing-intelligence, and financial-services settings, IDP AutoOpt achieved 90.2% accuracy vs. 81.6% human-expert accuracy at 4.6× lower per-page cost. Configuration time dropped from weeks to under two hours. A hard threshold in agent LLM capability was identified below which optimization fails. Curated domain skills outperformed raw source-code access, which degraded performance when unstructured.
AI.conclusion: The approach generalizes beyond IDP to any configurable enterprise AI system (e.g., RAG, multi-agent workflows) where configuration bottlenecks deployment. Key practical insights include the necessity of sufficient LLM capability, the superiority of structured domain skills over raw code access, and lessons on context management and variance mitigation.

title: ClinLens: Towards Long-Horizon Coding Agents for Longitudinal Multimodal Clinical Data Science
summary: Clinical data-science agents must transform heterogeneous longitudinal records into auditable analyses, yet existing benchmarks largely isolate medical question answering, structured-table reasoning, or generic scientific repositories. We introduce CLINLENS, a benchmark of 200 executable tasks over five linked MIMIC resources spanning structured electronic health records, notes, electrocardiograms, chest radiographs, and echocardiograms. A 4 x 5 taxonomy crosses four patient-time scopes with five analysis capabilities. Program-first reverse synthesis pairs each bounded semi-raw package with an evaluator-private reference workflow and checks required artifacts, cohort and temporal semantics, and the final answer. On a fixed 126-task suite, the strongest of 24 standardized model-scaffold configurations achieves 56.3% scope-macro STRICTPASS despite 100% EXECSUCCESS. For reference, a separately configured coding agent solves 83 of 126 tasks, while five biomedical systems adapted to GPT-4o-mini reach at most 2.9% scope-macro STRICTPASS. These results expose a substantial gap between runnable submissions and correct clinical analyses.

AI.tldr: CLINLENS is a benchmark of 200 executable clinical data-science tasks over five linked MIMIC resources, using a 4×5 taxonomy of patient-time scopes and analysis capabilities. The best model-scaffold configuration achieves only 56.3% STRICTPASS despite 100% execution success, exposing a large gap between runnable code and clinically correct analyses.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for clinical data-science agents focus on isolated tasks (medical QA, structured-table reasoning, or generic scientific repositories) and fail to capture the real-world challenge of transforming heterogeneous longitudinal clinical records into auditable, executable analyses.
AI.method: The authors introduce CLINLENS, a benchmark comprising 200 executable tasks spanning five linked MIMIC resources (structured EHRs, notes, ECGs, chest radiographs, echocardiograms). Tasks are organized via a 4×5 taxonomy crossing four patient-time scopes with five analysis capabilities. A "program-first reverse synthesis" methodology pairs each bounded semi-raw data package with an evaluator-private reference workflow, checking required artifacts, cohort and temporal semantics, and final answer correctness.
AI.result: Across a fixed 126-task suite, 24 standardized model-scaffold configurations were evaluated. The strongest configuration achieved 56.3% scope-macro STRICTPASS despite 100% EXECSUCCESS. A separately configured coding agent solved 83/126 tasks, while five biomedical systems adapted to GPT-4o-mini reached at most 2.9% scope-macro STRICTPASS.
AI.conclusion: There exists a substantial and underexplored gap between producing runnable submissions and generating correct clinical analyses, highlighting the need for benchmarks like CLINLENS that emphasize execution traceability and semantic correctness in clinical data science.

title: A Reference-Free Score for Detecting Silent Reasoning Failures in Large Language Models
summary: Mathematical chain of thought (CoT) evaluation is commonly reduced to whether the final answer matches a reference. This conflates producing a correct conclusion with producing a valid derivation an invalid chain can accidentally reach the right answer, while a valid calculation can be followed by a transcription error. We call this mismatch the reasoning answer consistency gap. This framework paper introduces the Reasoning Answer Faithfulness Score (RAFS), a reference free, instance level diagnostic of whether an emitted mathematical trace is locally credible, supports its answer, and is stable under resampling and targeted counterfactual interventions. RAFS combines step validity, reasoning to answer entailment and counterfactual sensitivity, answer consensus, and conditional reasoning stability. It evaluates transcript level agreement, not a models private computation and not factual correctness outside the tested mathematical setting. We retain a preregistered, results blind confirmatory study on GSM8K and MATH, with hypotheses, admissibility rules, calibration, and tests fixed before confirmatory outcomes are inspected. A separate feasibility pilot is specified to verify end to end execution and estimate interven tion coverage before that freeze numerical pilot claims are re ported only when trace level artifacts are available. We formalize four reasoning answer outcomes, justify the non compensatory aggregator, instantiate semantic trace distance, quantify compute and abstention tradeoffs, and define verifier independence and power analyses. RAFS is intended to complement mathematical answer accuracy with an auditable warning signal for silent reasoning failures and answer extraction errors

AI.tldr: RAFS is a reference-free, instance-level metric that diagnoses whether a mathematical chain-of-thought trace is internally coherent, supports its answer, and remains stable under counterfactual interventions — addressing the "reasoning-answer consistency gap" where final-answer matching alone fails to distinguish valid reasoning from lucky guesswork.
AI.motivation: Current mathematical CoT evaluation relies solely on final-answer matching, which conflates correct conclusions with valid derivations. A flawed chain can accidentally yield the right answer, and a valid chain can be marred by a transcription error. The authors identify this as the reasoning-answer consistency gap and argue that answer accuracy alone provides no signal about reasoning quality, silent failures, or answer extraction errors.
AI.method: RAFS is a composite, non-compensatory diagnostic score combining five components: (1) step validity — local credibility of each reasoning step; (2) reasoning-to-answer entailment — whether the trace logically supports the final answer; (3) counterfactual sensitivity — stability under targeted interventions; (4) answer consensus — agreement under resampling; and (5) conditional reasoning stability. The framework is evaluated via a preregistered, results-blind confirmatory study on GSM8K and MATH, with hypotheses, admissibility rules, calibration, and statistical tests fixed before outcomes are inspected. A separate feasibility pilot verifies end-to-end execution and intervention coverage.
AI.result: Numerical results are reported only when trace-level artifacts are available (pilot claims). The paper formalizes four reasoning-answer outcome categories, justifies the non-compensatory aggregator, instantiates semantic trace distance, quantifies compute-abstention tradeoffs, and defines verifier independence and power analyses. Confirmatory outcomes remain under blind until the preregistered freeze is lifted.
AI.conclusion: RAFS is intended to complement mathematical answer accuracy with an auditable warning signal for silent reasoning failures and answer extraction errors, providing a more faithful picture of model reasoning capability than final-answer matching alone.

title: Living-Harness Is an Interactive-Agent Evolver
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents may recover from a failure within an episode or after a retry, yet the same execution failure can recur in later tasks because post-episode feedback rarely revises the persistent harness that guides future interactions. Static harnesses improve reliability through fixed tools, context, memory, and workflow structures, but remain unchanged after deployment. We propose $\textbf{Living-Harness}$, a self-evolving agent harness that converts each completed trajectory and its evaluator signals into posterior evidence for bounded harness updates. Guided by a domain-level $\textbf{Evolution-SOP}$ ($\textbf{S}$tandard $\textbf{O}$perating $\textbf{P}$rocedure), Living-Harness extracts an episode abstraction and structured update evidence, and writes two complementary forms of procedural knowledge: episodic memory that records trigger conditions, failure patterns, and recovery actions, and a state graph that records state nodes, repair edges, and transition rules. The updated harness state is retrieved to guide future interactions, while tools and base context remain frozen, allowing procedural repairs to accumulate across evolution cycles. On eight interactive environments derived from $τ^2$-Bench and MultiWOZ-2.4, Living-Harness improves average Pass@1 over the strongest interactive baseline by 10.07 and 9.91 percentage points, respectively, and supports retrieval-only reuse of the evolved harness state across model backbones.

AI.tldr: Living-Harness is a self-evolving agent framework that converts completed task trajectories and evaluator feedback into persistent procedural knowledge (episodic memory and state graphs), governed by an Evolution-SOP, enabling LLM agents to avoid repeating failures across episodes without modifying frozen tools or base context.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents can recover from failures within an episode or after retries, but the same failures recur in later tasks because post-episode feedback does not update the persistent harness (tools, context, memory, workflow) that guides future interactions. Static harnesses remain unchanged after deployment, limiting long-term reliability improvement.
AI.method: Living-Harness introduces a self-evolving harness that processes each completed trajectory and evaluator signals into bounded harness updates. Guided by a domain-level Evolution-SOP (Standard Operating Procedure), it extracts episode abstractions and structured update evidence, then writes two forms of procedural knowledge: (1) episodic memory capturing trigger conditions, failure patterns, and recovery actions; and (2) a state graph with state nodes, repair edges, and transition rules. The updated harness is retrieved for future interactions while tools and base context remain frozen, allowing procedural repairs to accumulate across evolution cycles.
AI.result: On eight interactive environments from τ²-Bench and MultiWOZ-2.4, Living-Harness improves average Pass@1 over the strongest interactive baseline by 10.07 and 9.91 percentage points, respectively. It also supports retrieval-only reuse of the evolved harness state across different model backbones.
AI.conclusion: Living-Harness demonstrates that persistent, structured procedural knowledge extracted from prior trajectories can significantly reduce recurring failures in LLM agents, offering a practical path toward self-improving agent systems without modifying underlying model weights or static tool configurations.

title: Meta-Learned Reward Shaping for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
summary: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is the standard approach for aligning large language models with human preferences, but its quality is limited by static, task-agnostic reward models. This mismatch leads to sparse learning signals and suboptimal alignment. We introduce MeRLa (Meta-Learned Reward Shaping), a principled framework that meta-learns a task-aware shaping function $Φ(x,y;φ)$ across auxiliary tasks before RLHF training. The learned shaping produces a composite reward that preserves policy optimality while providing task-specific learning signals. Our meta-objective combines task discrimination, entropy regularization, and potential-based conservation for stable convergence. We provide theoretical guarantees for policy invariance, analyze representation drift sensitivity, and formally address incentive misalignment from entropy maximization. Experiments on LLaMA-3-8B across four benchmarks show consistent improvements over PPO, DPO, GRPO, and DAPO, achieving a 90.8% length-controlled win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0 and a score of 9.14 on MT-Bench, with 41% less training instability. MeRLa retains its benefits when combined with process-based and rubric-based enhanced rewards.

AI.tldr: MeRLa introduces a meta-learned, task-aware reward shaping function for RLHF that provides dense, task-specific learning signals while preserving policy optimality. It achieves superior alignment performance (90.8% LC win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0, 9.14 on MT-Bench) with 41% less training instability on LLaMA-3-8B.
AI.motivation: Standard RLHF relies on static, task-agnostic reward models that produce sparse learning signals, creating a mismatch between training and the diverse tasks encountered at deployment. This leads to suboptimal alignment, training instability, and poor sample efficiency.
AI.method: MeRLa meta-learns a task-aware shaping function Φ(x,y;φ) across auxiliary tasks prior to RLHF training. The shaping function produces a composite reward (original reward + shaped component) that is guaranteed to preserve policy optimality via potential-based shaping. The meta-objective combines three components: (1) task discrimination to ensure the shaping is task-aware, (2) entropy regularization for stable convergence, and (3) potential-based conservation to maintain policy invariance. The authors provide theoretical analysis of policy invariance guarantees, representation drift sensitivity, and formal treatment of incentive misalignment from entropy maximization.
AI.result: Experiments on LLaMA-3-8B across four benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over PPO, DPO, GRPO, and DAPO. MeRLa achieves a 90.8% length-controlled win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0, a score of 9.14 on MT-Bench, and 41% reduction in training instability. Benefits persist when combined with process-based and rubric-based enhanced rewards.
AI.conclusion: Task-aware reward shaping via meta-learning is a principled and effective approach to improving RLHF, addressing the fundamental limitation of static reward models. MeRLa provides strong empirical gains and formal theoretical guarantees, and generalizes well when combined with other reward enhancement techniques.

title: FinCacheServe: Dependency-Consistent Answer Reuse for Cost-Efficient RAG Serving over Mutable Enterprise Documents
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation services over mutable enterprise documents repeatedly execute semantically equivalent analysis requests. Answer reuse can remove GPU-bound generation work, yet response caches require dependency consistency when filings, evidence chunks, and tool outputs change. FinCacheServe treats each generated answer as a serving object indexed by enterprise intent and guarded by document versions, evidence fingerprints, tool fingerprints, model identity, and decoding configuration. A vLLM implementation evaluates SEC-derived financial-document workloads with Qwen2.5 models. On a 2,230-request hosted 7B trace, FinCacheServe skips 53.27% of LLM calls with zero observed dependency-stale outputs. Across three hosted 32B operator-suite seeds, it skips 53.31% of 544 requests, compared with 38.97% for versioned semantic caching and 22.43% for grounded-style reuse. Capacity, backend, and SLO replays show oracle-bounded cache management, 100k-entry transactional metadata behavior, and 44.30% lower estimated Wh per dependency-fresh 2s-SLO success than versioned semantic caching.

AI.tldr: FinCacheServe is a caching system for retrieval-augmented generation over mutable enterprise documents that treats answers as versioned serving objects indexed by intent, achieving 53%+ LLM call reduction with zero stale outputs by tracking dependency fingerprints across documents, evidence, tools, models, and decoding configs.
AI.motivation: Enterprise RAG services repeatedly execute semantically equivalent queries over mutable documents (filings, evidence chunks, tool outputs). Naive response caching risks serving stale answers when underlying dependencies change. Existing approaches (versioned semantic caching, grounded-style reuse) either miss reuse opportunities or fail to guarantee dependency consistency, wasting GPU compute on redundant generation.
AI.method: FinCacheServe models each generated answer as a serving object with a compound cache key: enterprise intent (semantic query fingerprint) plus a dependency vector consisting of document versions, evidence chunk fingerprints, tool output fingerprints, model identity, and decoding configuration. Cache lookup matches intent and validates that all dependency fingerprints remain current. The system is implemented atop vLLM and evaluated on SEC-derived financial document workloads using Qwen2.5 models (7B and 32B).
AI.result: On a 2,230-request 7B trace: 53.27% LLM calls skipped, zero dependency-stale outputs. On three 32B operator-suite seeds (544 requests): 53.31% skip rate vs. 38.97% for versioned semantic caching and 22.43% for grounded-style reuse. Capacity/backend/SLO replays demonstrate oracle-bounded cache management, transactional metadata handling at 100k-entry scale, and 44.30% lower estimated energy (Wh) per dependency-fresh 2s-SLO success versus versioned semantic caching.
AI.conclusion: Precise dependency fingerprinting — spanning document versions, evidence, tools, model, and decoding config — enables safe, high-hit-rate answer reuse in enterprise RAG. FinCacheServe demonstrates that co-designing cache keys with RAG dependency semantics yields substantial GPU savings and energy efficiency while maintaining strict correctness guarantees.

title: When benchmark inferences do not compose: Projectibility in AI evaluation
comment: 35 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Substantially rewritten and retitled; supersedes arXiv:2510.15236, whose homeostatic property-cluster account and proposed centrality-prior and cluster-stability measures are withdrawn. The argument, apparatus, and empirical companion are new. Code and empirical companion: https://github.com/BrettRey/benchmark-inference-composition
summary: An AI benchmark result rarely reaches a consequential claim in one step. Evaluators generalize it to further cases, interpret it as evidence of capability, extrapolate it to new tasks, transport it to another system or site, and combine it with assumptions about human review and downstream consequences. Validity-centred approaches require evidence for each claim. This paper identifies a further epistemic problem: warranted links don't automatically make a warranted chain. The target of one study may not be the source of the next; system, population, outcome, or conditions may change at the interface; and shared data or model lineage may make apparently independent support dependent. Projectibility concerns whether a bounded extension from observed to unobserved cases is warranted. Goodman supplies the problem of rival extensions; argument-based validity supplies an architecture for testing them. The paper's distinctive claim is a non-composition principle: support for adjacent projections warrants their composition only when endpoints and assumptions align and dependence and uncertainty are carried through. A legal-research case shows how benchmark evidence and a deployment study can each be sound while remaining parallel. A reanalysis and simulation show why aggregate stability can erase distinctions a later projection requires. The resulting projectibility audit diagnoses unsupported joins in benchmark-to-use arguments.

AI.tldr: Benchmark-based AI evaluation arguments often fail because individually valid evidential links do not compose into a valid chain. The paper introduces a "non-composition principle" and a projectibility audit to diagnose unsupported joins when extending benchmark results to real-world deployment claims.
AI.motivation: AI benchmark results are routinely generalized, extrapolated, and transported across contexts to support consequential claims about real-world capability. While validity-centred approaches require evidence for each inferential step, an underexamined problem remains: even when each link in an argument chain is individually warranted, the chain as a whole may fail due to misaligned endpoints, shifting conditions, unaccounted dependence, or loss of relevant variation. The paper aims to identify and formalize this composition failure.
AI.method: The paper develops a conceptual framework drawing on Nelson Goodman's "new riddle of induction" (the problem of rival extensions) and argument-based validity from educational measurement. It proposes a "non-composition principle" governing when adjacent projections can be validly composed. The framework is demonstrated through: (1) a legal-research case study showing how benchmark evidence and a deployment study can each be sound yet remain parallel rather than composable, and (2) a reanalysis with simulation showing how aggregate stability masks distinctions that later projections require, producing a "projectibility audit" that diagnoses unsupported joins in benchmark-to-use arguments.
AI.result: The legal-research case demonstrates that individually sound benchmark evidence and a deployment study can fail to compose because endpoints, populations, or conditions differ at the interface. The reanalysis and simulation show that aggregate stability can erase distinctions (e.g., subgroup or condition-specific variation) that become critical in downstream projections, rendering the chain unsupported despite apparent empirical coherence.
AI.conclusion: Warranted links do not automatically yield a warranted chain in benchmark-to-use arguments. The non-composition principle requires that endpoints and assumptions align and that dependence and uncertainty are carried through each interface. The projectibility audit offers a systematic diagnostic for identifying where argument chains break, providing a tool for more rigorous evaluation of AI capability claims.

title: GPT-Red: Automated Red Teaming via Self-Play at Scale
comment: 28 pages.13 main pages and 13 main figures
summary: We introduce \textbf{GPT-Red}, an automated red-teaming agent that is trained to discover novel prompt injection attacks against frontier LLMs. The goal of this model is to evaluate and improve the robustness of our production systems. To this end, we use it to adversarially train GPT-5.6, our most robust model to prompt injections to date. To create GPT-Red, we design a scalable self-play algorithm where the model is tasked with attacking a diverse population of simultaneously-trained defender agents. We train the model on realistic red-teaming environments using compute on the same scale as some of our largest RL post-training runs, making it the single-largest LLM safety training run ever documented. GPT-Red excels at red-teaming: it reliably breaks our past models up to GPT-5.5, it finds more successful attacks than human red-teamers, and it generalizes to held-out environments, defender models, and harnesses. In the future, we expect that as we improve the robustness of each new GPT model, it will in turn will provide better learning signal for \textit{even stronger} red-teamer agents, thus unlocking a self-improvement flywheel.

AI.tldr: GPT-Red is an automated red-teaming agent trained via self-play to discover novel prompt injection attacks. It is used to adversarially train GPT-5.6, achieving state-of-the-art robustness. The model outperforms human red-teamers and was trained at a scale comparable to large RL post-training runs, representing the largest documented LLM safety training run.
AI.motivation: To evaluate and improve the robustness of production LLMs against prompt injection attacks, and to establish a self-improving safety flywheel where stronger models provide better training signal for even stronger red-teamers.
AI.method: A scalable self-play algorithm where GPT-Red attacks a diverse population of simultaneously-trained defender agents in realistic red-teaming environments. The training uses compute at the scale of the largest RL post-training runs. The resulting red-teamer is then used to adversarially train GPT-5.6.
AI.result: GPT-Red reliably breaks models up to GPT-5.5, discovers more successful attacks than human red-teamers, and generalizes to held-out environments, defender models, and harnesses. GPT-5.6 emerges as the most prompt-injection-robust model to date.
AI.conclusion: Automated red-teaming via self-play is a scalable and effective approach to hardening frontier LLMs against prompt injections. The authors anticipate a self-improvement flywheel: each more robust model yields better training signal for even stronger red-teaming agents.

title: DREvo: Distilling Recalibrated Historical Experience for Harness Self-Evolution
summary: Harness plays a critical role in large language model agent performance, and building a high-performing harness requires substantial expert effort. Therefore, recent research has increasingly explored harness self-evolution, which iteratively proposes, evaluates, and improves harnesses using historical trial experience. However, accumulated historical experience does not always translate into stable search guidance, and performance often fluctuates substantially across evolution iterations, making it difficult to reliably discover high-performing harnesses under a limited evolution budget. We identify two limitations in how existing harness self-evolution methods leverage historical experience: (1) Lack of dynamic reassessment of whether historical experience remains valid for the current harness, and (2) Lack of explicit mechanisms for translating valid historical experience into actionable search directions. To address these limitations, we propose a new harness self-evolution method, named DREvo, which integrates function-level evidence anchoring, state-dependent evidence recalibration, and role-conditioned search intent distillation to determine which historical evidence remains valid and where the harness should evolve next. Under limited evolution budgets, DREvo exhibits smoother evolution trajectories, achieves the highest accuracy on all five benchmarks, and delivers average gains of 16.2% and 14.2% over the evaluated baselines on domain reasoning and agentic tasks, respectively.

AI.tldr: DREvo is a harness self-evolution method for LLM agents that addresses two key limitations in how existing methods use historical experience — lack of dynamic validity reassessment and lack of actionable search direction mechanisms. By integrating evidence anchoring, recalibration, and search intent distillation, DREvo achieves smoother evolution trajectories and outperforms baselines by 16.2% on domain reasoning and 14.2% on agentic tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing harness self-evolution methods suffer from unstable performance across iterations because accumulated historical experience does not reliably guide search. Two specific shortcomings are identified: (1) no dynamic reassessment of whether past experience remains valid for the current harness, and (2) no explicit mechanism to translate valid historical experience into concrete, actionable search directions. These limitations make it hard to discover high-performing harnesses under limited evolution budgets.
AI.method: DREvo introduces three integrated components: (1) Function-level evidence anchoring — to ground historical experience at a granular, functional level. (2) State-dependent evidence recalibration — to dynamically reassess whether prior evidence remains valid given the current harness state. (3) Role-conditioned search intent distillation — to translate recalibrated evidence into explicit, actionable search directions for the next evolution step.
AI.result: Under limited evolution budgets, DREvo exhibits smoother evolution trajectories with less performance fluctuation. It achieves the highest accuracy across all five evaluated benchmarks, with average improvements of 16.2% over baselines on domain reasoning tasks and 14.2% on agentic tasks.
AI.conclusion: The two identified limitations in historical experience usage are critical bottlenecks in harness self-evolution. DREvo's approach of dynamically anchoring, recalibrating, and distilling historical evidence into actionable guidance effectively overcomes these limitations, enabling more reliable and efficient harness discovery.

title: Data Fusion and Contrastive Alignment for Unconstrained IR Molecular Structure Elucidation
summary: Automated molecular structure elucidation from infrared (IR) spectroscopy data has seen significant advancements in recent years, but its broad applicability is limited by a reliance on pre-determined chemical formulas provided as auxiliary model inputs. This limits model predictions to isomer identification rather than full molecular structure prediction. Although transformer models have been shown to identify molecular isomers with high accuracy, their reliability for unconstrained structure elucidation is comparatively low and poorly understood. In this work, we propose and evaluate key modifications to the traditional encoder-decoder transformer. To better address the vast chemical space of the unconstrained problem, we implement a novel Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) decoder module that utilizes non-additive aggregation via linear-order statistics and the Choquet integral. We further modify the transformer to utilize these non-additive operators when aggregating spectral representations as well. Together with an auxiliary contrastive alignment loss term, these enhancements improve Top-K prediction accuracy by over 10 percentage points compared to baseline IR-only models. Through sub-structure fragment analysis of molecular predictions, we further confirm that infrared spectra encode the vast majority of relevant chemical information, implying that the higher performance of isomer-ranking models is largely due to underrepresented or overlapping absorption bands for molecules in the explored chemical space.
