Ultimately, by demonstrating the efficacy of automated molecular structure elucidation from measured IR spectra, this work serves to significantly broaden the utility of AI in analytical chemistry.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes enhancements to encoder-decoder transformers—specifically a Mixture-of-Experts decoder using the Choquet integral and linear-order statistics for non-additive aggregation, plus a contrastive alignment loss—to improve unconstrained molecular structure elucidation directly from IR spectra without pre-determined chemical formulas. The approach improves Top-K accuracy by over 10 percentage points and demonstrates that IR spectra encode most relevant chemical information.
AI.motivation: Current transformer models for molecular structure elucidation from IR spectroscopy rely on pre-determined chemical formulas, limiting them to isomer identification rather than full structure prediction. Their reliability for unconstrained structure elucidation is low and poorly understood, motivating the need for methods that can handle the vast chemical space without auxiliary formula inputs.
AI.method: The authors modify the traditional encoder-decoder transformer with (1) a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) decoder that employs non-additive aggregation via linear-order statistics and the Choquet integral, (2) non-additive operators for aggregating spectral representations in the encoder, and (3) an auxiliary contrastive alignment loss term to improve representation learning.
AI.result: The proposed enhancements improve Top-K prediction accuracy by over 10 percentage points compared to baseline IR-only models. Sub-structure fragment analysis confirms that IR spectra encode the vast majority of relevant chemical information, suggesting that the superior performance of isomer-ranking models stems from underrepresented or overlapping absorption bands in the explored chemical space.
AI.conclusion: By demonstrating effective automated molecular structure elucidation from measured IR spectra without pre-determined formulas, this work significantly broadens the applicability of AI in analytical chemistry, moving beyond isomer identification toward full molecular structure prediction.

title: Cross-Model Cross-Language AI Coding Agent Performance: Accuracy and Speed of Parallel CLRS Algorithms
summary: AI coding agents have quickly become omnipresent in software engineering. Their serial performance, both in terms of accuracy and speed, has been extensively covered. However, recent initial results suggest their parallel programming capabilities lag behind serial programming capabilities. This paper presents a cross-language evaluation of three coding agents -- Cursor's Composer 2.0, GPT 5.4, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 -- on parallel code generation across three algorithm categories -- sorting, graph traversal, and search -- in C++, Python, and Julia. For each algorithm and language pair, we prompt a coding agent to produce a parallel implementation from a serial baseline, track the prompting effort required to achieve both functional correctness and performance improvements, and measure speedup against both custom serial baselines and third-party library implementations. We find that coding agents can produce correct parallel implementations with modest prompting effort, but that achieving meaningful speedup is heavily algorithm- and language-dependent. Sonnet 4.6 delivers the strongest overall performance gains, whereas GPT 5.4 produces no measurable speedups despite consistent correctness. C++ is most consistently parallelizable for graph algorithms, while Python and Julia achieve the largest speedups on search algorithms: no single language dominates across all categories. Python and Julia each achieve speedup on some graph algorithms but regress on others. These findings underscore the impact of including runtime performance efficiency as a main LLM performance metric, in addition to accuracy, particularly for parallel implementations.

AI.tldr: A cross-language evaluation of three AI coding agents (Cursor's Composer 2.0, GPT 5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6) on parallel code generation across C++, Python, and Julia reveals that while agents can produce functionally correct parallel code, achieving meaningful speedup is algorithm- and language-dependent. Sonnet 4.6 performs best overall, while GPT 5.4 yields no measurable speedup despite correctness. The authors argue for including runtime performance as a key LLM evaluation metric.
AI.motivation: AI coding agents are widely adopted, but their parallel programming capabilities remain underexplored. Initial evidence suggests a gap between serial and parallel code generation performance. The authors aim to systematically evaluate whether current coding agents can generate parallel code that is not only correct but also delivers genuine runtime speedup across multiple languages and algorithm types.
AI.method: Three coding agents (Cursor's Composer 2.0, GPT 5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6) are prompted to produce parallel implementations from serial baselines across three algorithm categories (sorting, graph traversal, search) in three languages (C++, Python, Julia). For each algorithm–language pair, the authors track prompting effort to achieve functional correctness and performance improvement, then measure speedup against custom serial baselines and third-party library implementations.
AI.result: Agents achieve correct parallel implementations with modest prompting effort. However, meaningful speedup is heavily algorithm- and language-dependent. Sonnet 4.6 delivers the strongest overall performance gains; GPT 5.4 produces no measurable speedups despite correctness. C++ parallelizes most consistently for graph algorithms; Python and Julia achieve largest speedups on search. No language dominates all categories. Python and Julia show speedup gains on some graph algorithms but regressions on others.
AI.conclusion: Runtime performance efficiency should be adopted as a primary LLM evaluation metric alongside accuracy, especially for parallel implementations. The algorithm- and language-dependent nature of achieved speedups highlights that functional correctness alone is an insufficient benchmark for parallel code generation quality.

title: Hakka Kitchen: Engagement with Culinary Cultural Heritage Through Immersive Game Play
summary: Intangible Cultural Heritage (ICH) experiences are difficult to share with the public because they are essentially processes that rely on physical interactions with embodied, tacit, and situated phenomena in specific cultural contexts. We consume non-interactive media such as videos and books to learn about culinary ICH experiences, but they do not allow us to grasp actual interactive procedures that embody the cultural knowledge. To engage people in a traditional cooking experience, we created a gamified VR experience Hakka Kitchen, where players are guided by a chef of Hakka cuisine through a modeled physical process of making the traditional dish of stuffed bitter melon. Compared against watching a video in VR providing the same information in a between-subjects study (N=40), Hakka Kitchen led to increased sensory, imaginative engagement, positive affect, and willingness to transmit awareness for the culinary ICH. Heritage recognition is mode-dependent: the cognitive load of enactment suppressed players' uptake of concurrent cultural narration; however, it generated somatic and memory anchors that fostered a deeper, implicit kinesthetic form of empathy for the artisan's labor and cultural background. Our work shows how representing interactive procedures instead of static content may empower cultural awareness in a virtual form of ICH practice.

AI.tldr: A gamified VR experience for traditional Hakka cooking was compared against passive VR video viewing. The interactive game increased sensory engagement, positive affect, and willingness to share cultural heritage, but cognitive load from enactment suppressed explicit heritage recognition while fostering deeper kinesthetic empathy through somatic and memory anchors.
AI.motivation: Intangible Cultural Heritage (ICH), such as traditional cooking, is inherently processual, embodied, tacit, and situated — making it difficult to convey through non-interactive media like videos or books. The authors aim to explore whether interactive VR experiences can better engage users with culinary ICH by representing interactive procedures rather than static content.
AI.method: The authors developed Hakka Kitchen, a gamified VR experience where players are guided by a Hakka cuisine chef through the modeled physical process of making stuffed bitter melon. A between-subjects study (N=40) compared this interactive experience against a VR video providing identical informational content. Outcomes measured included sensory engagement, imaginative engagement, positive affect, willingness to transmit heritage awareness, heritage recognition, and kinesthetic empathy.
AI.result: Hakka Kitchen led to significantly increased sensory engagement, imaginative engagement, positive affect, and willingness to transmit awareness of culinary ICH. However, heritage recognition was mode-dependent: the cognitive load of physical enactment suppressed players' uptake of concurrent cultural narration. Paradoxically, this enactment generated somatic and memory anchors that fostered a deeper, implicit kinesthetic empathy for the artisan's labor and cultural background.
AI.conclusion: Representing interactive procedures — rather than static content — in virtual environments can empower cultural awareness by creating embodied, somatic connections to ICH practices. The trade-off between explicit heritage recognition and implicit kinesthetic empathy suggests that interactive VR offers a qualitatively distinct, complementary mode of cultural transmission compared to passive media.

title: Embedding Items at Scale: Comparing GNN-Based and ID-Based Item Embeddings in the Yandex Ecosystem
summary: Transformer-based sequential recommendation models, which process sequences of user-item interactions, rely heavily on the item embedding strategy. Existing approaches either use pretrained item embeddings or learn them end-to-end with the transformer. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has compared these options from both cost and quality perspectives in a large-scale industrial setting. This paper is a case study that compares pretrained industrial graph neural network item embeddings with end-to-end trainable item embeddings across two mature production recommendation systems at Yandex: Yandex Market and Yandex Music. We additionally evaluate both approaches on a low-resource dataset sampled from Yandex Lavka production logs, for which both the data and code are publicly available for demonstration purposes. Our results show that a separate pretraining stage helps when training data is limited, but provides no worthwhile benefit for large-scale models trained on extensive datasets.

AI.tldr: This paper compares pretrained GNN-based item embeddings with end-to-end learned embeddings for transformer-based sequential recommenders across three Yandex production systems. The key finding: pretraining helps when data is scarce, but offers negligible benefit for large-scale models with abundant training data.
AI.motivation: No prior work has systematically compared pretrained versus end-to-end item embeddings for transformer-based sequential recommendation in large-scale industrial settings, leaving practitioners without evidence-based guidance on which strategy to adopt under different data regimes.
AI.method: Case study across two mature production systems (Yandex Market, Yandex Music) and one low-resource public dataset (Yandex Lavka). The authors compare industrial GNN-pretrained item embeddings against embeddings learned end-to-end with the transformer, evaluating both recommendation quality and computational cost. Code and data for the low-resource setting are publicly released.
AI.result: Pretraining GNN item embeddings yields measurable quality improvements when training data is limited (Lavka scenario). However, for the large-scale production systems (Market, Music) with extensive training data, end-to-end learned embeddings perform comparably, making the additional pretraining stage an unnecessary cost with no worthwhile benefit.
AI.conclusion: The decision to pretrain item embeddings should be guided by data scale: a separate pretraining stage is valuable in low-resource settings but becomes redundant for industrial-scale models with sufficient training data, where end-to-end learning suffices and avoids extra engineering complexity.

title: GuideSkill: Evolving Executable LLM Agent Skills for Guideline-Grounded Clinical Reasoning
summary: Clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) encode diagnostic criteria, but LLM systems typically retrieve guideline text or absorb it through training rather than execute its rules. We introduce GuideSkill, an external reasoning layer that compiles disease-specific criteria into executable functions returning ordinal diagnostic-support scores. GuideSkill-Zero is initialized from guidelines, while GuideSkill-Evo uses case--diagnosis pairs to refine covered skills and add missing diagnoses. At inference, an LLM proposes a differential diagnosis, grounds the features required by each matched skill, and fuses its ranking with the executed skill scores. Across four benchmarks and four backbones, GuideSkill-Zero improves macro-average accuracy over guideline RAG by 13.45% on average. GuideSkill-Evo achieves the highest macro-average for every backbone, improves over direct inference by 18.49% relatively, and increases gold-label skill coverage from 56.5% to 99.5%. On Qwen3.5-9B, it also exceeds the strongest parameter-update baseline by 11.16% without updating the backbone. Expert evaluation further indicates that GuideSkill produces clinically sound and broadly acceptable skills, suggesting that its initialized and evolved rules are reliable and practically meaningful. These results support executable skills as a model-agnostic mechanism for combining guideline-derived procedures with case-derived diagnostic patterns.

AI.tldr: GuideSkill introduces an external reasoning layer that compiles clinical practice guideline criteria into executable functions, returning ordinal diagnostic-support scores. It comes in two variants: GuideSkill-Zero (initialized from guidelines) and GuideSkill-Evo (refined using case-diagnosis pairs). At inference, an LLM proposes differential diagnoses, grounds features for each matched skill, and fuses its ranking with executed skill scores. Across four benchmarks and four backbones, both variants substantially outperform guideline RAG and direct inference, with GuideSkill-Evo reaching 99.5% gold-label skill coverage and surpassing the strongest parameter-update baseline on Qwen3.5-9B by 11.16% without any backbone fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Current LLM systems handle clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) by retrieving or training on guideline text rather than executing their diagnostic rules. This passive use of guidelines limits structured, interpretable, and procedurally faithful diagnostic reasoning. The authors aim to bridge this gap by making guideline criteria directly executable while remaining model-agnostic.
AI.method: GuideSkill comprises three stages: (1) Skill Initialization — disease-specific diagnostic criteria from CPGs are compiled into executable functions yielding ordinal support scores; (2) Skill Evolution (GuideSkill-Evo only) — case-diagnosis pairs are used to refine existing skills and add skills for previously uncovered diagnoses; (3) Inference — the LLM proposes a differential diagnosis, grounds the required features for each matched skill, executes the skills to obtain scores, and fuses these scores with the LLM's own ranking to produce the final diagnostic output.
AI.result: GuideSkill-Zero improves macro-average accuracy over guideline RAG by 13.45% on average across four benchmarks and four backbones. GuideSkill-Evo achieves the highest macro-average accuracy for every backbone tested, improves over direct inference by 18.49% relatively, and raises gold-label skill coverage from 56.5% to 99.5%. On Qwen3.5-9B, GuideSkill-Evo exceeds the strongest parameter-update baseline by 11.16% without updating backbone weights. Expert evaluation confirms the skills are clinically sound and broadly acceptable.
AI.conclusion: Executable skills serve as a model-agnostic, interpretable mechanism that synergistically combines guideline-derived procedures with case-derived diagnostic patterns. GuideSkill demonstrates that structured rule execution can significantly enhance LLM diagnostic performance without requiring parameter updates, offering a practical path toward clinically faithful and auditable AI-assisted diagnosis.

title: (EC)2: Event-Centric Explainability for Cybersecurity Through Multi-Agent LLM Investigations
summary: Security operations centers rely on anomaly detection systems to flag suspicious events. Feature-level explanations for anomaly detectors offer limited value for operational investigations. To effectively handle alerts, analysts need to know contextual relationships and need actionable understanding of the entities involved. This paper introduces an event-centric detector-agnostic approach for explaining cybersecurity alerts in small- to medium-sized enterprise networks. We present (EC)2, a multi-agent framework that performs structured, hypothesis-driven investigation to provide explanations grounded in verifiable evidence. Evaluation results show that the proposed framework improves post-detection analysis by generating operationally meaningful explanations, which also enhance event classification accuracy.

AI.tldr: (EC)2 is a multi-agent, detector-agnostic framework that provides hypothesis-driven, evidence-grounded explanations for cybersecurity alerts, improving both post-detection analysis and event classification accuracy in SME networks.
AI.motivation: Existing anomaly detection systems provide feature-level explanations that lack the contextual relationships and actionable entity understanding analysts need for operational investigations. There is a gap between raw alert generation and actionable investigative insight, particularly in small- to medium-sized enterprise environments.
AI.method: The authors propose (EC)2, an event-centric, detector-agnostic multi-agent framework that performs structured, hypothesis-driven investigation. It generates explanations grounded in verifiable evidence, emphasizing contextual relationships among entities rather than purely feature-level justifications.
AI.result: Evaluation shows that (EC)2 improves post-detection analysis by producing operationally meaningful explanations. Additionally, the framework enhances event classification accuracy compared to baseline approaches.
AI.conclusion: Shifting from feature-level to evidence-grounded, context-rich explanations significantly benefits security operations. The (EC)2 framework effectively bridges the gap between anomaly detection and actionable investigation in SME networks.

title: Cross-organisational Process Mining from Message Logs
comment: This paper is the full version of an extended abstract with the same title, presented at the third International workshop on Collaboration Mining for Distributed Systems (COMINDS 2024) held in conjunction with ICPM 2024 in Copenhagen
summary: Enterprise nets and Industry nets are specific Petri net models that together form a framework for the modelling of collaborating business processes and the specification of interactions between them. In this set-up, individual business process are modelled as Enterprise nets, while Industry nets consist of Enterprise nets that interact by exchanging messages through unidirectional channels. In previous contributions (see [21,22]), it was established how to leverage algorithms for the discovery of single processes (modelled as Enterprise nets) from event logs (consisting of finite sequences of executed actions), to synthesise systems consisting of asynchronously communicating processes (modelled as Industry nets). However, in general, it may be difficult to work with event logs from different organisations or even get access to them. Recordings of message exchanges between processes may be easier available.Therefore, we focus in this paper on the communications between different processes and turn to the investigation of message logs, \ie collections of recordings of communications in the form of message exchanges (output and input events) between two processes. In particular, the question is addressed of how a message log can be transformed into a description of the communication behaviour in the form of an event log such that the causal order on message events is preserved. Following the approach from [21,22], this event log can then be used to synthesis an Industry net.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses how to transform message logs (recordings of inter-process communications) into event logs that preserve causal order, enabling the synthesis of Industry nets when direct access to organizational event logs is unavailable.
AI.motivation: Previous work showed how to synthesize asynchronously communicating processes (Industry nets) from event logs of individual processes (Enterprise nets). However, obtaining event logs from different organizations is often difficult. Message logs—recordings of output/input message exchanges between processes—are typically more accessible. The challenge is how to leverage these message logs for process synthesis.
AI.method: The paper investigates transforming message logs (collections of message exchange recordings between two processes) into event logs that preserve the causal ordering of message events. This transformation then feeds into the existing synthesis framework from prior work [21,22] to generate Industry nets.
AI.result: The paper provides a method for converting message logs into causally-ordered event logs suitable for synthesizing an Industry net.
AI.conclusion: Message logs can serve as a viable alternative data source for synthesizing communicating process models (Industry nets) when organization-specific event logs are inaccessible, by first transforming them into appropriately structured event logs that maintain causal dependencies.

title: Shared SFT Lessons Across Alignment, Model Organisms, and Toy Models
summary: Alignment training, model organisms, and toy models are usually treated as separate research areas. But projects in all three frequently use supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to pursue the same underlying goals. When projects share a goal, we should test whether lessons learned from one area transfer to the other areas. We study three such transfers, each taking a lesson developed in one SFT setting and testing it in another. First, we port a lesson about behavior generalization from alignment training into toy models. Training on the reason for a behavior, as in Teaching Claude Why, can make the behavior generalize better than training on examples of the behavior alone. Second, we port a lesson about capability preservation from model organisms into the Model-Spec Midtraining alignment setting. SFT on outputs written by a model other than the student (off-model outputs) can damage capabilities when trained on. Mixing in benign on-model (and on-policy) data into our training can prevent most of this damage while still embedding the target behavior. Third, we port a lesson about robustness from model organisms into the same alignment setting. We find that follow-up benign SFT can erase the alignment behavior while preserving capabilities, showing that capability preservation alone does not ensure robustness to subsequent training. Our work illustrates how porting SFT lessons between different research fields can uplift them all, suggesting more researchers should borrow techniques from outside their own areas.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that lessons learned from supervised fine-tuning (SFT) in one research area can successfully transfer to others, using three case studies: (1) behavior generalization from alignment training to toy models, (2) capability preservation from model organisms to alignment, and (3) robustness against subsequent benign SFT from model organisms to alignment. The authors advocate for greater cross-pollination between alignment training, model organisms, and toy model research.
AI.motivation: Alignment training, model organisms, and toy models are typically treated as separate research areas despite all frequently using supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for similar underlying goals. The authors argue that when projects share goals, researchers should test whether insights transfer between domains, yet this is rarely done. The paper aims to demonstrate the value of such cross-area transfer.
AI.method:
The authors conduct three transfer experiments, each taking a lesson from one SFT setting and testing it in another:

1. **Behavior generalization (alignment training → toy models):** Training on the *reason* for a behavior (inspired by "Teaching Claude Why") is compared against training on behavioral examples alone in a toy model setting.

2. **Capability preservation (model organisms → alignment):** Off-model SFT outputs are shown to damage capabilities; mixing in benign on-model/on-policy data is tested as a mitigation in the Model-Spec Midtraining setting.

3. **Robustness to subsequent training (model organisms → alignment):** Follow-up benign SFT is applied after alignment training to test whether capability preservation alone ensures robustness.
AI.result:
1. Training on the reason for a behavior improved generalization in toy models, confirming the lesson from alignment training.

2. Mixing benign on-model (and on-policy) data with off-model SFT data prevented most capability damage while still embedding the target behavior.

3. Follow-up benign SFT erased alignment behavior while preserving capabilities, demonstrating that capability preservation alone does not guarantee robustness to subsequent training.
AI.conclusion: Lessons from SFT experiments transfer effectively across alignment training, model organisms, and toy model research areas. The authors encourage more researchers to borrow techniques and insights from outside their own subfields, as cross-pollination can uplift all areas involved.

title: Large Language Models for Software Engineering Diagrams: A Systematic Review of UML and ER modelling
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to diagram-based software and data modelling. Among various modelling notations, UML and entity-relationship (ER) diagrams are the most widely adopted for software modelling and data modelling, respectively. Recent literature has investigated various applications of LLMs in diagram modelling; however, their effectiveness and limitations have not been extensively discussed. This systematic literature review analyses 64 studies published between 2023 and 2025, examining diagram coverage, modelling tasks, technical approaches, evaluation practices, and limitations. Our findings reveal significant concentration patterns and gaps. UML-based software modelling strongly dominates, with class diagrams receiving the most attention whilst behavioural diagrams and data modelling remain underrepresented. Diagram construction from natural language is the primary focus, with limited work on transformation, quality assurance, and consistency checking. GPT-based models are heavily prevalent, raising concerns about reproducibility and vendor dependence. Evaluation practices are heterogeneous, employing diverse metrics and custom datasets with limited benchmark reuse and inconsistent reporting of robustness and statistical significance. Common limitations include semantic inaccuracies, hallucinated diagram elements, sensitivity to prompt formulation, and reproducibility constraints. This survey provides the first systematic synthesis of LLM-based diagram modelling research, highlighting needs for standardised benchmarks, stronger evaluation protocols, broader diagram coverage, and techniques for improving semantic reliability and multi-view consistency.

AI.tldr: A systematic review of 64 studies (2023–2025) on LLMs for UML and ER diagram modelling reveals heavy concentration on class diagrams and GPT-based models, heterogeneous evaluation practices, and persistent issues with semantic inaccuracies and reproducibility. The survey calls for standardised benchmarks, broader diagram coverage, and improved multi-view consistency.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for diagram-based software and data modelling (UML, ER), but no comprehensive synthesis exists of their effectiveness, limitations, and the landscape of research in this area.
AI.method: Systematic literature review of 64 studies published between 2023 and 2025, analysing five dimensions: diagram coverage, modelling tasks, technical approaches, evaluation practices, and limitations.
AI.result: (1) UML class diagrams dominate; behavioural and data modelling diagrams are underrepresented. (2) Construction from natural language is the primary task; transformation, QA, and consistency checking are under-explored. (3) GPT-based models prevail, raising vendor lock-in and reproducibility concerns. (4) Evaluation is inconsistent — diverse metrics, custom datasets, limited benchmark reuse, and poor reporting of robustness/statistical significance. (5) Common limitations include semantic inaccuracies, hallucination, prompt sensitivity, and reproducibility issues.
AI.conclusion: The first systematic synthesis of LLM-based diagram modelling research, identifying critical gaps and recommending standardised benchmarks, stronger evaluation protocols, broader diagram coverage, and techniques for semantic reliability and multi-view consistency.

title: How Wrangling Tools Shape Wrangling: A Technical Dimensions Analysis
summary: Wrangling consumes a disproportionate share of the effort associated with any data project. While a variety of tools support it, relatively little is known about how their differing interface forms shape the way people actually wrangle. We conduct a between-subjects (N=40) observational study of data cleaning tasks performed in tools spanning distinct interface paradigms: Jupyter (notebook), Excel (spreadsheet), ChatGPT (conversational AI), and OpenRefine (visual wranglers). We situate our observations within the Technical Dimensions of Programming Systems framework, which we use as a conceptual scaffold for comparing across interface paradigms. Within the context of our study, the results suggest that tool affordances steer user strategies but do not determine outcomes. There is no consistent advantage of any single tool, nor convergence of results within tools observed across our outcome measures. Instead, we identify trade-offs and connect them with observed practice. For example, a key tension is between data- and abstraction-centered interfaces, where data-centered interfaces encourage opportunistic cleaning rather than systematic, planned transformations found in abstraction-focused tools (but come with a cognitive burden). Tool design, beyond mere functionality, plays a structuring role in how data work unfolds.

AI.tldr: A study comparing four data wrangling tools (Jupyter, Excel, ChatGPT, OpenRefine) finds that interface design shapes user strategies but doesn't determine outcomes; no single tool consistently outperforms others, and key trade-offs exist between data-centered and abstraction-centered interfaces.
AI.motivation: Data wrangling is disproportionately time-consuming in data projects, yet little is known about how different interface paradigms actually influence the way people perform cleaning tasks. The authors seek to fill this gap with a systematic, comparative observational study.
AI.method: A between-subjects observational study (N=40) where participants performed data cleaning tasks using one of four tools representing distinct interface paradigms: Jupyter (notebook), Excel (spreadsheet), ChatGPT (conversational AI), and OpenRefine (visual wrangler). Observations were analyzed through the lens of the Technical Dimensions of Programming Systems framework as a conceptual scaffold for cross-paradigm comparison.
AI.result: Tool affordances steer user strategies but do not determine outcomes. No single tool showed a consistent advantage, nor did results converge within tools across outcome measures. A key tension emerged between data-centered interfaces (encouraging opportunistic cleaning) and abstraction-centered interfaces (promoting systematic, planned transformations, but with higher cognitive burden).
AI.conclusion: Tool design plays a structuring role in how data work unfolds, beyond mere functionality. The findings highlight trade-offs rather than universal superiority, suggesting that interface paradigm choice should be guided by task context and user needs rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.

title: Large-Scale ChatBot Validation Through Customer Digital Twin Simulations
summary: LLM-based chatbots are transforming customer service in regulated domains such as banking, but scalable and cost-effective validation remains a critical barrier to safe deployment. We present a two-part contribution for large-scale chatbot validation. First, we introduce a methodology for creating high-fidelity synthetic customer agents (SCAs) as digital twins, grounded in real transactional and conversational data, that enables automatic generation and behavioral conditioning to simulate diverse customer profiles and interaction styles. Evaluation demonstrates that SCAs achieve high semantic alignment with real customers, low hallucination rates, and successful personality trait reproduction with controllable interventions. Second, we develop an SCA-based validation framework combining automated LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation, human expert testing, and adversarial probing. Scenario-based validation across emotional states, demographic groups, and linguistic factors confirms robust performance. Our approach was used to validate a customer facing chatbot at a leading UK bank, providing financial institutions with a scalable pathway toward regulatory compliance.

AI.tldr: A two-part framework for validating LLM chatbots in banking: (1) synthetic customer agents (SCAs) built from real data as digital twins, and (2) an SCA-based validation framework combining automated evaluation, human testing, and adversarial probing. Deployed successfully at a leading UK bank.
AI.motivation: LLM chatbots are increasingly deployed in regulated domains like banking, but scalable, cost-effective validation remains a critical barrier to safe deployment and regulatory compliance.
AI.method: Two-part contribution: (1) Methodology for creating high-fidelity synthetic customer agents (SCAs) as digital twins, grounded in real transactional and conversational data, with behavioral conditioning for diverse customer profiles and interaction styles. (2) An SCA-based validation framework integrating automated LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation, human expert testing, and adversarial probing across emotional states, demographic groups, and linguistic factors.
AI.result: SCAs demonstrated high semantic alignment with real customers, low hallucination rates, and successful personality trait reproduction with controllable interventions. Scenario-based validation confirmed robust performance across emotional, demographic, and linguistic dimensions. The approach was successfully deployed to validate a customer-facing chatbot at a leading UK bank.
AI.conclusion: The SCA-based validation methodology provides financial institutions with a scalable, cost-effective pathway toward regulatory compliance for LLM chatbot deployment, bridging the gap between innovation and safe operational practice in regulated environments.

title: Continuous Online Evaluation of Recommendation Strategies in Social Science Academic Search
comment: 21 pages, 1 figure. Accepted for publication at the 30th International Conference on Theory and Practice of Digital Libraries (TPDL 2026)
summary: Delivering relevant recommendations in academic search engines is a complex task due to the diversity of subject areas, information types, and user preferences. In this case study, we address these challenges by integrating and evaluating a range of recommendation systems within GESIS Search - a domain-specific search engine for the social sciences that provides researchers with access to research data, publications, variables, and measurement instruments. To support continuous, real-time evaluation of multiple recommendation strategies with actual platform users, we utilize the STELLA evaluation framework. We implement and compare a diverse set of algorithms, including traditional lexical similarity, semantic document similarity by using transformer-based embeddings, and session-based recommendations based on click paths from historical user sessions. Our results show that users prefer recommendations based on semantic similarity, which outperformed term-similarity and session-based methods. However, the performance of recommenders varies across categories within GESIS Search, suggesting that information-seeking behavior differs by information type. Overall, our study provides insights into how continuous evaluation can be incorporated to develop recommendations that better align with the preferences in academic search portals.

AI.tldr: Integrating and evaluating multiple recommendation strategies (lexical, semantic embedding-based, and session-based) in a social science academic search engine using the STELLA framework for continuous real-time evaluation. Semantic similarity recommenders outperformed others, but performance varied by information type.
AI.motivation: Academic search engines face challenges in delivering relevant recommendations due to diverse subject areas, information types, and user preferences. There is a need to systematically evaluate multiple recommendation strategies in real-world, domain-specific settings.
AI.method: A case study integrating multiple recommendation algorithms (traditional lexical similarity, transformer-based semantic document embeddings, and session-based click-path recommendations) into GESIS Search, a social science search engine. Continuous, real-time evaluation was conducted with actual platform users using the STELLA evaluation framework.
AI.result: Semantic-similarity-based recommendations were preferred by users and outperformed both term-similarity and session-based methods. However, recommender performance varied across different content categories within GESIS Search, indicating that information-seeking behavior differs by information type.
AI.conclusion: Continuous evaluation via frameworks like STELLA enables effective development and tuning of recommendations for academic search portals. Semantic approaches are most promising, but the optimal strategy may depend on the specific information type being recommended.

title: GoGoTB: Agentic RTL Verification with Specification-Grounded Coverage Closure
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables. Xin Xin and Jincheng Lou contributed equally to this work and share first authorship
summary: Functional verification dominates integrated circuit (IC) front-end engineering effort, and a single missed bug that escapes to silicon can trigger a costly respin. Recent large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to automate this process, yet existing LLM-based approaches generate each component through independent single-turn calls with no shared context, leaving interface mismatches undetected and reported coverage disconnected from specification requirements. To address these challenges, we present GoGoTB, an agentic framework that achieves end-to-end verification closure through three subsystems: an agentic execution control layer, an evolvable knowledge system, and specification-grounded coverage closure. The execution control layer separates deterministic enforcement from LLM reasoning at every tool and stage boundary. The knowledge system dispatches methodology and design-specific expertise on demand. The coverage framework anchors every bin to a named specification behavior so that each residual gap has a diagnosable root cause and a targeted remedy. Tested on 8 register transfer level (RTL) designs without any human intervention, GoGoTB achieves 100\% environment generation success and averages 98.4\% line, 97.2\% branch, 97.0\% toggle, and 83.2\% functional coverage. No prior work successfully generates a complete verification environment or achieves meaningful coverage on the same benchmarks.

AI.tldr: GoGoTB is an agentic LLM-based framework for automated IC verification that achieves end-to-end closure via three subsystems: agentic execution control, evolvable knowledge, and specification-grounded coverage. On 8 RTL designs without human intervention, it reaches 100% environment generation success and high coverage (98.4% line, 97.2% branch, 97.0% toggle, 83.2% functional), outperforming all prior work.
AI.motivation: Functional verification dominates IC front-end effort, and missed bugs can cause costly silicon respins. LLMs offer automation potential, but existing approaches use independent single-turn calls with no shared context, causing undetected interface mismatches and coverage disconnected from specification requirements. A holistic, context-aware solution is needed.
AI.method: GoGoTB comprises three subsystems: (1) an agentic execution control layer that separates deterministic enforcement from LLM reasoning at every tool/stage boundary; (2) an evolvable knowledge system that dispatches methodology and design-specific expertise on demand; (3) a specification-grounded coverage framework that anchors every coverage bin to a named specification behavior, enabling diagnosable root causes and targeted remedies for residual gaps.
AI.result: Tested on 8 RTL designs with zero human intervention, GoGoTB achieved 100% environment generation success, averaging 98.4% line coverage, 97.2% branch coverage, 97.0% toggle coverage, and 83.2% functional coverage. No prior work successfully generates a complete verification environment or achieves meaningful coverage on the same benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: GoGoTB demonstrates that an agentic, specification-grounded architecture can overcome the fragmentation and context-isolation limitations of prior LLM-based verification approaches, delivering the first fully automated, end-to-end verification closure system with competitive coverage metrics across multiple RTL designs.

title: On Exercising Governance Power in Decentralized Autonomous Organizations
comment: To Appear in 8th edition of the International Conference on Blockchain Computing and Applications (BCCA 2026)
summary: A decentralized autonomous organization (DAO) is a governance entity that allows its stakeholders to manage blockchain-based protocols through smart contracts. The DAO explicitly specifies how stakeholders make and enforce decisions concerning a protocol's operation in a smart contract, aptly referred to as its governance contract. The design of this governance contract, therefore, has far-reaching implications for the security (trust) and privacy (transparency) of the smart contracts managed by the DAO and its stakeholders. In this work, we (i) explicate the trust and transparency trade-offs of the design choices in implementing a DAO and (ii) highlight how poor choices introduce critical vulnerabilities, using real-world examples as case studies. To this end, we analyze $48$ public, actively used Ethereum-based DAOs that control a vast capital. We classify the design choices into a handful of key dimensions that succinctly capture how a DAO's stakeholders initiate a protocol change, vote on it, and, based on the voting outcome, execute that change. Our analyses crucially uncover a new class of attacks, which we call governance attacks, that directly exploit the fundamental design of a DAO's governance mechanisms, even if we assume bug-free implementations.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the design of DAO governance contracts, examining 48 Ethereum-based DAOs to classify governance design choices, reveal trust-transparency trade-offs, and identify a novel class of "governance attacks" that exploit fundamental governance mechanisms regardless of implementation correctness.
AI.motivation: DAO governance contracts explicitly encode how stakeholders make and enforce decisions about protocol operation. The design of these contracts has profound implications for security and privacy, yet the trust-transparency trade-offs inherent in different design choices are poorly understood. The authors aim to systematically analyze these trade-offs and uncover vulnerabilities stemming from governance design itself, not merely implementation bugs.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 48 public, actively used Ethereum-based DAOs controlling substantial capital. They classified governance design choices along key dimensions capturing how stakeholders initiate protocol changes, vote on them, and execute changes based on voting outcomes. Real-world case studies were used to illustrate how poor design choices introduce critical vulnerabilities.
AI.result: The analysis revealed that DAO governance designs can be categorized along a few key dimensions (proposal initiation, voting, and execution). Crucially, the authors uncovered a new class of attacks — "governance attacks" — that exploit the fundamental structure of DAO governance mechanisms, even under the assumption of bug-free smart contract implementations.
AI.conclusion: DAO governance contract design involves critical trust-transparency trade-offs, and poor choices can lead to severe vulnerabilities. The discovery of governance attacks demonstrates that security risks are inherent to governance mechanism design and cannot be eliminated solely through correct implementation.

title: Learning Implicit Causal World Models from Multi-Agent Demonstrations
summary: In model-based reinforcement learning, world models exist as internal simulators, but their training often conflates statistical correlations with causal mechanisms. This problem is exacerbated in multi-agent systems where physical transitions are intertwined with strategic agent intents, causing world models to fail under distribution shift. We introduce Implicit Causal World Models to recover environmental dynamics from offline demonstrations without requiring pre-defined causal graphs. By incorporating policy variance, we render world models discoverable via the sequential backdoor condition. Evaluations across coordination tasks (Two-Door, Navigation, and Giveway) demonstrate that these models provide interpretable causal representations under both full and partial observability, with model accuracy scaling directly with interventional strength.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Implicit Causal World Models, which recover environmental dynamics from offline demonstrations in multi-agent RL without requiring pre-defined causal graphs, using policy variance to satisfy the sequential backdoor condition.
AI.motivation: World models in model-based RL conflate statistical correlations with causal mechanisms, and this issue worsens in multi-agent systems where physical transitions are entangled with strategic agent intents, causing failures under distribution shift.
AI.method: The authors propose Implicit Causal World Models that leverage policy variance to render world models discoverable via the sequential backdoor condition, enabling causal structure recovery from offline demonstrations without pre-defined causal graphs.
AI.result: Evaluations on coordination tasks (Two-Door, Navigation, Giveway) show the models provide interpretable causal representations under full and partial observability, with model accuracy scaling directly with interventional strength.
AI.conclusion: Implicit causal modeling via policy variance offers a principled approach to disentangle causal mechanisms from spurious correlations in multi-agent world model learning, improving robustness under distribution shift.

title: Dynamic Parameterization Is Not Dynamic Inference
summary: Input-dependent controller coefficients are often treated as evidence of dynamic inference or computational savings. This interpretation conflates three properties: coefficient variation, dependence of a frozen model on how coefficients are assigned to inputs, and conditional execution. We focus on the second property and formulate a general principle of frozen-controller auditing. We provide one concrete implementation, Frozen-Controller Auditing (FCA), which caches the complete coefficient tensor along an unperturbed trajectory, disables the controller, and replays the frozen model with cross-input reassignment, token shuffling, and static profiles estimated from an independent calibration set. Because the coefficients are cached before any intervention, performance changes under replay measure assignment dependence without feedback from recomputing the controller on perturbed hidden states. Across seven independently trained 76M FeatureGate Transformers and three 504M models, static layerwise profiles retain 98.70% and 99.43% of the Correct-to-GlobalMean performance gap, respectively. Layer identity explains 87% to 96% of the coefficient variance. FeatureGate nevertheless executes every Transformer block, and its measured inference is 30.8% slower than Dense. On the public MUDDPythia-1.4B checkpoint, cross-input reassignment and token shuffling increase NLL by 1.9067 and 2.9637, respectively. These penalties show that the model depends strongly on content-conditioned cross-layer assignment. MUDDPythia also executes every Transformer block. The results show that dynamic parameterization alone does not establish dynamic inference and that functional dynamics do not establish computational savings. Claims about dynamic models should separately report coefficient variation, functional dependence of the frozen model, and actual execution.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Frozen-Controller Auditing (FCA), a method to isolate whether input-dependent controller coefficients in dynamic models reflect genuine assignment dependence rather than mere coefficient variation. Applied to FeatureGate Transformers and MUDDPythia-1.4B, FCA reveals that static profiles recover nearly all performance, that layer identity explains most coefficient variance, and that dynamic parameterization alone does not imply either dynamic inference or computational savings.
AI.motivation: Input-dependent controller coefficients in dynamic architectures are frequently cited as evidence of dynamic inference and computational efficiency. The authors argue this conflates three distinct properties — coefficient variation, assignment dependence of the frozen model, and conditional execution — and that these must be disentangled to avoid misleading claims about model dynamics.
AI.method: FCA operates by caching the complete coefficient tensor from an unperturbed forward pass, then disabling the controller and replaying the frozen model under three interventions: (1) cross-input reassignment (coefficients from input A applied to input B), (2) token shuffling, and (3) static layerwise profiles estimated from a calibration set. Because coefficients are cached pre-intervention, performance changes isolate assignment dependence without feedback loops from recomputing the controller on perturbed hidden states.
AI.result: On seven 76M FeatureGate Transformers and three 504M models, static layerwise profiles retain 98.70% and 99.43% of the Correct-to-GlobalMean performance gap. Layer identity explains 87–96% of coefficient variance. On the public MUDDPythia-1.4B checkpoint, cross-input reassignment and token shuffling increase NLL by 1.9067 and 2.9637, indicating strong content-conditioned assignment dependence. Despite dynamic coefficients, both FeatureGate and MUDDPythia execute every transformer block; FeatureGate inference is 30.8% slower than a dense baseline.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic parameterization alone does not establish dynamic inference, and functional dynamics do not establish computational savings. The authors recommend that claims about dynamic models separately report: (1) coefficient variation, (2) functional dependence of the frozen model on assignment, and (3) actual execution behavior.

title: Validating ETCS Data with the B Mathematical Language: An Industrial Pipeline and a Blueprint for LLM Integration
summary: Can large language models participate in the production and validation of ERTMS/ETCS data without undermining the certification arguments required by CENELEC EN 50128/50716? ERTMS/ETCS is a distributed safety-critical system (trackside, onboard, radio-block centre) whose behaviour is parameterised by large volumes of data drawn from the UNISIG Subsets; errors in that data propagate through the distributed architecture. This paper reports the current status of an ongoing industrial research effort at CLEARSY, ValidAItion, that bridges the ERTMS Operational Simulator to the CLEARSY Data Solver and applies rules expressed in the B mathematical language to that trackside data. During construction, a large language model (Claude) has authored the rule corpus and the parsers through a Model Context Protocol server; every proposal is adjudicated by the downstream toolchain and by systematic human review, and the toolchain has already rejected a syntactically valid but semantically illegal generated scenario. The contribution is architectural and industrial, not algorithmic: the work combines frameworks already in use at CLEARSY (CLEARSY Data Solver, ERTMS Operational Simulator) with a conversational authoring loop, rather than proposing a new formal method. It is a progress report: rule coverage is growing, the human-review campaign is underway, and the quantitative results will be published separately. The paper argues, on the evidence gathered so far, that formal rules in the mathematical language of B must remain the source of truth, while the language model serves as the fenced assistant in a distributed safety-critical railway system: AI proposes, the formal oracle disposes, the human confirms.

AI.tldr: This paper reports on an industrial research effort that integrates a large language model (Claude) into the ERTMS/ETCS data production pipeline via a Model Context Protocol server, where the LLM authors B-language rules and parsers, but all proposals are adjudicated by a formal toolchain and systematic human review. The core principle is "AI proposes, the formal oracle disposes, the human confirms."
AI.motivation: To explore whether large language models can assist in producing and validating safety-critical ERTMS/ETCS data without compromising CENELEC EN 50128/50716 certification arguments, given that errors in trackside data propagate through the distributed railway architecture.
AI.method: The ValidAItion project bridges the ERTMS Operational Simulator to the CLEARSY Data Solver, using rules expressed in the B mathematical language. An LLM (Claude) authors rule corpora and parsers through a Model Context Protocol server. Every LLM-generated proposal is adjudicated by the downstream formal toolchain and systematic human review; the toolchain has already rejected a syntactically valid but semantically illegal generated scenario.
AI.result: The toolchain successfully rejected at least one syntactically valid but semantically illegal LLM-generated scenario. Rule coverage is growing, and the human-review campaign is underway. Quantitative results are pending separate publication.
AI.conclusion: Formal rules in the B mathematical language must remain the source of truth for safety-critical railway systems. The LLM functions as a fenced assistant within a distributed safety-critical system, governed by the principle that the formal oracle disposes and the human confirms.

title: Reading Between the Curly Braces: On Textual Data Serialization Format Usability
summary: Textual data serialization formats, such as JSON or XML, are ubiquitous, supporting tasks like software configuration and data tabularization. Despite their prominence, little is known about their usability. What makes one good or bad? Is there a best one for cognitive efficiency? We explore these questions via a (N=215) crowd work study and a (N=9) semi-structured interview study. We find that format distinctions (like indentation versus curly braces) do not consistently translate into substantial usability differences. While HJSON and YAML performed better than other formats in certain modification tasks, these advantages disappeared in more realistic settings where task complexity was either trivial or highly demanding. Instead, usability appears driven by sociotechnical ecosystems: the tooling, documentation, and community practices surrounding a format matter more than syntax.

AI.tldr: A crowd study (N=215) and interviews (N=9) reveal that syntax differences among textual data serialization formats (JSON, XML, YAML, HJSON) do not consistently affect usability. Slight performance advantages for HJSON/YAML vanish at extremes of task complexity. Usability is shaped more by sociotechnical ecosystems—tooling, documentation, and community—than by format syntax alone.
AI.motivation: Despite the widespread use of textual data serialization formats like JSON, XML, YAML, and HJSON in software configuration and data tabularization, there is little empirical knowledge about their usability. The authors aim to determine what makes a format cognitively efficient and whether a "best" format exists for usability.
AI.method: A mixed-methods approach: (1) a crowd-sourced experiment with 215 participants performing modification tasks across different serialization formats to measure quantitative usability differences; (2) semi-structured interviews with 9 participants to gather qualitative insights on real-world format usage, tooling, and community factors.
AI.result: Format-level syntactic distinctions (e.g., indentation vs. curly braces) did not produce consistent, substantial usability differences. HJSON and YAML showed marginal performance gains on certain modification tasks, but these advantages disappeared when task complexity was either very low or very high. The dominant usability drivers were sociotechnical: surrounding tooling, documentation quality, and community practices.
AI.conclusion: Usability of data serialization formats is not primarily determined by syntax design. Instead, the sociotechnical ecosystem—editors, linters, documentation, and community norms—plays the decisive role. Researchers and practitioners should focus less on syntax wars and more on building robust ecosystems around chosen formats.

title: Do Methods Support the Claims? Intra-Paper Verification for Peer Review
comment: 9 pages, 8 figures. Source code, prompts, evaluation materials, and supporting data available at https://github.com/Ranjitha2493/intra-paper-claim-method-verification
summary: The growing volume of scientific submissions has motivated interest in using large language models (LLMs) to assist peer review. Existing automated novelty assessment approaches typically compare a paper's claimed contributions against prior literature, implicitly assuming that these contributions are accurately realized in the work itself. Human reviewers, however, frequently challenge novelty claims not because similar ideas already exist, but because the methodological evidence presented in the paper does not adequately support them. This internal mismatch between claimed contributions and methodological realization is rarely examined by current LLM-based review systems. To address this gap, we introduce intra-paper claim verification, a framework that evaluates whether novelty claims articulated in a paper are substantiated by the methods used to realize them. The framework employs an LLM to extract novelty claims from the introduction, retrieve claim-relevant methodological evidence, and assess whether the methods substantiate the stated contributions. Assessment is guided by reviewer-inspired evaluation criteria derived inductively from human peer reviews collected from 182 ICLR 2025 papers. These criteria capture recurring reviewer concerns related to novelty, methodology, clarity, and other issues and are used to generate structured reviewer-style assessments of claim substantiation. We evaluate the framework by comparing LLM-generated review comments against human reviewer concerns on a balanced subset of accepted and rejected papers. Human evaluation demonstrates significant alignment between framework-generated assessments and human reviewer concerns, particularly for novelty-related issues. BERTScore further distinguishes corresponding human-LLM review pairs from mismatched controls, indicating that the framework captures concerns consistent with human reviewer observations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces intra-paper claim verification, an LLM-based framework that assesses whether a paper's novelty claims are substantiated by its own methodological evidence, rather than merely checking novelty against prior literature. Using reviewer-inspired criteria derived from 182 ICLR 2025 reviews, the framework generates structured assessments that align closely with human reviewer concerns.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based novelty assessment only compares claimed contributions against prior literature, ignoring the frequent peer review scenario where novelty claims fail due to insufficient methodological support within the paper itself. This internal mismatch between claims and methods is unaddressed by current systems.
AI.method: A framework with three stages: (1) LLM extracts novelty claims from the introduction; (2) retrieval of claim-relevant methodological evidence from the paper; (3) LLM assesses whether methods substantiate the claims using evaluation criteria inductively derived from 182 ICLR 2025 human peer reviews, covering novelty, methodology, clarity, and other concerns. Generates structured reviewer-style assessments.
AI.result: Human evaluation on a balanced subset of accepted/rejected ICLR 2025 papers shows significant alignment between framework-generated and human reviewer concerns, especially for novelty-related issues. BERTScore confirms that corresponding human-LLM review pairs score higher than mismatched controls.
AI.conclusion: Intra-paper claim verification fills a critical gap in automated peer review by evaluating the internal consistency between claims and methods. The framework produces assessments that capture concerns consistent with human reviewer observations, demonstrating its practical utility.

title: DIRECTOR: Dynamic Index-based Recommendation with Transport-Optimized Retrieval
summary: Reranking is a combinatorial decision problem that aims to select and order a high-utility slate from a request-specific candidate set. A major line of generative rerankers adopts autoregressive (AR) models, which construct the slate one position at a time to capture inter-position dependencies. However, under practical greedy or bounded-width decoding, prefix-based search may prematurely prune globally promising permutations and incurs inherently sequential latency, restricting the effective search space under a fixed serving budget. Non-autoregressive (NAR) alternatives alleviate this efficiency bottleneck through position-parallel prediction, but naive position-wise factorization treats different positions too independently, leading to insufficient cross-position coordination and potentially duplicate or conflicting item selections. To retain parallel efficiency while introducing global structural coordination, we propose Dynamic Index-based RECommendation with Transport-Optimized Retrieval (DIRECTOR), a transport-guided parallel reranking framework. DIRECTOR maps candidate items into a continuous latent space and generates request-conditioned dynamic retrieval indices for all target positions in parallel. During training, it uses entropy-regularized OT to provide conflict-aware supervision; at inference, it directly performs global hard matching on similarity matrix, producing duplicate-free slates without iterative transport. To further align the generator with an opaque list-wise evaluator that returns only a scalar utility, we introduce a prefix-anchored credit assignment mechanism that converts the global reward into position-specific training signals. Extensive offline and online experiments demonstrate that DIRECTOR consistently outperforms strong reranking baselines, achieving significant improvement in large-scale industrial recommendation scenarios.

AI.tldr: DIRECTOR is a non-autoregressive reranking framework that uses optimal transport to generate globally-coordinated, duplicate-free recommendation slates in parallel, outperforming both autoregressive and naive NAR baselines in large-scale industrial settings.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive rerankers capture inter-position dependencies but suffer from sequential latency and premature pruning of good permutations under greedy/bounded decoding. Non-autoregressive methods are faster but treat positions too independently, causing duplicates and poor cross-position coordination. The goal is to achieve both parallel efficiency and global structural coordination.
AI.method: DIRECTOR maps candidate items into a continuous latent space and generates request-conditioned dynamic retrieval indices for all positions in parallel. Training uses entropy-regularized optimal transport (OT) for conflict-aware supervision; inference uses global hard matching on a similarity matrix for duplicate-free slates without iterative transport. A prefix-anchored credit assignment mechanism converts a scalar list-wise reward into position-specific training signals to align with opaque evaluators.
AI.result: Extensive offline and online experiments show DIRECTOR consistently outperforms strong reranking baselines, achieving significant improvements in large-scale industrial recommendation scenarios.
AI.conclusion: DIRECTOR successfully combines the parallel efficiency of non-autoregressive generation with global slate-level coordination via optimal transport, making it a practical and effective solution for industrial-scale reranking.

title: Position: Evaluation Scores Are Perishable Knowledge Claims
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Published at the Fifth Workshop on Generation, Evaluation and Metrics (GEM), ACL 2026, San Diego
summary: Evaluation methodologies for language models increasingly combine multiple signals, from automated metrics and LLM-as-judge ratings to human assessments and benchmark suite results. When these signals are aggregated via averaging, evaluation confidence can then substantially exceed the reliability of the weakest signal: a phenomenon we call trust inflation in evaluation. We argue that evaluation scores should be treated as epistemic claims with three properties: formality (human evaluation provides stronger evidence than an automated metric), scope (a benchmark result applies to the tested distribution, not universally), and validity windows (benchmark results expire as contamination accumulates and distributions shift). Several converging research traditions (chain-of-thought analysis, possibilistic logic, and algebraic theory) establish weakest-link aggregation as the conservative endpoint of a parameterized operator family controlled by a single pessimism parameter. Drawing on those traditions, and on concrete lessons from building an evaluation harness for agentic AI, we propose that evaluation results carry explicit metadata (formality tier, scope declaration, and expiration date) to make their epistemic status transparent. We illustrate the cost of mean aggregation on the public HELM leaderboard: across 54 frontier models on ten scenarios, the top-five models ranked by mean score and by weakest-link are completely disjoint.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "trust inflation" in language model evaluation, where averaging multiple signals produces confidence exceeding the weakest signal's reliability. It proposes treating evaluation scores as epistemic claims with formality, scope, and validity windows, advocates weakest-link aggregation as a conservative alternative, and calls for explicit metadata on evaluation results.
AI.motivation: Current LM evaluation practices aggregate heterogeneous signals (automated metrics, LLM-as-judge, human assessments, benchmarks) via simple averaging, which masks the unreliability of individual components. This creates a dangerous illusion of robustness—evaluation confidence inflated beyond what any single signal warrants—leading to potentially misleading model comparisons and rankings.
AI.method: The authors draw on three converging research traditions—chain-of-thought analysis, possibilistic logic, and algebraic theory—to establish weakest-link aggregation as the conservative endpoint of a parameterized operator family governed by a pessimism parameter. They illustrate the cost of mean aggregation empirically by comparing rankings on the HELM leaderboard (54 frontier models, 10 scenarios), where top-5 models by mean versus weakest-link are entirely disjoint.
AI.result: On the HELM leaderboard, ranking 54 frontier models across 10 scenarios reveals that the top-five models by mean score and by weakest-link aggregation are completely disjoint sets—demonstrating that common aggregation choices dramatically alter conclusions about which models are "best."
AI.conclusion: Evaluation results should carry explicit metadata (formality tier, scope declaration, expiration date) to make their epistemic status transparent. Weakest-link aggregation provides a conservative baseline, and practitioners should be aware of where their chosen aggregation method falls on the pessimism-optimism spectrum.

title: Learning the Word Problem: Geodesic Lengths and Cryptographic Applications
summary: The Word Problem has been a subject of intensive mathematical study for over a century, initially driving advances in combinatorial group theory and more recently emerging as a foundational hardness assumption in post-quantum cryptography (PQC). While generally undecidable, several families of infinite non-abelian groups exhibit solvable or algorithmically fast word problems, making them attractive platforms for cryptographic design. This paper introduces WPNet, a novel Graph Neural Network architecture capable of solving the Word Problem heuristically, which is demonstrated on the Baumslag-Solitar group $BS(1,2)$ and on an Artin group. By mapping unreduced words to dynamic graph structures, the model learns to cluster algebraically equivalent elements in a continuous embedding space, effectively identifying the geodesic representative of a word without executing discrete reduction steps. As an application, a model variant is developed that can predict the geodesic length of an unreduced word in both groups. To demonstrate the cryptographic severity of this structural leakage, WPNet is successfully deployed against the Wagner-Magyarik public-key cryptosystem.

AI.tldr: WPNet introduces a Graph Neural Network that heuristically solves the Word Problem in certain infinite non-abelian groups (BS(1,2) and Artin groups) by learning to cluster algebraically equivalent words in an embedding space, and demonstrates cryptographic vulnerability by breaking the Wagner-Magyarik public-key cryptosystem.
AI.motivation: The Word Problem is foundational to combinatorial group theory and has recently emerged as a hardness assumption in post-quantum cryptography. While undecidable in general, certain infinite non-abelian groups have efficiently solvable word problems, making them attractive for cryptographic design. The authors aim to show that neural network approaches can exploit structural leakage in such group-theoretic cryptosystems.
AI.method: WPNet maps unreduced words to dynamic graph structures and trains a Graph Neural Network to learn continuous embeddings where algebraically equivalent elements cluster together. This allows the model to identify geodesic representatives without executing discrete algebraic reduction steps. The approach is demonstrated on the Baumslag-Solitar group BS(1,2) and an Artin group. A variant also predicts geodesic length.
AI.result: WPNet successfully learns to solve the Word Problem heuristically on BS(1,2) and Artin groups. It clusters equivalent words in embedding space and identifies geodesic representatives. The model variant accurately predicts geodesic length. Most significantly, WPNet is successfully deployed to break the Wagner-Magyarik public-key cryptosystem, demonstrating the cryptographic severity of this structural leakage.
AI.conclusion: Graph Neural Networks can effectively learn algebraic structure from unreduced words in certain infinite non-abelian groups, solving the Word Problem heuristically. This constitutes a form of structural leakage with direct cryptanalytic consequences, as evidenced by the successful attack on the Wagner-Magyarik cryptosystem.

title: Partner Capability Estimation for Task-Agnostic Adaptation in Ad-Hoc Teamwork
summary: Effective collaboration with novel and diverse partners is a crucial skill for autonomous agents. Most current ad-hoc teamwork (AHT) approaches assume that agents will collaborate on a single, fixed task and that the partner's capabilities, their ability to successfully execute the desired action, are already known. In reality, a partner's true capabilities are often hidden, and human collaborators may act sub-optimally on tasks with multiple valid strategies. To address these limitations, we extend ad-hoc teamwork into a multi-task setting by re-framing it as a problem of joint planning with decentralised execution under hidden partner capabilities. We introduce CE-CM (Capability Estimation via Contextual Models), an approximate Bayesian method that infers task-invariant capability vectors. By using simulation-based sampling, the agent estimates capabilities and induces a contextual Multi-agent Markov Decision Processes for planning. This approach requires no population pre-training and refines its beliefs online from just a few tasks. To account for human unpredictability, we propose CE-CM-Div, an extension that evaluates capability hypotheses against diverse planner rollouts rather than a single optimal trajectory. Simulated experiments demonstrate that CE-CM rapidly recovers hidden capabilities, reduces infeasible action assignments, and adapts to changes over time. Furthermore, in an offline human study of 225 trajectories from 15 participants, CE-CM-Div substantially improved capability estimates over the baseline CE-CM method. Our results suggest capability-based modelling is a promising interpretable, task-agnostic representation in the studied settings, demonstrating that accounting for behavioural diversity is essential for robust human-AI teaming.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CE-CM, a Bayesian method for ad-hoc teamwork in multi-task settings where partner capabilities are hidden. By inferring task-invariant capability vectors and using simulation-based planning, it enables agents to collaborate effectively without pre-training. An extension, CE-CM-Div, accounts for human unpredictability by evaluating against diverse rollouts, significantly improving capability estimation in human studies.
AI.motivation: Current ad-hoc teamwork research is limited to single, fixed tasks with known partner capabilities. In reality, partners (especially humans) have hidden capabilities and may act sub-optimally across tasks with multiple valid strategies. There is a need for agents that can infer capabilities online across multiple tasks without population pre-training.
AI.method: The authors introduce CE-CM (Capability Estimation via Contextual Models), an approximate Bayesian inference method that estimates task-invariant capability vectors from observed behavior across tasks. It uses simulation-based sampling to infer capabilities and induces a contextual Multi-agent Markov Decision Process for decentralized joint planning. CE-CM-Div extends this by evaluating capability hypotheses against diverse planner rollouts (rather than a single optimal trajectory) to account for human behavioral diversity.
AI.result: In simulated experiments, CE-CM rapidly recovers hidden capabilities, reduces infeasible action assignments, and adapts to changes over time. In an offline human study with 225 trajectories from 15 participants, CE-CM-Div substantially outperformed baseline CE-CM in capability estimation accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Capability-based modeling offers a promising interpretable, task-agnostic representation for human-AI teaming. Accounting for behavioral diversity (via CE-CM-Div) is essential for robust collaboration with human partners who may deviate from optimality.

title: Weak-to-Strong On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD), which aligns a student with the teacher's token-level distribution on the student's own rollouts, is an effective paradigm for transferring capabilities across LLMs. Prevailing approaches assume a teacher at least as capable as the student: they either distill a larger model into a smaller one, which fails at the frontier where no larger teacher exists, or consolidate multiple domain experts trained from a shared base, which requires costly training at the student's scale. We introduce Weak-to-Strong On-Policy Distillation (W2S-OPD), a simple yet effective OPD framework that improves the strong student by distilling from multiple weak models. W2S-OPD constructs a proxy teacher in logit space from a contrast pair of a positive and a negative model, both smaller than the student and cheap to obtain. Their logit difference isolates the capability direction, which is added to the student's own base model, yielding a proxy teacher that couples this direction while staying distributionally adjacent to the student. The student then distills it by minimizing the per-token reverse KL on its own rollouts. We instantiate the contrast pair as i) a post-RL expert against its pre-RL initialization, isolating the skill RL instills, ii) a larger against a smaller base model, isolating the capability from scale, and iii) a small base model with correct versus wrong hints, isolating the instance-level direction toward the solution. Across four math and three code benchmarks, W2S-OPD outperforms OPD, enables the student to surpass the domain teacher, and keeps improving the student even when every supervision source is weaker. Analysis shows different contrasts yield distinct signals: the post-RL and hint contrasts emphasize reasoning frameworks, while the scale contrast emphasizes the solving procedure. Our code will be available at https://github.com/Yu-Fangxu/W2S-OPD.

AI.tldr: W2S-OPD introduces a framework where a strong student improves by distilling from multiple weak models via a contrastive proxy teacher constructed in logit space, enabling the student to surpass all weak supervision sources.
