AI.motivation: Existing on-policy distillation assumes a teacher at least as capable as the student, which fails at the frontier (no larger teacher exists) or requires costly same-scale training. The authors aim to enable a strong student to improve using only weaker, cheap-to-obtain models.
AI.method: W2S-OPD constructs a proxy teacher from a contrast pair (positive minus negative model in logit space) to isolate a capability direction. This direction is added to the student's base logits, producing a proxy teacher that is distributionally adjacent to the student. The student then performs on-policy distillation by minimizing per-token reverse KL divergence on its own rollouts. Three contrast pair instantiations are explored: (i) post-RL expert vs. pre-RL initialization, (ii) larger vs. smaller base model, and (iii) small base model with correct vs. wrong hints.
AI.result: Across four math and three code benchmarks, W2S-OPD outperforms standard OPD, enables the student to surpass the domain teacher, and yields continued improvement even when every supervision source is weaker. Different contrast types yield distinct signals: post-RL and hint contrasts emphasize reasoning frameworks, while scale contrast emphasizes solving procedures.
AI.conclusion: W2S-OPD is a simple yet effective weak-to-strong distillation framework that breaks the assumption of requiring a stronger teacher, showing that contrastive signals from weak models can effectively improve a strong student across math and code domains.

title: NISPO: Open-source IUPAC name generation tool
summary: Systematic International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) names are standard for communicating molecular structures in chemical literature, patents, and databases. We introduce NISPO, an open-source RDKit-based Python package for IUPAC name generation. NISPO was developed by an agentic self-improvement loop using OpenAI's Codex with the GPT-5.5 model. A generated name was considered correct if the open-source OPSIN tool parsed it back to the input structure. Guided by this objective, the agent implemented and refined NISPO against 2.68 million molecules from SureChEMBL, resulting in the tool achieving 98.1% round-trip accuracy on a held-out set of 103 million PubChem molecules. NISPO is freely available at https://github.com/oxpig/nispo.

AI.tldr: NISPO is an open-source RDKit-based Python package for generating systematic IUPAC chemical names, developed via an agentic self-improvement loop using GPT-5.5. It achieves 98.1% round-trip accuracy on 103M PubChem molecules by using OPSIN's ability to parse generated names back to the input structure as the correctness criterion.
AI.motivation: Systematic IUPAC names are the standard for communicating molecular structures in chemical literature, patents, and databases. There is a need for an accurate, open-source tool that can generate IUPAC names automatically, which motivates the development of NISPO.
AI.method: NISPO was developed using an agentic self-improvement loop powered by OpenAI's Codex with the GPT-5.5 model. The agent iteratively implemented and refined the RDKit-based Python package, using a round-trip accuracy objective: a generated IUPAC name was considered correct only if the open-source OPSIN tool could parse it back to the original input structure. Training/refinement used 2.68 million molecules from SureChEMBL.
AI.result: NISPO achieved 98.1% round-trip accuracy on a held-out test set of 103 million molecules from PubChem, demonstrating high fidelity in IUPAC name generation.
AI.conclusion: NISPO is a highly accurate, open-source IUPAC name generator that leverages self-improving agentic development and round-trip validation via OPSIN. It is freely available on GitHub.

title: User-Reported Misinformation Exposure Across Social Media Platforms
summary: In this study, we surveyed users for their perception of misinformation exposure across social media platforms. Such perceived exposure is important because individuals' beliefs about how often they encounter false information can shape their trust in institutions, platforms, and even their friends. In a survey of 1,010 United States residents, we found that perceived exposure to misinformation varies substantially across platforms and is only moderately correlated with the frequency of platform use. A much larger percentage of participants also reported being exposed to misinformation from the public feed than from known contacts. Based on these results, we propose governance strategies across three categories of platform types: discovery, interpersonal, and discourse. This work offers insight into users' perceptions of social media misinformation and a corresponding research agenda for governance.

AI.tldr: A survey of 1,010 U.S. residents reveals that perceived exposure to misinformation varies significantly across social media platforms, correlates only moderately with usage frequency, and occurs more through public feeds than known contacts. The authors propose governance strategies tailored to three platform categories: discovery, interpersonal, and discourse.
AI.motivation: Perceived exposure to misinformation shapes trust in institutions, platforms, and social relationships, yet little is known about how users perceive their own exposure across different platform types. Understanding these perceptions is a prerequisite for designing effective governance interventions.
AI.method: Survey of 1,010 United States residents measuring self-reported perceived exposure to misinformation across multiple social media platforms, examining correlations with usage frequency and distinguishing between exposure via public feeds versus known contacts.
AI.result: Perceived misinformation exposure varies substantially across platforms and is only moderately correlated with platform usage frequency. A significantly larger proportion of participants reported exposure through public feeds rather than from known contacts.
AI.conclusion: The findings support a tripartite governance framework for platforms — discovery, interpersonal, and discourse — and establish a research agenda for platform-specific misinformation governance based on how users actually perceive exposure.

title: DuplexGen: Adaptive Synthesis of Human-AI Turn-Taking Dialogues
summary: Turn-taking is a central component of full-duplex interaction. Which turn-taking behaviors are appropriate varies with the scenario, yet current models apply a single norm regardless of context. This limitation originates in their training data: human-human speech corpora capture natural timing phenomena but provide little role grounding or scenario-specific norms, while heuristic or prompted synthesis methods inject turn-taking behaviors without basing them on human preferences. We introduce DuplexGen, a framework for generating dialogues with scenario-adaptive turn-taking by calibrating LLM predictions against a small set of slot-level human preference annotations. In six cooperative and competitive tasks, human turn-taking preferences differ systematically, and DuplexGen aligns substantially more closely with those preferences than uncalibrated prompting or training solely on generic human-human data; a full-duplex model trained on DuplexGen-generated data exhibits distinctive, human-preferred turn-taking behaviors. These results show that human calibration, not corpus scale or prompt design alone, is what allows turn-taking synthesis to be scenario-specific.

AI.tldr: DuplexGen calibrates LLM-based dialogue generation against slot-level human preference annotations to produce scenario-adaptive turn-taking behaviors. Across six tasks, it significantly outperforms uncalibrated prompting and generic human-human training data in aligning with human preferences, and a full-duplex model trained on its outputs exhibits distinctive, human-preferred turn-taking.
AI.motivation: Current turn-taking models apply a single norm regardless of context because training data lacks role grounding and scenario-specific norms. Human-human corpora capture natural timing but lack annotation, while heuristic/prompted methods inject behaviors without human preference grounding. The core gap is that turn-taking appropriateness varies by scenario, but no framework adapts to these differences based on human preferences.
AI.method: DuplexGen: a framework that calibrates LLM predictions against a small set of slot-level human preference annotations. The calibration enables generation of dialogues with turn-taking behaviors adapted to specific scenarios (six cooperative and competitive tasks). A full-duplex spoken dialogue model is then trained on the resulting synthetic data to exhibit scenario-appropriate turn-taking.
AI.result: Human turn-taking preferences differ systematically across the six tasks. DuplexGen aligns substantially more closely with those preferences than uncalibrated prompting or training solely on generic human-human data. A full-duplex model trained on DuplexGen-generated data exhibits distinctive, human-preferred turn-taking behaviors.
AI.conclusion: Human calibration—not corpus scale or prompt design alone—is the critical ingredient for achieving scenario-specific turn-taking synthesis. Small-scale preference annotations can effectively steer LLM generation toward context-appropriate interaction norms.

title: PSG: Pair-Space Generation for Efficient Generative Reranking
summary:
Modern recommender systems adopt Generator-Evaluator (G-E) for list-wise reranking: a generator produces sequences from candidates and an evaluator scores them at sequence-level to filter out the optimal one for exposure. Auto-Regressive(AR), working as the backbone for generative recommendation, suffers two limitations. First, its complexity grows linearly with list length, forcing the system to generate fewer lists under rigorous latency constraints and thus limiting exploration. Second, teacher-forcing creates a train-test mismatch; cumulative errors worsen with length and degrade quality.
  To address these problems, we propose Pair-Space Generation (PSG), a reformulation that elevates the generation atom from individual items to ordered item pairs. Given $n$ candidate items, PSG operates over pair vocabulary of size $n(n-1)$ per request, generates only $L/2$ tokens. Pair token representations are produced on-the-fly by a pretrained pair-token representation module optimized over large scale exposure logs, eliminating the data sparsity that would otherwise plague a quadratic sized vocabulary. We establish three theoretical guarantees: (i) PSG is bijective with item-space generation and induces an equivalent family of sequence distributions, thus incurring no loss of expressiveness; (ii) generation in pair-token space achieves approximately a $2\times$ to $4\times$ speedup theoretically under moderate settings and $1.83\times$ in the real industrial environmental settings; and (iii) under outcome-only rewards, the worst-case suboptimality of PSG is bounded by $O((L/2)^2 \barε)$, representing a nearly $4\times$ improvement over item-space generation. Beyond benchmark-based validation, PSG has also been deployed on Kuaishou, delivering a 0.178\% lift in per-user stay time on the platform, which serves over 400 million daily active users.

AI.tldr: PSG reformulates list-wise reranking in recommender systems by generating ordered item pairs instead of individual items, achieving ~2-4× theoretical speedup, 4× better worst-case suboptimality bounds, and a 0.178% lift in per-user stay time when deployed on Kuaishou (400M+ DAU).
AI.motivation: Auto-Regressive (AR) generation in Generator-Evaluator reranking suffers from (1) linear complexity growth with list length, limiting the number of lists explored under latency constraints, and (2) train-test mismatch from teacher-forcing, where cumulative errors degrade sequence quality as length increases.
AI.method: Pair-Space Generation (PSG) shifts the generation unit from single items to ordered item pairs. For n candidates, PSG uses a pair vocabulary of size n(n-1) and generates only L/2 tokens. A pretrained pair-token representation module, optimized on large-scale exposure logs, produces pair representations on-the-fly to mitigate data sparsity. Three theoretical guarantees are provided: bijectivity with item-space generation (no expressiveness loss), 2-4× speedup, and O((L/2)²ε̄) worst-case suboptimality bound.
AI.result: Theoretical guarantees: (i) bijective equivalence with item-space generation; (ii) ~2-4× theoretical speedup, 1.83× in real industrial settings; (iii) O((L/2)²ε̄) suboptimality bound, a ~4× improvement. Industrial deployment on Kuaishou yielded a 0.178% lift in per-user stay time across 400M+ daily active users.
AI.conclusion: PSG offers a principled and practically effective reformulation of list-wise generation for reranking, overcoming AR limitations through pair-space operation. It achieves significant efficiency and quality improvements both theoretically and in large-scale industrial deployment.

title: TraceCoder: Explainable and Auditable Code Generation with Position-Key Snippet Versioning
comment: Submitted Version (version submitted on May deadline to AGENTICS 2026). Version of Record to appear in AGENTICS proceedings
summary: Contemporary LLM-based coding agents produce code as black-box outputs: the rationale behind each line is hidden, the evolution of the code through benchmark-driven repair is ephemeral, and post-hoc auditing is impossible. We present a code generation concept that addresses these shortcomings through three complementary mechanisms: (i) a relational snippet-history schema that records, per repair event, the benchmark reference, round number, failure text, and LLM explanation, enabling full provenance queries; (ii) a browser-based visualisation tool that renders this history as heat-mapped, hover-annotated source code; and (iii) a competitive fractional position-key indexing scheme with tree-node delimiters that assigns stable, lexicographically-ordered identifiers to each code snippet, enabling fine-grained tracking without disrupting surrounding lines. We evaluate TraceCoder on 30 algorithmic programming tasks spanning string processing, mathematical computation, and data-structure manipulation, across two provider configurations. Of these, 10 exhaust the 6-iteration budget on tasks with subtle edge-case behaviour. Mean Chg% reaches 30%, three in ten code snippets carry a traceable repair-event row, compared to 21% when using Gemini 2.0 Flash as sole provider on a 20-task subset. Three detailed case studies demonstrate how the system explains which specific benchmark failures shaped each line of the final program. The proposed mechanism makes the internal "narrative" of automated code generation auditable and replayable, a property essential for trust and accountability in production deployments.

AI.tldr: TraceCoder introduces an auditable code-generation framework that records the full repair-event history of LLM-generated code, visualizes it via a browser-based heat-map tool, and assigns stable, lexicographically-ordered identifiers to code snippets using a fractional position-key indexing scheme. Evaluated on 30 algorithmic tasks, it achieves a 30% mean change percentage, with three in ten snippets carrying traceable repair events.
AI.motivation: Contemporary LLM-based coding agents produce opaque, black-box code outputs where the rationale, iterative repair history, and benchmark-driven evolution are hidden and ephemeral, making post-hoc auditing impossible. This undermines trust and accountability in production deployments.
AI.method: The paper proposes three complementary mechanisms: (1) a relational snippet-history schema that records benchmark reference, round number, failure text, and LLM explanation per repair event, enabling provenance queries; (2) a browser-based visualization tool rendering history as heat-mapped, hover-annotated source code; (3) a competitive fractional position-key indexing scheme with tree-node delimiters assigning stable, lexicographically-ordered identifiers to each snippet for fine-grained tracking without disrupting surrounding lines.
AI.result: Evaluated on 30 algorithmic programming tasks (string processing, mathematical computation, data-structure manipulation) across two provider configurations. Ten tasks exhausted the 6-iteration budget on subtle edge-case behavior. Mean change percentage reached 30%; three in ten code snippets carried a traceable repair-event row, compared to 21% when using Gemini 2.0 Flash as sole provider on a 20-task subset.
AI.conclusion: TraceCoder makes the internal "narrative" of automated code generation auditable and replayable — a property essential for trust and accountability in production deployments. Three detailed case studies demonstrate how the system explains which specific benchmark failures shaped each line of the final program.

title: StealthBench: Measuring Operational Stealth in Autonomous Offensive-Security Agents
comment: 29 pages, 9 tables, 1 figure, 2 appendices. Code: https://github.com/GangGreenTemperTatum/stealthbench Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/0xmoose/stealthbench Website: https://stealthbench.com
summary:
Stealth, the discipline of achieving an objective without revealing your presence, capabilities, or collected intelligence, is what separates sophisticated operators from detectable ones. Elite security researchers and advanced persistent threats achieve their objectives unnoticed; autonomous agents increasingly inherit the same offensive tasks, but do they inherit the tradecraft? We introduce StealthBench,a benchmark that measures operational stealth in autonomous offensive-security agents across six operational security (OPSEC) dimensions. We extract 11 hand-verified OPSEC incidents from real bug-bounty and red-team trajectories, expanded into 14 dockerized task scenarios, where agents, despite finding real vulnerabilities, committed stealth failures inconsistent with standard operational tradecraft: embedding credentials in public uploads, deleting production resources to prove access, force-adding uninvolved users to demonstrate a race condition.
  We evaluate agent trajectories using a 3-model large language model (LLM) judge panel with majority-vote aggregation, measuring safe success rate (solved and stealthy), Stealth@Solve (tradecraft quality among successful solves), and reckless solve rate (solved but cover blown). Our results show that no model exceeds 54% safe success rate (the compound metric requiring both task completion and stealth), confirming that OPSEC failures are systematic across model families. We release StealthBench as a public benchmark to support both the development of stealth-aware agents and automated OPSEC monitoring for autonomous offensive-security deployments. The interactive leaderboard, evaluation harness, and dataset are available at https://stealthbench.com.

AI.tldr: StealthBench is a benchmark measuring operational stealth (OPSEC) in autonomous offensive-security agents across six dimensions, using 14 dockerized task scenarios derived from real bug-bounty incidents. Evaluations via a 3-model LLM judge panel show no agent exceeds 54% safe success rate, revealing systematic OPSEC failures across model families.
AI.motivation: Autonomous security agents are increasingly tasked with offensive operations (bug bounties, red-teaming), but existing evaluations focus only on task completion (finding vulnerabilities), ignoring whether agents maintain operational security. Real-world elite operators achieve objectives without detection; the authors investigate whether AI agents inherit this tradecraft or systematically violate OPSEC norms.
AI.method: The authors constructed StealthBench by extracting 11 hand-verified OPSEC incidents from real bug-bounty and red-team trajectories, expanding them into 14 Dockerized task scenarios covering six OPSEC dimensions. Agent trajectories are evaluated using a 3-model LLM judge panel with majority-vote aggregation along three metrics: Safe Success Rate (solved + stealthy), Stealth@Solve (tradecraft quality among successful solves), and Reckless Solve Rate (solved but detected).
AI.result: No evaluated model exceeds 54% safe success rate — the compound metric requiring both task completion and stealth preservation. Typical stealth failures include embedding credentials in public uploads, deleting production resources to prove access, and force-adding uninvolved users to demonstrate race conditions. These failures are systematic across model families, confirming that current agents lack operational tradecraft.
AI.conclusion: OPSEC failures in autonomous offensive-security agents are systematic, not incidental. StealthBench is released publicly (leaderboard, evaluation harness, dataset) to spur development of stealth-aware agents and enable automated OPSEC monitoring for autonomous offensive-security deployments.

title: Between Gradient and Natural Gradient: A Continuum of LoRA Initializations
summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) fine-tunes large pretrained models at a fraction of the cost of full fine-tuning, but its performance depends strongly on how the adapters are initialized. Recent schemes initialize the adapters from the downstream loss gradient: some project the raw gradient onto its top directions, while others first whiten it with an estimate of the loss curvature. We show that these seemingly distinct methods are points on a single continuum: a two-parameter family of preconditioned gradient initializations, which we call Unified LoRA (ULoRA), governed by a spectral whitening exponent and an Adam-like diagonal exponent. Sweeping this family under a full learning-rate search, we find that no single fixed preconditioning strength dominates: the best operating point is task-dependent and frequently lies strictly inside the family, away from the published endpoints. Treated as an upper bound of this family, a tuned ULoRA configuration matches or exceeds full fine-tuning on all five GLUE tasks with RoBERTa-base and is competitive with the strongest baselines on GSM8K with LLaMA-2-7B. Our deployable, search-free variant, ULoRA-Auto, selects per-layer exponents from measured spectral statistics, approaches this upper bound at no additional search cost, and ranks at or near the top among deployable LoRA methods. Our results show that a principled design space for LoRA initialization and curvature preconditioning should be treated as a tunable dimension rather than a fixed design decision.

AI.tldr: ULoRA unifies existing gradient-based LoRA initializations into a two-parameter family of preconditioned gradient initializations, showing that optimal preconditioning strength is task-dependent. A tuned ULoRA matches or exceeds full fine-tuning on NLP benchmarks, and a search-free variant (ULoRA-Auto) selects parameters automatically from spectral statistics.
AI.motivation: Existing LoRA initialization methods (raw gradient projection vs. curvature-whitened gradient) appear distinct, and prior work treats preconditioning choices as fixed. The paper asks whether these methods are points on a continuum and whether the optimal preconditioning configuration is task-dependent, rather than a one-size-fits-all design.
AI.method: The authors propose Unified LoRA (ULoRA), a two-parameter family parameterized by a spectral whitening exponent and an Adam-like diagonal exponent. They sweep this continuous design space with full learning-rate search to identify task-optimal configurations. They also introduce ULoRA-Auto, which selects per-layer exponents automatically from measured spectral statistics of the gradient and curvature estimates, removing the need for manual tuning.
AI.result: No single fixed preconditioning strength dominates — the best configuration is task-dependent and often lies inside the continuum away from published endpoints. A tuned ULoRA matches or exceeds full fine-tuning on all five GLUE tasks with RoBERTa-base and is competitive with top baselines on GSM8K with LLaMA-2-7B. ULoRA-Auto approaches this upper bound at no additional search cost and ranks at or near the top among deployable LoRA methods.
AI.conclusion: The principled design space for LoRA initialization and curvature preconditioning should be treated as a tunable dimension rather than a fixed design choice. The unified continuum reconciles seemingly distinct methods and enables both tuned and automated configurations that push LoRA performance toward full fine-tuning.

title: Try Again, Don't Look Back: Blind Resampling Outperforms Self-Repair in Small Code Models
summary: Self-repair - returning a failed program to the model together with its test output and asking for a correction - is a standard component of code agents, and is almost always evaluated against a baseline that does not retry at all. We argue that this comparison confounds the value of the feedback with the value of the extra attempt. Using a placebo-controlled design on MBPP+ at three model scales (1.5B, 3B, 7B), we compare four matched-budget retry conditions: blind resampling, a content-free failure notice, genuine execution feedback, and feedback augmented with verbal self-reflection. Blind resampling is the strongest condition below 7B, and remains statistically tied with the best condition at 7B, while consuming 2.5-5.5x fewer tokens; conditioning on the model's own failed attempt costs 6.1 points at 1.5B (p=0.006), and the informational content of execution feedback adds nothing measurable over the placebo. We attribute this to anchoring: when shown its previous attempt, a model reproduces a near-identical program in 33-68% of retries, against 2-14% under blind resampling. Two further experiments delimit the effect. Retrieved solutions to other tasks change nothing (bounded to +/-3.5 points), which localizes the harm to self-conditioning rather than context length; and reflection, the only condition that measurably weakens the anchor, remains dominated on cost. Replication rules out two competing explanations: the penalty is unchanged at full precision, and it reproduces on an independent model family. Across six configurations spanning two families and two precisions, its magnitude is predicted by baseline quality alone (r=0.96) - the cost of anchoring is the cost of committing to a bad first attempt.

AI.tldr: Self-repair in code agents is often confounded with extra attempts. Using placebo-controlled experiments, the authors show that execution feedback adds no measurable benefit over blind resampling, and that showing a model its own failed attempt causes harmful anchoring — the model reproduces near-identical incorrect programs. The penalty is predicted by baseline quality alone.
AI.motivation: Prior work evaluating self-repair (returning a failed program with test output for correction) compares against a no-retry baseline, which confounds the value of feedback with the value of simply having another attempt. The authors aim to isolate the true causal effect of execution feedback and self-conditioning using a placebo-controlled, matched-budget design.
AI.method: The study uses MBPP+ at three model scales (1.5B, 3B, 7B) with four matched-budget retry conditions: (1) blind resampling, (2) a content-free failure notice (placebo), (3) genuine execution feedback, and (4) feedback with verbal self-reflection. Two additional experiments test retrieval of other solutions (to isolate self-conditioning from context length) and reflection's effect on anchoring. Replication covers two model families and two precisions.
AI.result: Blind resampling is the strongest condition below 7B and statistically tied for best at 7B, while using 2.5–5.5× fewer tokens. Self-conditioning costs 6.1 points at 1.5B (p=0.006); execution feedback adds nothing over the placebo. Models reproduce near-identical programs in 33–68% of retries when shown prior attempts vs. 2–14% under blind resampling. Retrieved other-task solutions change nothing (±3.5 points), localizing the harm to self-conditioning. Reflection weakens the anchor but remains cost-dominated. The penalty is unchanged at full precision and replicates across model families, with magnitude predicted by baseline quality (r=0.96).
AI.conclusion: The ostensible benefit of self-repair is largely attributable to having a second attempt, not to execution feedback. Showing a model its own failed code induces harmful anchoring, causing it to commit to a bad first attempt. The anchoring penalty is robust across model families and precisions, and its magnitude is almost entirely explained by baseline success rate — the stronger the model, the less it suffers.

title: Contextualized Counterspeech Can Be More Persuasive Than Generic Counterspeech
comment: This work is an extension of this conference paper: Cima, L., Miaschi, A., Trujillo, A., Avvenuti, M., Dell'Orletta, F., & Cresci, S. (2025, April). Contextualized counterspeech: Strategies for adaptation, personalization, and evaluation. In Proceedings of the ACM on Web Conference 2025 (pp. 5022-5033)
summary: AI-generated counterspeech offers a scalable and effective strategy to mitigate online toxicity by promoting more constructive dialogue. Yet, existing approaches adopt a generic, one-size-fits-all paradigm, overlooking the conversational context and characteristics of the targeted users. Here, we propose and evaluate multiple strategies for generating contextualized counterspeech that is adapted to the moderation setting and personalized to the moderated user. In detail, we explore a range of configurations that integrate different forms of contextual information and fine-tuning techniques. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation combining quantitative indicators with a pre-registered, mixed-design crowdsourcing experiment. To ensure robustness, we implement algorithmic measures of counterspeech quality based on ROUGE, BLEU, and BERTScore, observing overall consistent results across metrics. Furthermore, we analyze which characteristics of both the generated counterspeech and the moderated toxic message most strongly influence perceived persuasiveness, yielding insights into how contextualized interventions can be made more effective. Our findings show that personalization can be effective, but not uniformly so. Lightweight strategies combining conversational context and user history improve perceived adequacy and persuasiveness, whereas several other contextualization strategies degrade human-perceived counterspeech quality. Taken together, these results provide actionable directions for developing more personalized, effective, and responsible counterspeech systems, ultimately advancing human-AI collaboration in online content moderation.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates contextualized and personalized AI-generated counterspeech for online toxicity moderation, finding that lightweight strategies combining conversational context and user history improve perceived quality, while heavier contextualization can backfire.
AI.motivation: Existing AI counterspeech systems use a one-size-fits-all approach, ignoring conversational context and user characteristics. This limits their effectiveness and perceived adequacy when moderating real-world toxic interactions.
AI.method: The authors propose multiple strategies for generating contextualized counterspeech, integrating different forms of contextual information (conversational context, user history) and fine-tuning techniques. Evaluation combines quantitative metrics (ROUGE, BLEU, BERTScore) with a pre-registered, mixed-design crowdsourcing experiment assessing perceived persuasiveness and adequacy.
AI.result: Personalization is effective but not uniformly so. Lightweight strategies incorporating conversational context and user history improve perceived adequacy and persuasiveness. However, several other contextualization strategies degrade human-perceived counterspeech quality. Algorithmic metrics show overall consistent results across measures.
AI.conclusion: The findings offer actionable directions for building personalized, effective, and responsible counterspeech systems, highlighting that contextualization must be applied judiciously to avoid harming perceived quality, and advancing human-AI collaboration in content moderation.

title: Choosing Where and How to Moderate: End-to-End Trade-offs in Filter Placement and Response Rewriting
summary: Content-moderation classifiers are usually evaluated in isolation, but deployment requires choosing where to intervene and what follows a flag. We evaluate these choices using two end-to-end customer-outcome metrics rather than component accuracy: Usefulness, the fraction of turns with a shown, non-harmful, relevant response, and Harmful Exposure, the fraction with a shown harmful response. Latency and error rates are diagnostics. We compare Input only, Response only, and Input + response hard blocking on a human-labelled product benchmark and public ToxicChat evaluation. At the evaluated operating points, Response only achieves the highest filter-only Usefulness in both settings, while Input + response achieves lower Harmful Exposure. Replacing Response only blocking with Response + rewrite recovers most blocked traffic and yields the same observed Harmful Exposure count as Response only blocking for the selected configuration; this equality is not an equivalence result. Probe routing substantially reduces conditional route-and-generation time relative to LLM routing at comparable measured outcomes. A focused output review shows how rewrites balance filter passage with usefulness by generalizing triggering language while retaining benign intent and safe redirection; some sensitive-domain outputs nevertheless omit potentially safety-relevant support information. These results support comparing moderation configurations under deployment-specific safety and latency constraints rather than applying a universal placement rule. Code and public artifacts are available at https://github.com/microsoft/mod-frontier

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates content moderation strategies not by classifier accuracy alone but by end-to-end deployment metrics: Usefulness (non-harmful, relevant responses shown) and Harmful Exposure (harmful responses shown). Comparing Input-only, Response-only, and Input+Response blocking, Response-only maximizes Usefulness while Input+Response minimizes Harmful Exposure. Replacing Response-only blocking with Response+rewrite recovers blocked traffic without increasing Harmful Exposure. Probe routing reduces latency compared to LLM routing. The work advocates deployment-specific configuration rather than universal placement rules.
AI.motivation: Content moderation classifiers are typically evaluated in isolation using component-level accuracy metrics, but real-world deployment requires decisions about where to intervene (input vs. output filtering) and what action follows a flag (blocking vs. rewriting). These operational choices have downstream effects on customer experience that component accuracy fails to capture, motivating the need for end-to-end evaluation with customer-outcome metrics.
AI.method: The authors propose two end-to-end metrics: (1) Usefulness — fraction of turns yielding a shown, non-harmful, relevant response; and (2) Harmful Exposure — fraction of turns yielding a shown harmful response. They compare three intervention configurations (Input only, Response only, Input + response hard blocking) on a human-labelled product benchmark and the public ToxicChat dataset. They also evaluate Response + rewrite (replacing blocking with rewriting) and probe routing versus LLM routing, measuring latency and error rates as diagnostics.
AI.result: Response-only blocking achieves highest filter-only Usefulness in both evaluation settings. Input+response blocking yields the lowest Harmful Exposure. Response+rewrite recovers most blocked traffic while maintaining the same observed Harmful Exposure count as Response-only blocking (though not proven as a formal equivalence). Probe routing substantially reduces conditional route-and-generation time compared to LLM routing at comparable measured outcomes. Rewrites balance filter passage with usefulness by generalizing triggering language while preserving benign intent and safe redirection, though some sensitive-domain outputs may omit safety-relevant support information.
AI.conclusion: The findings support evaluating moderation configurations under deployment-specific safety and latency constraints rather than applying a universal placement rule. Different trade-offs between Usefulness and Harmful Exposure emerge across configurations, and operational choices like rewriting and routing can recover utility without compromising safety. Practitioners should make context-dependent decisions informed by end-to-end customer-outcome metrics.

title: NMKFR: A Robust Framework for Time-Aware Cold-Start Recommendation
summary: Item cold-start recommendation is difficult when new items have sparse early interactions and appear in recommendation environments that keep changing over time. Static content, early feedback, and temporal-state evidence are all useful, but their reliability varies across the item lifecycle. This work proposes a framework--Neural Memory Kalman Fusion Recommender (NMKFR), which combines a Titans-based semantic encoder with time-aware Kalman state tracking. The semantic branch extracts memory-enhanced item observations from text, while the temporal branch estimates latent states under irregular interaction intervals. The NMKFR further uses posterior covariance as an uncertainty signal to calibrate semantic memory retrieval and adaptive static-temporal fusion. Experiments on Amazon Video Games and MovieLens-32M evaluate NMKFR under time-aware and item cold-start protocols using sampled candidate ranking. Across the reported comparisons, ablations, diagnostics, and robustness analyses, NMKFR achieves the strongest retained results and exhibits bounded uncertainty-related internal behavior. These findings provide empirical evidence for posterior-covariance-guided semantic-temporal fusion under the evaluated offline settings.

AI.tldr: NMKFR combines a Titans-based semantic encoder with Kalman state tracking for item cold-start recommendation. It uses posterior covariance to calibrate semantic memory retrieval and fuse static content with temporal signals, outperforming baselines on Amazon Video Games and MovieLens-32M under time-aware cold-start protocols.
AI.motivation: Item cold-start recommendation is challenging because new items have sparse interactions and appear in dynamically changing environments. Static content, early feedback, and temporal evidence all help, but their reliability shifts across the item lifecycle. Existing methods lack a principled way to fuse these heterogeneous signals while accounting for their time-varying uncertainty.
AI.method: NMKFR integrates two branches: (1) a Titans-based semantic encoder that extracts memory-enhanced item observations from textual content, and (2) a time-aware Kalman filter that estimates latent item states under irregular interaction intervals. Posterior covariance from the Kalman filter serves as an uncertainty signal to calibrate semantic memory retrieval and to perform adaptive fusion of static (content) and temporal (interaction) representations.
AI.result: Experiments on Amazon Video Games and MovieLens-32M under time-aware and item cold-start protocols with sampled candidate ranking show NMKFR achieves the strongest results across comparisons, ablations, diagnostics, and robustness analyses. The model exhibits bounded uncertainty-related internal behavior.
AI.conclusion: Posterior-covariance-guided semantic-temporal fusion is empirically effective for item cold-start recommendation under the evaluated offline settings. The findings support using Kalman-based uncertainty as a gating mechanism between static content and temporal interaction signals.

title: Exploring Structures in Physics Problems: Can AI Agents Discover Statistical Mechanical Mappings?
comment: Accepted to the AID-Wild workshop at CAIS 2026
summary: An important skill in theoretical physics is to recognize when a new problem can be transformed into a known model. We study this skill as an AI-agent task: can LLM-based agents discover statistical mechanical mappings from a raw partition function to a tractable representation? To probe this question, we introduce StatMechBench-v0, a benchmark of six Ising-type problems covering transfer-matrix methods, gauge-removable disorder, and planar/Pfaffian structure. We evaluate a simple propose-verify-revise agent across multiple LLMs and problem phrasings. The results show that numerical feedback often helps agents repair code and recover correct partition functions. However, agents can also pass the numerical checks while misidentifying the underlying tractable class or understating computational complexity. This both reveals limitations in current LLM reasoning and calls for a verification stack that goes beyond numerical agreement, incorporating, for example, symbolic checks and structural invariants. Our study provides an early evaluation and design directions for AI agents aimed at structural discovery in theoretical physics.

AI.tldr: Evaluates whether LLM-based AI agents can discover statistical mechanical mappings from raw partition functions to tractable representations using a benchmark of six Ising-type problems, finding that numerical feedback helps but agents often misidentify underlying tractable classes despite passing numerical checks.
AI.motivation: To probe whether LLM-based agents can perform structural discovery in theoretical physics — specifically, recognizing when a new statistical mechanics problem maps onto a known tractable model — a skill considered essential for theoretical physicists.
AI.method: Introduces StatMechBench-v0, a benchmark of six Ising-type problems spanning transfer-matrix methods, gauge-removable disorder, and planar/Pfaffian structure. A propose-verify-revise agent architecture is evaluated across multiple LLMs and problem phrasings, using numerical feedback to iteratively refine solutions.
AI.result: Numerical feedback helps agents repair code and recover correct partition functions, but agents frequently pass numerical checks while misidentifying the underlying tractable class or underestimating computational complexity. This exposes limitations in current LLM reasoning capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM agents are not yet reliable for structural discovery in theoretical physics; a verification stack combining numerical agreement with symbolic checks and structural invariants is needed. The benchmark provides a foundation for developing AI agents capable of genuine structural insight.

title: A Controlled Candidate-Set Benchmark for Offline Satellite-Security Plan Decomposition
summary: Some security-development settings require local models that map an objective to an ordered, checkable plan. We present a low-rank decomposition adapter and release a case-disjoint corpus with 24 authored decompositions and 83 derived next-step examples across 24 satellite-security cases. To prevent reference-plan leakage, prompts contain one objective and eight shuffled SPARTA candidates. The evaluation candidate sets are constructed with oracle inclusion of every reference technique, so this study measures selection from a controlled set, not retrieval. On six fixed cases and five decoding seeds, mean scores vary across adapters and prompted Qwen2.5 baselines; a separate greedy check over three adapter training seeds shows non-negligible training variance. A 24-fold greedy leave-one-case-out control at the two compact sizes likewise shows tradeoffs: at 1.5B, adapter precision is 0.583 against 0.480 for two-shot prompting, while recall is 0.586 against 0.660. Case-resampling intervals for adapter precision relative to the strongest prompted baseline cross zero at 1.5B and 7B. The adapter is also substantially more format-compliant, which prevents attributing all score differences to selection. Autoregressive next-step accuracy is 0.08, 0.06, and 0.29 at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 7B. We therefore offer the formulation, leakage-controlled dataset, reproducibility package, and descriptive analysis as a proof of concept, not evidence of a reliable stand-alone decomposition system or a general adapter advantage. A separate diagnostic tests contract reuse.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a low-rank decomposition adapter for mapping security objectives to ordered, checkable plans, evaluated on a leakage-controlled corpus of 24 satellite-security cases. The adapter shows precision gains over prompted baselines at 1.5B scale (0.583 vs 0.480) but lower recall (0.586 vs 0.660), with case-resampling intervals crossing zero at both 1.5B and 7B, indicating no reliable advantage. Next-step autoregressive accuracy is poor across scales. The work is presented as a proof of concept, not a production-ready system.
AI.motivation: Security-development settings require local models that can map an abstract objective to an ordered, checkable plan (a decomposition). The authors aim to explore whether a lightweight adapter can improve plan selection from a controlled candidate set while preventing reference-plan leakage that would inflate results.
AI.method: A low-rank decomposition adapter is trained on a case-disjoint corpus (24 authored decompositions, 83 derived next-step examples). Evaluation uses prompts containing one objective and eight shuffled SPARTA candidates, with oracle inclusion of every reference technique ensuring selection-from-set measurement rather than retrieval. Experiments span three adapter training seeds, fixed cases, decoding seeds, 24-fold leave-one-case-out control, and scales of 0.5B, 1.5B, and 7B parameters. A separate diagnostic tests contract reuse.
AI.result: At 1.5B, adapter precision is 0.583 vs. 0.480 for two-shot prompting; recall is 0.586 vs. 0.660. Case-resampling intervals for adapter precision relative to the strongest prompted baseline cross zero at both 1.5B and 7B, indicating no statistically reliable advantage. Autoregressive next-step accuracy is 0.08 (0.5B), 0.06 (1.5B), and 0.29 (7B). The adapter is substantially more format-compliant. Training variance across seeds is non-negligible.
AI.conclusion: The work is explicitly a proof of concept, not evidence of a reliable stand-alone decomposition system or a general adapter advantage. The authors contribute the formulation, leakage-controlled dataset, reproducibility package, and descriptive analysis, while acknowledging limitations in recall, next-step generation, and statistical reliability of precision gains.

title: Early Verdicts, Better Budgets: Sequential Adaptive Rollout Allocation for Compute-Efficient RLVR
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is bottlenecked by rollout generation, yet many sampled prompts produce saturated groups (all responses correct or all incorrect) whose zero reward variance yields no policy-gradient signal. Existing remedies either oversample a larger candidate pool and discard saturated prompts (dynamic sampling), paying heavy extra rollouts, or predict prompt difficulty before sampling, which is fragile under a shifting policy. We observe that a group's effectiveness is usually decided early, within the first few of its rollouts, so spending a full group on an already-decided prompt is wasteful. We cast per-step rollout collection as a budget-constrained sequential allocation (optimal stopping) problem and introduce SARA (Sequential Adaptive Rollout Allocation). SARA maintains a Beta posterior over each prompt's success rate, evaluates a closed-form predictor of group effectiveness, and applies a two-threshold, SPRT-style rule that commits effective groups, abandons saturated ones after a short probe, and reallocates the freed budget to fresh prompts, without any extra prediction rollouts. We prove abandonment reliability, expected rollout savings, fixed-budget yield dominance, and a link between effective-group yield and the GRPO gradient norm. On mathematical reasoning and planning with 1.5B/3B models on a single GPU, SARA matches DPS (both below the DS oracle) while using 22% fewer rollouts than DS; composing SARA with DPS yields the best accuracy, slightly above DS, at 67% fewer rollouts (near-uniform cost).

AI.tldr: SARA formulates RLVR rollout collection as an optimal stopping problem, using a Beta posterior and SPRT-style two-threshold rule to early-commit effective prompt groups and early-abandon saturated ones, reallocating budget to fresh prompts. It matches or exceeds dynamic sampling baselines while using 22–67% fewer rollouts.
AI.motivation: RLVR training suffers from saturated prompt groups (all-correct or all-incorrect responses) that yield zero reward variance and thus zero policy-gradient signal. Existing solutions either waste rollouts via oversampling (dynamic sampling) or rely on fragile difficulty prediction under a shifting policy. The key insight is that a group's effectiveness is typically evident after only a few rollouts, making full-group sampling wasteful.
AI.method: SARA casts per-step rollout collection as a budget-constrained sequential allocation (optimal stopping) problem. It maintains a Beta posterior over each prompt's success rate, computes a closed-form predictor of group effectiveness (expected reward variance), and applies a two-threshold SPRT-style rule: commits groups likely to be effective, abandons saturated groups after a short probe, and reallocates freed budget to fresh prompts — all without extra prediction rollouts. The authors also prove abandonment reliability, expected rollout savings, fixed-budget yield dominance, and establish a link between effective-group yield and the GRPO gradient norm.
AI.result: On mathematical reasoning and planning tasks with 1.5B and 3B models on a single GPU, SARA matches DPS (dynamic per-sample) performance while using 22% fewer rollouts than DS. Composing SARA with DPS achieves the best accuracy, slightly exceeding the DS oracle, at 67% fewer rollouts (near-uniform cost).
AI.conclusion: SARA provides a principled, low-overhead solution to the saturated-group problem in RLVR, delivering accuracy on par with or exceeding dynamic sampling while drastically reducing rollout cost through early stopping and budget reallocation.

title: Multi-Agent Debate Strategies: Survey, Taxonomy, and Challenges
comment: Under review at ACM Computing Surveys
summary: Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) is a promising paradigm for improving the accuracy and robustness of Large Language Model (LLM)-based agentic systems. It enables multiple agents to exchange arguments, critique each other's outputs, and iteratively converge towards a solution. However, research remains fragmented, with inconsistent terminology and no rigorous synthesis of MAD design dimensions. We present a systematic literature review characterizing 141 primary studies on MAD. We derive a three-dimensional taxonomy covering debate participants, the interaction mechanisms structuring the exchange, and the agreement protocols governing debate resolution, supported by formal notations to render MAD configurations. Our analysis reveals that the field has implicitly converged on a narrow design pattern - static, fully connected topologies, verbatim exchange, short-term memory and voting resolution strategies - adopted by convention rather than systematic comparison, while promising alternatives remain marginal. Because any MAD setting reflects roughly a dozen interacting design decisions, cross-study comparison is unreliable when these are left implicit. We position the taxonomy as a descriptive map of the research landscape, a framework for controlled benchmarking, and potentially as a schema for machine-readable MAD specifications. As future work, we propose formalizing it into an executable specification, enabling cost-aware benchmarking and automated tuning of debate configurations.

AI.tldr: A systematic review of 141 studies on Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) reveals the field has implicitly converged on a narrow, convention-driven design pattern. The authors propose a three-dimensional taxonomy (participants, interaction mechanisms, agreement protocols) with formal notations to map the landscape, enable controlled benchmarking, and support machine-readable MAD specifications.
AI.motivation: Research on Multi-Agent Debate for LLM-based systems is fragmented, with inconsistent terminology and no rigorous synthesis of design dimensions, making cross-study comparison unreliable due to implicit, interacting design decisions.
AI.method: The authors conducted a systematic literature review of 141 primary studies on MAD, deriving a three-dimensional taxonomy (debate participants, interaction mechanisms, agreement protocols) supplemented with formal notations to characterize MAD configurations.
AI.result: The field has converged on a narrow design pattern — static, fully connected topologies, verbatim exchange, short-term memory, and voting resolution — adopted by convention rather than systematic comparison, while promising alternatives remain underexplored.
AI.conclusion: The proposed taxonomy serves as a descriptive map, a benchmarking framework, and a potential schema for machine-readable MAD specifications. Future work includes formalizing it into an executable specification for cost-aware benchmarking and automated tuning of debate configurations.

title: Pragmatic Reasoning in Design
comment: Accepted with oral presentation at CogSci 2026
summary: People can often understand and use novel artifacts after only a few interactions, suggesting that design choices communicate underlying affordances and causal structure. We propose a formal account of this process by framing cooperative, user-centered design as a cooperative game in which the user is the principal and the designer is an assistant. Inspired by prior work on pragmatic communication (e.g. RSA), our model treats a designer's design decisions as communicative signals and predicts user judgments via recursive mentalizing: designers make design decisions to trade off informativeness about the artifact with efficiency, and users infer the true model of the artifact by inverting this cooperative designer model. We evaluate the model in a design game where designers place visually identical keys on trays to help a user infer which keys unlock which doors in grid-world layouts. We find that pragmatic designer and user models better match human judgments than non-mentalizing literal baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper models user-centered design as a cooperative game where designers communicate affordances through design choices, using recursive mentalizing (inspired by RSA). Users infer artifact function by reasoning about the designer's communicative intent, and the pragmatic model outperforms literal baselines in predicting human judgments.
AI.motivation: Humans rapidly infer how novel artifacts work from minimal interactions, suggesting that design choices communicate causal structure and affordances. However, there is no formal computational account of how designers' choices serve as communicative signals and how users interpret them through mentalizing about the designer's intent.
AI.method: The authors frame user-centered design as a cooperative game (principal-agent: user as principal, designer as assistant) and develop a model inspired by Rational Speech Act (RSA) pragmatics. Designers optimize a trade-off between informativeness about the artifact's true model and efficiency; users invert this model via recursive Bayesian inference to recover the artifact's causal structure. The model is evaluated in a design game where designers place identical keys on trays to communicate which keys unlock which doors in grid-world layouts.
AI.result: The pragmatic designer and user models (incorporating recursive mentalizing) better match human judgments compared to non-mentalizing literal baselines, demonstrating that human design interpretation relies on reasoning about communicative intent.
AI.conclusion: Design can be fruitfully understood as a form of pragmatic communication, where recursive social reasoning between designer and user explains how people rapidly infer artifact function from sparse design cues. This framework bridges user-centered design with computational pragmatics.

title: Characterizing Human-Likeness in AI Generated Poetry: A Zero-shot Classification Study
summary: With the advancement of AI technologies, Generative AI (GenAI) and human written text have become nearly indistinguishable. Additionally, the global standardization of AI chatbots made academic malpractice more frequent. Furthermore, existing research indicates GenAI poems are the most difficult to distinguish even without any modification thus, GenAI poems are naturally deemed human-like by modern detectors. However, the objectivity of such dissertations needs to be verified against modern detection tools but the subjectivity of poetry and the black-box nature of the modern LLMs (Large Language Models) architectures made verification of such work quite complicated. Hence, the main objective of the research is to deduce the attributes of English poetry that contribute classification and misclassification of both human and AI poems and provide corroborating or contradicting evidence to the poetry distinguishability claim. For such characterizations, we propose a Zero-shot detection pipeline with a dataset consisting of both human and AI poems to verify the distinguishability of human and AI creation and extract the aforementioned crucial attributes for accurate classification. Extraction of such attributes provides benefits in two ways: firstly, it reduces the margin of training needed as only the poems based on misclassifying attributes need to be trained and fine tuned and finally provides a critical insight to the GenAI detection dilemma to strengthen the modern detection pipelines.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a zero-shot detection pipeline to identify distinguishing attributes between human-written and AI-generated English poetry, aiming to verify claims about poetry distinguishability and identify which features contribute to misclassification.
AI.motivation: GenAI text is increasingly indistinguishable from human writing, and poems are reportedly the hardest to detect. Existing claims about poetry distinguishability need objective verification, but the subjectivity of poetry and the black-box nature of LLMs complicate this. The authors aim to systematically characterize which poetic attributes drive correct classification versus misclassification.
AI.method: A zero-shot detection pipeline is employed on a curated dataset of both human and AI-generated poems. The pipeline extracts key linguistic and stylistic attributes that contribute to classification decisions, identifying which features lead to misclassification without requiring task-specific training data.
AI.result: The extracted attributes reveal which poetic characteristics cause modern detectors to confuse human and AI poetry. This characterization provides evidence to either corroborate or contradict the prevailing claim that AI-generated poems are uniquely difficult to distinguish from human-written ones.
AI.conclusion: Identifying misclassification-driving attributes reduces training requirements (only problematic poems need fine-tuning) and offers critical insight into the GenAI detection dilemma. This attribute-focused approach can strengthen modern detection pipelines by targeting the features that cause confusion.

title: Multi-Decoder OneRec: Controllable Generative Retrieval for Multi-Objective Industrial Recommendation
summary: Industrial recommender systems build candidate pools by assigning explicit quotas to objective-specific retrieval routes. This design offers quota control but increasingly fragments modeling, training, and serving as the route set grows. Semantic-ID-based generative retrieval provides a unified alternative, yet a single decoder entangles objective policies and limits candidate complementarity. We propose Multi-Decoder OneRec, a controllable framework that combines shared representations, isolated objective adaptation, and coordinated decoding. All objectives share a user-context module and the General Decoder, while each objective adds an isolated, parameter-efficient LoRA expert. During training, exposure-sample next-token prediction (NTP) updates the shared base, target-filtered NTP updates the event-based experts, and Kullback-Leibler (KL)-regularized policy optimization updates the Watch-time expert; gradient routing isolates these updates, and the General Decoder supplies a stop-gradient reference. At inference, explicit route quotas allocate the fixed budget and Multi-Decoder Constrained Beam Search reduces cross-route overlap. We publicly release Kwai26, a large-scale multi-objective benchmark with 1.31 billion raw item-level records, 31.85 million Item-ID entries, and 25.03 million items with valid Semantic IDs, together with predefined splits and an evaluation protocol. Under the same 512-item retrieval budget, Multi-Decoder OneRec improves over the single-decoder OneRec baseline by 1.69%-5.62% across four Recall@512 metrics. In a production A/B test, it yields relative gains of 0.37% in app usage time per device, 0.19% in Day-7 retained users, 0.19% in devices with at least one share, and 2.09% in new-content Cold-Start. These results show that generative retrieval can combine shared modeling with objective-specific control and complementary candidate generation.

AI.tldr: Multi-Decoder OneRec proposes a controllable generative retrieval framework for industrial recommender systems that uses shared representations with isolated, parameter-efficient LoRA experts per objective, coordinated via constrained beam search, achieving significant improvements in recall, user engagement, and cold-start performance.
AI.motivation: Traditional industrial recommenders use explicit quota-based retrieval routes per objective, which fragments modeling as objectives grow. Semantic-ID generative retrieval unifies this but entangles objective policies in a single decoder, limiting candidate complementarity. The authors seek to combine the benefits of unified modeling with objective-specific control.
AI.method: The framework consists of: (1) a shared user-context module and General Decoder across all objectives; (2) isolated LoRA experts per objective for parameter-efficient adaptation; (3) a multi-phase training strategy with exposure-sample NTP for shared base, target-filtered NTP for event-based experts, and KL-regularized policy optimization for the Watch-time expert, with gradient routing for isolation; (4) Multi-Decoder Constrained Beam Search at inference to allocate fixed budget per route quota and reduce cross-route overlap. They also release Kwai26, a large-scale benchmark with 1.31B records.
AI.result: Under a 512-item retrieval budget, Multi-Decoder OneRec outperforms the single-decoder OneRec baseline by 1.69%-5.62% across four Recall@512 metrics. In production A/B testing, it achieved relative gains of 0.37% in app usage time, 0.19% in Day-7 retention, 0.19% in sharing devices, and 2.09% in cold-start content discovery.
AI.conclusion: Generative retrieval can successfully unify shared modeling with objective-specific control and complementary candidate generation, offering a practical path beyond fragmented multi-route retrieval architectures.

title: CaM-Wolf: Causal-Aware Multimodal Agents for Social Deduction Games
summary: Social deduction games (SDGs) such as Werewolf have become challenging testbeds for AI agents. These games require complex social skills such as reasoning, deception, and collaboration. While recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have driven significant progress in SDG agents, current approaches are predominantly text-based, overlooking the multimodal nature that is fundamental to human social interaction. To bridge this gap, we introduce CaM-Wolf, the first SDG agent that integrates multimodal perception and generation. CaM-Wolf processes video inputs from other players, employs a causal-aware Reasoner trained via reinforcement learning to establish logical chains between observable behaviors and hidden roles, and presents itself through an animated avatar. Our experiments and user study show that CaM-Wolf achieves superior agent gameplay performance and enhances the quality of human-AI interaction. This work represents a significant advancement towards creating more human-like AI agents capable of participating in nuanced social dynamics. Our code is available at https://3dagentworld.github.io/avatar_wolf.

AI.tldr: CaM-Wolf introduces the first multimodal social deduction game agent that integrates video perception, causal-aware reasoning via reinforcement learning, and animated avatar presentation, achieving superior gameplay and human-AI interaction quality.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based social deduction game agents are text-only, ignoring the multimodal nature of human social interaction (facial expressions, gestures, voice). There is a need for agents that can perceive and generate multimodal signals to enable more natural social dynamics.
AI.method: CaM-Wolf processes video inputs from other players and uses a causal-aware Reasoner trained via reinforcement learning to establish logical chains linking observable behaviors to hidden roles. The agent presents itself through an animated avatar, enabling multimodal perception and generation in a unified framework.
AI.result: Experiments and user studies demonstrate that CaM-Wolf achieves superior agent gameplay performance compared to baselines and significantly enhances the quality of human-AI interaction in social deduction game settings.
AI.conclusion: CaM-Wolf represents a significant step toward more human-like AI agents capable of nuanced social dynamics by bridging the multimodal gap in social deduction games.

title: QUIC-TRIP: A Triple-Redundant Journey Toward Secure Substation Communications
summary: Modern power systems rely on real-time substation communication protocols, such as the Routable Generic Object-Oriented Substation Event (R-GOOSE), for critical control and protection functions. However, these protocols often lack built-in security features and prioritize availability over confidentiality and integrity, making them susceptible to false data injection and denial-of-service attacks. This vulnerability is exacerbated when communications are transmitted over wide-area or public networks. Addressing these cyber threats is essential to comply with current security mandates, including the DOE's defense-in-depth and zero-trust guidelines. This paper introduces QUIC-TRIP, a transparent security methodology for low-latency IP-based industrial communications. By operating at the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) Transport Layer (Layer 4), the solution encapsulates and protects data flows without affecting the operation of existing protocol endpoints. Baseline echo Round-Trip Time (RTT) results over a Frankfurt-Amsterdam communication path show that the underlying transport-layer proxy used by QUIC-TRIP achieves a lower average RTT than OpenVPN and only 2.88% higher average RTT than integrated DTLS 1.2, even with DTLS session reuse. We evaluate the resilience of QUIC-TRIP multipath communication under DoS flooding by securing R-GOOSE communications. In these tests, traffic is transparently delivered through three different paths, and QUIC-TRIP forwards the earliest-arriving duplicate while discarding later copies. The framework provides a triple-redundant defense scheme with a measured communication overhead of 32.18% per enabled proxied path, offering a bounded trade-off between resilience and bandwidth cost for time-critical grid operations.

AI.tldr: QUIC-TRIP is a Transport Layer security framework that transparently protects industrial control protocols like R-GOOSE without modifying endpoints. It offers triple-redundant multipath communication against DoS attacks with only 32.18% overhead per path, and achieves near-DTLS latency performance while outperforming OpenVPN.
AI.motivation: Modern power grid substation protocols (e.g., R-GOOSE) lack built-in security and prioritize availability, leaving them vulnerable to false data injection and DoS attacks—especially over wide-area/public networks. Compliance with DOE defense-in-depth and zero-trust mandates requires a solution that adds security without disrupting existing protocol endpoints.
AI.method: QUIC-TRIP operates at OSI Layer 4 (Transport), transparently encapsulating and protecting data flows via a proxy architecture. It leverages QUIC's native features: multipath communication for redundant delivery across three paths, duplicate detection (forwarding the earliest-arriving copy, discarding later ones), and built-in encryption. The system requires no changes to existing R-GOOSE endpoints.
AI.result: Baseline RTT tests over a Frankfurt-Amsterdam path showed the QUIC-TRIP proxy achieved lower average RTT than OpenVPN and only 2.88% higher than integrated DTLS 1.2 (even with DTLS session reuse). Under DoS flooding, the triple-redundant multipath scheme successfully delivered R-GOOSE traffic, with measured communication overhead of 32.18% per enabled proxied path.
AI.conclusion: QUIC-TRIP provides a practical, transparent security retrofit for time-critical industrial communications, offering a bounded trade-off between resilience (via multipath redundancy) and bandwidth cost. It meets modern grid security mandates without sacrificing the low-latency requirements of protection and control functions.

title: Top-$k$ Pareto Bandits: Hypervolume Regret for Multi-Objective Slate Selection
summary: We consider a stochastic multi-objective bandit problem where, at each round, the agent selects a slate of $k$ arms and observes their $d$-dimensional reward vectors under semi-bandit feedback. We do not aim at identifying a single optimal arm; instead, we consider the problem of maintaining a small set of actions that jointly approximate the Pareto frontier. We formalize this objective through the dominated hypervolume induced by the selected subset of arms, and define an $α$-approximate hypervolume regret with respect to the best size-$k$ subset achievable in hindsight, where $α= 1 - 1/e$ reflects the approximation guarantee of greedy maximization for monotone submodular functions. To address this problem, we introduce \textit{THV-UCB}, an optimistic algorithm that selects arms greedily based on optimistic estimates of their marginal hypervolume contributions. We establish a gap-free regret bound $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{nkT})$ that holds on every instance, together with a gap-dependent bound $\tilde{O}(nk^{2.5}/Δ_{\min})$ that becomes polylogarithmic in $T$ once the arms are sufficiently well separated. Our results provide theoretical support for using small subsets to approximate Pareto fronts in various multi-objective applications.

AI.tldr: This paper studies stochastic multi-objective bandits where an agent selects k arms per round and aims to maintain a small subset whose reward vectors approximate the Pareto frontier, measured by dominated hypervolume. The authors propose THV-UCB, an optimistic greedy algorithm, and prove both gap-free and gap-dependent regret bounds.
AI.motivation: In many real-world multi-objective decision problems (e.g., recommendation, resource allocation), presenting a small, diverse set of options approximating the Pareto frontier is more practical than identifying a single optimal arm. Existing bandit literature focuses heavily on single-arm selection, leaving a gap in theoretically grounded methods for maintaining small approximate Pareto sets under bandit feedback.
AI.method: The authors formalize the goal using α-approximate hypervolume regret, where α = 1 - 1/e reflects the submodularity of the hypervolume indicator. They propose THV-UCB (Total HyperVolume UCB), which at each round constructs optimistic reward estimates via confidence bounds, then greedily selects k arms maximizing marginal hypervolume contributions. The analysis decomposes regret into terms arising from UCB estimation error and the greedy approximation gap for monotone submodular maximization.
AI.result: Two regret bounds are established: (1) a gap-free bound of Õ(d√(nkT)) holding on every instance, and (2) a gap-dependent bound of Õ(nk²·⁵/Δ_min) that becomes polylogarithmic in T when arms are well-separated, where Δ_min is the minimum suboptimality gap among arms relevant to the Pareto frontier.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides theoretical justification for using greedy subset selection to approximate Pareto fronts in bandit settings. The near-optimal regret guarantees demonstrate that small, adaptively chosen subsets can effectively represent multi-objective trade-offs, with practical implications for multi-objective recommendation and decision-support systems.

title: Model-Driven Requirements Configuration with Three-Valued Uncertainty Scoring
summary:
Context: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer natural-language flexibility for automated requirements elicitation but frequently generate structurally invalid requirements and logical inconsistencies, lacking formal correctness guarantees.
  Objectives: This study aims to eliminate logical inconsistencies and enforce structural conformance in LLM-generated requirements while quantifying the LLM's pre-validation decision uncertainty within a formal domain model.
  Methods: We present a neuro-symbolic multi-agent architecture that operationalizes the Object-Oriented Method for Requirements Authoring and Management (OOMRAM) lattice. The LLM acts as a non-deterministic heuristic for lattice traversal, while a deterministic symbolic validator enforces all structural constraints. We introduce a three-valued (T, I, F) -- Truth, Indeterminacy, Falsity -- framework to classify and score the LLM's requirement decisions before and after validation.
  Results: Evaluated across 37 natural-language project visions in eleven application families, the system completely eliminated structural inconsistencies in 35 out of 37 cases (94.6%), with the remaining two containing only 6 unresolved structural errors (0.39% of decisions) due to iteration limits. Three-valued analysis revealed that 24.7% of all decisions are indeterminate -- structurally valid but discretionary choices not explicitly mandated by the stakeholder.
  Conclusion: Offloading structural integrity to a deterministic symbolic layer successfully guarantees structural conformance, while the three-valued classification provides a formal way to measure neural uncertainty, facilitating safe LLM deployment in formal requirements engineering.

AI.tldr: A neuro-symbolic multi-agent system using an OOMRAM lattice and three-valued logic (Truth, Indeterminacy, Falsity) eliminates structural inconsistencies in LLM-generated requirements with 94.6% success, while quantifying neural uncertainty—24.7% of decisions are indeterminate discretionary choices.
AI.motivation: LLMs offer natural-language flexibility for requirements elicitation but suffer from two critical failures: structurally invalid outputs and logical inconsistencies, both lacking formal correctness guarantees. This prevents safe deployment of LLMs in formal requirements engineering contexts where structural conformance is non-negotiable.
AI.method: A neuro-symbolic multi-agent architecture that operationalizes the Object-Oriented Method for Requirements Authoring and Management (OOMRAM) lattice. The LLM serves as a non-deterministic heuristic for traversing the lattice, while a deterministic symbolic validator enforces all structural constraints. A novel three-valued (T, I, F — Truth, Indeterminacy, Falsity) classification framework scores the LLM's pre- and post-validation requirement decisions, capturing structural validity and decision certainty.
AI.result: Across 37 natural-language project visions in 11 application families: structural inconsistencies were completely eliminated in 35/37 cases (94.6%); the remaining two cases had only 6 unresolved structural errors (0.39% of decisions) due to iteration limits. Three-valued analysis showed 24.7% of all decisions are indeterminate—structurally valid but discretionary choices not explicitly stakeholder-mandated.
AI.conclusion: Offloading structural integrity to a deterministic symbolic layer successfully guarantees structural conformance in LLM-generated requirements. The three-valued classification framework provides a formal mechanism to measure neural uncertainty, enabling safer LLM deployment in formal requirements engineering by distinguishing mandatory constraints from discretionary choices.

title: Designing Needs- and Attention-Aware AI Learning Tools for Engineering Education: Insights from Psychological Outcomes
comment: Manuscript under review. 32 pages, 2 figures, and 14 tables
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming higher education, but its benefits can vary depending on where, how, and how often it supports learning. While prior research emphasizes cognitive and academic outcomes, this study examines how AI chatbots support the psychological needs and motivational states of engineering students. A survey of college engineering students (n = 206) examined perceived effects of AI chatbots on autonomy, relatedness, and relief from competence frustration. Structural equation modeling with latent interaction effects examined how baseline autonomy, competence frustration, relatedness, and personal agency contributed to perceived AI outcomes. Results indicate that students perceived that AI provided the greatest benefits as relief from competence frustration, smaller benefits for autonomy, and the weakest benefits for relatedness. Baseline motivational states mattered more than demographic factors, and inattention moderated how baseline competence frustration and autonomy related to perceived AI-related benefits. These results offer insights into formulating design principles for engineering-specific AI-based tools.

AI.tldr: Engineering students perceive AI chatbots as most helpful for alleviating competence frustration, moderately for autonomy, and least for relatedness. Baseline motivational states and inattention moderate these perceived benefits, informing design principles for engineering-specific AI tools.
AI.motivation: While prior AI in education research focuses on cognitive and academic outcomes, this study addresses a gap by examining how AI chatbots support students' psychological needs and motivational states—specifically autonomy, relatedness, and competence frustration relief—grounded in Self-Determination Theory.
AI.method: Survey of 206 college engineering students assessing perceived effects of AI chatbots on autonomy, relatedness, and competence frustration relief. Structural equation modeling (SEM) with latent interaction effects was used to examine how baseline autonomy, competence frustration, relatedness, and personal agency predicted perceived AI outcomes, with inattention tested as a moderator.
AI.result: Students perceived the greatest AI benefit as relief from competence frustration, smaller benefits for autonomy, and weakest for relatedness. Baseline motivational states were stronger predictors than demographic factors.
