Inattention significantly moderated the relationships between baseline competence frustration/autonomy and perceived AI benefits.
AI.conclusion: AI chatbots serve primarily as a compensatory tool for competence-related struggles rather than for fostering social connection. Design principles for engineering-specific AI tools should account for students' baseline motivational profiles and attentional characteristics.

title: Steering Instruction Hierarchies at Inference Time
comment: Published as a conference paper at COLM '26; the first two authors contributed equally to the work. 24 pages, 9 figures
summary: Instruction hierarchies are a core safety assumption of language model deployment: higher priority inputs, such as system prompts, should override conflicting lower priority inputs from users or tools. Yet frontier LLMs often violate this hierarchy. We introduce V-Steer, a training-free inference time method that restores privileged influence by editing cached value vectors at prompt positions. Using direct logit attribution on the first next token prediction, V-Steer identifies heads where lower priority spans dominate privileged ones, then boosts privileged spans and suppresses conflicting lower priority spans through in-place multiplicative edits to cached V tensors. Since the method acts only on cached values, it remains compatible with fused attention backends and adds only a one time prefill overhead. Across models from 7B to 70B, this attribution guided intervention raises primary constraint accuracy from under 18% up to 92% on controlled role conflict benchmarks, and on broader instruction hierarchy evaluations substantially outperforms prompt only baselines while matching or exceeding SoTA training based methods on 3 of 4 scales of LLMs, with negligible decoding-speed overhead. The code is available at https://github.com/cindy2000sh/v-steer.

AI.tldr: V-Steer is a training-free, inference-time method that restores instruction hierarchy in LLMs by editing cached value vectors (V tensors) at specific attention heads. Using direct logit attribution, it identifies where lower-priority spans override privileged ones, then applies multiplicative edits to boost privileged and suppress conflicting lower-priority information. It achieves up to 92% primary constraint accuracy (up from <18%) with negligible speed overhead, matching or exceeding training-based methods.
AI.motivation: Instruction hierarchies (system prompts > user inputs > tool outputs) are critical for safe LLM deployment, but frontier models frequently violate this hierarchy. Existing solutions require expensive training, while training-free prompt-based methods are insufficient. A lightweight, plug-and-play inference-time intervention is needed.
AI.method: V-Steer uses direct logit attribution on the first next-token prediction to identify attention heads where lower-priority token spans dominate privileged ones. It then performs in-place multiplicative edits to cached V (value) tensors at those heads: boosting the privileged span's representation and suppressing conflicting lower-priority spans. This operates solely on KV caches, making it compatible with fused attention backends and incurring only a one-time prefill overhead.
AI.result: On controlled role-conflict benchmarks, V-Steer raises primary constraint accuracy from under 18% to up to 92% across models from 7B to 70B. On broader instruction hierarchy evaluations, it substantially outperforms prompt-only baselines and matches or exceeds state-of-the-art training-based methods on 3 of 4 LLM scales, with negligible decoding-speed overhead.
AI.conclusion: V-Steer demonstrates that targeted, attribution-guided editing of value vectors at inference time can effectively restore instruction hierarchy without retraining, offering a practical safety mechanism compatible with existing inference infrastructure.

title: ASARL: Autonomous Social-Aware Relevance Learning for QQ Search
summary: The rapid growth of online social platforms has transformed communication and information retrieval, giving rise to social search, where queries-titles are typically expressed in informal, community-specific language. While large language models provide strong general-purpose semantic understanding, their effectiveness in social search is constrained by contextual discrepancy, data scarcity, and behavior-driven dynamics. To address these challenges, we propose the Autonomous Social-Aware Relevance Learning (ASARL), a fully automated framework that integrates multi-agent data curation with staged model training. ASARL leverages a collaborative agent system: ReasonAgent generates interpretable relevance labels grounded in social attributes, CriticAgent validates and ensures logical consistency, and GenAgent augments long-tail data through synthetic query-title pairs. Building on the curated dataset, ASARL employs three-stage training: Social Context Training (SCT) to capture social language patterns, Preference-Guided Optimization (PGO) to align model predictions with behavioral signals, and Social Distillation (SD) to transfer these improvements into compact models for efficient deployment. Extensive offline and online experiments on the QQ search platform demonstrate significant improvements in both offline relevance metrics and online user engagement indicators, along with enhanced annotation efficiency. These results validate the effectiveness of combining autonomous, socially grounded data governance with preference-aligned training in practical search systems.

AI.tldr: ASARL is a fully automated framework for social search relevance that combines multi-agent data curation (ReasonAgent, CriticAgent, GenAgent) with a three-stage training pipeline (Social Context Training, Preference-Guided Optimization, Social Distillation) to address informal language, data scarcity, and alignment with user behavior. Validated on QQ search, it improves both offline relevance metrics and online engagement.
AI.motivation: Social search queries use informal, community-specific language that general-purpose LLMs struggle with due to three key challenges: (1) contextual discrepancy between formal training data and social platform language, (2) data scarcity, particularly for long-tail queries, and (3) behavior-driven dynamics where user engagement signals don't align with surface-level semantic relevance. Existing approaches lack automated, socially-aware solutions that address all three simultaneously.
AI.method: ASARL has two core components: (1) A multi-agent data curation system where ReasonAgent generates relevance labels grounded in social attributes, CriticAgent validates logical consistency of these labels, and GenAgent synthesizes query-title pairs to augment long-tail data. (2) A three-stage training pipeline: Social Context Training (SCT) captures social language patterns via pretraining on curated social data; Preference-Guided Optimization (PGO) aligns model predictions with behavioral signals using preference optimization; and Social Distillation (SD) transfers improvements into compact, deployable models via knowledge distillation.
AI.result: Extensive offline and online experiments on the QQ search platform show significant improvements in offline relevance metrics, online user engagement indicators, and annotation efficiency. The framework demonstrates that combining autonomous, socially grounded data governance with preference-aligned training yields practical gains in real-world social search systems.
AI.conclusion: The ASARL framework validates that integrating autonomous multi-agent data curation with staged, socially-aware training effectively addresses the unique challenges of social search. The approach bridges the gap between general-purpose semantic models and community-specific search needs, offering both improved relevance and deployment efficiency.

title: CG-World: A Large-Scale World-State Dataset and Protocol for World Models
summary: World models must learn the joint dynamics of states, actions, events, and observations, yet existing video, robotics, and simulation datasets usually capture only part of this structure. We introduce CG-World, a large-scale world-state dataset and protocol derived from industrial computer graphics production pipelines. CG-World explicitly records intermediate states, including multimodal semantics, spatial structure, skeletal and controller states, motion curves, camera and lighting parameters, physics caches, contact events, and multi-pass renderings. CG-World v1 contains approximately 850,000 temporally aligned segments of 1-5 seconds. It separates latent states, observations, relations, events, and branch metadata, and organizes them into unified spatiotemporal samples. To support intervention learning and counterfactual reasoning, CG-World defines a branch lineage covering factual trajectories, observation interventions, action interventions, mechanism interventions, and strict counterfactual branches, with intervention targets, invariants, and alternative outcomes explicitly recorded. We evaluate the dataset on geometry-conditioned video generation, action prediction, and closed-loop vision-language-action policy transfer. Results show that CG-World provides reusable structured supervision for controlled generation, action modeling, and embodied policy transfer. We plan to expand CG-World through continued data collection and community collaboration toward a shared data infrastructure for world models, Physical AI, and embodied intelligence.

AI.tldr: CG-World is a large-scale dataset (~850K segments) derived from CGI production pipelines that explicitly captures intermediate world states—geometry, skeletal data, physics, events, and multi-pass renderings—along with counterfactual intervention branches, enabling structured supervision for world models, controlled generation, and embodied policy transfer.
AI.motivation: Existing datasets for world models (video, robotics, simulation) capture only partial structure of the joint dynamics among states, actions, events, and observations. There is no large-scale dataset that explicitly records the full intermediate state chain with intervention and counterfactual branches, limiting progress in controlled generation, causal reasoning, and embodied AI.
AI.method: The authors leverage industrial computer graphics production pipelines to construct CG-World, a dataset that records comprehensive intermediate states (multimodal semantics, spatial structure, skeletal/controller states, motion curves, camera/lighting parameters, physics caches, contact events, multi-pass renderings) as temporally aligned segments of 1–5 seconds. The dataset is organized into latent states, observations, relations, events, and branch metadata. A branch lineage is defined with five trajectory types: factual, observation interventions, action interventions, mechanism interventions, and strict counterfactual branches, each with explicit intervention targets, invariants, and alternative outcomes.
AI.result: Evaluation on geometry-conditioned video generation, action prediction, and closed-loop vision-language-action policy transfer demonstrates that CG-World provides reusable structured supervision, improving controlled generation, action modeling, and embodied policy transfer performance.
AI.conclusion: CG-World fills a critical gap in structured world-state data and shows strong utility across multiple downstream tasks. The authors plan to expand the dataset through continued collection and community collaboration, aiming to establish a shared data infrastructure for world models, Physical AI, and embodied intelligence.

title: Recover, Decode, Reguard: Guard-Agnostic Defense Amplification againstEncoded VLM Jailbreaks
summary: Safety classifiers ("guards") are the dominant black-box defense for vision-language models, yet they judge an input's surface form, not its meaning: a harmful request re-encoded as set theory, formal logic, a rare language, code, or an image of text slips past a guard that would block it in plain language -- the decode gap. The natural fix is a guard-agnostic recover-and-decode amplifier that transcribes image content and restates encoded text into its plain payload before the guard, so any off-the-shelf classifier can screen the true request. We build this amplifier and evaluate it against the attacker's best case: an ensemble of eleven attacks, scoring a behavior as broken if any succeeds (best-of-suite, following AutoAttack) -- rarely reported for jailbreak defenses, yet ~3.5x the per-attack mean. This exposes our central finding: an empirical safety-utility ceiling for the non-iterative recovery defenses we evaluate, across five guards and two target VLMs. The amplifier only partly closes the gap -- the undefended ensemble breaks 89-91% of behaviors, and the best guard-plus-amplifier still leaves 63-65% -- and its gain over the guard alone is significant in only four of ten guard-target pairs. It is guard-agnostic at the interface, but not uniformly so in effect. A modular reguard layer closes much of the residual, yet drives benign over-refusal to 81-92% for well-calibrated guards; the one laxer guard that stays usable never reaches deployable safety (48% ensemble ASR). No configuration we evaluate reaches both low attack-success and low over-refusal, for the pipeline we study and for representation-shifting attacks -- encodings and cross-modal renders that leave a legible payload, not pixel- or embedding-space attacks. We contribute the amplifier, an ensemble evaluation that makes the trade-off visible, and a map of where recovery-based VLM defense works and where it does not.

AI.tldr: Safety classifiers for vision-language models suffer from a "decode gap" where harmful requests encoded in non-plain-language forms (code, logic, rare languages, images of text) bypass detection. The authors build a recover-and-decode amplifier to extract the plain-text payload before the guard, but find it only partially closes the gap. An ensemble evaluation reveals a persistent safety-utility ceiling: no configuration achieves both low attack success and low benign over-refusal, mapping where recovery-based defenses succeed and fail.
AI.motivation: Existing black-box safety classifiers (guards) for vision-language models operate on surface form rather than semantic meaning, creating a "decode gap": harmful content re-encoded as formal logic, code, rare languages, or images of text easily evades detection. The motivation is to characterize and attempt to close this gap with a guard-agnostic recovery mechanism, while rigorously evaluating whether the approach can achieve practical safety.
AI.method: The authors build a recover-and-decode amplifier that transcribes image content and restates encoded text into plain language before passing it to an off-the-shelf safety guard. They evaluate using an ensemble of eleven attacks under a best-of-suite metric (following AutoAttack methodology), where a behavior is considered broken if any single attack succeeds. Evaluation spans five guards, two target VLMs, and includes a modular "reguard" layer. The ensemble metric is ~3.5× the per-attack mean, revealing trade-offs that single-attack evaluations obscure.
AI.result: The undefended ensemble breaks 89–91% of behaviors. The best guard-plus-amplifier configuration still leaves 63–65% attack success. The amplifier's improvement over guard-alone is statistically significant in only 4 of 10 guard–target pairs. Adding a reguard layer reduces residual attacks but drives benign over-refusal to 81–92% for well-calibrated guards. The one laxer guard that remains usable never reaches deployable safety (48% ensemble ASR). No configuration achieves both low attack success and low over-refusal for representation-shifting attacks.
AI.conclusion: There exists an empirical safety-utility ceiling for non-iterative recovery-based defenses against representation-shifting attacks on VLMs. The recover-and-decode amplifier is guard-agnostic at the interface but not uniformly effective in practice. The work contributes the amplifier, an ensemble evaluation methodology that surfaces the trade-off, and a systematic map of where recovery-based VLM defense succeeds and fails.

title: FloDR: An invertible dimensionality reduction method based on a normalising flow
summary: It is common for two-dimensional embeddings of high-dimensional data to be read far beyond what they can support. Distances in and between clusters, the meaning behind empty spaces, and the amount of structure hidden at each point are generally invisible in the output of methods such as t-SNE and UMAP. This is because the information that could support the meaning of these properties is discarded during the optimisation process. Here, we present FloDR, a dimensionality reduction method that embeds data through an invertible normalising flow. While FloDR only uses the first two output coordinates to create a two-dimensional embedding, it retains the remaining coordinates rather than discarding them. In addition to the embedding, an exact inverse and an exact density are properties of a trained mapping, which enable diagnostic visualisations that are computed from the exact inverse of the model that drew the layout rather than from an approximate one. Specifically, we draw two fields, the conditional spread, which measures how much of the original data remains undetermined at each embedding position in input units, and the hidden contrast, which measures how much information about a labelled contrast the two plotted coordinates discard. Both fields are rendered with a prespecified test against a held out portion of the input data and a bootstrap confidence. A field that fails the test is reported as refused.

AI.tldr: FloDR is an invertible normalising flow-based dimensionality reduction method that retains discarded coordinates to compute diagnostic visualisations — conditional spread and hidden contrast — which reveal how much information is lost or hidden in a 2D embedding, with statistical confidence testing.
AI.motivation: Traditional dimensionality reduction methods like t-SNE and UMAP discard information during optimisation, making it impossible to assess how faithfully the 2D embedding represents the high-dimensional data. Users often over-interpret distances, cluster separations, and empty spaces without knowing what information has been lost.
AI.method: FloDR uses an invertible normalising flow to embed high-dimensional data into two dimensions while retaining all remaining coordinates. The method provides an exact inverse mapping and exact density. From these, two diagnostic fields are computed: (1) conditional spread — measuring undetermined data variation at each embedding position in input units; (2) hidden contrast — measuring how much label-discriminative information the 2D embedding discards. Both fields are rendered with bootstrap confidence intervals and tested against a held-out dataset; fields failing the test are marked as refused.
AI.result: FloDR produces a 2D embedding alongside diagnostic visualisations that quantify information loss. The conditional spread and hidden contrast fields, computed via exact inversion, reveal where the embedding is reliable versus where critical information is hidden, with statistical rigour through held-out testing and bootstrapping.
AI.conclusion: FloDR addresses a critical gap in dimensionality reduction by making the invisible visible — it quantifies and visualises the information discarded by 2D embeddings. The invertible flow architecture enables exact diagnostics that prevent over-interpretation of low-dimensional layouts, promoting more honest and statistically principled use of embedding visualisations.

title: Do Code Language Models Use Tests? A Behavioral and Representational Study of Test-Driven Code Generation
summary: Public tests are widely used to guide large language model code generation, but whether models treat them as executable specifications or merely as extra prompt context remains unclear. We study test-driven code generation on HumanEval+, MBPP+, and recent LiveCodeBench tasks using Qwen2.5-Coder-7B and Qwen3.6-27B. We compare natural-language-only prompts with relevant visible tests, shuffled outputs, irrelevant tests, assertion-only tests, and stronger-model-generated synthetic tests. Evaluation combines hidden or private test pass rates with task-level behavior flips, linear probes, and layer-wise hidden-state shifts. Visible tests substantially improve Qwen2.5 performance on MBPP+ but have little or unstable effect on HumanEval+ and LiveCodeBench. For Qwen3.6 on LiveCodeBench, the natural-language-only pass rate rises from 13.1% to 39.4%, yet relevant original tests add only 2.9 percentage points (p = .458), and synthetic high5 tests add 1.7 points over their matched baseline (p = .701). More tests produce larger representation shifts, but accuracy gains quickly saturate or disappear; assertion-only and irrelevant-test prompts can strongly alter hidden states without improving correctness. After controlling for prompt length, task-level shifts are associated with both beneficial and harmful flips, with a substantially stronger association for harms. These results show that tests influence code models through both semantic guidance and prompt-context perturbation, and that representational change alone does not demonstrate effective test utilization.

AI.tldr: Tests improve code generation mainly through prompt-context perturbation rather than semantic specification; representation shifts don't imply effective test utilization, and accuracy gains are unstable and saturate quickly.
AI.motivation: To determine whether LLMs treat visible tests as executable specifications or merely as extra prompt context during code generation, and to disentangle semantic guidance from superficial prompt-length effects.
AI.method: The authors compare multiple prompt variants (natural-language-only, relevant visible tests, shuffled outputs, irrelevant tests, assertion-only tests, synthetic tests from stronger models) across HumanEval+, MBPP+, and LiveCodeBench using Qwen2.5-Coder-7B and Qwen3.6-27B. They evaluate using hidden/private test pass rates, task-level behavior flips, linear probes, and layer-wise hidden-state shifts, controlling for prompt length.
AI.result: Visible tests substantially help Qwen2.5 on MBPP+ but show little or unstable effect on HumanEval+ and LiveCodeBench. For Qwen3.6 on LiveCodeBench, natural-language-only gets 39.4% pass rate, but relevant tests add only 2.9pp (p=.458) and synthetic tests add 1.7pp over baseline (p=.701). More tests produce larger representation shifts but accuracy gains saturate or disappear; assertion-only and irrelevant-test prompts strongly alter hidden states without improving correctness. Task-level shifts associate with both beneficial and harmful flips, with stronger association for harms.
AI.conclusion: Tests influence code models through both semantic guidance and prompt-context perturbation. Representational change alone does not demonstrate effective test utilization, and the benefits of visible tests are far less robust than commonly assumed.

title: Sensor-Placement-Agnostic Sonomyography: Toward Continuous High-Dimensional Control by Users with Tetraplegia
comment: Vikram Athithan, Emma Ferran, Maria Herrera, and Carson J. Wynn contributed equally to this work. Copyright 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses, in any current or future media
summary:
Sonomyography (SMG) enables continuous device control via ultrasound-measured muscle deformation signals, but existing SMG interfaces generally require substantial user- and sensor-location-specific training data and provide only one proportional signal or task-specific classification. We present a real-time, sensor-placement-agnostic SMG control system based on sparse optical flow tracking that enables continuous 1-DOF control after minimal calibration (3 pose definitions). We also present a preliminary expansion of this method that augments this algorithm with a short computer-aided calibration to enable 2-DOF control.
  We evaluate both 1- and 2-DOF systems' performance for a preliminary cohort of 3 cervical spinal cord injury survivors and 6 uninjured individuals across 6 sensor placements spanning the arm, neck, and upper torso. As assessed by a cursor trajectory tracking task, all participants achieved continuous 1-DOF control at all tested sensor locations (even those that relied on passive tissue motions), with all participants achieving <5.5% tracking error using at least one placement (and many <4% across many). All participants were also able to modulate 2D cursor position via the 2-DOF system, with varying levels of control authority, and several were able to complete a 2D drawing task, constituting the first (to our knowledge) demonstration of location-agnostic multi-DOF continuous SMG-based control. These results highlight the promise of SMG to enable rapidly calibratable, high-dimensional, sensor-placement-agnostic device control by users with tetraplegia, and also illuminate key challenges in both signal processing and practical system deployment. To enable further development by scientific and user communities, developed algorithms have been open-sourced as part of the OpenMyoControl project on SimTK (simtk.org/projects/openmyocontrol).

AI.tldr: A real-time, sensor-placement-agnostic sonomyography (SMG) control system using sparse optical flow enables 1-DOF continuous control with minimal calibration and can be extended to 2-DOF. Evaluated on spinal cord injury survivors and uninjured individuals across diverse sensor locations, results demonstrate low tracking error and the first multi-DOF continuous SMG control, with algorithms open-sourced.
AI.motivation: Existing SMG interfaces require extensive user- and location-specific training data and are limited to single proportional signals or task-specific classification, hindering practical, flexible device control — especially for individuals with tetraplegia.
AI.method: The authors propose a real-time SMG control system based on sparse optical flow tracking of ultrasound-measured muscle deformation. For 1-DOF control, only 3 pose definitions are needed for calibration. For 2-DOF, the algorithm is augmented with a short computer-aided calibration. The system was evaluated on 3 cervical spinal cord injury survivors and 6 uninjured individuals across 6 sensor placements (arm, neck, upper torso) using a cursor trajectory tracking task.
AI.result: All participants achieved continuous 1-DOF control at all sensor locations, with <5.5% tracking error using at least one placement (many <4%). All participants modulated 2D cursor position via the 2-DOF system with varying control authority; several completed a 2D drawing task — the first demonstration of location-agnostic multi-DOF continuous SMG-based control.
AI.conclusion: SMG shows strong promise for rapidly calibratable, high-dimensional, sensor-placement-agnostic device control for users with tetraplegia. Key challenges remain in signal processing and practical deployment. Algorithms are open-sourced via the OpenMyoControl project on SimTK to foster further development.

title: A large-scale corpus of religious radio broadcast transcripts from webstream recordings in the United States
summary: Religious radio is a widespread but understudied form of mass communication in the United States, and content-level analysis of it has been constrained by the absence of large-scale transcript data. This Data Descriptor presents a corpus of transcribed English-language religious radio broadcasts captured from live webstreams over a one-month period in July 2025. Fifteen-minute segments were recorded on a rolling schedule from 785 distinct streams, which together rebroadcast the signals of more than two thousand AM and FM stations, yielding over 700,000 recordings and more than 60 million diarized lines of speech. Each recording was transcribed and speaker-diarized with an automated pipeline, and segmented and labeled by programming format and topic using a large language model. The corpus is organized as linked tables of stream metadata, recording metadata, and transcript lines. It supports descriptive study of religious broadcasting across regions and traditions, analysis of how social and political issues are discussed in religious media, and speech-processing research in an underrepresented domain.

AI.tldr: This Data Descriptor presents a large-scale corpus of transcribed English-language religious radio broadcasts captured from 785 webstreams (representing 2,000+ AM/FM stations) over July 2025, yielding 700,000+ recordings and 60M+ diarized speech lines, automatically transcribed, speaker-diarized, and LLM-labeled by format and topic.
AI.motivation: Religious radio is a widespread yet understudied form of mass communication in the U.S., with content-level analysis historically constrained by the absence of large-scale transcript data. This corpus addresses that gap.
AI.method: Fifteen-minute segments were recorded on a rolling schedule from 785 distinct live webstreams over one month (July 2025). An automated pipeline performed transcription and speaker diarization. A large language model segmented and labeled each recording by programming format and topic. The resulting data is organized as linked tables of stream metadata, recording metadata, and transcript lines.
AI.result: The corpus comprises over 700,000 recordings and more than 60 million diarized lines of speech, spanning more than 2,000 AM and FM stations, organized into linked relational tables ready for analysis.
AI.conclusion: The corpus enables descriptive study of religious broadcasting across regions and traditions, analysis of social and political discourse in religious media, and speech-processing research in a domain that has been underrepresented in available datasets.

title: WhisperRec: Latent Reasoning for Efficient Foundation Recommendation Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong reasoning capabilities, motivating their adoption as backbones for foundation recommendation models (FRMs). Existing approaches typically enhance recommendation with explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) under the Think-then-Answer paradigm. However, generating lengthy rationales introduces substantial inference overhead, while fixed CoT templates struggle to model diverse, dynamic, and context-dependent user interests. We propose WhisperRec, an efficient latent reasoning framework for FRMs. WhisperRec compresses teacher-generated CoT into learnable latent reasoning tokens, enabling a Latent-Reason-then-Answer paradigm that performs reasoning in latent space without producing verbose rationales. This design retains decision-relevant reasoning information while avoiding the latency bottleneck of autoregressive rationale generation. Specifically, it first introduces Multi-View Adaptive CoT (MV-ACoT) to construct diverse, high-quality supervision from complementary perspectives on user interests. MV-ACoT also adapts reasoning complexity to each instance, applying lightweight analysis to clear cases and targeted multi-factor reasoning to challenging ones. Building on a pre-trained FRM, WhisperRec then employs a three-stage Latent Reasoning Alignment procedure to progressively internalize teacher CoT into latent representations. Finally, curriculum-based post-training activates latent-token reasoning for downstream recommendation while preserving standard recommendation capability. Experiments on an industrial-scale Kuaishou dataset and the public Kuaishou LLM-Rec benchmark show that WhisperRec consistently outperforms explicit-CoT methods and conventional baselines. Compared with explicit CoT Think and No-Think variants, WhisperRec improves SID@64 by 17.44% and 9.33%, respectively, and achieves over 10x higher online inference throughput.

AI.tldr: WhisperRec proposes an efficient latent reasoning framework for foundation recommendation models that compresses Chain-of-Thought reasoning into learnable latent tokens, replacing verbose rationale generation with a "Latent-Reason-then-Answer" paradigm. It achieves 17.44% and 9.33% SID@64 improvements over explicit CoT Think and No-Think variants, respectively, with over 10x higher inference throughput.
AI.motivation: LLMs as FRMs benefit from CoT reasoning, but generating lengthy rationales causes substantial inference overhead, and fixed CoT templates fail to capture diverse, dynamic, context-dependent user interests. There is a need for efficient reasoning that retains decision-relevant information without the latency bottleneck.
AI.method: WhisperRec consists of three components: (1) Multi-View Adaptive CoT (MV-ACoT) constructs diverse supervision from complementary user interest perspectives and adapts reasoning complexity per instance; (2) a three-stage Latent Reasoning Alignment procedure progressively internalizes teacher CoT into latent representations on a pre-trained FRM; (3) curriculum-based post-training activates latent-token reasoning for downstream recommendation while preserving standard capability.
AI.result: On an industrial-scale Kuaishou dataset and the public Kuaishou LLM-Rec benchmark, WhisperRec consistently outperforms explicit CoT methods and conventional baselines. Compared with explicit CoT Think and No-Think variants, it improves SID@64 by 17.44% and 9.33%, respectively, and achieves over 10x higher online inference throughput.
AI.conclusion: WhisperRec demonstrates that latent-space reasoning can effectively replace explicit CoT in FRMs, simultaneously improving both recommendation quality and inference efficiency. The MV-ACoT and curriculum-based post-training strategies prove effective for internalizing reasoning into compact latent tokens.

title: MultivationBench: A Benchmark for Multimodal Sequential Motivation Reasoning
comment: 31 pages, including appendices; 6 figures and 22 tables. Code: https://github.com/HKUST-KnowComp/MultivationBench
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models have sparked significant interest due to their potential for social intelligence; however, their ability to perform sequential motivation reasoning remains insufficiently studied. Existing evaluations predominantly examine static text or isolated visual snapshots, which do not reflect the cumulative nature of real-world behavioral drivers. To address this gap, we introduce MultivationBench, a benchmark designed to rigorously evaluate multimodal motivation reasoning within story-driven visual narratives. The benchmark builds upon established psychological frameworks - Maslow's hierarchy and Reiss's basic desires - and requires models to integrate accumulated multimodal context to infer evolving motivations. Results indicate that MultivationBench presents a significant challenge: all tested models struggle to maintain consistent motivation reasoning across sequential contexts, revealing a critical disconnect between static recognition capabilities and the dynamic reasoning essential for human-like social understanding.

AI.tldr: MultivationBench is a benchmark evaluating multimodal LLMs on sequential motivation reasoning within story-driven visual narratives, grounded in Maslow's hierarchy and Reiss's basic desires. All tested models struggle with consistent motivation reasoning across sequential contexts, exposing a gap between static recognition and dynamic social understanding.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of multimodal LLMs focus on static text or isolated images, failing to capture the cumulative, evolving nature of real-world behavioral drivers. Sequential motivation reasoning—the ability to infer how motivations shift over time using accumulated multimodal context—remains critically understudied.
AI.method: The authors introduce MultivationBench, a benchmark grounded in two established psychological frameworks: Maslow's hierarchy of needs and Reiss's basic desires. The benchmark presents story-driven visual narratives that require models to integrate accumulated multimodal context across sequential frames to infer evolving character motivations.
AI.result: All tested multimodal LLMs struggle to maintain consistent motivation reasoning across sequential contexts. Results reveal a critical disconnect between models' static recognition capabilities and the dynamic reasoning required for human-like social intelligence.
AI.conclusion: Current multimodal LLMs lack robust sequential motivation reasoning, highlighting a significant limitation in their social intelligence. The benchmark serves as a valuable diagnostic tool for future model development targeting dynamic, narrative-driven understanding.

title: CDN Tsunami: Exploiting HTTP/3-HTTP/1.1 Conversion for DoS Attacks
comment: This paper has been accepted for publication at the IEEE International Symposium on Reliable Distributed Systems (SRDS) 2026
summary:
Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) provide high availability, accelerate content delivery for their host websites, but are also vulnerable to different types of Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks. Prior works have studied a variety of DoS attacks with HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 connections, but most of them are being fixed, making CDNs robust against such attacks. One unexplored research area is how the recent introduction of HTTP/3 at CDNs affects the DoS attack landscape, especially when there are heterogeneous deployments of HTTP/3 and HTTP/1.1 between CDNs and host websites.
  In this paper, we design the first study of DoS attacks against HTTP/3 protocols deployed at CDNs. Our key insight is that when the CDN adopts HTTP/3 but the host websites use HTTP/1.1, an adversary can utilize the disparity to amplify a small amount of traffic to the CDN using HTTP/3 to a large amount from the CDN to the host website using HTTP/1.1. More specifically, we design two attack variations-HTTP/3 Bandwidth Amplification (HBA) and HTTP/3 Connection Amplification (HCA)-targeting the bandwidth and the number of connections, respectively. Furthermore, we conduct a large-scale measurement upon the Tranco Top 1M domain list to quantify the real-world impact of these attacks, identifying 42,330 subdomains that are potentially vulnerable to our attacks. Finally, we responsibly disclose the details of our attacks to the affected CDN vendors: so far, two vendors have already acknowledged their vulnerabilities with bounties and have deployed our mitigations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces novel DoS attacks exploiting the HTTP/3 to HTTP/1.1 protocol translation at CDNs, enabling traffic amplification attacks (bandwidth and connection-based) that affect tens of thousands of real-world subdomains.
AI.motivation: Prior DoS attacks on CDNs over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 have been largely mitigated. The introduction of HTTP/3 creates a new, unexplored attack surface, particularly due to heterogeneous deployments where CDNs speak HTTP/3 to clients but HTTP/1.1 to origin servers.
AI.method: The authors design two attack variants: HTTP/3 Bandwidth Amplification (HBA), which amplifies client-to-CDN traffic into larger CDN-to-origin traffic, and HTTP/3 Connection Amplification (HCA), which amplifies the number of connections at the origin. A large-scale measurement on the Tranco Top 1M domain list quantifies real-world impact.
AI.result: The measurement identified 42,330 subdomains potentially vulnerable to the attacks. Two affected CDN vendors acknowledged the vulnerabilities, awarded bounties, and deployed the proposed mitigations.
AI.conclusion: HTTP/3 adoption at CDNs introduces significant new DoS vulnerabilities due to protocol-translation amplification effects. Responsible disclosure led to real-world mitigations, but the findings highlight the need for careful deployment of HTTP/3 in heterogeneous environments.

title: Entity Resolution in Practice: Lessons from a Self-Serve Pipeline
summary: We built and evaluated a self-serve entity resolution (ER) system on six benchmarks spanning 864 to 5M records, and three lessons emerged that are absent from existing ER literature. (1) No single matching algorithm wins everywhere - a self-serve pipeline cannot predict its next dataset, so we recommend training several algorithm families per dataset and letting an automatic bake-off pick the winner. (2) Precision and recall need separate fixes, not a shared threshold - precision needs hard rule-based vetoes, recall needs more diverse candidate retrieval. (3) One false-positive link can silently merge unrelated entities - assuming "A matches B" and "B matches C" implies "A matches C" lets a single bad link chain hundreds of records together, so every cross-group merge must be actively re-verified. We hope these lessons save practitioners the months of dead-end experiments that led us to them.

AI.tldr: A self-serve entity resolution system was built and evaluated on six diverse benchmarks. Three practical lessons emerged: (1) no single matching algorithm is universally best, necessitating an ensemble-based bake-off; (2) precision and recall require independent tuning strategies; (3) transitive closure of matches risks catastrophic chaining from a single false positive, requiring explicit re-verification of cross-group merges.
AI.motivation: Entity resolution (ER) is critical for data integration, yet practitioners face months of trial-and-error. The authors aim to distill practical, actionable lessons from building a self-serve ER pipeline — one that must work out-of-the-box on unseen datasets without manual tuning — filling a gap in the literature where such hard-won operational insights are rarely documented.
AI.method: A self-serve ER pipeline was constructed and evaluated across six benchmarks ranging from 864 to 5 million records. The pipeline trains multiple algorithm families in parallel per dataset and employs an automatic bake-off to select the best performer. Precision is addressed via hard rule-based vetoes (not merely threshold tuning), recall is addressed via diverse candidate retrieval strategies, and transitive clustering is augmented with active re-verification of every cross-group merge to prevent cascading errors.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) No single matching algorithm dominates across all benchmarks — ensemble training with automatic bake-off is necessary for robustness. (2) Precision and recall respond to different interventions: rule-based vetoes effectively eliminate false positives without harming recall, while diverse candidate retrieval improves recall. (3) A single false-positive link, when transitive closure is applied naively, can silently chain hundreds of records into one erroneous entity; mandatory re-verification of cross-group merges prevents this.
AI.conclusion: The three lessons — algorithmic diversity with automatic bake-off, decoupled precision/recall optimization, and active re-verification of merge transitivity — are practical design principles for robust self-serve ER systems. The authors offer these to help practitioners avoid common dead-end experiments and build more reliable pipelines.

title: SARC-DQ: Runtime Data-Quality Gating for Agentic AI: Silent Evidence Defects, the Incompetence Shield, and Downstream-Only Remediation
summary: Agentic systems act, so a defect in the evidence they retrieve becomes a wrong action with a currency cost. The most dangerous enterprise defects are metadata-borne: a stale price or a superseded record, perfectly well-formed in the payload and betrayed only by freshness, lineage, or provenance. Such a defect never enters the agent's context, and an agent cannot doubt data it cannot see. On a priced replenishment benchmark, a competent agent silently converts an injected metadata-borne defect into a costly action about 60% of the time, with zero data-quality flags and behavioral doubt markers at chance (AUC <= 0.50). Across four model tiers spanning roughly 15x in inference price, the rate stays flat: capability does not buy skepticism. A metadata-aware pre-action gate with downstream-only remediation recovers the loss fully on the signals its predicates cover and not at all on those they miss. A model-free oracle derived from the task's decision geometry tracks the measured rates with MAE 0.015 (Pearson r = 0.876, interval coverage 15/16 cells), giving the flat ladder an analytical form. Evidence integrity is a systems axis distinct from model capability; mitigation depends on enforcement placement and predicate coverage. Code, frozen results, and a deterministic analysis pipeline: https://github.com/besanson/dqSarc

AI.tldr: Agentic systems are systematically vulnerable to metadata-borne data defects (e.g., staleness, provenance issues) that are invisible in payload content. Experiments show agents silently convert these defects into costly actions ~60% of the time, regardless of model capability tier. A metadata-aware gating mechanism can fully recover losses when predicates cover the defect, but misses entirely otherwise. An oracle model derived from decision geometry accurately predicts failure rates, demonstrating that evidence integrity is a distinct systems axis from model capability.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems that retrieve evidence and take actions are vulnerable to a class of defects that prior data-quality research has overlooked: metadata-borne defects. Unlike malformed payloads, these defects (stale prices, superseded records) are structurally valid but betrayed only by freshness, lineage, or provenance — information that never enters the agent's context window. The authors argue this represents a dangerous blind spot: agents cannot doubt evidence they cannot see, yet their actions carry real currency costs. No existing work systematically quantifies how metadata-blindness translates into costly agent failures.
AI.method: The authors construct a priced replenishment benchmark where metadata-borne defects (staleness, supersession) are injected into evidence served to agents. They test four model tiers spanning ~15x inference cost. They measure: (1) the rate at which agents silently convert defects into costly actions, (2) whether agents exhibit behavioral doubt markers or data-quality flags, and (3) whether capability scales with skepticism (AUC for doubt markers). They then introduce a metadata-aware pre-action gate with downstream-only remediation, evaluating recovery as a function of predicate coverage. Finally, they derive a model-free oracle from the task's decision geometry and validate it against measured rates (MAE, Pearson r, interval coverage).
AI.result: Agents silently convert injected metadata-borne defects into costly actions ~60% of the time. Data-quality flags and behavioral doubt markers perform at chance (AUC ≤ 0.50). The failure rate remains flat across all four model tiers despite ~15x inference cost difference — capability does not buy skepticism. The metadata-aware pre-action gate fully recovers losses on covered predicates but zero on uncovered ones. The decision-geometry oracle matches measured rates with MAE 0.015, Pearson r = 0.876, and interval coverage of 15/16 cells, giving the flat failure ladder a formal analytical structure.
AI.conclusion: Evidence integrity constitutes a systems axis orthogonal to model capability; more capable models are not more skeptical of metadata-blind defects. Effective mitigation depends entirely on enforcement placement (pre-action gating) and predicate coverage, not on model scaling. The decision-geometry oracle provides a predictive framework for reasoning about these failures without empirical testing. The work implies that agentic system safety requires explicit, out-of-context metadata verification architectures rather than reliance on model reasoning improvements.

title: FleetScape: A Mixed Reality Sandtable for Spatial Supervision and Control of Scalable Drone Fleets
summary: As autonomous drone deployments scale from individual units to coordinated swarms, the human operator's role shifts from direct piloting to high-level supervision. Current interfaces often treat multi-drone control as a scaled-up version of single-drone operation. We instead investigate how reframing fleet supervision as spatial interaction can better support the spatial, temporal, and safety demands of complex missions. We present FleetScape, a Mixed Reality (MR) sandtable system that externalizes layered real-time mission, safety, and environmental data while enabling fluid transitions between manual intervention and autonomous supervision. We developed a high-fidelity building inspection simulation that generates and streams synchronized multi-drone and environmental data for MR visualizations. We used this prototype to conduct a user study with six experienced drone pilots managing fleets of up to 15 drones. Our findings show that FleetScape supports situational awareness through layered spatial representations and clarifies control mode transitions. However, a limit to situational awareness was observed as fleet size increases, leading to different supervisory strategies. Finally, we derive design implications for supporting scalable drone fleet supervision.

AI.tldr: FleetScape is a Mixed Reality sandtable system that reframes multi-drone fleet supervision as spatial interaction, using layered real-time data visualizations to support situational awareness and fluid control transitions, with scalability limits observed beyond certain fleet sizes.
AI.motivation: As drone operations scale from individual units to swarms, human operators transition from direct piloting to high-level supervision, yet existing interfaces merely scale up single-drone control paradigms. The authors argue that fleet supervision has distinct spatial, temporal, and safety demands requiring a fundamentally different interaction approach grounded in spatial cognition.
AI.method: The authors designed FleetScape, a Mixed Reality sandtable prototype that externalizes layered mission, safety, and environmental data in real time. They built a high-fidelity building inspection simulation generating synchronized multi-drone and environmental data for MR visualization. A user study was conducted with six experienced drone pilots managing fleets of up to 15 drones to evaluate situational awareness and control mode transitions.
AI.result: FleetScape effectively supported situational awareness through layered spatial representations and clarified transitions between manual intervention and autonomous supervision modes. However, situational awareness degraded as fleet size increased, prompting pilots to adopt different supervisory strategies to cope with cognitive scaling limits.
AI.conclusion: Reframing fleet supervision as spatial interaction in MR offers clear benefits for operator situational awareness and control fluidity. The observed scalability ceiling yields concrete design implications for future systems supporting large-scale autonomous drone fleet supervision.

title: Robostreet Flow: A Lightweight, Ultra-Low-Drag Electric Tractor and Four-Truck Hybrid Convoy Architecture for Minimum-Cost Point-to-Point Freight
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems 2026
summary: Line-haul trucking costs are dominated by three comparably sized components: energy, driver labor, and equipment. Most efficiency technologies address only one component at a time. This paper presents Robostreet Flow, a freight architecture that jointly optimizes the vehicle, convoy formation, and operating model to minimize cost per ton-mile on high-volume point-to-point corridors. The Flow platform is a battery-electric 6x4 tractor with a teardrop single-seat cab and a drag coefficient of 0.35, approximately 40% below that of conventional Class 8 tractors. A carbon-composite monocoque and structurally integrated batteries reduce net vehicle weight by 50%. A 513 kWh tractor battery and a 340 kWh powered trailer battery provide a 500-mile single-charge range. Four Flow trucks operate as a coordinated convoy with a safety driver only in the lead vehicle, while three followers operate in SAE Level 4 automated mode. Computational fluid dynamics simulations show that close following at an 8 m gap reduces follower drag coefficients by 42-48% and follower peak frontal pressure by approximately a factor of four relative to the exposed lead vehicle. A longitudinal energy model calibrated to these results predicts fleet-average consumption of 1.27 kWh/mi in convoy, compared with 1.60 kWh/mi for an isolated vehicle, for a 20.5% energy saving. Electricity cost is approximately 17% of the equivalent diesel fuel cost. Amortizing one driver across four trucks and accounting for the additional payload enabled by lightweighting reduce operating cost from 9.4 to 4.1 cents per ton-mile, a 56% reduction relative to a diesel baseline. Sensitivity analysis, a hub-to-hub operating concept, and regulatory implications are also presented.

AI.tldr: Robostreet Flow proposes a freight system combining a lightweight, aerodynamic battery-electric tractor-trailer with coordinated four-truck convoys (one human driver, three Level 4 automated followers) to slash line-haul trucking costs by 56% relative to diesel, achieving 4.1 cents/ton-mile through joint optimization of vehicle design, convoy aerodynamics, and operating model.
AI.motivation: Line-haul trucking costs are dominated by three roughly equal components — energy, driver labor, and equipment — yet most efficiency technologies target only one at a time. The authors seek a holistic solution that simultaneously optimizes all three cost levers to achieve substantial cost reduction on high-volume point-to-point corridors.
AI.method: The paper presents the Robostreet Flow architecture: a battery-electric 6x4 tractor with a teardrop single-seat cab (Cd=0.35, ~40% below conventional Class 8), carbon-composite monocoque with structurally integrated batteries (50% weight reduction), and 513 kWh tractor + 340 kWh powered trailer batteries (500-mile range). Four trucks operate in coordinated convoy at 8 m gaps, with a safety driver only in the lead vehicle; the three followers run SAE Level 4 automation. CFD simulations quantify drag reduction for followers (42-48% Cd reduction). A longitudinal energy model calibrated to CFD results computes fleet-average energy consumption. Operating cost modeling amortizes one driver across four trucks and accounts for lightweighting-enabled payload gains, benchmarked against a diesel baseline.
AI.result: CFD simulations show 8 m close-following reduces follower Cd by 42-48% and peak frontal pressure by ~4×. Fleet-average energy consumption is 1.27 kWh/mi in convoy vs. 1.60 kWh/mi isolated, yielding 20.5% energy savings. Electricity cost is ~17% of equivalent diesel fuel cost. Combined driver amortization and payload gains reduce operating cost from 9.4 to 4.1 cents/ton-mile — a 56% reduction versus diesel baseline.
AI.conclusion: Joint optimization of vehicle design, convoy formation, and operating model yields transformative cost reductions in line-haul trucking. The Robostreet Flow architecture demonstrates that battery-electric automated convoys on hub-to-hub corridors can achieve a 56% per-ton-mile cost reduction relative to conventional diesel operations, with significant energy, labor, and equipment savings. Sensitivity analysis and regulatory considerations are also addressed.

title: CaIRec: Calibrated Modality Imputation for Incomplete Multimodal Recommendation
summary: Real-world multimodal recommender systems often face incomplete modality observations, where items lack images, text, or other content features. Such incompleteness weakens item representations and degrades recommendation performance. Existing modality imputation methods estimate missing representations from available item content, but two challenges remain. First, they optimize the recovered representation itself without explicitly considering its relations with other modalities of the same item. The completed modalities may therefore form inconsistent cross-modal relations, causing Cross-modal Structural Distortion. Second, even structurally coherent recovered information may remain ineffective for personalized ranking. Recovered representations receive limited ranking-oriented guidance, while modality missingness disrupts the item neighborhoods required for preference propagation, resulting in a Preference Adaptation Gap. To address these challenges, we propose Calibrated Imputation for Incomplete Multimodal Recommendation (CaIRec), a two-stage framework. Structural Imputation Calibration (SIC) estimates missing-modality representations from shared information inferred from available modalities and calibrates their cross-modal organization through structural regularization and correspondence supervision from observed modality pairs. Preference-oriented Representation Calibration (PRC) performs recommendation-specific adaptation at both the representation and relation levels. It constructs pseudo-missing instances to align recovered representations with observed counterparts shaped by ranking supervision in the recommendation space. It further builds completion-aware item graphs by integrating completed content relations with collaborative evidence. Extensive experiments on three datasets under different modality-missing settings demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of CaIRec.

AI.tldr: CaIRec is a two-stage framework for incomplete multimodal recommendation that addresses cross-modal structural distortion and preference adaptation gaps via structural imputation calibration and preference-oriented representation calibration.
AI.motivation: Real-world multimodal recommenders suffer from incomplete modality observations (missing images, text, etc.), which weakens item representations. Existing imputation methods fail to (1) preserve consistent cross-modal relations, causing Cross-modal Structural Distortion, and (2) align recovered representations with ranking objectives, resulting in a Preference Adaptation Gap.
AI.method: A two-stage framework, CaIRec: (1) Structural Imputation Calibration (SIC) estimates missing modality representations from shared information across available modalities and calibrates cross-modal organization via structural regularization and correspondence supervision from observed modality pairs. (2) Preference-oriented Representation Calibration (PRC) aligns recovered representations with ranking-supervised observed counterparts using pseudo-missing instances and builds completion-aware item graphs that fuse completed content relations with collaborative evidence.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three datasets under different modality-missing settings demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of CaIRec.
AI.conclusion: CaIRec effectively addresses both cross-modal structural distortion and the preference adaptation gap in incomplete multimodal recommendation, outperforming existing imputation approaches across diverse missing-modality scenarios.

title: EvoPINN: Agentic Discovery of Executable Algorithms for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for solving partial differential equations (PDEs), yet their performance heavily relies on the manual, trial-and-error engineering of neural representations, loss formulations, and optimization dynamics. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a promising avenue for automated design, unconstrained code generation often yields mathematically invalid or numerically unstable solutions under strict scientific computing constraints. To bridge this gap, we propose \textbf{EvoPINN}, an agentic framework that reformulates PINN development from labor-intensive manual design into a rigorous, execution-grounded algorithm discovery problem. EvoPINN navigates a modular search space by decoupling neural representations from training programs, utilizing an LLM agent to iteratively propose memory-conditioned programmatic modifications. To ensure scientific validity, all candidates undergo strict structural verification and budget-matched PDE evaluation. Extensive experiments across diverse PDE regimes (oscillatory, elliptic, dissipative, and nonlinear transport) demonstrate that EvoPINN discovers PDE-specialized learning algorithms that significantly reduce relative $L_{2}$ error compared to baselines. Crucially, EvoPINN autonomously invented SLRC-PINN, a novel architecture whose performance gains persist under rigorous parameter-matched comparisons, establishing the viability of execution-grounded agents for discovering genuinely new scientific computing mechanisms.

AI.tldr: EvoPINN is an agentic framework that uses LLM agents to automatically discover physics-informed neural network architectures and training algorithms through execution-grounded search, outperforming manually designed baselines and autonomously inventing a novel architecture called SLRC-PINN.
AI.motivation: PINN development currently requires labor-intensive manual trial-and-error for designing neural representations, loss formulations, and optimization dynamics. While LLMs could automate this, unconstrained code generation often produces mathematically invalid or numerically unstable solutions. A rigorous, execution-grounded approach is needed to enable reliable automated discovery of PDE-solving algorithms.
AI.method: EvoPINN decouples neural representations from training programs within a modular search space. An LLM agent iteratively proposes memory-conditioned programmatic modifications. All candidates undergo strict structural verification and budget-matched PDE evaluation to ensure scientific validity before acceptance.
AI.result: Across diverse PDE regimes (oscillatory, elliptic, dissipative, nonlinear transport), EvoPINN discovers specialized learning algorithms that significantly reduce relative L2 error compared to baselines. It autonomously invented SLRC-PINN, a novel architecture whose performance gains persist under rigorous parameter-matched comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Execution-grounded agentic frameworks like EvoPINN are viable for discovering genuinely new scientific computing mechanisms, moving beyond manual design toward automated algorithm discovery with built-in mathematical rigor.

title: Guarding Organizations Against Malware Risk: A Novel Graph-Based Malware Detection Method
summary: Organizational digitalization expands cybersecurity risks, making cybersecurity an increasingly important research area in Information Systems (IS). Among these risks, malware has become a pervasive and destructive threat. Byte-based machine learning (ML) methods are widely used for malware detection but remain vulnerable to evasive behaviors that manipulate raw bytes to evade detection. Graph-based methods are less affected by such manipulations because they represent software as program graphs that capture execution behavior. However, they do not explicitly identify cohesive groups of basic blocks that jointly realize meaningful program behaviors, nor do they learn sufficiently expressive program graph representations for accurate detection. To this end, we propose MalGuard, a graph-based malware detection method for organizational malware risk management. MalGuard introduces two methodological innovations: an operational role identification approach and a program graph representation learning method. The former identifies these cohesive groups of basic blocks as operational roles, enabling the detector to capture program behaviors that may not be visible from isolated basic blocks. The latter learns expressive program graph representations by modeling interactions among operational roles, preserving sparse malicious signals, and capturing hierarchical graph structure. Extensive experiments show that MalGuard improves detection performance and reduces the expected cost of undetected malware.

AI.tldr: MalGuard is a graph-based malware detection method that introduces operational role identification and hierarchical program graph representation learning to better capture program behaviors, outperforming byte-based ML methods that are vulnerable to byte-level evasion.
AI.motivation: Existing byte-based ML malware detectors are vulnerable to evasive manipulations of raw bytes. Graph-based methods are more robust but suffer from two limitations: they fail to explicitly identify cohesive groups of basic blocks that jointly realize meaningful program behaviors, and they do not learn sufficiently expressive program graph representations.
AI.method: MalGuard proposes two innovations: (1) an operational role identification approach that groups cohesive basic blocks into "operational roles" capturing joint program behaviors, and (2) a program graph representation learning method that models interactions among operational roles, preserves sparse malicious signals, and captures hierarchical graph structure.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that MalGuard improves detection performance and reduces the expected cost of undetected malware compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: MalGuard provides a more robust and expressive graph-based malware detection framework for organizational cybersecurity risk management, addressing key weaknesses in prior graph-based and byte-based methods.

title: Impossible to hide secret ...: Uncovering Security and Privacy Issues in LLM-native IDEs
summary: LLM-native IDEs (Integrated Development Environments), aka LIDEs, are designed from the ground up to work with Large Language Models (LLMs). LIDEs have found remarkable success in Software Engineering (SE) tasks such as coding, debugging, and program comprehension. LIDEs are software systems, and, like any system, they can exhibit vulnerabilities. In this paper, we study the security and privacy issues that developers reported while using popular LIDEs in their development tasks. We collected 1.1M posts from 29 popular subreddits related to LIDEs. We identified 446 posts and analyzed over 6K comments to the posts that discussed security and privacy issues in almost all popular LIDEs, such as Cursor, Copilot, Codex, etc. Using a mix of qualitative and quantitative methods, we constructed a taxonomy of the reported security and privacy issues. Our results show that most issues in LIDEs stem from system-level design choices, rather than the underlying LLMs, such as user data access, unchecked autonomous actions, etc. To overcome these issues, developers frequently relied on external safeguards like code sandboxing and manual reviewing, highlighting prevalent mistrust among developers about LIDEs. We share lessons from our study to support future design of secure and privacy-aware LIDEs.

AI.tldr: A study analyzing 1.1M Reddit posts from 29 subreddits to identify security and privacy vulnerabilities in LLM-native IDEs (LIDEs) like Cursor, Copilot, and Codex. The authors constructed a taxonomy of reported issues, finding that most stem from system-level design choices rather than the underlying LLMs, and that developers frequently resort to external safeguards due to mistrust.
AI.motivation: LLM-native IDEs (LIDEs) have gained significant traction in software engineering, yet their security and privacy vulnerabilities remain poorly understood. As software systems themselves, LIDEs can introduce novel risks distinct from those of standalone LLMs, warranting systematic investigation of real-world security and privacy concerns reported by practitioners.
AI.method: The authors collected 1.1 million posts from 29 popular subreddits related to LIDEs. From these, they identified 446 posts and analyzed over 6,000 associated comments discussing security and privacy issues across major LIDEs (Cursor, Copilot, Codex, etc.). They employed a mixed-methods approach combining qualitative and quantitative analysis to construct a taxonomy of reported security and privacy issues.
AI.result: The analysis revealed that most security and privacy issues in LIDEs originate from system-level design choices (e.g., user data access, unchecked autonomous actions) rather than from the underlying LLMs themselves. Developers commonly relied on external safeguards such as code sandboxing and manual review, indicating widespread mistrust of LIDEs. A comprehensive taxonomy of these issues was developed.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight that LIDE security is primarily a systems-design problem, not an LLM problem. The prevalent developer mistrust and reliance on external safeguards underscore the need for more secure, privacy-aware LIDE architectures. The authors distill lessons from their study to inform future design of trustworthy LIDEs.

title: How Do Researchers Manage Visualization Experiment Stimuli?
comment: Accepted to IEEE VIS 2026 Full Paper, 11 pages, 2 figures, and 2 tables
summary: Visualization experiments need a set of "good" stimuli that effectively address research questions and hypotheses. Creating, managing, and deploying stimuli are often challenging, as these tasks require tremendous care. Inappropriate stimuli can make the outcome invalid or uninteresting, wasting both researchers' and participants' resources. As the speed of science increases, better support for stimuli-related tasks is essential, yet we lack a closer look at how visualization researchers deal with them. To understand the experiences of visualization experimenters and guide future improvements, we interviewed 19 visualization researchers with diverse backgrounds and experiences. Our findings describe practices and challenges across the life cycle of stimuli, from exploration and selection through shipment, deployment, and analysis. For example, stimuli management and deployment require tedious manual effort, which does not scale for experiments with many levels and complex conditioning. We also discuss both concerns and optimism around AI-assisted visualization experiment design. We conclude with future research opportunities in supporting stimuli creation, automated stimuli inspection, and experimental apparatus concerns.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an interview study with 19 visualization researchers investigating practices and challenges across the entire stimuli lifecycle—from creation and selection to deployment and analysis—revealing significant manual effort bottlenecks and scaling issues, and identifies opportunities for AI-assisted experiment design and automated stimuli inspection.
AI.motivation: Visualization experiments require carefully crafted stimuli, but creating, managing, and deploying them is challenging and error-prone. Inappropriate stimuli can invalidate results and waste resources. Despite the accelerating pace of science, there is a lack of systematic understanding of how visualization researchers handle stimuli-related tasks, motivating a need for closer examination to guide better tooling and support.
AI.method: The authors conducted semi-structured interviews with 19 visualization researchers possessing diverse backgrounds and experience levels. The interviews probed practices, challenges, and pain points across the full stimuli lifecycle, including stimuli exploration, selection, creation, shipment, deployment, and post-experiment analysis. Qualitative analysis of interview data yielded thematic findings.
AI.result: The study reveals that stimuli management and deployment involve tedious, non-scalable manual effort, particularly for experiments with many conditions or complex factorial designs. Researchers face challenges at every lifecycle stage, from finding suitable existing stimuli to ensuring consistent presentation across participants. The findings also surface mixed sentiments—both concerns and optimism—regarding the role of AI in assisting visualization experiment design.
AI.conclusion: The authors outline future research directions including better tool support for stimuli creation, techniques for automated stimuli inspection and quality assurance, and improved experimental apparatus that reduces manual overhead. These improvements are essential to keep pace with the increasing speed and complexity of visualization research.

title: Evaluating Prompt Scope and Demonstration Similarity in Local LLM Machine Translation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as general-purpose translation systems, but their behavior is usually evaluated under a single prompt shape: translate one source sentence into one target language. In practice, users may ask for one target language, for several related languages at once, or for translations conditioned on examples. This paper studies prompt scope and demonstration selection as experimental variables for local LLM machine translation. We evaluate English-to-Romance and English-to-Germanic translation on the full FLORES devtest split for nine official European Union languages. We compare three local instruction-tuned LLMs, llama3.2:3b, mistral:latest, and qwen2.5:14b, against dedicated MT baselines from OPUS-MT and NLLB-200. We test zero-shot prompting and k=5 few-shot prompting with random, lexical-similarity, and embedding-similarity demonstration selection. We also compare single-target prompts with JSON-formatted family-scope prompts that request all languages in a family at once. Results show that dedicated MT systems remain strongest overall, especially for Germanic languages. Few-shot prompting helps mistral:latest and qwen2.5:14b, but hurts llama3.2:3b; embedding retrieval is best on average for the stronger LLMs, but its advantage over random and lexical examples is modest. Family-scope prompting is feasible for stronger local LLMs but exposes structured-output failures in smaller models. These findings motivate evaluating LLM translation not only by language pair and metric, but also by prompt scope, retrieval strategy, and multi-target compliance.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates how prompt scope (single-target vs. family-scope JSON requests) and few-shot demonstration selection strategies (random, lexical-similarity, embedding-similarity) affect local LLM translation performance across English-to-Romance and English-to-Germanic language families, comparing three instruction-tuned LLMs against dedicated MT baselines.
AI.motivation: Current LLM translation evaluation is narrow, typically using only single-sentence, single-target prompts. Real-world usage involves varied prompt formats—multi-target requests, language-family bundles, and example-conditioned translation—yet these variables remain largely unexamined, especially for local (non-API) LLMs.
AI.method: Authors evaluate three local instruction-tuned LLMs (llama3.2:3b, mistral:latest, qwen2.5:14b) against OPUS-MT and NLLB-200 baselines on the full FLORES devtest for nine EU languages (Romance and Germanic families). They test zero-shot and k=5 few-shot translation using three demonstration selection methods: random, lexical-similarity, and embedding-similarity retrieval. They also compare standard single-target prompts against JSON-formatted family-scope prompts requesting all languages in a family simultaneously.
AI.result: Dedicated MT systems (OPUS-MT, NLLB-200) outperform all LLMs overall, especially for Germanic languages. Few-shot prompting benefits mistral:latest and qwen2.5:14b but degrades llama3.2:3b performance. Embedding-based retrieval yields the best average results for stronger LLMs, though its advantage over random and lexical selection is modest. Family-scope JSON prompting is viable for larger LLMs but exposes structured-output failures in smaller models like llama3.2:3b.
AI.conclusion: LLM translation evaluation should extend beyond language-pair and metric comparisons to account for prompt scope, demonstration retrieval strategy, and multi-target output compliance. Smaller local LLMs are not yet robust enough for structured multi-target translation tasks.

title: MediaWiki Code2Code Search: Neural Retrieval for the Semantic Discovery of Open-Source Software Entities
summary: Code search in large-scale ecosystems is often hindered by the lexical gap between user queries and implementation details, alongside the trade-off between the low latency of traditional Information Retrieval (IR) and the precision of Deep Learning (DL). We present MediaWiki Code2Code Search, a neural retrieval system for semantic code-to-code discovery. By indexing 1.29 million structural entities (functions, types, and templates) across 2,500+ MediaWiki repositories, our system enables retrieval based on computational intent rather than surface tokens. We employ a split-build architecture, decoupling GPU-intensive offline indexing from a CPU-only serving layer; our FAISS IVF-PQ index occupies 168.6 MB: a 96.6\% reduction compared to a flat float32 baseline, and achieves a median query latency of 1.85 seconds on commodity hardware, satisfying the 6 GiB RAM constraint of Wikimedia Toolforge. Our evaluation across a 27-query benchmark demonstrates superior performance over the BM25 baseline, achieving a P@10 of 0.87 compared to 0.64 (0.52 versus 0.34 for strict matching). Gains are most pronounced in name-obfuscated tasks where lexical methods fail. The system is available at https://code2codesearch.toolforge.org under the Apache 2.0 licence and provides an open RESTful API.

AI.tldr: MediaWiki Code2Code Search is a neural semantic code retrieval system that bridges the lexical gap in code search by indexing 1.29M structural entities across 2,500+ repositories. It uses a split-build architecture with FAISS IVF-PQ indexing (168.6 MB, 96.6% compression), achieves 1.85s median latency under 6 GiB RAM, and attains P@10 of 0.87 vs. BM25's 0.64 on a 27-query benchmark.
AI.motivation: Code search in large-scale ecosystems suffers from the lexical gap between natural-language or surface-form queries and actual implementation details. Traditional IR (e.g., BM25) offers low latency but poor semantic precision, while deep learning methods improve precision at the cost of high latency. The authors aim to reconcile this trade-off in the resource-constrained Wikimedia Toolforge environment.
AI.method: A split-build architecture: GPU-intensive neural encoding and FAISS IVF-PQ index construction are performed offline, while a CPU-only serving layer handles online queries. The system indexes 1.29 million structural entities (functions, types, templates) from 2,500+ MediaWiki repositories. FAISS IVF-PQ compresses the index from a flat float32 baseline to 168.6 MB (96.6% reduction), enabling deployment within a 6 GiB RAM budget.
AI.result: On a 27-query benchmark, the system achieves P@10 of 0.87 versus BM25's 0.64 (strict matching: 0.52 vs. 0.34). Name-obfuscated tasks show the largest gains, confirming the system's ability to capture computational intent beyond surface tokens. Median query latency is 1.85 seconds on commodity hardware.
AI.conclusion: The system successfully demonstrates that neural semantic code-to-code search can be deployed under stringent resource constraints (6 GiB RAM) while outperforming lexical baselines, particularly for semantically motivated but lexically divergent queries. It is publicly available under Apache 2.0 with a RESTful API.

title: Evidence-Ledger Adjudication for Claim-Evidence Traceability
summary: AI agents can draft claims faster than authors can check whether the cited or retrieved evidence supports them.
