We study evidence-ledger adjudication: a claim-evidence traceability workflow that pairs each claim with an evidence packet, assigns a support relation, and routes unsupported, contradicted, or mixed-evidence claims back to the author. The empirical core is a 2,335-row blind benchmark built from independent external labels in AVeriTeC, CLIMATE-FEVER, and SciFact. Gold relations and source evidence labels are hidden during prediction and joined only for scoring. On this benchmark, the agent evidence-ledger condition achieves 0.676 relation accuracy and 0.601 macro-F1, compared with 0.383 accuracy and 0.303 macro-F1 for the best non-agent baseline. It also routes 1270/1435 claims whose gold labels indicate contradiction, missing evidence, or mixed evidence, while routing 295/900 supported claims. These results show that evidence-ledger adjudication can turn heterogeneous evidence packets into an auditable traceability layer for AI-assisted writing.

AI.tldr: AI agents can draft claims rapidly, but verification lags. This paper introduces evidence-ledger adjudication, a claim-evidence traceability workflow that pairs claims with evidence packets, classifies support relations, and routes problematic claims back to authors. Evaluated on a 2,335-row blind benchmark combining AVeriTeC, CLIMATE-FEVER, and SciFact, the agent-based approach achieves 0.676 relation accuracy and 0.601 macro-F1, substantially outperforming non-agent baselines (0.383 accuracy, 0.303 macro-F1). It successfully routes 1270/1435 contradicted/mixed/missing-evidence claims and 295/900 supported claims.
AI.motivation: AI-assisted writing tools can generate claims faster than human authors can verify the supporting evidence. There is a need for an auditable, structured workflow that traces each claim back to its evidence, adjudicates the support relationship, and flags unreliable claims for author review, ensuring accountability in AI-augmented writing.
AI.method: The authors propose an evidence-ledger adjudication workflow: each claim is paired with an evidence packet and assigned a support relation (supported, contradicted, missing evidence, or mixed). Problematic claims are routed back to the author. The system is evaluated using a blind benchmark of 2,335 rows derived from three existing fact-checking datasets (AVeriTeC, CLIMATE-FEVER, SciFact), with gold relation labels and source evidence hidden during prediction and revealed only for scoring. An agent-based implementation is compared against non-agent baselines.
AI.result: The agent evidence-ledger condition achieves 0.676 relation accuracy and 0.601 macro-F1 on the blind benchmark. The best non-agent baseline reaches only 0.383 accuracy and 0.303 macro-F1. For routing, the system correctly flags 1270 out of 1435 claims with gold labels indicating contradiction, missing evidence, or mixed evidence, while routing 295 out of 900 fully supported claims.
AI.conclusion: Evidence-ledger adjudication effectively transforms heterogeneous evidence packets into an auditable traceability layer for AI-assisted writing, enabling reliable claim verification and selective author intervention at scale.

title: Borrowed Strength: Best-of-N Search over a Code EncodingBreaks Self-Check Jailbreak Defenses
summary: A self-check defense asks the target model to assess a request before answering it; SAGE, the strongest published instance, reports an average 99% defense success rate. We show it can be breached by composing two attacks that are individually harmless against it: an established code-completion encoding and an established best-of-N search, neither of which exceeds 4.7% of behaviors alone. Composed, with the search budget spent on the encoding, they reach 67/22/15% across three open targets, and the effect persists on a 70B target. We then explain the composition rather than only reporting it. First, a self-check defense borrows its strength from the target: SAGE does not detect the attack, it asks the model to, and the four targets convert that request into an explicit refusal between 32% and 97% of the time, which orders the spread in defended coverage even though undefended reach is near-identical. Second, which attack survives is decided by the type of defense, and it inverts: against transform defenses the code encoding retains far more of its undefended reach than the character search, while against gate defenses the ordering flips. We account for this with the number of independent probes an attack delivers to a defense's decision boundary. Finally, we report a validity defect we found and repaired in our own pipeline, a deterministic attack under greedy decoding has no best-of-N variation channel at all, and give the one-line diagnostic that detects it. All claims rest on 310,000 generations scored by a human-validated judge.

AI.tldr: A self-check defense (SAGE) achieves 99% success but can be broken by composing two individually weak attacks—code-completion encoding and best-of-N search—reaching up to 67% attack success. The paper explains why: self-check relies on the target model to refuse, not on detection, and attack effectiveness inverts depending on defense type (transform vs. gate), determined by how many independent probes strike the defense's decision boundary.
AI.motivation: Published self-check defenses like SAGE report near-perfect defense success rates (~99%), but their robustness under adaptive, composed attack strategies remains underexplored. The authors aim to systematically breach SAGE, explain the mechanisms behind the breach, and reveal fundamental properties of self-check defenses and their interaction with different attack types.
AI.method: The authors compose two established attacks—code-completion encoding and best-of-N search—that are individually weak against SAGE (<5% success each). They evaluate across three open-weight targets and one 70B model, generating 310,000 outputs scored by a human-validated judge. They analyze why composition works by distinguishing between transform defenses and gate defenses, measuring how often the model converts the self-check request into an explicit refusal, and counting independent probes an attack delivers to the defense's decision boundary. They also diagnose a validity defect in their pipeline involving deterministic greedy decoding's lack of best-of-N variation.
AI.result: The composed attack achieves 67%, 22%, and 15% success rates on three open targets, with effects persisting on a 70B model. Self-check defenses rely on the target model refusing 32–97% of the time rather than on intrinsic detection. Attack effectiveness inverts by defense type: code encoding retains more reach against transform defenses, while character search performs better against gate defenses, explained by the number of independent probes hitting the decision boundary.
AI.conclusion: Self-check defenses like SAGE are vulnerable to composition of individually weak attacks. Their strength derives entirely from the target model's propensity to refuse, not from detecting attacks. The interaction between attack type and defense type (transform vs. gate) inverts effectiveness, governed by the number of independent probes at the decision boundary. The findings underscore the need for more robust defense evaluation and provide practical diagnostics for pipeline validity.

title: RAGuard: A Layered Defense Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems Against Data Poisoning
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS ResponsibleFM 2025, AAAI FrontierIR 2026
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems ground large language models (LLMs) in external corpora, but this reliance exposes them to corpus poisoning: maliciously injected passages that manipulate retrieved evidence. We introduce RAGuard, a layered defense against \emph{factual} corpus-poisoning attacks on RAG pipelines. The first layer adversarially fine-tunes a dense retriever on synthetic poisoned documents (fabricated facts, contradictions, and reasoning traps), teaching it to downrank malicious passages before generation. The second layer, the Zero-Knowledge Inference Patch ZKIP, is a label-free, black-box filter: for each retrieved document, it performs a leave-one-out decode and scores the document by the semantic shift and output-entropy change that its removal induces. ZKIP requires no poison labels, no ground-truth answers, and no access to model internals; it compares the model's own answers under counterfactual contexts. On poisoned Natural Questions at 5--30\% poison ratios, adversarial retriever training alone reduces but does not eliminate attack success, while ZKIP drives the measured attack success rate to 0.000 in every defended configuration, keeping Recall@5 within 0.03 of the clean-corpus baseline. Supervised analyses on both Natural Questions and BEIR (NFCorpus) confirm that the counterfactual signals ZKIP relies on carry learnable poison structure. The defense costs $k{+}1$ generator passes per query ($6\times$ for $k{=}5$); we analyze batching and early-stopping approximations that reduce this overhead. We also show that keyword-preserving poisons leave lexical retrievers such as BM25 essentially unaffected, an observation that delineates the boundary of the threat model. Code, datasets, and evaluation harnesses are released for reproducibility.

AI.tldr: RAGuard is a two-layer defense against factual corpus poisoning in RAG systems: (1) adversarial fine-tuning of a dense retriever to downrank poisoned passages, and (2) ZKIP, a black-box filter that scores documents by measuring semantic shift and entropy changes from leave-one-out decoding, reducing attack success rate to zero while preserving retrieval quality.
AI.motivation: RAG systems rely on external corpora, making them vulnerable to corpus poisoning attacks where malicious passages are injected to manipulate retrieved evidence and distort LLM outputs. Existing defenses are insufficient, motivating a robust, layered approach.
AI.method: Layer 1: Adversarially fine-tune a dense retriever on synthetic poisoned documents (fabricated facts, contradictions, reasoning traps) to downrank malicious passages. Layer 2: ZKIP, a label-free, black-box filter that performs leave-one-out decoding, scoring each document by the semantic shift and output-entropy change induced by its removal, requiring no poison labels, ground truth, or model internals.
AI.result: On poisoned Natural Questions (5–30% poison ratios), adversarial retriever training alone reduces but does not eliminate attack success. ZKIP drives attack success rate to 0.000 in all defended configurations, with Recall@5 within 0.03 of the clean baseline. BEIR (NFCorpus) analyses confirm that ZKIP's counterfactual signals carry learnable poison structure. BM25 is shown to be largely unaffected by keyword-preserving poisons, bounding the threat model.
AI.conclusion: The two-layer RAGuard defense effectively neutralizes factual corpus poisoning attacks with minimal retrieval degradation. ZKIP's zero-knowledge, black-box design is practical and broadly applicable, though the k+1 generator-pass cost invites future efficiency optimizations.

title: ExplainBench: Evaluating Code Explanations from Agents
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have seen rapid adoption in software engineering. As agents take a greater role in the actual generation of code, they are making larger changes, spanning tens to hundreds of lines. This makes manual review of agent results increasingly infeasible, leading developers to turn to explanations to understand enacted changes. Despite this, there are no benchmarks that evaluate the trustworthiness of agent-generated explanations. To bridge this gap, we propose ExplainBench, a benchmark to automatically evaluate explanations from coding agents. ExplainBench is based on the intuition that informative explanations should enable an LLM to correctly answer questions, allowing quantitative comparison of explanation quality between agents. With this observation, we construct a suite of questions that evaluates whether explanations accurately describe (1) the intended behavior of buggy code and (2) the effect of applying the agent patch itself. Experiments first reveal that explanation quality is a distinct axis of agent evaluation: ExplainBench ranks agents differently from the widely-used SWE-bench Verified benchmark. A deeper breakdown of explanation quality in agents shows frequent problems in explanations, such that explanations often claim that a patch is correct when it is not. Based on this insight, we implement and evaluate an explanation audit agent which runs additional tests to validate and refine explanations. This agent improved the explanations of all evaluated agents, demonstrating agent explanations can be automatically made more trustworthy.

AI.tldr: ExplainBench is a benchmark for automatically evaluating the quality and trustworthiness of explanations generated by LLM coding agents. It assesses whether explanations accurately describe buggy code behavior and patch effects via question-answering. Experiments show explanation quality is a distinct evaluation axis from correctness, explanations often falsely claim patches are correct, and an explanation audit agent can automatically improve explanation trustworthiness.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents increasingly generate large code changes, manual review becomes infeasible, and developers rely on agent-generated explanations. However, no benchmarks exist to evaluate the trustworthiness of these explanations, creating a critical gap between agent capability assessment and developer trust.
AI.method: ExplainBench constructs a suite of questions testing whether explanations accurately capture (1) intended behavior of buggy code and (2) the effect of applying the agent's patch. Explanation quality is measured by how well an LLM can answer these questions given the explanation. The authors also implement an explanation audit agent that runs additional tests to validate and refine explanations automatically.
AI.result: ExplainBench ranks agents differently from SWE-bench Verified, showing explanation quality is a distinct evaluation axis. Frequent problems were found: explanations often claim a patch is correct when it is not. The audit agent improved explanations across all evaluated agents, demonstrating automatic improvement of explanation trustworthiness is feasible.
AI.conclusion: Explanation quality in coding agents is a critical, under-evaluated dimension that diverges from functional correctness benchmarks. Automated auditing can enhance explanation trustworthiness, offering a path toward more reliable agent-generated explanations in software engineering workflows.

title: Repair as Representational Work: Integration Bottlenecks in AI-Assisted Development
comment: Preprint submitted to International Journal of Human-Computer Studies. 18-case corpus study with controlled multi-turn probe. 1 figure, 7 tables
summary: Research on AI-assisted programming has concentrated on the gulf of execution -- how users write successful prompts. We report a candidate phenomenon, an integration bottleneck, that lies in Norman's gulf of evaluation: a repair-relevant contribution reaches the user and fails to become actionable at the point of receipt. Two cases in an eighteen-case corpus of publicly shared AI-assisted-development accounts report this, from a peer and from the system's own output; both fall at evaluation's interpretation stage, and a third, which would fall at comparison, is reached only on an inferential reading and reported as a boundary case. A within-case contrast is consistent with actionability turning on whether the contribution can be restated as an instruction without an intervening judgement. We report this as a candidate warranting dedicated study, not an established regularity; its evidence base is retrospective author self-reports. On the submission side, medium alone did not sort the corpus contrasts; immediate uptake aligned with a checkable condition across four decisive contrasts, while a fifth case shows checkability sufficient for immediate uptake did not guarantee persistence. A twenty-trial multi-turn probe across two current models observed no constraint loss in fifteen judgeable narrow trials, and a ten-trial extension with an explicit restructuring request none in eight. Study 2 is not a replication attempt: it isolates regeneration, the mechanism the corpus authors invoke, and removes it as a sufficient explanation. We specify four interaction requirements for an accepted-constraint ledger; a conformance analysis of twelve mechanisms found none documented to satisfy all four.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies an "integration bottleneck" in AI-assisted programming — a phenomenon where relevant, repair-worthy contributions reach the user but fail to become actionable at the point of receipt, situated in Norman's gulf of evaluation. Through corpus analysis and a multi-turn probe, the authors argue this is a candidate phenomenon distinct from prompt-writing challenges, and find that no existing mechanism satisfies all four proposed requirements for an "accepted-constraint ledger."
AI.motivation: AI-assisted programming research has focused heavily on the gulf of execution (crafting effective prompts), while neglecting the gulf of evaluation — specifically, why useful repair contributions that reach the user sometimes fail to be acted upon. The authors aim to identify and characterize this underexplored breakdown point in human-AI programming interaction.
AI.method: Two-part methodology: (1) An eighteen-case corpus analysis of publicly shared AI-assisted development accounts, identifying instances of the integration bottleneck, with within-case contrasts to isolate conditions for actionability. (2) A twenty-trial multi-turn probe across two current models testing for constraint loss, with a ten-trial extension using explicit restructuring requests, to isolate and eliminate "regeneration" as a sufficient explanation for the phenomenon.
AI.result: Two clear cases (plus one inferential boundary case) of the integration bottleneck were found in the corpus, both at the interpretation stage of evaluation. Within-case contrasts suggested actionability hinges on whether a contribution can be restated as an instruction without intervening judgment. In Study 2, 15 of 20 narrow trials showed no constraint loss, and 8 of 10 extended trials likewise; regeneration was removed as a sufficient explanation. Twelve existing mechanisms were analyzed against four requirements for an accepted-constraint ledger; none satisfied all four.
AI.conclusion: The integration bottleneck is reported as a candidate phenomenon warranting dedicated study, not an established regularity, given the retrospective self-report nature of the evidence. The paper specifies four interaction requirements for an accepted-constraint ledger and demonstrates that no currently documented mechanism meets them all, pointing to a design gap in AI-assisted programming tools.

title: AgentGUI: An Interface for Observing and Steering Long-Running AI Agents
summary: AI agents are increasingly adept at tackling complex, long-running tasks. With the rapid surge of autonomous capabilities, human oversight is systematically lagging behind due to limited human-centered interfacing. Aiming to address this, we introduce AgentGUI, a user-friendly, locally hosted GUI for seamlessly observing and steering AI agents amid multiple concurrent, long-running sessions. AgentGUI features 1) rich agent trajectory visualizations, 2) effective manual and automated steering, and 3) integration with and coordination between open-source and frontier agent frameworks. A controlled user study demonstrates statistically significant reduction in the time it takes to identify key elements from agent traces (38% faster, p = 0.023). In a preliminary experiment, AgentGUI's automated drift prevention feature raises the task completion rate of small local agents by as high as 34pp across a 0.8B--9B model ladder (N=50 runs per model). AgentGUI is publicly available through its project website (https://agent-gui-project.github.io) and open-source repository (https://github.com/eth-medical-ai-lab/agent-gui), along with a demo video (https://youtube.com/watch?v=GSDyxN1gTF0).

AI.tldr: AgentGUI is a locally hosted GUI that enables seamless human observation and steering of multiple concurrent AI agents, featuring trajectory visualizations, manual/automated intervention tools, and cross-framework integration. User studies show 38% faster trace analysis and up to 34pp improvement in task completion via automated drift prevention.
AI.motivation: As AI agents grow more autonomous in handling complex, long-running tasks, human oversight interfaces have not kept pace. There is a critical gap in human-centered tooling for monitoring and intervening across multiple concurrent agent sessions, which AgentGUI aims to fill.
AI.method: AgentGUI is built as a locally hosted GUI with three core capabilities: (1) rich visualizations of agent trajectories, (2) manual and automated steering mechanisms (including drift prevention), and (3) integration with both open-source and frontier agent frameworks. Evaluation consists of a controlled user study measuring time-to-identify key elements in agent traces, and a preliminary experiment testing automated drift prevention across models ranging from 0.8B to 9B parameters (N=50 runs per model).
AI.result: The controlled user study demonstrates a statistically significant 38% reduction in time required to identify key elements from agent traces (p = 0.023). The automated drift prevention feature improves task completion rates by up to 34 percentage points across the 0.8B–9B model ladder in preliminary experiments (N=50 per model).
AI.conclusion: AgentGUI effectively bridges the gap between autonomous agent capabilities and human oversight, providing measurable benefits in both human efficiency (faster trace analysis) and agent performance (improved task completion via drift prevention). The open-source release promotes further adoption and development.

title: Beyond Action Imitation: Learning a Decision-Aware User Simulator for Online Advertising
summary: Recent advances in LLM-based user simulation have shown promise for offline evaluation of recommendation and advertising systems. However, existing simulators typically infer user preferences from single-domain interaction histories and are primarily optimized to reproduce observable actions such as clicks. Consequently, they capture only a partial view of user preferences, while action-only prediction easily induces model shortcuts and limits both the fidelity and diagnostic value of simulation. To address these challenges, we propose DASH, a decision-aware user simulator that jointly generates thinking traces and predicts behavioral actions from heterogeneous cross-domain histories. DASH first introduces a Context Engineering stage that folds heterogeneous cross-domain histories into decision-relevant context, together with prompt optimization for effective reasoning over the folded context. To train a user simulator, DASH distills thinking trajectories from strong LLMs as SFT data, and further tailors a rubric-based reward model that evaluates thinking traces along form, content, and logic for RL training. Combined with the action reward, these signals jointly improve action prediction and thinking quality. Extensive experiments on real-world Tencent advertising data spanning five heterogeneous content domains demonstrate the effectiveness, efficiency, fidelity, and diagnostic value of DASH.

AI.tldr: DASH is a decision-aware user simulator that jointly generates thinking traces and predicts actions from heterogeneous cross-domain histories, using context engineering, LLM distillation, and rubric-based RL to improve simulation fidelity and diagnostic value for recommendation/advertising systems.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based user simulators for recommendation and advertising (1) infer preferences from only single-domain histories, yielding a partial view of user preferences, and (2) optimize solely for action reproduction (e.g., clicks), which induces model shortcuts and limits simulation fidelity and diagnostic value.
AI.method: DASH operates in two stages: (1) Context Engineering — folds heterogeneous cross-domain histories into decision-relevant context with prompt optimization for effective reasoning; (2) Simulator Training — distills thinking trajectories from strong LLMs as SFT data, then designs a rubric-based reward model evaluating thinking traces along form, content, and logic dimensions, combined with action rewards for RL training to jointly improve action prediction and thinking quality.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on real-world Tencent advertising data across five heterogeneous content domains demonstrate DASH's effectiveness, efficiency, fidelity, and diagnostic value.
AI.conclusion: DASH advances user simulation by incorporating cross-domain reasoning traces alongside action prediction, overcoming the limitations of single-domain, action-only simulators and providing a more faithful and diagnostically useful tool for offline evaluation of advertising and recommendation systems.

title: Eco3S: Complex Socio-Economic System Simulation via Agent-Based Models
summary: The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) has renewed interest in agent-based modeling (ABM). However, current LLM-based ABM research faces several key challenges: modeling evolving agent-environment interactions, enabling flexible counterfactual reasoning, and automating simulation workflows for scientific research. In this paper, we propose Eco3S, a socio-economic system simulation framework for economic research and policy analysis that addresses these challenges through three key mechanisms: (1) Co-evolving Environment Design, a bidirectional feedback loop where agents and the environment co-evolve, producing realistic emergent behaviors; (2) Structural Causal Simulation, a structural causal model (SCM)-inspired counterfactual mechanism that allows flexible interventions for diverse causal inference tasks; (3) Simulation-Analysis-Refinement Paradigm, a self-corrective mechanism that iteratively refines experimental designs based on prior simulation results. Experiments on diverse economic scenarios confirm \textit{Eco3S}'s effectiveness in replicating multiple established economic studies (canal decay, origins of governance, and information propagation) and phenomena across domains. Additional results further demonstrate its scalability and generalizability, highlighting the framework's potential for rigorous economic research and policy-making.

AI.tldr: Eco3S is an LLM-based socio-economic simulation framework featuring co-evolving agent-environment dynamics, SCM-inspired counterfactual reasoning, and an iterative self-corrective paradigm, validated across multiple economic scenarios.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based ABM research suffers from three limitations: inability to model evolving agent-environment interactions, lack of flexible counterfactual reasoning mechanisms, and absence of automated simulation workflow refinement for rigorous scientific inquiry.
AI.method: Eco3S introduces three mechanisms: (1) Co-evolving Environment Design — a bidirectional feedback loop between agents and environment; (2) Structural Causal Simulation — an SCM-inspired intervention mechanism for causal inference; (3) Simulation-Analysis-Refinement Paradigm — iterative, self-corrective experimental design refinement based on prior results.
AI.result: Eco3S successfully replicates multiple established economic studies — canal decay, origins of governance, and information propagation — and demonstrates scalability and generalizability across diverse economic domains.
AI.conclusion: Eco3S offers a robust, generalizable, and scalable framework suitable for rigorous economic research and evidence-based policy-making, advancing the state of LLM-driven ABM.

title: Fingerprint-Driven Automation: Coupling Reconnaissance with POC Verification
summary: In the field of network security confrontation, reconnaissance is the first and most critical step. Accurate, efficient, and comprehensive reconnaissance can help network security workers more fully understand the target's current state, identify potential weaknesses, and formulate a targeted attack strategy. However, there are some problems in the existing tools on the market, such as low accuracy of the collected information, lack of concealment, time-consuming, low or high integration of tools, which makes them difficult to start using. With the continuous development of technology, systems need to continuously upgrade their technologies and strategies, and expand new functions. The scalability of tool functions is also one of the factors that need to be taken into consideration. These problems in the practice of network security have a serious impact on user experience and work efficiency. In view of this, a more user-friendly, more automated reconnaissance and vulnerability verification tool is designed.This paper proposes to develop a highly automated reconnaissance and vulnerability verification tool. This paper presents the tool functions and conducts the basic design. Finally, we implement and test all the functions specifically to verify the feasibility of the tool functions and highlight the advantages of this tool in terms of automation, retrieval, and use in network security operations.Through the test of the online security simulation range, the results show that this tool can complete the automatic reconnaissance and in-depth data processing of specific targets, and conduct automatic vulnerability detection and verification.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the design, implementation, and testing of a highly automated reconnaissance and vulnerability verification tool aimed at overcoming limitations of existing network security tools, such as low accuracy, poor concealment, high time consumption, and poor scalability.
AI.motivation: Existing network reconnaissance tools suffer from low information accuracy, lack of stealth, time-consuming operation, and either excessively low or high integration — making them difficult to use. Additionally, limited extensibility hampers adaptation to evolving technologies. These issues severely degrade user experience and operational efficiency in network security practice.
AI.method: The authors propose and design a highly automated reconnaissance and vulnerability verification tool. They specify tool functions, conduct basic design, implement all functions, and perform testing on an online security simulation range to validate feasibility and highlight advantages in automation, information retrieval, and usability.
AI.result: Testing on the online security simulation range demonstrates that the tool successfully performs automatic reconnaissance with in-depth data processing on specific targets, and conducts automated vulnerability detection and verification.
AI.conclusion: The implemented tool proves feasible and offers significant advantages in automation, retrieval, and ease of use for network security operations, addressing the key deficiencies of existing reconnaissance tools.

title: Automorphism-Induced Non-Canonicity in Top-k Explanations of Graph Neural Networks
summary: A gradient-based GNN explainer given a molecule with two chemically equivalent nitro groups assigns them attribution scores that are equal to the last bit. It cannot do otherwise: message passing is exactly permutation equivariant, so any automorphism of the input leaves every attribution invariant. Yet the standard report, the top-k edges, names one of the two, and which one is settled by the order of an array. We show this is a structural obstruction rather than an implementation slip. When no minimal valid explanation is fixed by the input's automorphism group, no rule can be single-valued, minimal and symmetry-respecting at once. For the exact-k reports used in practice we give a parameter-free criterion, mechanised in Lean 4 with no axiom dependencies, that decides from the graph alone whether every score-optimal report of that size must split an orbit. Across 21298 instance-budget decisions the criterion agrees with a mechanical model-equivalence check without exception, and no severing case we found admitted a neutral alternative. The obstruction is common. Nontrivial automorphisms occur in 93.4% of Mutagenicity, the dataset the seminal explainability papers use, so the measure-zero dismissal of symmetric inputs, sound on the continuous domains it was made for, collapses here. At the sparsity budget those papers report, 24.0% of molecules with two interchangeable nitro groups (6 of 25) surface exactly one of them, every one arbitrary under mechanical verification. A model's blindness also manufactures symmetry: every MUTAG molecule contains atoms chemistry separates and the network provably cannot, and a matched control shows the resolution is set by what the model reads rather than how it is parameterised. Reporting orbits removes the arbitrariness at 0.11 ms and 0.43 extra edges per graph.

AI.tldr: GNN explainers produce arbitrary, symmetry-breaking attributions for chemically equivalent substructures because the explanation task itself admits no single-valued, minimal, symmetry-respecting rule when the input's automorphism group does not fix a unique minimal explanation. The paper provides a parameter-free criterion, mechanised in Lean 4, to detect this obstruction, shows it is widespread in benchmark datasets like Mutagenicity, and advocates reporting entire orbits instead of top-k edges to eliminate arbitrariness.
AI.motivation: Current GNN explainers report top-k edges, but due to permutation equivariance, chemically equivalent substructures (e.g., two nitro groups related by molecular symmetry) receive identical attribution scores. When forced to select a subset, the tie is broken arbitrarily by implementation details like array ordering, producing explanations that appear scientifically meaningful but are in fact spurious artifacts. The authors argue this is not merely an implementation bug but a fundamental structural obstruction: the explainability task itself is ill-posed under symmetry constraints.
AI.method: The authors formalise the problem as a tension between three desiderata — single-valuedness, minimality, and symmetry-respect — and prove that when no minimal valid explanation is fixed pointwise by the input's automorphism group, no explanation rule can satisfy all three simultaneously. They develop a parameter-free, graph-theoretic criterion that decides, for exact-k reports, whether every score-optimal report must split an orbit. This criterion is fully mechanised in the Lean 4 proof assistant with no axiom dependencies. The criterion is validated against a mechanical model-equivalence check across 21,298 instance-budget decisions with zero discrepancies. They further analyse the prevalence of nontrivial automorphisms in the Mutagenicity dataset and demonstrate that even chemically distinct atoms can become indistinguishable to a GNN, manufacturing additional symmetry.
AI.result: Nontrivial automorphisms occur in 93.4% of Mutagenicity molecules. At standard sparsity budgets, 24.0% of molecules containing two interchangeable nitro groups (6 of 25) surface exactly one arbitrarily. The proposed orbit-based reporting resolves this arbitrariness at a cost of only 0.11 ms and 0.43 extra edges per graph. The Lean 4 mechanised criterion matches model-equivalence checks across all 21,298 tested cases. Additionally, every MUTAG molecule contains atoms that chemistry distinguishes but the GNN provably cannot, meaning the network itself manufactures symmetry beyond molecular topology.
AI.conclusion: The arbitrariness in GNN explanations from symmetric inputs is a structural inevitability, not an implementation flaw. Reporting entire automorphism orbits rather than individual edges eliminates the problem at negligible computational cost. Researchers should adopt orbit-level reporting as standard practice, and the Lean-formalised criterion provides a rigorous, machine-checkable test for when this obstruction arises.

title: MultiFixer: A Coordinator-Proposer Based Multi-Agent Framework For Fixing Multi-Hunk Bugs
comment: Accepted to 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026)
summary: Automated Program Repair (APR) has benefited greatly from Large Language Models (LLMs), but existing LLM-based APR methods still struggle with multi-hunk bugs that require coordinated changes across multiple locations. These bugs demand repository-level context understanding, repair-order scheduling, and effective hunk-level patch generation and selection. To address these challenges, we propose MultiFixer, a novel Coordinator-Proposer based multi-agent framework for multi-hunk repair. MultiFixer performs tool-augmented bug analysis, constructs fine-grained repair context, iteratively generates patches through a Coordinator-Proposer architecture, and applies two-stage patch refinement for syntactic and semantic correctness. We evaluate MultiFixer on 835 bugs from Defects4J and three vulnerability benchmarks. On Defects4J, MultiFixer fixes 326 bugs, including 62 multi-method and 27 multi-file bugs, and outperforms prior APR baselines in the reported comparisons with the same base model. Moreover, MultiFixer also fixes 46 multi-hunk bugs among 95 unique fixes. When combined with Claude-3.5-Sonnet, MultiFixer repairs 420 bugs, establishing a new state of the art on Defects4J. On VUL4J, MultiFixer repairs 24 real-world vulnerabilities, including 5 multi-hunk cases. On the multi-hunk subsets of SEC-bench and PatchEval, MultiFixer fixes 11 and 19 vulnerabilities, respectively, outperforming all compared baselines under GPT-3.5. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of MultiFixer for multi-hunk repair.

AI.tldr: MultiFixer is a multi-agent APR framework using a Coordinator-Proposer architecture with tool-augmented bug analysis and two-stage patch refinement, achieving state-of-the-art results on Defects4J (420 bugs fixed with Claude-3.5-Sonnet) and excelling at multi-hunk bug repair across vulnerability benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based APR methods struggle with multi-hunk bugs requiring coordinated changes across multiple locations, due to three core challenges: repository-level context understanding, repair-order scheduling, and effective hunk-level patch generation and selection.
AI.method: MultiFixer is a Coordinator-Proposer multi-agent framework featuring: (1) tool-augmented bug analysis for fine-grained repair context construction, (2) an iterative Coordinator-Proposer architecture that schedules and generates hunk-level patches, and (3) a two-stage patch refinement process addressing both syntactic and semantic correctness.
AI.result: On Defects4J (835 bugs), MultiFixer fixes 326 bugs (including 62 multi-method and 27 multi-file bugs) and achieves 46 multi-hunk fixes among 95 unique fixes. With Claude-3.5-Sonnet, it repairs 420 bugs — a new SOTA. On VUL4J, it fixes 24 real-world vulnerabilities (5 multi-hunk). On SEC-bench and PatchEval multi-hunk subsets, it fixes 11 and 19 vulnerabilities respectively, outperforming all GPT-3.5 baselines.
AI.conclusion: MultiFixer demonstrates that a coordinated multi-agent approach with structured repair context and iterative refinement substantially improves multi-hunk bug repair, establishing new state-of-the-art performance on Defects4J and strong results across vulnerability benchmarks.

title: A Design Study on Voice-based Interaction for Immersive Network Visualization and Analysis
summary: Visual network analysis leverages network visualization authoring techniques to facilitate sensemaking, serendipitous discovery, and hypothesis verification on network data. However, transferring the same paradigm to immersive environments is non-trivial due to insufficient UI affordance for authoring operations. Researchers have studied combining multiple modalities for interactions, but the high learning curve of such input systems limits their adoption by typical data analysts, let alone for network analytics. In this work, we investigate the advantages and limitations of voice as the primary input modality with a research-through-design (RtD) study, in which we design a system that supports voice-based interactions for immersive network visualization facilitated by Large Language Models (LLMs). Through a user study on social network data analysis with participants from social science and computer science backgrounds, we find that voice interactions can improve perceived usability relative to controller-based interaction and lower the cognitive effort of formulating commands, since users can express intent in natural language rather than compressing it into terse instructions. We discuss design implications for immersive visualizations, highlighting how usability limits adoption while simplified interactions and voice-based controls enhance fluidity and support complex, multi-parameter operations.

AI.tldr: This paper explores voice as a primary input modality for immersive network visualization, using LLMs to interpret natural language commands. A user study shows voice interaction improves perceived usability and reduces cognitive effort compared to controller-based input, with design implications for immersive analytics.
AI.motivation: Transferring visual network analysis to immersive environments (VR/AR) is challenging because existing UI affordances for authoring operations are insufficient. While multimodal interaction has been explored, the high learning curve of such systems limits adoption by typical data analysts. The authors investigate whether voice input, facilitated by LLMs, can overcome these barriers.
AI.method: A research-through-design (RtD) methodology is employed. The authors designed a system supporting voice-based interactions for immersive network visualization, powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) to interpret natural language commands. A user study was conducted on social network data analysis with participants from both social science and computer science backgrounds, comparing voice interaction against controller-based interaction.
AI.result: Voice interactions improved perceived usability relative to controller-based interaction and lowered the cognitive effort of formulating commands. Users benefited from expressing intent in natural language rather than compressing it into terse instructions.
AI.conclusion: Usability limits the adoption of immersive visualizations. Simplified interactions and voice-based controls enhance fluidity and support complex, multi-parameter operations. The paper provides design implications for future immersive visualization systems incorporating voice as a primary modality.

title: When Synthetic Users Fail: A Cross-Domain Benchmark of LLM-Simulated Human Survey Responses
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Preprint; under review
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as synthetic users, stand-ins for human respondents whose simulated answers feed product, policy, and market decisions. We ask when this substitution is valid and when it fails, and package the answer as an evaluation framework for intelligent synthetic-user systems. A single protocol, run across four models spanning two families and an 8B-to-frontier capability range, is applied to two independent domains of real human-response data: U.S. general social attitudes (General Social Survey) and cross-cultural values (World Values Survey). Every model is benchmarked against a suite of non-LLM baselines fit on held-out human data. Under demographic prompting and the survey-simulation protocols we test, two failures replicate across both domains, all four models, and both families. First, at the individual level no LLM beats even the strongest baseline; on cross-cultural values every model falls well below it, and the gap survives distance-aware and proper scoring. Second, models systematically over-determine demographics, treating identity as far more predictive of attitudes than it is among real people, a distortion present for nearly every question-group combination and robust to a coding-invariant measure. Neither failure is remedied by a larger, more capable model. A decision-impact analysis shows why this matters in practice: on a segment-targeting task the models inflate between-segment gaps two to fourfold, would direct a team to the wrong segment in half of U.S. and most cross-cultural cases, and manufacture segment splits that do not exist in real people. We make the cross-domain benchmark and the evaluation framework available on request, so that teams can determine in advance when synthetic-user evidence is safe for decision support and when it is not.

AI.tldr: LLMs used as synthetic users for survey responses fail at the individual level (no model beats strong non-LLM baselines) and systematically over-determine demographics, treating identity as far more predictive of attitudes than in real humans. These failures persist across models, domains, and capabilities, and cause inflating between-segment gaps and targeting errors in practical decisions.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed as synthetic users — stand-ins for human respondents in surveys that inform product, policy, and market decisions. The authors ask when this substitution is valid versus when it fails, and aim to build an evaluation framework so teams can determine in advance whether synthetic-user evidence is safe for decision support.
AI.method: A single evaluation protocol is applied across four models (spanning two model families and an 8B-to-frontier capability range) on two independent real human-response datasets: the U.S. General Social Survey and the World Values Survey (cross-cultural values). Each LLM is benchmarked against multiple non-LLM baselines fitted on held-out human data. Demographic prompting and standard survey-simulation protocols are used. Metrics include individual-level accuracy, proper scoring rules, distance-aware scoring, a coding-invariant measure of demographic over-determination, and a decision-impact analysis via a segment-targeting task.
AI.result: Two failures replicate across both domains, all four models, and both families: (1) No LLM beats the strongest non-LLM baseline at the individual level; on cross-cultural values all models fall well below it. (2) Models systematically over-determine demographics, treating identity as far more predictive of attitudes than in real people — this holds for nearly every question-group combination. Larger, more capable models do not remedy either failure. The decision-impact analysis shows models inflate between-segment gaps 2–4×, direct teams to the wrong segment in half of U.S. cases and most cross-cultural cases, and manufacture non-existent segment splits.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based synthetic users are not yet reliable substitutes for human respondents under current survey-simulation protocols. The failures are systematic, robust, and not resolved by scaling model capability. The authors offer their cross-domain benchmark and evaluation framework so practitioners can assess when synthetic-user evidence is safe for decision support and when human data remains indispensable.

title: IMFuse: Instance-Aware Multi-Layer Fusion for LLM-Enhanced Sequential Recommendation
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, and 9 tables. Yuheng Zheng and Yu Cui contributed equally. Jiawei Chen is the corresponding author
summary: Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly enhanced sequential recommendation by encoding rich item textual information into semantic representations. However, existing methods typically rely on the final-layer hidden states of LLMs, overlooking potentially useful semantic signals encoded in other layers. Through empirical analysis, we reveal the limitations of this practice: final-layer representations often suffer from dimensional collapse, whereas intermediate layers preserve complementary, coarse-to-fine semantic knowledge. Furthermore, we observe that different items exhibit heterogeneous layer-wise representation evolution, making a uniform layer selection sub-optimal. To bridge this gap, we propose IMFuse, an instance-aware multi-layer fusion strategy designed for LLM-enhanced recommendation. Instead of relying on a single layer, IMFuse adaptively aggregates multi-layer semantic information by learning global dimension-wise layer preferences to capture general semantic contributions. To address item-level heterogeneity, IMFuse introduces an instance-aware expert modulation mechanism that dynamically adjusts these global preferences, generating personalized, item-specific semantic representations. Extensive experiments across four real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of IMFuse. It consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with an average relative improvement of 6.72%, while introducing limited parameter and computational overhead.

AI.tldr: IMFuse proposes an adaptive multi-layer fusion strategy for LLM-enhanced sequential recommendation that dynamically aggregates semantic representations from all transformer layers rather than relying solely on the final layer, addressing both dimensional collapse in final-layer states and item-level heterogeneity in layer-wise representation evolution.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based sequential recommendation methods use only final-layer hidden states, but empirical analysis reveals two key limitations: (1) final-layer representations suffer from dimensional collapse, losing semantic diversity; (2) intermediate layers encode complementary coarse-to-fine semantic knowledge. Additionally, different items exhibit heterogeneous layer-wise representation evolution, making uniform layer selection sub-optimal.
AI.method: IMFuse introduces two core components: (1) global dimension-wise layer preferences that are learned to capture general semantic contributions across layers; (2) an instance-aware expert modulation mechanism that dynamically adjusts these global preferences per item, generating personalized item-specific semantic representations through adaptive multi-layer aggregation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets show IMFuse consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with an average relative improvement of 6.72%, while introducing limited parameter and computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: Multi-layer semantic fusion with instance-aware modulation is an effective and efficient approach for LLM-enhanced sequential recommendation, overcoming the limitations of single-layer representations and addressing item-level heterogeneity.

title: Fewer Clarifications, Better Code: Benchmarking Cross-Session Personalized Ambiguity Adaptation in Coding Assistants
summary: AI-assisted coding increasingly translates informal user intent into executable software, yet coding requests often contain ambiguities that recur in user-specific ways across tasks and sessions. Existing disambiguation methods typically address each ambiguous request in isolation within the current coding session, often through eliciting additional clarification. However, whether resolved session history from the same user can serve as memory for resolving recurring personalized ambiguity in a newly opened session remains underexplored. We formulate personalized ambiguity adaptation as a new task: given a user's previously resolved coding sessions and a new ambiguous request, an assistant should identify the recurring ambiguity pattern, produce the intended executable solution, and minimize clarification. To benchmark this task, we introduce CAPA, which characterizes personalized coding ambiguity through six mechanisms and injects these mechanisms into unambiguous executable tasks using a controlled three-stage generation pipeline. CAPA contains 600 coding sessions across 60 balanced user--ambiguity cells, including 300 held-out evaluation sessions. We evaluate 12 recent LLMs under no-history and same-user-history conditions using executable success, first-turn success, and turns-to-completion. Our analyses examine task difficulty, user identity, and memory-based history use, and we further propose same-user history gating as a lightweight inference-time method. CAPA provides a foundation for developing long-term coding assistants that better align generated code with user intent while reducing repeated clarification.

AI.tldr: CAPA is a benchmark for evaluating how well AI coding assistants leverage a user's past resolved sessions to disambiguate recurring personalized ambiguities in new coding requests, featuring 600 sessions across 60 user-ambiguity cells with six ambiguity mechanisms, and evaluating 12 LLMs under different history conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing disambiguation methods treat each ambiguous coding request in isolation within a single session, requiring repeated clarification. The core insight is that users exhibit recurring, personalized ambiguity patterns across tasks and sessions, yet leveraging prior resolved session history as memory for resolving such ambiguities in new sessions remains underexplored.
AI.method: The authors formalize personalized ambiguity adaptation as a new task and introduce CAPA, a benchmark constructed via a controlled three-stage generation pipeline. CAPA characterizes personalized coding ambiguity through six distinct mechanisms, injected into unambiguous executable tasks. The dataset contains 600 coding sessions across 60 user-ambiguity cells (balanced design), with 300 held-out evaluation sessions. Evaluation uses executable success, first-turn success, and turns-to-completion as metrics under no-history and same-user-history conditions across 12 recent LLMs. They also propose same-user history gating as a lightweight inference-time method.
AI.result: Evaluation of 12 LLMs reveals performance variations under no-history versus same-user-history conditions across the three metrics. The analyses examine task difficulty effects, user identity effects, and memory-based history utilization patterns, with the proposed history gating method offering a lightweight approach to improve ambiguity resolution.
AI.conclusion: CAPA provides a foundation for developing long-term coding assistants that better align generated code with user intent while reducing repeated clarification, highlighting the underexplored potential of session history as personalized memory.

title: Graph Is the Verifier: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Interprocedural Vulnerability Detection
summary: Real-world vulnerabilities often span multiple functions, yet most learning-based detectors classify each function in isolation: on a sample of real CVEs, we find that 71.7% of vulnerable functions require evidence from outside the function to be classified correctly. Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) could close this gap by enabling a model to gather that evidence itself, but it lacks a reliable reward, since a reward defined on the final verdict alone can be obtained without performing any investigation. We propose VulAgentRL, an agentic RL framework for interprocedural vulnerability detection built on a Code Property Graph (CPG). The CPG serves two roles: at inference time the policy queries it for callers, callees, dataflow, and other queries, and at training time the same graph verifies the evidence the policy cites. Because every CPG node carries a persistent integer identifier, this verification is an exact comparison rather than a textual match, so the reward credits verdicts that are supported by evidence. We further initialize the policy by distilling teacher investigations, and show that this warm start is necessary, since RL cannot acquire tool-use behavior it never samples. Under a repository-level split that prevents leakage, VulAgentRL outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, including frontier models, on the strict pair-wise-correct metric while issuing fewer tool calls, and its advantage persists on an out-of-distribution corpus and under class imbalance.

AI.tldr: VulAgentRL is an agentic reinforcement learning framework that detects interprocedural vulnerabilities by training a policy to query a Code Property Graph (CPG) for cross-function evidence, with graph-based reward verification ensuring verdicts are evidence-backed; it achieves state-of-the-art performance under strict repository-level splits.
AI.motivation: 71.7% of vulnerable functions in real CVEs require evidence from outside the function for correct classification, yet current learning-based detectors operate per-function in isolation. Agentic RL could address this by letting models gather evidence autonomously, but lacks a reliable reward signal — a reward based solely on final verdict can be achieved without meaningful investigation.
AI.method: VulAgentRL uses a Code Property Graph (CPG) for both inference and training. At inference, the policy queries the CPG for callers, callees, and dataflow information. At training, the CPG verifies cited evidence via persistent integer node identifiers, enabling exact comparison (not fuzzy text matching) to reward only evidence-supported verdicts. The policy is warm-started by distilling teacher investigations, which is shown necessary since RL cannot discover tool-use behaviors it never samples.
AI.result: Under a repository-level split preventing data leakage, VulAgentRL outperforms state-of-the-art baselines (including frontier models) on the strict pair-wise-correct metric while issuing fewer tool calls. Its advantage persists on out-of-distribution corpora and under class imbalance.
AI.conclusion: Agentic RL with CPG-based evidence verification is a viable and effective approach for interprocedural vulnerability detection. Warm-start initialization via distillation is critical for enabling tool-use behavior in RL, and the framework generalizes robustly beyond its training distribution.

title: MetaKoopman: Bayesian Meta-Learning of Koopman Operators for Modeling Structured Dynamics under Distribution Shifts
summary: Modeling and forecasting nonlinear dynamics under distribution shifts is essential for robust decision-making in real-world systems. In this work, we propose MetaKoopman, a Bayesian meta-learning framework for modeling nonlinear dynamics through linear latent representations. MetaKoopman learns a Matrix Normal-Inverse Wishart (MNIW) prior over the Koopman operator, enabling closed-form Bayesian updates conditioned on recent trajectory segments. Moreover, it provides a closed-form posterior predictive distribution over future state trajectories, capturing both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty in the learned dynamics. We evaluate MetaKoopman on a full-scale autonomous truck and trailer system across a wide range of adverse winter scenarios, including snow, ice, and mixed-friction conditions, as well as in simulated control tasks with diverse distribution shifts. MetaKoopman consistently outperforms prior approaches in multi-step prediction accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and robustness to distributional shifts. Field experiments further demonstrate its effectiveness in dynamically feasible motion planning, particularly during evasive maneuvers and operation at the limits of traction. Project website: https://mahmoud-selim.github.io/MetaKoopman/

AI.tldr: MetaKoopman is a Bayesian meta-learning framework that models nonlinear dynamics via linear latent representations with a Matrix Normal-Inverse Wishart prior over the Koopman operator, enabling closed-form Bayesian updates and posterior predictive distributions. It outperforms prior methods in prediction accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and robustness under distribution shifts, demonstrated on autonomous truck-trailer systems in adverse winter conditions.
AI.motivation: Real-world autonomous systems must model and forecast nonlinear dynamics under distribution shifts (e.g., varying road friction due to snow/ice). Existing approaches lack robust uncertainty quantification and fast adaptation, motivating a framework that combines Koopman operator theory with Bayesian meta-learning for reliable, uncertainty-aware predictions.
AI.method: MetaKoopman learns a Koopman operator—a linear latent representation of nonlinear dynamics—within a Bayesian meta-learning framework. It places a Matrix Normal-Inverse Wishart (MNIW) prior over the Koopman operator, which admits closed-form Bayesian updates given recent trajectory segments and yields a closed-form posterior predictive distribution over future states, capturing both epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty.
AI.result: MetaKoopman consistently outperforms prior approaches in multi-step prediction accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and robustness to distribution shifts. Evaluations include a full-scale autonomous truck-trailer system across snow, ice, and mixed-friction winter scenarios, simulated control tasks with diverse shifts, and field experiments demonstrating effective dynamically feasible motion planning during evasive maneuvers and at traction limits.
AI.conclusion: MetaKoopman provides a principled, uncertainty-aware approach to nonlinear dynamics modeling under distribution shifts, with strong empirical validation on safety-critical autonomous vehicle tasks. Its closed-form inference and predictive capabilities make it practical for real-time decision-making in dynamically challenging environments.

title: Tangling Pull Requests: Curating a Commit Untangling Dataset from Merged PRs
summary:
Composite commits (CC), in which multiple unrelated changes are bundled into a single commit, are frequent in software development and significantly hinder code comprehension and maintenance. Although machine learning-based methods have been developed to ``untangle'' such commits into smaller, coherent change sets, these methods require large-scale training data with correct untangling labels. Preparing such datasets is costly and typically requires expert labelling.
  In this study, we propose a scalable and cost-effective method for dataset construction by leveraging commits extracted from open-source repositories' pull requests (PRs). We empirically validated our dataset and found that when applying our filtering rules, PRs that, when viewed as a single commit, are tangled, yet each individual commit on the feature branch is atomic (ideal PRs), increased from 9.5% to 55%. This composite commits dataset is more than 5.7 times larger than previous heuristic-based datasets.
  Using our new dataset, we find that the PR-based dataset differs statistically from previous datasets directly constructed using Herzig's proposed heuristics even after accounting for our proposed rules that may alter CC or STS sizes. When constructing datasets using the previous heuristics, they differ statistically along dimensions that impact the confidence voters and are likely to impact learning-based approaches. We validate the impact on the original Herzig \etal method, which used confidence voters across our dataset.
  To show that our approach extends to other languages, we also create a Python dataset which we empirically validate, finding comparable rates for ideal PRs (56.5%).

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a scalable, cost-effective method for constructing composite commit datasets by leveraging pull requests from open-source repositories. Applying filtering rules increases the proportion of ideal PRs from 9.5% to 55%, yielding a dataset over 5.7× larger than prior heuristic-based datasets. The authors demonstrate statistical differences between their PR-based dataset and previous ones, validate these differences affect confidence-voter-based methods, and extend their approach to Python with comparable results (56.5%).
AI.motivation: Existing machine learning-based commit untangling methods require large-scale training data with correct labels, which is costly and typically demands expert annotation. The authors aim to address this bottleneck by developing a scalable, cost-effective dataset construction approach.
AI.method: The method extracts commits from open-source repositories' pull requests (PRs). Filtering rules are applied to identify "ideal PRs" — PRs that appear tangled when viewed as a single commit but whose individual feature-branch commits are each atomic. The resulting dataset is empirically validated and compared statistically against prior heuristic-based datasets (Herzig et al.) along dimensions affecting confidence voters.
AI.result: Filtering rules increased ideal PR rates from 9.5% to 55%. The resulting dataset is 5.7× larger than previous heuristic-based datasets. Statistical analysis reveals significant differences between the PR-based dataset and Herzig-style heuristic datasets, even after controlling for rule-induced size changes. These differences impact confidence-voter-based untangling methods. Extension to Python achieved a comparable ideal PR rate of 56.5%.
AI.conclusion: PR-based dataset construction is a viable, scalable, and cost-effective alternative to expert-labeled or purely heuristic-based datasets for commit untangling research. The approach generalizes across programming languages (Java, Python) and produces datasets that differ meaningfully from prior heuristic-derived datasets, with implications for training and evaluating learning-based untangling methods.

title: Galvanic Vestibular Stimulation in Latent Space
summary: Galvanic vestibular stimulation (GVS) is widely used to modulate self-orientation, balance, and motion perception; the discriminability of frequency-encoded cues further suggests its potential as a standalone modality for embodied feedback. However, synthesizing GVS waveforms congruent with target events or bodily states remains challenging. GVS waveforms combine current direction, intensity, duration, and onset and offset transitions, yet how these parameters jointly shape users' perceptual and associative responses remains underexplored. To address this gap, we contribute a dataset linking GVS waveforms to free-form experience descriptions, as well as a retrieval-guided generative model for synthesizing candidate waveforms from target descriptions. The dataset comprises 100 GVS waveforms and 1,526 valid free-form sensation descriptions collected from 16 participants. Semantic analysis revealed diverse motion- and force-related sensations, localized bodily sensations, and situational associations. Compared with a participant-preserving permutation baseline, descriptions elicited by the same waveform covered fewer semantic categories (8.18 vs. 9.45) and exhibited a higher dominant-category proportion (26.97% vs. 21.25%; both P < 0.001). Building on this dataset, we implemented the generative model as a retrieval-guided one-dimensional convolutional variational autoencoder. An independent behavioral study recruited 10 participants who had not contributed to the dataset collection. Performance in discriminating congruent from incongruent waveform-visual cue pairings was significantly above chance, with an accuracy of 63.33%, d-prime = 0.70, and p < 0.001. Together, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of text-conditioned GVS synthesis and support the development of GVS as a programmable modality for semantically congruent embodied feedback across interactive scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a dataset linking GVS waveforms to free-form sensation descriptions and a retrieval-guided 1D convolutional VAE that synthesizes GVS waveforms from text. A behavioral study confirmed that generated waveforms produce semantically congruent sensations, with 63.33% discrimination accuracy (d'=0.70), establishing GVS as a programmable modality for embodied feedback.
AI.motivation: Synthesizing GVS waveforms that are semantically congruent with target events or bodily states is challenging because the joint influence of current direction, intensity, duration, and onset/offset transitions on users' perceptual and associative responses remains underexplored. The authors aim to bridge this gap to enable GVS as a standalone, programmable modality for embodied feedback.
AI.method: The authors collected a dataset of 100 GVS waveforms and 1,526 free-form descriptions from 16 participants. Semantic analysis validated within-waveform consistency. They then built a retrieval-guided one-dimensional convolutional variational autoencoder (VAE) to generate candidate GVS waveforms conditioned on text descriptions. An independent behavioral study with 10 naive participants tested discrimination of congruent vs. incongruent waveform-visual cue pairings.
AI.result: Same-waveform descriptions covered significantly fewer semantic categories (8.18 vs. 9.45) with higher dominant-category proportion (26.97% vs. 21.25%, both P<0.001) versus baseline. The generative model achieved 63.33% discrimination accuracy (d'=0.70, p<0.001), significantly above chance.
AI.conclusion: Text-conditioned GVS waveform synthesis is feasible. The results support developing GVS as a programmable modality for semantically congruent embodied feedback in interactive scenarios.

title: Symphony of Bias: Exploring Gender Associations with Musical Instruments in Multimodal LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in everyday life and widely used for information seeking, raising concerns about their potential to perpetuate social biases and reinforce stereotypes. In this study, we investigate gender bias in LLMs through the lens of their associations with musical instruments. Building on social-science research on the cultural gender-typing of instruments, we introduce Symphony-Bias, a parallel multimodal dataset spanning text, vision, and audio. We evaluate ten multimodal models with diverse architectures and scales across 22 musical instruments, analyzing how they associate each instrument with three gender categories: {male, female, non-binary}, across three modalities: {text, vision, audio}. Our results show that 92\% of instrument-level outcomes align with prior social-science findings, with the harp and drums showing particularly consistent gendered associations across all evaluated models and modalities. We further find that alignment with social stereotypes is weakest in audio, stronger in vision, and strongest in text, suggesting that modality-specific representations can differentially amplify gendered associations with musical instruments.\footnote{The Symphony-Bias dataset will be publicly released upon acceptance of the paper.}

AI.tldr: This study introduces Symphony-Bias, a multimodal dataset to evaluate gender bias in LLMs through musical instrument associations, finding that 92% of outcomes align with prior social-science research, with bias strongest in text and weakest in audio modalities.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for information seeking in everyday life, raising concerns about perpetuating social biases. Prior social-science research has documented cultural gender-typing of musical instruments, but how multimodal models encode and amplify these associations across text, vision, and audio remains underexplored.
AI.method: The authors construct Symphony-Bias, a parallel multimodal dataset covering text, vision, and audio. They evaluate ten multimodal models with diverse architectures and scales across 22 musical instruments, probing associations with three gender categories (male, female, non-binary) across all three modalities.
AI.result: 92% of instrument-level outcomes align with prior social-science gender-typing findings. The harp and drums show particularly consistent gendered associations across all models and modalities. Modality-specific analysis reveals alignment with stereotypes is weakest in audio, stronger in vision, and strongest in text.
AI.conclusion: Modality-specific representations differentially amplify gendered associations with musical instruments, with text-based representations exhibiting the strongest stereotypical alignment. This highlights the need for debiasing strategies that account for modality-specific bias amplification in multimodal AI systems.

title: Learning from the Future: Privileged Self-Distillation for Sequential Recommendation
summary:
Sequential recommenders are commonly trained with one-hot next-item labels under a causal (prefix-only) objective aligned with inference. While deployment-compatible, this supervision offers little insight into relative preferences among non-target items. Yet logged interaction sequences contain an additional supervisory source: interactions following the target often reveal how user intent evolves, making the target easier to interpret. We treat these future interactions as training-only privileged information, available during learning but not at inference. This raises a natural question: can future interactions provide richer supervision while keeping training aligned with inference-time prediction?
  We propose Privileged Self-Distillation (PSD), a framework that separates learning-time information from inference-time information. PSD applies two attention masks to the same backbone: a future-aware view yields a privileged teacher distribution conditioned on past and future interactions, while a prefix-only view yields the student distribution used for deployment. Distilling the privileged distribution converts future interactions into training-only supervision rather than inference-time inputs. Since both views share a backbone, the teacher's advantage is purely informational, not architectural, removing the need for a separately pretrained teacher and letting its supervision adapt as the student evolves. PSD further uses an advantage-reachability gate to focus distillation on teacher signals likely supported by the observed prefix, along with a momentum-averaged teacher for stable targets. The framework is optimized end-to-end in a single stage, leaving the deployed model and inference cost unchanged. Experiments across public benchmarks and diverse backbones show consistent improvements.

AI.tldr: PSD uses future interactions as privileged training-only information to distil richer relative-preference signals into a standard prefix-only sequential recommender, requiring no architectural changes at inference.
AI.motivation: Standard causal sequential recommenders use one-hot next-item labels, which provide no relative preference signal among non-target items. However, logged sequences contain future interactions beyond the immediate target that reveal how user intent evolves. The challenge is leveraging this extra information without altering the inference-time model.
AI.method: Privileged Self-Distillation (PSD) applies two attention masks to a shared backbone: a future-aware mask produces a privileged teacher distribution (conditioned on past + future), and a prefix-only mask produces the student distribution (deployment-compatible). Distillation loss aligns the student to the teacher. An advantage-reachability gate focuses distillation on teacher signals plausibly supported by the observed prefix, and a momentum-averaged teacher stabilizes targets. Both views share one backbone, trained end-to-end in a single stage.
AI.result: PSD yields consistent improvements across public benchmarks and diverse backbone architectures without altering inference cost or deployed model structure.
AI.conclusion: Future interactions, treated as privileged information via self-distillation with a shared backbone, provide effective enriched supervision for sequential recommenders. The approach is architecture-agnostic, single-stage, and inference-cost-free.

title: AlphaSchema: Exploring the Space of Trading Semantics for LLM-Based Alpha Mining
summary: Automated alpha mining has increasingly adopted large language model (LLM) agents for factor generation and iterative discovery. However, existing LLM-based systems often delegate both factor construction and search decisions to the agent itself, without an explicit exploration space or a principled mechanism for navigating that space. As a result, exploration remains largely implicit and difficult to control or optimize systematically. We introduce AlphaSchema, which constructs and explores a structured space of trading semantics for alpha mining. Each point in this space is a schema plan composed of Event, Context, Qualities, Direction, and Output, specifying the semantics of a candidate factor before implementation. AlphaSchema decouples exploration from implementation: an LLM translates selected schema plans into executable factors, while evaluated rewards are accumulated to learn a surrogate model over the semantic space. An iterative selection mechanism uses this model to balance global exploration, surrogate-guided exploitation, and local mutation. Experiments on the Chinese stock market show that AlphaSchema discovers factor pools with strong predictive and portfolio performance. Further analyses show that the semantic search process navigates diverse regions while increasingly allocating evaluations toward high-reward regions, and that implementations of the same schema plans by different LLMs exhibit comparable predictive quality, suggesting that alpha mining quality is largely robust to the choice of LLM within our framework.

AI.tldr: AlphaSchema introduces a structured semantic space for alpha mining, decoupling exploration (schema plan selection) from implementation (LLM-based factor coding). An iterative surrogate-guided mechanism balances exploration and exploitation, yielding robust factor pools on Chinese stock market data.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based alpha mining systems conflate factor construction with search strategy, leaving exploration implicit and unsystematic. There is no explicit exploration space or principled navigation mechanism, making the process hard to control or optimize.
AI.method: AlphaSchema defines a structured semantic space where each point is a schema plan with five components: Event, Context, Qualities, Direction, and Output. Exploration is decoupled from implementation — an LLM translates selected schemas into executable factors. Evaluated rewards (predictive performance) are used to train a surrogate model over the semantic space. An iterative selection mechanism balances three strategies: global exploration, surrogate-guided exploitation, and local mutation of high-performing schemas.
AI.result: The discovered factor pools demonstrate strong predictive power and portfolio performance on the Chinese stock market. The semantic search navigates diverse regions while increasingly concentrating evaluations in high-reward areas. Additionally, different LLMs implementing the same schema plans yield comparable predictive quality, indicating robustness to LLM choice.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling semantic exploration from implementation via a structured schema space enables systematic, controllable alpha mining. The surrogate-guided search effectively balances exploration-exploitation trade-offs, and the framework is largely robust to the choice of underlying LLM, suggesting that the semantic schema plan is the primary driver of factor quality.

title: Not In My Git Yard: Catching Backdoors at Commit and Release Time
summary: Code-level backdoors-stealthy code changes that grant hidden privileges via secret triggers-pose a persistent threat to opensource software.
