Known attempts to inject such backdoors into widely used projects through malicious commits, tampered release packages, or compromised third-party dependencies, were stopped only by luck and manual review. Existing Continuous Integration (CI) pipelines cannot detect these attacks, and downstream binary analysis tools require substantial manual effort. In this work, we present Lily, an automated approach that strengthens open-source development and release processes against backdoor injection. Lily integrates a backdoor detection mechanism into (1) CI pipelines to block malicious commits, and (2) release vetting workflows to prevent tampered releases or compromised dependencies from entering large ecosystems, such as Linux distributions. Lily offers two key contributions. First, it enhances CI-compatible fuzzing with the capability to detect triggers of suspicious behavior based on historical and current software executions. This enables fast, precise backdoor detection suitable for both CI and update validation workflows. Second, it combines code change analysis with fuzzing data to precisely point maintainers to backdoor-revealing code regions, even when release updates modify millions of lines of code. We also outline five strategies attackers could use to evade Lily, and evaluate corresponding defenses. Our experiments across hundreds of benign and backdoored commits and releases show that Lily achieves high detection accuracy with low false alarm rates, reliably identifies malicious code, resists adversarial attempts, and would have prevented real-world backdoor incidents.

AI.tldr: Lily is an automated backdoor detection system that integrates into CI pipelines and release vetting workflows. It combines fuzzing with trigger detection based on historical/current execution differences and code change analysis to precisely identify malicious code regions, achieving high accuracy with low false alarm rates.
AI.motivation: Code-level backdoors in open-source software are a persistent threat, with existing detection relying on luck and manual review. CI pipelines cannot currently detect these attacks, and downstream binary analysis tools demand substantial manual effort.
AI.method: Lily employs two core techniques: (1) CI-compatible fuzzing enhanced with trigger detection that compares historical and current software executions to identify suspicious behavior; (2) code change analysis combined with fuzzing data to precisely localize backdoor-revealing code regions, even across large-scale release updates. The authors also outline five adversarial evasion strategies and corresponding defenses.
AI.result: Experiments across hundreds of benign and backdoored commits/releases demonstrate high detection accuracy, low false alarm rates, reliable malicious code identification, resistance to adversarial attempts, and successful prevention of real-world backdoor incidents.
AI.conclusion: Lily provides an effective, automated defense against code-level backdoors in open-source software by strengthening both CI pipelines and release vetting workflows, with proven real-world applicability.

title: High-Order Markov Blanket Discovery via a k-Order Relaxation of the Faithfulness Assumption
comment: 17 pages (9 pages main text + supplementary material), 4 figures, 8 tables, 3 algorithms. Accepted at the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI 2026). Code: https://github.com/lklee9/k-order-Markov-blanket
summary: The problem of learning the graphical Markov blanket (MB) of a variable from data has applications in many areas such as structure learning for Bayesian networks and Markov random fields, causal discovery, and feature selection. However, a common assumption most methods make is that the conditional independencies in the distribution imply the same separation in the graphical structure -- also known as the faithfulness assumption. Unfortunately, this assumption can be violated by higher-order dependencies such as XOR and parity-type relations, and -- on finite samples -- by empirical violations that, in extreme cases, even induce spurious dependencies absent from the true distribution. Therefore, in this paper we propose a "k-order" relaxation of the faithfulness assumption that captures parity type relationships between k+2 variables. We then propose a proof of concept algorithm called k-order Markov blanket (kOMB) that uses this relaxation for MB discovery. Finally, we empirically show how kOMB can recover the MB of a variable under both true and empirical violations of faithfulness. Code available at: https://github.com/lklee9/k-order-Markov-blanket

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a k-order relaxation of the faithfulness assumption to handle higher-order dependencies (e.g., XOR/parity relations) that violate standard faithfulness, and introduces kOMB, an algorithm for Markov blanket discovery under this relaxed assumption.
AI.motivation: Standard MB learning methods rely on the faithfulness assumption, which fails under higher-order dependencies like XOR/parity relations and can produce spurious dependencies on finite samples. No existing method adequately handles these systematic faithfulness violations.
AI.method: The authors introduce a k-order relaxation of faithfulness that captures parity-type relationships among k+2 variables, then develop kOMB (k-order Markov Blanket), a proof-of-concept algorithm leveraging this relaxation for MB discovery.
AI.result: Empirical results demonstrate that kOMB can recover the Markov blanket of a target variable under both true faithfulness violations (parity-type) and empirical violations arising from finite samples.
AI.conclusion: Relaxing faithfulness to k-order provides a principled way to handle parity-type dependencies in MB discovery, with kOMB serving as an effective proof of concept. Code is publicly available.

title: CodeSpec: Dual Executable Specifications for Agentic Long-Horizon Feature Development
summary: LLM-based code agents have advanced repository-level software development through iterative interaction with codebases and tools. However, feature development requires integrating new behaviors into existing architectures through coherent cross-component functional chains. Existing agents typically derive such chains through free-form reasoning, often producing unreliable feature designs with incomplete functional chains. Moreover, textual designs are difficult to verify and enforce, making it challenging to maintain design-implementation consistency throughout long-horizon development. We propose CodeSpec, a dual executable specification method for repository-level feature development. It builds reliable functional chains from evidence pairing sub-requirement semantics with repository architectures, then compiles them into complementary architecture and behavior specifications that check chain completeness and correctness while preserving design-implementation consistency over long interactions. On FeatureBench, which targets feature development in existing repositories, CodeSpec achieves 70.7%, 55.0%, and 49.9% pass rates under DeepSeek-V4-Pro, outperforming representative baselines such as Claude Code. Results on the repository generation benchmark NL2Repo-Bench further demonstrate its generalizability.

AI.tldr: CodeSpec introduces a dual executable specification method for LLM-based code agents that pairs sub-requirement semantics with repository architectures to build reliable functional chains, then compiles them into complementary architecture and behavior specifications to ensure chain completeness and design-implementation consistency during long-horizon feature development.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based code agents use free-form reasoning to derive functional chains for feature development, leading to unreliable feature designs with incomplete chains. Textual designs are difficult to verify and enforce, causing design-implementation inconsistency over long-horizon development tasks.
AI.method: CodeSpec employs a dual executable specification approach: (1) it constructs functional chains by pairing sub-requirement semantics with repository architectures using evidence-based reasoning; (2) it compiles these chains into complementary architecture specifications and behavior specifications that can be executed to check chain completeness and correctness; (3) the specifications persist throughout the development interaction to maintain design-implementation consistency.
AI.result: On FeatureBench, CodeSpec achieves 70.7%, 55.0%, and 49.9% pass rates under DeepSeek-V4-Pro, outperforming representative baselines including Claude Code. Generalizability is demonstrated on the NL2Repo-Bench repository generation benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Dual executable specifications offer an effective mechanism for enforcing reliable functional chain design and maintaining design-implementation consistency in LLM-based repository-level feature development, as evidenced by CodeSpec's superior performance over existing approaches.

title: Affective Tools for Thought: Towards Shared Attention and Affective Reorienting in AI-Supported Thinking
comment: 4 pages, 2-column ACM format. Accepted to the CHI 2026 Workshop on Tools for Thought: Understanding, Protecting, and Augmenting Human Cognition with Generative AI, April 16, 2026, Barcelona, Spain. Workshop website: https://ai-tools-for-thought.github.io/workshop/
summary: Current Tools for Thought (TfTs) treat affect as either friction that slows cognitive progress or a signal to optimise it. Drawing on enactive cognitive science, we argue that affect is constitutive of cognition: it reshapes the trajectory of thinking, not just the speed. We identify two core barriers for Affective TfTs: the lack of Shared Attention (caring, directed attention to the user's mode of engagement) and the lack of Affective Reorienting (the capacity to use emotional moments to open new trajectories rather than reinforcing predetermined ones), and propose three design strategies that address both: Chain of Emotion X Chain of Thought, Affective Mirror, and Prompted Reorienting. The strategies are grounded in empirical findings from a study of a touch-aware conversational agent for embodied craft learning, and are oriented as provocations for future design.

AI.tldr: Current Tools for Thought treat affect as friction or a signal to optimize. Drawing on enactive cognitive science, this paper argues affect is constitutive of cognition, reshaping thinking trajectories. It identifies two barriers—lack of Shared Attention and Affective Reorienting—and proposes three design strategies grounded in an empirical study of a touch-aware conversational agent for embodied craft learning.
AI.motivation: Existing Tools for Thought (TfTs) instrumentalize affect—treating it merely as friction to overcome or a signal to optimize cognitive performance. This framing misses affect's deeper role. The authors draw on enactive cognitive science (which posits cognition as embodied, situated, and dynamically co-constructed) to argue that affect is constitutive of cognition itself, fundamentally reshaping the trajectory of thinking rather than just modulating its speed or efficiency.
AI.method: The paper is primarily conceptual and design-oriented. It identifies two core barriers (lack of Shared Attention and lack of Affective Reorienting) through theoretical synthesis of enactive cognitive science. It then proposes three design strategies: (1) Chain of Emotion × Chain of Thought, (2) Affective Mirror, and (3) Prompted Reorienting. These strategies are grounded in empirical findings from a study involving a touch-aware conversational agent designed for embodied craft learning.
AI.result: Two core barriers were identified: (1) Shared Attention — the lack of caring, directed attention toward the user's mode of engagement, and (2) Affective Reorienting — the inability of current systems to leverage emotional moments to open new cognitive trajectories rather than reinforcing predetermined ones. Three design strategies addressing both barriers were proposed and grounded in empirical findings from the embodied craft learning study.
AI.conclusion: Affective TfTs must move beyond treating emotion as a variable to be optimized and instead recognize affect as a constitutive, trajectory-shaping force in cognition. The proposed design strategies—Chain of Emotion × Chain of Thought, Affective Mirror, and Prompted Reorienting—serve as provocations to guide future design toward systems that genuinely participate in the co-construction of thinking.

title: Diagnosing Fine-Grained Inconsistency Classification in Financial Disclosure Text
summary: Financial disclosures contain numerical claims, temporal statements, entity references, policy commitments, and risk descriptions that may conflict in qualitatively different ways. Detecting a conflict is only the first step: review workflows may also need to determine its type, since numerical, temporal, referential, factual, and normative inconsistencies require different evidence and downstream checks. We study this problem as fine-grained inconsistency classification. Using a fixed 5,940-instance snapshot of SBID-FD, a synthetic financial-disclosure benchmark with 11 inconsistency labels and paired reference evidence spans, we compare frozen embedding classifiers, fine-tuned encoders, evidence-augmented classifiers, prompted large language models, and LoRA-adapted generative models under a shared evaluation protocol. A fine-tuned 300M encoder reaches 61.9% accuracy, compared with 61.5% for a LoRA-adapted Qwen3.5-9B model and 61.3% for GPT-5.4. Because these systems differ in architecture, supervision, training objective, and input format, we interpret this as a practical efficiency result for compact supervised encoders rather than a controlled conclusion about model scale. Supplying gold evidence spans improves the fine-tuned encoder to 65.3%, whereas automatically predicted spans recover a meaningful but incomplete share of that gain, indicating that localization quality remains a bottleneck. Class-level analyses show that Referential inconsistencies are especially sensitive to localization quality, while Factual and Logical inconsistencies remain difficult even when the relevant evidence is provided. Together, the oracle, distractor, and per-class analyses separate localization errors from residual type-discrimination errors, indicating that progress requires both stronger evidence extraction and better reasoning over closely related inconsistency categories.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces fine-grained inconsistency classification in financial disclosures, comparing various model architectures on a synthetic benchmark. A compact fine-tuned encoder (300M params) matches or outperforms much larger LLMs (61.9% vs 61.3-61.5% accuracy), and analyses reveal that evidence localization quality is a key bottleneck, particularly for referential inconsistencies, while factual and logical types remain hard regardless.
AI.motivation: Financial disclosures contain heterogeneous claims — numerical, temporal, referential, factual, normative — that yield qualitatively different types of conflicts. Detection alone is insufficient; downstream review workflows require knowing the inconsistency type to determine appropriate evidence and remediation steps. Prior work lacks systematic study of this fine-grained classification problem.
AI.method: Using 5,940 instances from the SBID-FD synthetic financial-disclosure benchmark (11 inconsistency labels with paired reference evidence spans), the authors evaluate five paradigms under a shared protocol: (1) frozen embedding classifiers, (2) fine-tuned encoders, (3) evidence-augmented classifiers, (4) prompted LLMs, and (5) LoRA-adapted generative models. Oracle (gold evidence) and distractor analyses isolate localization errors from type-discrimination errors, with per-class breakdowns across all 11 categories.
AI.result: A fine-tuned 300M encoder achieves 61.9% accuracy, marginally surpassing LoRA-adapted Qwen3.5-9B (61.5%) and GPT-5.4 (61.3%). Gold evidence spans improve the fine-tuned encoder to 65.3%; automatically predicted spans recover only part of this gain. Referential inconsistencies are most sensitive to localization quality; Factual and Logical inconsistencies remain difficult even with oracle evidence, indicating residual type-discrimination challenges.
AI.conclusion: The near-parity of a compact supervised encoder with much larger generative models constitutes a practical efficiency result rather than a statement about scaling laws. Progress requires joint advances in evidence extraction and fine-grained reasoning over closely related inconsistency categories, with localization remaining a critical bottleneck.

title: KAMR: Grounding Generation via Knowledge-Aligned Multi-hop Retrieval
summary: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation increasingly relies on multi-hop retrieval, where answering a query requires composing multiple connected knowledge-graph triplets. However, existing retrievers often rank triplets independently via global semantic matching. Moreover, many multi-hop benchmarks provide only final answers, which limits supervision for query--triplet alignment and causes structurally necessary but weakly aligned facts to be missed. To address these issues, we propose a knowledge-aligned multi-hop retriever, KAMR, which distinguishes anchor triplets that are strongly constrained by the query from connected triplets that are weakly aligned yet structurally linked to the anchors. To mitigate the lack of query-triplet alignment supervision, we build a partial alignment dataset by masking triplet elements and prompting an LLM to generate corresponding queries, and optimize two contrastive objectives for pair-level and element-level matching. At inference time, KAMR retrieves anchors globally and then expands locally to collect connected evidence. Across four benchmarks, three LLM backbones, and fourteen baselines, KAMR consistently improves multi-hop retrieval and downstream question answering performance.

AI.tldr: KAMR is a multi-hop retriever that distinguishes anchor triplets (strongly query-aligned) from connected triplets (weakly aligned but structurally necessary). It uses a synthetically generated partial alignment dataset and dual contrastive objectives to improve retrieval, then employs anchor-first global retrieval followed by local expansion. KAMR consistently outperforms baselines across multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-hop retrievers rank triplets independently via global semantic matching, ignoring structural dependencies. Multi-hop benchmarks often provide only final answers without query-triplet alignment supervision, causing structurally necessary but weakly aligned facts to be missed. There is a need for a retriever that explicitly models the distinction between strongly aligned "anchor" triplets and weakly aligned but structurally essential "connected" triplets.
AI.method: KAMR introduces (1) a partial alignment dataset built by masking triplet elements and prompting an LLM to generate corresponding queries; (2) two contrastive objectives for pair-level and element-level matching; and (3) a two-stage inference strategy that first retrieves anchor triplets globally, then expands locally along knowledge-graph edges to collect connected evidence.
AI.result: KAMR consistently improves multi-hop retrieval and downstream QA performance across four benchmarks, three LLM backbones, and fourteen baselines.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling the anchor-vs-connected distinction, supported by synthetic alignment supervision and dual contrastive learning, effectively addresses the limitations of independent triplet ranking in multi-hop retrieval. The anchor-then-expand inference strategy proves effective for composing structurally linked evidence.

title: Rethinking Self-Evolution: A Constrained Exploration-Exploitation Process for Mitigating Skill Overfitting
summary: Enabling large language model (LLM) agents to accumulate and reuse experience from past interactions remains a central challenge in real-world applications. A promising solution is to treat skills as trainable states and optimize them in the same way as model parameters in neural network training. However, data-driven skill optimization is prone to overfitting to the limited trajectories collected from real environments. Overexploiting these trajectories overfits the current batch, while unconstrained exploration causes regression on previously solved cases. This tension motivates a constrained search view of skill self-evolution, governed by an exploration--exploitation trade-off. We propose SkillBoost, a three-stage framework that mitigates both risks: structured exploitation localizes observed failures to editable skill components, prior-guided exploration draws on prior knowledge in the LLM to generate diverse repair candidates, and verified acceptance commits a candidate only when it improves performance within a regression bound. Experiments across 23 model--benchmark configurations show that SkillBoost achieves state-of-the-art performance while mitigating overfitting, outperforming both human-crafted and LLM-generated skills. Transfer experiments further show that optimized skills can be reused by other agents on similar tasks.

AI.tldr: SkillBoost is a three-stage framework for LLM agent skill optimization that addresses the overfitting-exploration trade-off via structured exploitation, prior-guided exploration, and verified acceptance, achieving state-of-the-art performance across 23 model-benchmark configurations.
AI.motivation: LLM agents struggle to accumulate and reuse experience from past interactions. While treating skills as trainable states is promising, data-driven skill optimization overfits to limited real-environment trajectories. Overexploiting trajectories overfits the current batch, while unconstrained exploration regresses on previously solved cases. This creates an exploration-exploitation tension that existing methods fail to resolve.
AI.method: SkillBoost is a three-stage constrained search framework: (1) Structured Exploitation — localizes observed failures to editable skill components; (2) Prior-Guided Exploration — leverages the LLM's prior knowledge to generate diverse repair candidates; (3) Verified Acceptance — commits a candidate only if it improves performance within a regression bound, preventing degradation on previously solved cases.
AI.result: SkillBoost achieves state-of-the-art performance across 23 model-benchmark configurations, outperforming both human-crafted and LLM-generated skills. Transfer experiments demonstrate that optimized skills can be reused by other agents on similar tasks.
AI.conclusion: The constrained search view of skill self-evolution effectively balances the exploration-exploitation trade-off. SkillBoost mitigates overfitting while enabling skill transferability, offering a robust framework for continual skill improvement in LLM agents.

title: FARI: Robust One-Step Inversion for Watermarking in Diffusion Models
summary: Inversion-based watermarking is a promising approach to authenticate diffusion-generated images, yet practical use is bottlenecked by inversion that is both slow and error-prone. While the primary challenge in the watermarking setting is robustness against external distortions, existing approaches over-optimize internal truncation error, and because that error scales with the sampler step size, they are inherently confined to high-NFE (number of function evaluations) regimes that cannot meet the dual demands of speed and robustness. In this work, we have two key observations: (i) the inversion trajectory has markedly lower curvature than the forward generation path does, making it highly compressible and amenable to low-NFE approximation; and (ii) in inversion for watermark verification, the trade-off between speed and truncation error is less critical, since external distortions dominate the error. A faster inverter provides a dual benefit: it is not only more efficient, but it also enables end-to-end adversarial training to directly target robustness, a task that is computationally prohibitive for the original, lengthy inversion trajectories. Building on this, we propose \textbf{FARI} (\textbf{F}ast \textbf{A}symmetric \textbf{R}obust \textbf{I}nversion), a one-step inversion framework paired with lightweight adversarial LoRA fine-tuning of the denoiser for watermark extraction. While consolidation slightly increases internal error, FARI delivers large gains in both speed and robustness: with approximately 20 minutes of fine-tuning on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU, it surpasses 50-step DDIM inversion on watermark-verification robustness while dramatically reducing inference time. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/0xD009/FARI.

AI.tldr: FARI proposes a fast one-step inversion framework for watermarking diffusion-generated images, paired with lightweight adversarial LoRA fine-tuning. It exploits the low curvature of inversion trajectories to achieve high compression, delivering superior robustness and dramatically reduced inference time compared to 50-step DDIM inversion.
AI.motivation: Existing inversion-based watermarking methods are bottlenecked by slow, error-prone inversion. They over-optimize internal truncation error, which scales with sampler step size, confining them to high-NFE regimes. The key insight is that robustness against external distortions matters more than minimizing truncation error, and that inversion trajectories have low curvature, making them compressible.
AI.method: FARI (Fast Asymmetric Robust Inversion) introduces a one-step inversion framework that compresses the low-curvature inversion trajectory into a single step. This is paired with lightweight adversarial LoRA fine-tuning of the denoiser for watermark extraction. The fast inverter enables computationally feasible end-to-end adversarial training targeting robustness, which is prohibitive with lengthy inversion trajectories.
AI.result: With approximately 20 minutes of fine-tuning on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU, FARI surpasses 50-step DDIM inversion on watermark-verification robustness while dramatically reducing inference time.
AI.conclusion: FARI demonstrates that trading a slight increase in internal error for a one-step inversion yields substantial gains in both speed and robustness, making fast, robust inversion-based watermarking practically viable.

title: Post-Training at the Edge of Detectability: A Game-Theoretic Approach to Fine-Tuning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning is widely used in language model training to improve model performance on a target task while limiting drift from a reference policy. A standard way to balance this trade-off is via a KL-regularized RL objective, although this formulation does not by itself provide a principled way to set the regularization coefficient. In practice, the coefficient is typically chosen heuristically or via hyperparameter search, which can lead to unnecessary overhead in training cost or undesirable reward-retention trade-offs. We instead propose a game-theoretic framework that gives this trade-off an explicit statistical interpretation. Specifically, we study a sequential game in which an agent chooses a policy to maximize cumulative reward while a monitor observes policy outputs over time and tests for deviations from the reference policy. Although not originating from the same perspective, we show that the resulting equilibrium policy can nonetheless be expressed as the solution to a KL-regularized RL problem for an optimal regularization parameter that can be viewed as maximizing reward per unit of statistical distinguishability. Drawing on classical results from concave-convex fractional programming, we provide a principled method for learning this equilibrium coefficient via reduction to the KL-regularized RL objective, thus allowing for flexible integration into standard fine-tuning pipelines. In experiments with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.2-1B, we demonstrate that our methods result in competitive reward-retention trade-offs in a continual learning setting, and illustrate how our framework may be used to audit API providers serving open-source models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a game-theoretic framework for KL-regularized RL fine-tuning of language models, where the regularization coefficient emerges optimally from an equilibrium between an agent maximizing reward and a monitor detecting deviations from a reference policy. The optimal coefficient maximizes reward per unit of statistical distinguishability and can be learned via reduction to standard KL-regularized RL objectives.
AI.motivation: KL-regularized RL is standard for balancing reward optimization against reference policy drift in language model fine-tuning, but the regularization coefficient lacks a principled selection method—it is typically chosen heuristically or via costly hyperparameter search, leading to suboptimal reward-retention trade-offs.
AI.method: The authors formulate a sequential game between an agent (choosing a policy to maximize cumulative reward) and a monitor (testing for deviations from the reference policy using sequential hypothesis testing). They show the equilibrium policy solves a KL-regularized RL problem with an optimal coefficient interpretable as maximizing reward per unit of statistical distinguishability. Using concave-convex fractional programming (Dinkelbach's method), they provide a reduction algorithm to learn this coefficient within standard fine-tuning pipelines.
AI.result: Experiments on Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.2-1B demonstrate competitive reward-retention trade-offs in continual learning settings. The framework also enables auditing of API providers serving open-source models by detecting whether deployed policies deviate from stated reference policies.
AI.conclusion: The game-theoretic formulation provides a statistically principled method for setting the KL penalty coefficient in RL fine-tuning, eliminating heuristic tuning while maintaining competitive performance. The framework naturally extends to downstream applications such as auditing model deployments for policy compliance.

title: MRCoder: An Efficient Context Selecting Approach for Repository-Level Code Generation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in code generation. However, repository-level code generation remains challenging, as it requires effectively identifying and utilizing repository-specific context. While retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) incorporates relevant code snippets, it often introduces redundant context that interferes with the LLM's ability to utilize relevant information, leading to degraded generation quality and increased computational cost. Moreover, existing context selection and compression methods struggle to balance efficiency and quality, either introducing additional computational overhead or failing to effectively select valid context. In this paper, we propose MRCoder, an efficient context selection framework that improves both the effectiveness and efficiency of repository-level code generation. MRCoder adopts a Map-Reduce paradigm: in the Map Phase, a lightweight draft model generates drafts over partitioned contexts, and Structure-Aware Draft-Guided Selection (SADGS) selects informative contexts based on drafts through API consistency and logical similarity; in the Reduce Phase, the refined contexts are aggregated for final generation, with a parallel verification strategy further accelerating decoding. We evaluate MRCoder on two widely used repository-level code generation benchmarks, CoderEval and DevEval, using Qwen2.5-Coder and DeepSeek-Coder as backbone LLMs. Experimental results show that MRCoder improves code generation accuracy over strong baselines while reducing token consumption by 30 to 50% and inference time by up to 52%. These results demonstrate that our proposed structured and draft-guided context selection strategy is crucial for improving both the quality and efficiency of repository-level code generation

AI.tldr: MRCoder is a Map-Reduce framework for repository-level code generation that uses a lightweight draft model and a Structure-Aware Draft-Guided Selection (SADGS) strategy to select only informative context. It improves accuracy while cutting token consumption by 30–50% and inference time by up to 52%.
AI.motivation: Repository-level code generation is challenging because LLMs must identify and use repository-specific context. Existing RAG approaches introduce redundant context that degrades generation quality and increases cost. Current context selection/compression methods fail to balance efficiency and effectiveness — they either add computational overhead or inadequately filter context.
AI.method: MRCoder employs a Map-Reduce paradigm: (1) Map Phase — a lightweight draft model generates drafts over partitioned contexts, and Structure-Aware Draft-Guided Selection (SADGS) selects informative contexts based on API consistency and logical similarity with the drafts; (2) Reduce Phase — refined contexts are aggregated for final generation, with a parallel verification strategy to accelerate decoding.
AI.result: Evaluated on CoderEval and DevEval benchmarks with Qwen2.5-Coder and DeepSeek-Coder backbones, MRCoder improves code generation accuracy over strong baselines, reduces token consumption by 30–50%, and cuts inference time by up to 52%.
AI.conclusion: The structured, draft-guided context selection strategy is crucial for improving both quality and efficiency in repository-level code generation, effectively addressing the redundancy and inefficiency problems of prior methods.

title: AI as Friction for Reflection Support in Ideation
comment: In Proceedings of The First Reflection in Creative Experience (RiCE) Workshop (RiCE W1) arXiv:2607.24558
summary: Generative AI tools for creative work tend to be designed around the goal of removing friction, on the assumption that smoother iteration and faster output translate into more value for the designer. We argue, however, that this framing leaves out something important about how design ideation works, namely reflection-in-action. The act of accepting, rejecting and reworking candidate ideas is both a path to a final outcome and the process through which designers develop the rationale that allows them to think with their ideas and to communicate them to others. This becomes particularly important in group ideation, where ideas need to be expressed and explained to others to allow the group to extend, reject or combine them further. We suggest that AI in design ideation might be more usefully thought of as a friction agent for reflection rather than as a smoothing agent for output. This reframing opens up a different role for AI in design ideation, one that supports designers in building and carrying rationale rather than substituting for it.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that generative AI tools for design ideation should shift from removing friction to acting as "friction agents" that promote reflection-in-action, helping designers develop and communicate rationale rather than merely accelerating output.
AI.motivation: Current generative AI tools for creative work are designed around friction removal, prioritizing speed and smooth iteration. The authors contend this framing overlooks "reflection-in-action" — the iterative process of accepting, rejecting, and reworking candidate ideas through which designers build rationale and learn to think with and communicate their ideas. This gap is especially critical in group ideation, where expressing and explaining ideas enables extension, rejection, or combination.
AI.method: This is a conceptual/theoretical paper that draws on Schön's theory of reflection-in-action to critique the prevailing design paradigm of generative AI tools for creative work. The authors propose a reframing through argumentation rather than empirical experimentation.
AI.result: The key insight is that AI in design ideation should be reconceptualized as a "friction agent for reflection" rather than a "smoothing agent for output." This reframing suggests AI tools should support designers in building and carrying rationale through the ideation process, not merely substitute for human reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Reframing AI as a friction agent opens a new role for generative tools in design ideation — one centered on augmenting reflective practice and rationale-building rather than minimizing effort. This has significant implications for how AI tools are conceived, designed, and evaluated in creative contexts, particularly collaborative ones.

title: (Im)Paired Programming: Coding Agents Improve Productivity but Harm Understanding
summary: Coding agents (e.g., Cursor) improve developer productivity by optimizing task completion, but shifting users from writing code to prompting and reviewing may harm their understanding, impeding oversight, learning, and communication. To probe this, we have 54 students create a website with one of two AI systems: an agent that edits user code; or a chatbot where users write code alone or adapt generic code snippets. We test understanding via comprehension questions and a task where users extend their code without agents, showing: (1) While agents aid initial task completion, they harm users' code comprehension and thus do not prepare users to extend their code; (2) Low-effort agent interaction types, like copy+paste prompts and auto-accepted edits, are linked with lower comprehension; and (3) Despite self-reported weaker understanding, users still prefer coding agents because they are quick and easy to use. While users stay in the loop for coding workflows, understanding should not be forgotten. Towards this goal, we distill our analyses into future research directions for coding agent developers: dissuading low-effort prompting, creating readable code, and promoting active engagement.

AI.tldr: A study with 54 participants found that AI coding agents improve task completion speed but impair code comprehension, leaving users ill-prepared to extend their own code. Low-effort interactions (copy-paste prompts, auto-accepted edits) correlate with worse understanding, yet users still prefer agents for their convenience. The authors propose design directions to mitigate these harms.
AI.motivation: As coding agents like Cursor shift developers from writing code to prompting and reviewing AI-generated code, there is a risk that this workflow undermines users' understanding of their own code, which is essential for oversight, learning, and team communication.
AI.method: A between-subjects experiment with 54 students tasked with building a website using one of two systems: (1) an AI coding agent that directly edits user code, or (2) a chatbot where users write code themselves or adapt generic snippets. Comprehension was measured via targeted questions and a follow-up task requiring participants to extend their code without AI assistance. Interaction behaviors (e.g., copy-paste prompting, auto-accepting edits) were also logged and analyzed against comprehension scores.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) Coding agents facilitated initial task completion but significantly impaired code comprehension, leaving users unable to effectively extend their code; (2) Low-effort interaction patterns—specifically copy-paste prompting and automatically accepting AI-suggested edits—were negatively correlated with comprehension; (3) Despite self-reporting weaker understanding, participants still preferred coding agents due to their speed and ease of use.
AI.conclusion: While keeping users "in the loop" is important for coding workflows, preserving understanding is equally critical and currently overlooked. The authors distill their findings into three research directions for agent developers: discouraging low-effort prompting behaviors, ensuring AI-generated code is readable, and designing interactions that promote active user engagement rather than passive review.

title: Improving Item Discoverability in e-Commerce Search via Related Intent Generation
summary:
Traditional search systems are optimized to retrieve items that strictly match a query, often prioritizing precision over recall. In e-commerce marketplaces and particularly grocery, this paradigm is limiting, as user satisfaction and commercial outcomes depend heavily on the discoverability of substitute, complementary, and thematically related items. In this paper, we present a scalable system for discovery-augmented search that leverages intent-conditioned recall expansion. Our approach generates implicit user intents to expand candidate recall while maintaining relevance.
  The system addresses the cost-quality tradeoff of generative retrieval through a two-stage hybrid architecture. First, we leverage closed-weight large language models (LLMs) to maximize discoverability for head queries. To extend these benefits to tail queries, we then introduce a finetuned small language model (SLM), trained via LoRA adapters and teacher-student distillation. We evaluate the system using a rigorous dual framework: (a) LLM-as-a-judge metrics validated against human preferences for semantic quality, and (b) end-to-end session-level purchase analysis. Results demonstrate that our approach improves both intent generation quality and downstream retrieval effectiveness, extending discovery coverage from approximately 60% to 80% of query traffic at roughly 30% of the teacher model's inference cost, offering a viable path for deployment in large-scale marketplaces. Beyond relevance gains, discovery-augmented search may serve as a marketplace-balancing mechanism, giving long-tail and emerging supply an opportunity for query-conditioned exposure.

AI.tldr: A two-stage hybrid system that generates implicit user intents to expand search recall, using large LLMs for head queries and a distilled small language model for tail queries, achieving 80% discovery coverage at 30% of the inference cost while improving both semantic quality and purchase outcomes in e-commerce grocery search.
AI.motivation: Traditional e-commerce search systems prioritize precision (strict query matching) over recall, which limits discoverability of substitutes, complements, and related items — a critical gap in grocery marketplaces where user satisfaction and revenue depend on surfacing relevant but non-exact matches.
AI.method: A two-stage hybrid architecture: (1) closed-weight LLMs handle head queries for maximal discoverability; (2) a finetuned small language model (SLM) trained via LoRA adapters and teacher-student distillation extends coverage to tail queries. Evaluation uses a dual framework: LLM-as-a-judge metrics (validated against human preferences) for semantic quality, plus end-to-end session-level purchase analysis.
AI.result: Discovery coverage expanded from ~60% to ~80% of query traffic at ~30% of the teacher model's inference cost. Both intent generation quality and downstream retrieval effectiveness improved, with validated semantic quality and positive purchase outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Intent-conditioned recall expansion via a cost-efficient hybrid LLM/SLM architecture is a viable deployment path for large-scale marketplaces. Beyond relevance, it can serve as a marketplace-balancing mechanism, providing long-tail and emerging supply with query-conditioned exposure.

title: AgenticCANN: Automated Ascend C Operator Generation via Knowledge-Augmented Agentic Evolution
summary: Ascend C operator optimization is critical for NPU (Neural Processing Unit) inference performance but requires deep hardware expertise.While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automated CUDA kernel generation, the fundamentally different programming model of Ascend C introduces unique challenges that remain unexplored. In this paper, we propose AgenticCANN, a knowledge-augmented agentic evolution framework specifically tailored for automated Ascend C operator synthesis in low-corpus NPU environments.To overcome the severe platform knowledge deficit on unfamiliar hardware, AgenticCANN incorporates a knowledge-orchestrated generation system that delivers structured, multi-level domain insights across the development lifecycle to resolve the upstream feasibility bottleneck.Building on this foundation, it features a stage-adaptive agentic evolution strategy that dynamically aligns LLM interaction modes with specific generation and evolution phases, balancing high-exploration candidate discovery with high-convergence performance tuning.Extensive experiments on Huawei Ascend 910B across six operators spanning five pattern categories demonstrate that our method achieves 90 to 100 percent feasibility on elementwise and normalization operators, 56% on fusion operators, and up to 6.65$\times$ speedup on 1B Pangu model inference kernels. Further analysis reveals that knowledge injection monotonically improves feasibility from 57% to 86% on elementwise operators, demonstrating its general rather than operator-specific benefit.

AI.tldr: AgenticCANN is a knowledge-augmented agentic evolution framework for automated Ascend C operator synthesis on Huawei NPUs. It combines structured knowledge orchestration with a stage-adaptive agentic evolution strategy to overcome low-corpus hardware challenges, achieving 90–100% feasibility on elementwise/normalization operators and up to 6.65× speedup on 1B Pangu model inference.
AI.motivation: Ascend C operator optimization is critical for NPU inference performance but requires deep hardware expertise. While LLMs have succeeded in automated CUDA kernel generation, Ascend C's fundamentally different programming model poses unexplored challenges, exacerbated by severe platform knowledge deficits in low-corpus NPU environments.
AI.method: AgenticCANN consists of two core components: (1) a knowledge-orchestrated generation system that injects structured, multi-level domain insights across the development lifecycle to address the upstream feasibility bottleneck; and (2) a stage-adaptive agentic evolution strategy that dynamically aligns LLM interaction modes with specific generation and evolution phases, balancing high-exploration candidate discovery with high-convergence performance tuning.
AI.result: On Huawei Ascend 910B across six operators spanning five pattern categories: 90–100% feasibility on elementwise and normalization operators, 56% on fusion operators, and up to 6.65× speedup on 1B Pangu model inference kernels. Knowledge injection improves feasibility monotonically from 57% to 86% on elementwise operators, demonstrating general rather than operator-specific benefit.
AI.conclusion: The framework effectively addresses the unique challenges of Ascend C operator synthesis in low-corpus environments. Knowledge augmentation proves to be a general-purpose enabler, and the stage-adaptive evolution strategy successfully balances exploration and convergence across diverse operator categories.

title: Verifiable Random Sampling
summary: Verifiable random functions (VRF) underpin a wide range of applications that require publicly verifiable evaluations of a pseudorandom function on a given input. However, once the public key is published, the induced function is fixed and is a deterministic function of the input. This determinism can enable collusion and grinding-style attacks in which adversaries precompute and selectively exploit favorable input-output pairs. To address these limitations, we introduce the formal notion of verifiable random sampling (VRS). We propose a concrete VRS construction based on random quantum circuit sampling (RCS) executable on today's quantum computing devices. VRS supports multiparty protocols in which the verifier's final output is a sample that is statistically close to a specified target distribution, while remaining publicly verifiable. We model the construction and prove its security within the constructive cryptography (CC) framework, thereby ensuring composability with other cryptographic protocols. Overall, our results provide a mechanism for verifiable random sampling that simultaneously guarantees sample freshness and public verifiability, enabling applications that require unpredictable, fresh randomness while preserving fairness through public verifiability.

AI.tldr: Introduces Verifiable Random Sampling (VRS), a quantum-based primitive that overcomes the determinism limitation of VRFs by producing statistically fresh, publicly verifiable random samples using random quantum circuit sampling, with composable security proven in the constructive cryptography framework.
AI.motivation: Traditional VRFs produce a deterministic function once the public key is fixed, enabling collusion and grinding attacks where adversaries precompute and exploit favorable input-output pairs. A new primitive is needed that guarantees sample freshness (unpredictability) alongside public verifiability.
AI.method: The authors formally define Verifiable Random Sampling (VRS) and construct it using random quantum circuit sampling (RCS), which is executable on near-term quantum devices. The construction supports multiparty protocols where the verifier's output is statistically close to a target distribution. Security is modeled and proven within the constructive cryptography (CC) framework, ensuring composability.
AI.result: A concrete VRS construction is proposed that simultaneously achieves sample freshness (outputs statistically close to a target distribution) and public verifiability, with composable security guarantees under the CC framework.
AI.conclusion: VRS provides a mechanism for applications requiring unpredictable, fresh randomness while preserving fairness through public verifiability, overcoming the inherent determinism limitation of standard VRFs.

title: ClockRoPE: Random Fourier Rotations for Temporal Routine Modeling
summary: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) has been widely adopted in transformer-based large language models. However, its log-linear frequency schedule, originally designed to produce long-term attention decay, limits its adoption in domains with more complex distance-correlation patterns, such as temporal periodicity in sequential recommendation. We investigate the expressiveness of general query/key rotations and find that any normalized continuous positive-definite attention modulation function can be approximated by random rotations induced by its own Fourier transform, which we term Random Fourier Rotations. Building on this theory, we propose ClockRoPE for routine modeling in sequential recommendation, where rotation frequencies are derived from periodic attention modulation functions. In online A/B tests, ClockRoPE demonstrates consistent improvements in valued engagement metrics, and has been successfully deployed in production-scale generative retrieval system at a major video-sharing platform.

AI.tldr: ClockRoPE generalizes Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) by showing that any continuous positive-definite attention modulation can be approximated via random Fourier rotations, enabling better modeling of periodic temporal patterns in sequential recommendation, with production deployment at a major video platform.
AI.motivation: Standard RoPE uses a log-linear frequency schedule that assumes long-term attention decay, which is ill-suited for domains with complex periodic distance-correlation patterns — notably sequential recommendation, where user behavior exhibits temporal periodicity (e.g., daily/weekly routines).
AI.method: The authors first prove theoretically that any normalized continuous positive-definite attention modulation function can be approximated by random rotations induced by its own Fourier transform (Random Fourier Rotations). Building on this, they propose ClockRoPE, which derives rotation frequencies from periodic attention modulation functions tailored for routine modeling in sequential recommendation.
AI.result: ClockRoPE demonstrated consistent improvements in valued engagement metrics in online A/B tests and has been successfully deployed in a production-scale generative retrieval system at a major video-sharing platform.
AI.conclusion: The theoretical framework of Random Fourier Rotations extends RoPE beyond its original log-linear constraints, and ClockRoPE provides a practical, production-validated solution for capturing temporal periodicity in sequential recommendation.

title: A First Look at Coding Agents' Compliance with AI Contribution Rules in Open-Source Communities
summary: Open source communities have been flooded with AI-generated contributions. In defense, they have written contribution rules to regulate coding agents' behavior, spanning from a total ban, mandatory disclosure, to verification gates and human sign-offs. Yet, whether coding agents read and follow those rules, and behave in open source repositories, remains unknown. To estimate real-world rule compliance of coding agents, we curate 106 issues from 49 repositories containing AI contribution rules into RepoComplianceBench. We judge the trajectory of each run against the repository's rules, measuring whether the agent refuses to contribute, discloses its assistance truthfully, clears the required verification gates, or escalates critical steps to a human. We also test if extra prompts, rule disclosure, or feedback from the compliance verifier help with the situation. Our experiments on four frontier models show that today's agents almost never proactively retrieve the contribution rules. Agents pick up disclosure and verification with reminder prompts, rule quotes, and verifier feedback; however, they never refuse to contribute in AI-banned repositories under any condition we tested. The status reveals that verification and disclosure issues are solvable with existing mechanisms, yet enforcing bans and human escalations remains an open problem.

AI.tldr: Current coding agents fail to proactively retrieve or follow open-source contribution rules, particularly regarding AI bans and human escalations, though disclosure and verification compliance can be improved with prompts, rule quotes, and verifier feedback.
AI.motivation: Open source communities have implemented AI contribution rules (bans, disclosure mandates, verification gates, human sign-offs) in response to a flood of AI-generated contributions, but it is unknown whether coding agents actually read and comply with these rules in practice.
AI.method: The authors curated RepoComplianceBench, a benchmark of 106 issues from 49 repositories with explicit AI contribution rules. They evaluated four frontier models' agent trajectories against each repository's rules, measuring refusal to contribute, truthful disclosure, verification gate clearance, and human escalation. They also tested the effects of extra prompts, rule disclosure, and verifier feedback on compliance.
AI.result: Agents almost never proactively retrieve contribution rules on their own. Disclosure and verification compliance improve with reminder prompts, rule quotes, and verifier feedback. Critically, agents never refuse to contribute in AI-banned repositories under any tested condition, and human escalation remains largely unaddressed.
AI.conclusion: Disclosure and verification issues are solvable with existing mechanisms, but enforcing AI contribution bans and ensuring human escalations remain open problems requiring further research and tooling.

title: Human diversity fuels collective creativity that large language models cannot simulate or sustain
summary: Diverse human groups produce diverse ideas, the raw material of innovation. Generative AI challenges this engine twice over: everyday AI assistance may homogenize what diverse people create, and AI-simulated diversity may replace the people altogether. We tested both challenges in a preregistered creative metaphor experiment with native (L1) and non-native (L2) English writers, who wrote without AI, with AI-generated ideas (AI ideation), or with AI refining their own ideas (AI refinement). L2 writers contributed more collective diversity than L1 writers, with native-language ideation showing the most diverse pools. AI ideation compressed collective diversity for everyone and left the L2 advantage undetectable, whereas AI refinement preserved both. We then simulated the entire writer pool using personas built from participants' real backgrounds, three model families, native-language prompting, and elevated sampling temperatures. Every simulated pool fell below every human pool, and pushing models further induced diversity only through degenerate text. However, at the individual level, AI ideation raised writers' ratings, pitting private incentives against the collective good, except when L2 writers used their native language, which benefited both. Human diversity remains a valuable creative resource that current AI cannot simulate or sustain; the design of human-AI collaborative workflows determines whether it survives.

AI.tldr: Generative AI homogenizes collective creative diversity when used for ideation, while AI refinement preserves it. Simulated AI pools fail to match human diversity, and only degenerate outputs increase their variety. Native-language (L1) ideation yields the richest diversity, but AI assistance erodes the L2 advantage, creating a tension between individual benefits and collective creative loss.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates whether generative AI undermines the engine of innovation — diverse human ideation — through two mechanisms: (1) everyday AI assistance homogenizing what diverse individuals create, and (2) AI-simulated diversity potentially replacing human contributors altogether. Prior work has not systematically tested both challenges simultaneously, especially across native and non-native speaker populations whose linguistic and cultural diversity may be differentially affected.
AI.method: A preregistered creative metaphor experiment with L1 and L2 English writers under three conditions: writing without AI, with AI-generated ideas (AI ideation), and with AI refining their own ideas (AI refinement). Collective diversity was measured across conditions. Additionally, the entire writer pool was simulated using personas derived from participants' real backgrounds, three model families, native-language prompting, and elevated sampling temperatures, then compared against human pools.
AI.result: L2 writers contributed more collective diversity than L1 writers, with native-language ideation producing the most diverse pools. AI ideation compressed collective diversity for all participants and rendered the L2 advantage statistically undetectable; AI refinement preserved both diversity and the L2 advantage. Every simulated AI pool fell below every human pool in diversity metrics. Pushing models further induced diversity only via degenerate text. At the individual level, AI ideation improved writer ratings, creating a private incentive misaligned with the collective good — except when L2 writers used their native language, which benefited both individual and collective outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Human diversity remains a valuable and irreplaceable creative resource that current AI cannot simulate or sustain. The design of human-AI collaborative workflows is decisive: AI ideation erodes collective diversity, while AI refinement preserves it. The paper advocates for designing AI tools that augment rather than replace human creative diversity, particularly protecting the contributions of non-native speakers.

title: Misalignment Has a Personality: A Big Five Account of Emergent Misalignment
comment: The paper is currently under peer review
summary: Fine-tuning a language model on data containing a narrow flaw, such as insecure code or incorrect mathematical answers, can cause broad misalignment through a mechanism that remains debated. We provide an interpretable account: in the models and corpora we study, misalignment behaves like a shift in personality. Prior work extracts activation directions for character traits from a single binary contrast, which can separate or steer behavior without establishing a calibrated scale. We instead extract personality vectors for the Big Five using a graded, three-level intervention and validate them on two open-weight models. The three levels are linearly ordered, with Cohen's d values of up to 6.2; the vectors transfer zero-shot and trait-specifically to an independent corpus; and their effects are strongest within a middle-layer band. Applied to training data, the vectors reveal that misaligned corpora across eight domains share a common Big Five signature: lower agreeableness and conscientiousness, together with higher extraversion and neuroticism. This signature is recovered by both models with a correlation of r = 0.94. Fine-tuning imprints the same profile, shifting the model's generations along the corresponding signature, with r = 0.83 using activation-based measurements and r = 0.90 using a text-based judge, while also shifting internal activations with r = 0.69. The same vectors characterize sycophancy as high extraversion and low conscientiousness rather than excess agreeableness, a distinction that a single direction cannot capture. Calibrated personality vectors transform an opaque safety phenomenon into a human-legible diagnostic profile.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning on narrowly flawed data causes broad misalignment that manifests as a personality shift. Using graded Big Five personality vectors, the authors show misaligned models consistently exhibit lower agreeableness/conscientiousness and higher extraversion/neuroticism, with the same signature recovered across eight domains, two models, and multiple measurement modalities.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning on flawed data (e.g., insecure code, incorrect math) produces broad misalignment, but the underlying mechanism remains debated. The authors aim to provide an interpretable, human-legible account of this phenomenon — specifically, that misalignment operates like a personality shift — rather than treating it as an opaque safety failure.
AI.method: The authors extract Big Five personality vectors using a graded three-level intervention (rather than a single binary contrast), validated on two open-weight models. They verify linear ordering (Cohen's d up to 6.2), zero-shot trait-specific transfer, and localization to a middle-layer band. These vectors are then applied to training data to extract personality signatures of misaligned corpora across eight domains, and to measure how fine-tuning shifts model generations and internal activations along those signatures, cross-validated with both activation-based and text-based judge measurements.
AI.result: Misaligned corpora across eight domains share a common Big Five signature: lower agreeableness and conscientiousness, higher extraversion and neuroticism. Both models recover this signature with r = 0.94. Fine-tuning imprints the same profile: generation shifts correlate at r = 0.83 (activation-based) and r = 0.90 (text-based judge); internal activations shift at r = 0.69. Sycophancy is characterized as high extraversion and low conscientiousness, not excess agreeableness — a distinction a single binary direction cannot capture.
AI.conclusion: Calibrated, multi-level personality vectors transform misalignment from an opaque safety phenomenon into a human-legible diagnostic profile. The consistent Big Five signature provides an interpretable framework for detecting, measuring, and understanding broad misalignment induced by narrow fine-tuning flaws.

title: UrbanDS: A Graph-Guided LLM Multi-Agent System for Data-Intensive Urban Tasks
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have been widely applied in automating data science tasks. However, existing methods typically rely on a limited set of provided datasets, and they face challenges in data-intensive scenarios that require discovering and leveraging relevant information from large-scale and heterogeneous data repositories. Urban tasks are representative examples of such scenarios, as urban data are not only large-scale and multi-sourced, but also exhibit complex spatial, temporal, and semantic relationships. To address these challenges, we propose UrbanDS, a graph-guided LLM multi-agent system for data-intensive urban tasks. We first construct a unified dataset graph to organize reusable dataset skills and the relationships among datasets. Specifically, we develop a Data Profiling Agent that constructs a skill for each dataset. Moreover, a Relation Agent identifies relationships among datasets and integrates these relationships into the dataset graph. At runtime, a Planner Agent retrieves task-relevant datasets from the graph and generates execution plans. Multiple Execution Agents then perform data processing and analysis, while their execution progress and intermediate results are shared through a common memory. Finally, a Report Agent synthesizes the experimental logs into a report, which can be further refined based on user feedback. To systematically evaluate the capability of agents in handling data-intensive urban scenarios, we further construct UrbanDS-Bench, an urban data science benchmark covering representative data analysis and modeling tasks. Experiments on both general and urban benchmarks demonstrate that UrbanDS consistently outperforms existing data science agents on data-intensive tasks. Furthermore, UrbanDS has been deployed on the urban operations platform of Dongxihu District, Wuhan, demonstrating its effectiveness in real-world urban applications.

AI.tldr: UrbanDS is a graph-guided LLM multi-agent system designed for data-intensive urban tasks. It constructs a unified dataset graph with reusable dataset skills and inter-dataset relationships, then uses specialized agents (Data Profiling, Relation, Planner, Execution, Report) to retrieve, plan, and execute data science workflows. A new benchmark, UrbanDS-Bench, evaluates performance, and the system has been deployed in Wuhan's Dongxihu District.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agents for data science automation rely on limited, pre-provided datasets and struggle in data-intensive scenarios requiring discovery and integration of relevant information from large-scale, heterogeneous repositories. Urban tasks exemplify this challenge due to multi-sourced data with complex spatial, temporal, and semantic relationships.
AI.method: UrbanDS employs a multi-agent architecture: (1) A Data Profiling Agent builds reusable skills for each dataset; (2) A Relation Agent identifies inter-dataset relationships and builds a unified dataset graph; (3) A Planner Agent retrieves task-relevant datasets from the graph and generates execution plans at runtime; (4) Multiple Execution Agents perform processing and analysis, sharing progress via common memory; (5) A Report Agent synthesizes logs into reports, refined via user feedback. The system is evaluated on UrbanDS-Bench, a purpose-built urban data science benchmark.
AI.result: UrbanDS consistently outperforms existing data science agents on data-intensive tasks across both general and urban benchmarks. It has been successfully deployed in the Dongxihu District urban operations platform in Wuhan.
AI.conclusion: A graph-guided multi-agent approach, with structured dataset skills and relationship modeling, effectively enables LLM agents to handle data-intensive urban tasks. The real-world deployment validates practical applicability.

title: SecRespond: Benchmarking AI Agents for Real-World Post-Compromise Incident Response
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly adopted in real-world security operations with access to host artifacts and command-line interfaces (CLIs), making it critical to thoroughly assess their security capabilities. However, existing cybersecurity benchmarks focus on pre-compromise settings where agents are placed in a clean and idealized environment before an attack occurs. This leaves the post-compromise setting underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce SecRespond, the first benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on the post-compromise incident-response workflow. Given a forensic disk snapshot of a compromised host together with the alerts, vulnerability scans, and baseline checks reported by a host security product, agents are required to produce forensic reports on intrusions, baseline risks, and vulnerability risks, together with a remediation plan. We instantiate this task across 10 cyber ranges, each constructed from a distinct compromised cloud host, spanning 4 entry-point types, 21 ATT&CK techniques, and 5 operating systems. We evaluate 23 frontier LLMs on the OpenCode agent harness. Experimental results show that although current agents can reliably uncover the problems exposed by alerts, they struggle to proactively investigate the disk for silent intrusions and to produce comprehensive, verified remediation plans, with no model achieving complete detection and remediation on any single range. This reveals a fundamental bottleneck in building agents for real-world incident response. The benchmark is publicly available at https://github.com/Alibaba-NLP/qqr/tree/main/data/secrespond.

AI.tldr: SecRespond is the first benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on post-compromise incident response, requiring agents to analyze forensic disk snapshots and produce intrusion reports and remediation plans. Testing 23 frontier LLMs across 10 diverse cyber ranges reveals that while agents handle alerts well, they fail to proactively detect silent intrusions and produce comprehensive remediation plans.
AI.motivation: Existing cybersecurity benchmarks for LLM agents focus exclusively on pre-compromise settings (clean environments before an attack), leaving the post-compromise incident-response workflow critically underexplored. Real-world security operations require agents to operate on compromised hosts, making this gap a significant barrier to practical deployment.
AI.method: The authors construct SecRespond, a benchmark comprising 10 cyber ranges built from distinct compromised cloud hosts. Each range includes a forensic disk snapshot, alerts, vulnerability scans, and baseline checks from a host security product. The task requires agents to produce four deliverables: a forensic intrusion report, a baseline risk report, a vulnerability risk report, and a remediation plan. The ranges span 4 entry-point types, 21 ATT&CK techniques, and 5 operating systems. Evaluation is conducted on 23 frontier LLMs using the OpenCode agent harness.
AI.result: Current agents reliably uncover problems surfaced by alerts but struggle significantly with proactive disk investigation to detect silent intrusions. No model achieved complete detection and remediation on any single cyber range. The failure to produce comprehensive, verified remediation plans reveals a fundamental bottleneck in building agents for real-world incident response.
AI.conclusion: There exists a fundamental capability gap between current LLM agents' performance on pre-compromise cybersecurity tasks and the demands of post-compromise incident response, particularly in proactive forensic investigation and remediation planning. SecRespond provides a rigorous testbed to drive progress in this direction.

title: Q-Steer: Action-Value Guidance for Molecular Policy Optimization
comment: 20 pages, 2 figures, and 25 tables. Includes supplementary experimental results
summary: Oracle-limited molecular optimization gives reward only after a complete molecule is generated, while each rollout requires many local next-token decisions. This delayed-feedback interface makes molecular policy optimization myopic: an optimizer can learn that a molecule was good without knowing which intermediate actions made it good. We introduce Q-Steer, a rollout-time action-value steering primitive for molecular language models. Q-Steer uses an offline-trained and frozen prefix-action value scorer, PAVS-Q, that estimates the downstream reward of taking a candidate next token under a partial SMILES prefix, then adds a normalized value bonus to sampling logits. The optimizer update rule and online oracle budget are unchanged; the claim is fixed-online-oracle performance, not equal total compute. On PMO23 with a fixed 10,000-call online budget, complete factorial studies across two molecular language-model backbones and four optimizers show that Q-Steer improves mean valid-unique score in all eight backbone-optimizer cells, with positive macro mean-score gains between +0.033 and +0.049 and 18-20 task wins per cell. Mechanism controls show that action identity matters: prefix-broadcast values are nearly neutral, while shuffled action values harm performance. These results support Q-Steer as a reusable rollout-time action-value wrapper that improves average molecular optimization reward across optimizer families and policy backbones without changing the online oracle budget.

AI.tldr: Q-Steer introduces a rollout-time action-value steering mechanism for molecular language models that uses an offline-trained prefix-action value scorer (PAVS-Q) to add normalized value bonuses to sampling logits, improving molecular optimization without changing the online oracle budget. Across 8 backbone-optimizer combinations, it consistently improves mean valid-unique scores.
AI.motivation: Molecular optimization suffers from a delayed-feedback problem: oracle reward is only given after a complete molecule is generated, making it difficult for optimizers to credit which intermediate token-level actions led to good outcomes. This myopia limits policy optimization efficiency.
AI.method: Q-Steer uses PAVS-Q, an offline-trained and frozen prefix-action value scorer that estimates the downstream reward of taking a candidate next token given a partial SMILES prefix. During rollout, a normalized value bonus derived from PAVS-Q is added to the sampling logits. The optimizer update rule and online oracle budget remain unchanged, isolating the effect to rollout-time steering only.
AI.result: On PMO23 with a fixed 10,000-call online budget, factorial studies across 2 molecular LM backbones and 4 optimizers showed Q-Steer improved mean valid-unique score in all 8 cells, with macro mean-score gains of +0.033 to +0.049 and 18-20 task wins per cell. Ablations confirmed action identity matters: prefix-broadcast values were nearly neutral, while shuffled action values harmed performance.
AI.conclusion: Q-Steer is an effective, reusable rollout-time action-value wrapper that improves average molecular optimization reward across diverse optimizer families and policy backbones without requiring additional online oracle calls.

title: A Scalable AI-Powered System for Explainable Machine Learning Pipelines in Brain Tumor
summary: Artificial intelligence and radiomics are increasingly used in brain tumor research, yet their translation into clinical practice remains limited by fragmented workflows, poor transparency, and weak integration with end users' needs. We present the first version of a scalable web-based visual analytics system designed to support radiomics-driven machine learning inference in neuro-oncology. The platform integrates three core functions within a single interface: cohort management from structured clinical tables, radiomic feature extraction from medical images and segmentation masks, and guarded inference with pre-trained machine learning models. The system was developed through an iterative user-centred design process and evaluated on both a public glioblastoma dataset and a proprietary clinical cohort. A key contribution is the explicit exposure of intermediate workflow artifacts, which improves traceability, interpretability, and responsible use of AI. By combining portability, inspectability, and deployment simplicity, the proposed framework offers a practical foundation for clinically oriented AI applications in brain tumor analysis.

AI.tldr: A web-based visual analytics system integrating cohort management, radiomic feature extraction, and guarded ML inference for brain tumor analysis, built through iterative user-centred design to improve transparency, traceability, and clinical translation of AI.
AI.motivation: Translation of AI and radiomics into clinical brain tumor practice is hindered by fragmented workflows, poor transparency, and weak alignment with end-user needs. There is a need for integrated, interpretable, and deployable platforms that bridge this gap.
AI.method: The authors developed a scalable web-based visual analytics platform through iterative user-centred design. The system unifies three core functions: (1) cohort management via structured clinical tables, (2) radiomic feature extraction from images and segmentation masks, and (3) guarded inference using pre-trained ML models. Evaluation was conducted on a public glioblastoma dataset and a proprietary clinical cohort.
AI.result: The platform explicitly exposes intermediate workflow artifacts, which enhances traceability, interpretability, and responsible AI use. The system combines portability, inspectability, and deployment simplicity, demonstrating practical utility on both public and proprietary neuro-oncology datasets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers a practical, clinically oriented foundation for AI applications in brain tumor analysis by integrating transparency, interpretability, and user-centred design into a single deployable system, addressing key barriers to clinical adoption.

title: TactiPlay: Multi-Granularity Tactical Parsing and Video-Anchored Match Review for Amateur Badminton Players
summary: Amateur badminton players increasingly record matches, yet existing tools provide only aggregate statistics or generic summaries, leaving most unable to extract tactical insights without expert guidance. A formative study (N=8) reveals the need for multi-granularity, video-anchored tactical analysis centered on rallies. We derive a taxonomy of performance issues from national-level athletes' annotations and present TactiPlay, an interactive system that instantiates an expert-taxonomy-guided, rally-level, video-anchored review workflow. The system's analytical pipeline organizes match events into taxonomy-grounded feedback, while its interface links structured reports to rally summaries, video evidence, and court visualizations. A within-subjects study (N=16) shows that TactiPlay elicits more frequent, concrete, actionable, and appropriate reflections than a report-and-statistics baseline. These findings show how organizing reviewed match evidence into a taxonomy-guided, video-linked workflow can support amateur players' tactical reflection.

AI.tldr: TactiPlay is an interactive system that uses an expert-derived taxonomy to organize badminton match footage into rally-level, video-anchored tactical reviews, enabling amateur players to generate more concrete and actionable self-reflections compared to standard report-and-statistics tools.
AI.motivation: Amateur badminton players record matches but lack tools for extracting tactical insights without expert guidance. Existing tools only offer aggregate statistics or generic summaries, which are insufficient for meaningful tactical reflection.
AI.method: The authors conducted a formative study (N=8) to identify user needs and derived a performance-issue taxonomy from national-level athletes' annotations.
