They then built TactiPlay, an interactive system with an analytical pipeline that structures match events into taxonomy-grounded feedback, and an interface linking structured reports to rally summaries, video evidence, and court visualizations. A within-subjects study (N=16) compared TactiPlay against a report-and-statistics baseline.
AI.result: TactiPlay elicited significantly more frequent, concrete, actionable, and appropriate reflections from amateur players compared to the baseline condition.
AI.conclusion: Organizing reviewed match evidence into a taxonomy-guided, video-linked workflow effectively supports amateur players' tactical reflection, bridging the gap between raw footage and expert-level analysis.

title: Knowledge before Reasoning: EC-Reason-Bench, a Training-Free Diagnostic Benchmark for LLM Enzyme Classification
summary: Enzyme function prediction is a hierarchical, knowledge-intensive form of protein function classification. Existing benchmarks expose an anomaly: general LLMs often get the coarse first level right, yet once asked for a complete EC number their accuracy at levels two through four drops to almost zero, while specialized models and tools stay usable. We propose EC-Reason-Bench, a training-free, diagnostic evaluation protocol built to answer two questions: why general LLMs score close to nothing on EC number prediction, and how much of that loss can be recovered without updating a single weight. We break enzyme classification ability into four orthogonal levers that can each be measured on their own: output structure, external knowledge, reasoning structure, and reasoning robustness. We test each lever with an inference-time method against a shared zero-shot baseline reproducing previously reported near-zero performance. Experiments with several strong reasoning LLMs yield four main findings. First, external knowledge is decisive and must precede reasoning: uniformly low closed-book performance rises sharply with open-book access, narrowing model gaps. Second, in closed-book settings, whether cascading and chain-of-thought help or hurt depends on a model's tendency to abstain. Third, once evidence is available the aggregate score of the best LLM setting is indistinguishable from simply voting the EC numbers of the nearest retrieved neighbors; that tie is an artifact of averaging, and it hides a large gain on adversarial evidence set against an equally large loss on multi-functional enzymes. Reasoning over evidence therefore acts as an arbiter of conflicting neighbors rather than as a source of knowledge, and no single-number leaderboard can see it. Fourth, accuracy obeys a law of homology availability.

AI.tldr: General LLMs fail at fine-grained enzyme function prediction (EC numbers levels 2–4) despite passing level 1. EC-Reason-Bench isolates four orthogonal levers—output structure, external knowledge, reasoning structure, and reasoning robustness—to diagnose why. Key findings: external (open-book) knowledge is decisive and must precede reasoning; chain-of-thought effects depend on model abstention tendencies; with evidence, best LLMs tie nearest-neighbor voting but show complementary strengths on adversarial vs. multi-functional enzymes; and accuracy follows a "law of homology availability."
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks reveal a paradox: general LLMs achieve near-zero accuracy on full EC number prediction (levels 2–4) despite decent level-1 performance, while specialized tools remain usable. The authors aim to diagnose why this drop occurs and quantify how much can be recovered through inference-time interventions alone, without fine-tuning.
AI.method: EC-Reason-Bench, a training-free diagnostic protocol, decomposes enzyme classification into four measurable levers: (1) output structure, (2) external knowledge (closed-book vs. open-book), (3) reasoning structure (cascading, chain-of-thought), and (4) reasoning robustness. Each lever is tested via inference-time methods against a shared zero-shot baseline across multiple strong reasoning LLMs.
AI.result: Four main findings: (1) External knowledge is decisive—open-book access sharply raises performance and narrows inter-model gaps. (2) In closed-book settings, the effect of cascading/chain-of-thought depends on model abstention tendencies. (3) With evidence, the best LLM setting ties nearest-neighbor voting in aggregate but excels on adversarial evidence while losing on multi-functional enzymes—reasoning arbitrates conflicting neighbors rather than supplying knowledge. (4) Accuracy follows a law of homology availability.
AI.conclusion: EC number prediction exposes fundamental limitations in LLMs' hierarchical reasoning capabilities. External knowledge retrieval is the single most impactful lever, and reasoning over evidence serves primarily as an arbitration mechanism. Aggregate metrics mask complementary strengths and weaknesses, calling for more nuanced evaluation beyond single-number leaderboards.

title: CMT-RAG: Complementary Memory Traces for Multi-turn Multi-hop RAG
summary: Multi-turn information-seeking conversations require both multi-hop reasoning and long-range dependency tracking across turns. However, existing RAG systems typically represent conversational memory as raw dialogue history, rewritten queries, or unstructured summaries, making it difficult to recover the specific prior reasoning steps and evidence required for follow-up queries. Our key insight is to align conversational memory with retrieval by representing dialogue context as sub-question-level reasoning traces. Building on this insight, we introduce MuMu-QA, a benchmark for multi-turn multi-hop RAG with explicit cross-turn sub-question dependency annotations, and CMT-RAG, a complementary memory framework for this setting. At each turn, CMT-RAG employs a state-space trace generator, whose recurrent state serves as runtime memory, to incorporate recent conversational context and decompose the current query into structured trace drafts containing retrieval-oriented sub-questions and dependencies on earlier traces. It then grounds these drafts with retrieved evidence and stores them as persistent memory traces in a session-level DAG, enabling future turns to efficiently recover relevant prior reasoning and evidence. Experiments on MuMu-QA and corpus-level RAG benchmarks show that CMT-RAG consistently outperforms five categories of RAG baselines in answer accuracy.

AI.tldr: MuMu-QA is a new benchmark for multi-turn, multi-hop RAG with explicit cross-turn sub-question dependency annotations. CMT-RAG is a complementary framework that uses a state-space trace generator to decompose queries into structured trace drafts, grounds them with retrieved evidence, and stores them as persistent memory traces in a session-level DAG, enabling efficient recovery of prior reasoning for follow-up queries. CMT-RAG outperforms five categories of RAG baselines on both MuMu-QA and corpus-level benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG systems represent conversational memory as raw dialogue history, rewritten queries, or unstructured summaries, which makes it difficult to recover specific prior reasoning steps and evidence needed for follow-up queries in multi-turn, multi-hop information-seeking conversations. The authors aim to solve this by aligning conversational memory with retrieval through sub-question-level reasoning traces.
AI.method: The paper introduces two contributions: (1) MuMu-QA, a benchmark for multi-turn multi-hop RAG with explicit cross-turn sub-question dependency annotations; and (2) CMT-RAG, a complementary memory framework. At each turn, CMT-RAG uses a state-space trace generator with recurrent state as runtime memory to incorporate recent context and decompose the current query into structured trace drafts (retrieval-oriented sub-questions with dependencies on earlier traces). These drafts are grounded with retrieved evidence and stored as persistent memory traces in a session-level DAG, allowing future turns to efficiently recover relevant prior reasoning and evidence.
AI.result: Experiments on MuMu-QA and corpus-level RAG benchmarks demonstrate that CMT-RAG consistently outperforms five categories of RAG baselines in answer accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Aligning conversational memory with retrieval via sub-question-level reasoning traces, operationalized through CMT-RAG's state-space trace generator and session-level DAG memory, significantly improves multi-turn multi-hop RAG performance over existing approaches.

title: Do Latent Channels Actually Communicate? A Causal Audit of Latent Multi-Agent LLM
summary: Latent communication in large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) transmits continuous internal representations instead of text, but greater representational capacity does not establish that the receiver uses task-relevant information. End-task performance alone also cannot reveal whether an observed effect depends on message presence, content generated for the evaluated example, or information supplied by a separate agent. We introduce a causal audit that applies controlled message replacements at the boundary where the sender-produced representation enters the receiver. Four message settings support five measurements of encoded sender information, receiver sensitivity to message presence and identity, the task value of example-specific content, and the additional value supplied by a separate agent. We apply the audit to latent relay with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B on GSM8K, ARC-C, and MATH-500. On GSM8K, the Qwen3-4B overall performance effect of -1.00 percentage point decomposes into a -6.17-point effect retained by an other-example message and a +5.17-point effect attributable to example-specific content; both component directions reverse at 8B. On MATH-500, the Qwen3-4B gain of 15.00 points comprises 8.33 points retained by an other-example message and 6.67 points attributable to example-specific content, while the 8B gain is dominated by the former component. Self-substitution comparisons further show that example-specific content and other-agent value are distinct. These results show that aggregate accuracy does not identify how a latent message affects the receiver and motivate controlled message comparisons as a standard evaluation for latent communication.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a causal audit framework for latent communication in LLM-based multi-agent systems, decomposing end-task performance into components attributable to message presence, example-specific content, and separate-agent value. Applied to Qwen3 models on reasoning benchmarks, results reveal that aggregate accuracy masks opposing or distinct underlying effects, motivating controlled message comparisons as a standard evaluation practice.
AI.motivation: Latent communication in LLM-based MAS replaces text with continuous representations, but higher representational capacity does not guarantee that receivers use task-relevant information. End-task performance alone conflates multiple factors—message presence, example-specific content, and information from a separate agent—making it impossible to determine how a latent message actually affects receiver behavior.
AI.method: The authors propose a causal audit with controlled message replacements at the sender-receiver boundary. Four message settings (original, same-example other-agent, other-example same-agent, and other-example other-agent) support five measurements: encoded sender information, receiver sensitivity to message presence/identity, task value of example-specific content, and additional value from a separate agent. The audit is applied to latent relay with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B on GSM8K, ARC-C, and MATH-500.
AI.result: On GSM8K, Qwen3-4B's overall -1.00 pp effect decomposes into -6.17 pp from an other-example message and +5.17 pp from example-specific content; both directions reverse at 8B. On MATH-500, Qwen3-4B's +15.00 pp gain comprises +8.33 pp from other-example message and +6.67 pp from example-specific content; the 8B gain is dominated by the former. Self-substitution comparisons confirm that example-specific content and other-agent value are distinct factors.
AI.conclusion: Aggregate accuracy fails to identify how latent messages affect receivers. The proposed causal audit with controlled message comparisons should become a standard evaluation for latent communication, as it reveals the distinct and sometimes opposing components underlying overall performance effects.

title: Before Agents Speak: Pre-hoc Failure Risk Inference in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) have exhibited remarkable capabilities in collaborative reasoning and decision-making, yet their interconnected communications introduce new systemic risk: localized hallucinations can propagate along agent communication chain, amplify through interactions, and ultimately trigger cascading failures. Existing countermeasures predominantly follow a post-hoc paradigm, identifying failures only after unsafe behaviors emerge, by which time harmful effects may have already spread throughout the agent network. To tackle this problem, we investigate a complementary pre-hoc approach and propose HalluProp, a Propagation-aware Hallucination inference framework that estimates individual agent failures and emergent system-level hallucination risks before inter-agent interaction. First, we model intrinsic hallucination risks by identifying fine-grained semantic misalignment between agent roles and task queries. We then characterize inter-agent risk propagation by modeling both semantic influence and communication topology. Finally, we integrate these two risks via a differentiable Noisy-OR inference mechanism to derive a systemic diagnosis. Extensive experiments show that HalluProp accurately localizes faulty agents, achieving an average AUROC of 84.6%, while enabling sub-second diagnosis with over $65\times$ speedup over post-hoc methods. By facilitating early intervention through upstream screening, HalluProp effectively complements post-hoc methods, highlighting the potential of pre-hoc risk inference for building more reliable multi-agent systems.

AI.tldr: HalluProp is a pre-hoc framework that predicts hallucination propagation risks in LLM-based multi-agent systems before interactions occur, achieving 84.6% AUROC with 65× speedup over post-hoc methods by modeling semantic misalignment and communication topology.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches to hallucination in multi-agent systems are post-hoc—they detect failures only after unsafe behaviors have already spread through the agent network. A pre-hoc (upstream) method is needed to estimate risks before inter-agent communication, enabling early intervention.
AI.method: HalluProp operates in three stages: (1) modeling intrinsic hallucination risk via fine-grained semantic misalignment between agent roles and task queries; (2) characterizing inter-agent risk propagation by jointly modeling semantic influence and communication topology; (3) integrating both risks through a differentiable Noisy-OR inference mechanism to produce a systemic diagnosis of failure probabilities.
AI.result: HalluProp achieves an average AUROC of 84.6% for localizing faulty agents, delivers sub-second diagnosis, and offers over 65× speedup compared to post-hoc methods.
AI.conclusion: HalluProp demonstrates that pre-hoc risk inference is a viable and efficient complement to post-hoc methods, enabling upstream screening and early intervention for building more reliable multi-agent systems.

title: Flow Map Learning via Nongradient Vector Flow
summary: Diffusion and flow-based models benefit from simple regression losses, but inference incurs significant overhead because sampling requires integration. Consistency models address this by directly learning the flow maps along the ODE trajectory, opening a design space between one-step and many-step approaches. However, existing methods face computational challenges such as requiring model inverses or backpropagation through iterated model calls, and do not always prove that the desired ODE flow map is a solution to the loss. We introduce SGFlow, an approach for learning flow maps that bypasses explicit invertibility constraints and expensive differentiation through model iteration. SGFlow trains a model to compute both the ODE solutions and the implied velocity from scratch by following non-conservative dynamics with a stationary point at the desired flow map. On the CIFAR image benchmark, no single method attains the best FID at every step count: SGFlow attains the best FID at 10 sampling steps and remains competitive with flow matching, Meanflow, and Lagrangian map matching at other step counts, while being the only one with a proven stationary-point guarantee for its stopgrad-based dynamics.

AI.tldr: SGFlow introduces a stopgrad-based dynamics approach for learning flow maps that avoids invertibility constraints and backpropagation through iterated model calls, achieving competitive FID on CIFAR with a proven stationary-point guarantee at the desired ODE flow map.
AI.motivation: Existing consistency models for learning ODE flow maps require either model inverses or expensive backpropagation through iterated model calls, and often lack theoretical guarantees that the desired flow map is actually a solution to the loss. SGFlow addresses both the computational and theoretical gaps.
AI.method: SGFlow trains a model to compute both ODE solutions and implied velocity from scratch by following non-conservative dynamics with a stationary point at the desired flow map, bypassing explicit invertibility constraints and differentiation through model iteration. The stopgrad-based dynamics provide a stationary-point guarantee.
AI.result: On CIFAR, SGFlow attains the best FID at 10 sampling steps, and remains competitive with flow matching, Meanflow, and Lagrangian map matching at other step counts. It is the only method with a proven stationary-point guarantee.
AI.conclusion: SGFlow offers a computationally efficient and theoretically grounded alternative for learning flow maps in diffusion/flow-based generative models, with strong empirical performance particularly at intermediate step counts.

title: When Knowledge Changes: Metamorphic Testing of RAG Systems with Mutations
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-based LLM systems rely on external document corpora that can evolve and change over time. However, current evaluation methodologies (e.g., RAGAS) assess correctness against static snapshots, failing to detect faults when routine updates, factual changes, or noise alter the underlying data. We introduce a metamorphic testing framework that evaluates the consistency of RAG systems under corpus evolution. We formalise a fault taxonomy and 11 mutation operators that systematically perturb the system at both the pre-chunk (retrieval index) and post-chunk (retrieved context) levels. An empirical evaluation across five datasets and over 28k mutants reveals metamorphic violation rates of 4.9-10.2%. In a meta-evaluation against ground truth, our metamorphic oracle achieves F1 scores of 0.927-1.000, while the best RAGAS metric reaches only 0.570. Finally, we provide actionable insights into mitigating these faults through retrieval re-configuration, generator upgrades, and LLM-based reranking.

AI.tldr: Introduces a metamorphic testing framework for RAG systems that evaluates consistency under corpus evolution, using 11 mutation operators across 28k+ mutants, achieving significantly better fault detection (F1 0.927-1.000) than existing metrics like RAGAS (F1 0.570).
AI.motivation: Current RAG evaluation methods (e.g., RAGAS) assess correctness against static snapshots, making them blind to faults arising from routine corpus updates, factual changes, or noise in evolving document corpora. There is a need for evaluation that captures consistency degradation under realistic data evolution.
AI.method: Proposes a metamorphic testing framework with a formal fault taxonomy and 11 mutation operators that perturb RAG systems at two levels: pre-chunk (retrieval index mutations) and post-chunk (retrieved context mutations). Evaluated across 5 datasets with over 28,000 mutants, measuring metamorphic violation rates. A meta-evaluation compares the metamorphic oracle against ground truth and RAGAS metrics using F1 scores.
AI.result: Metamorphic violation rates ranged from 4.9% to 10.2% across datasets. The metamorphic oracle achieved F1 scores of 0.927-1.000 in meta-evaluation against ground truth, substantially outperforming the best RAGAS metric (0.570). Actionable mitigation strategies identified include retrieval re-configuration, generator upgrades, and LLM-based reranking.
AI.conclusion: Metamorphic testing is a highly effective approach for evaluating RAG system robustness under corpus evolution, far surpassing static snapshot-based metrics. The fault taxonomy and mutation operators provide a systematic basis for both evaluation and mitigation in production RAG deployments.

title: The Social Cost of an AI Teammate: How an Artificial Teammate Reshapes Human-Human Communication in Small-Team Decision-Making
summary: Conversational AI is increasingly positioned as a teammate rather than a tool, yet we know little about how its presence reshapes communication among the humans on the team. We examined sociocognitive communication dynamics in team decision-making using Group Communication Analysis (GCA), team surveys, and lexical analyses of team discourse. Teams completed a high-stakes moral-dilemma decision task in a randomized controlled study: 16 teams of two students plus an AI teammate, and 17 all-human teams of three. Across six GCA dimensions and survey outcomes, we find that the AI teammate was the single most talkative and self-cohesive member of every treatment team, yet its contributions carried the least new information and the lowest density. The presence of AI also reshaped communication amongst humans. In AI-human teams, human teammates showed lower responsivity and social impact toward one another and reported lower levels of belonging and status. Greater AI dominance in the conversation was associated with students feeling less valued as team members. Additionally, this social cost is immediate and present at baseline; it does not emerge over the course of the conversation. Drawing on these results, we discuss a research agenda extending to voice-based and longitudinal settings.

AI.tldr: In a controlled experiment comparing human-AI teams (2 humans + 1 AI) with all-human teams (3 humans), the AI teammate dominated conversationally but contributed the least novel information. Its presence reduced human-to-human responsivity, social impact, belonging, and perceived status—a social cost evident from the outset, not emerging over time.
AI.motivation: Conversational AI is increasingly framed as a teammate rather than a mere tool, yet little is known about how its presence alters sociocognitive communication dynamics among the human members of a team. The study aims to fill this gap by examining whether and how an AI teammate reshapes human-to-human interaction, team cohesion, and individual perceptions of belonging and status.
AI.method: A randomized controlled experiment with 33 teams: 16 AI-human teams (2 students + 1 AI) and 17 all-human teams (3 students). Teams completed a high-stakes moral-dilemma decision task. Analysis combined Group Communication Analysis (GCA) across six dimensions, team surveys, and lexical analysis of discourse. The study measured talkativeness, self-cohesion, information novelty, conversational density, responsivity, social impact, and subjective feelings of belonging and status.
AI.result: The AI teammate was the most talkative and self-cohesive member in every treatment team, yet its contributions had the lowest new information and density. In AI-human teams, humans showed lower responsivity and social impact toward each other and reported less belonging and status. Greater AI conversational dominance correlated with students feeling less valued. This social cost was immediate and present at baseline rather than emergent over time.
AI.conclusion: Introducing an AI teammate into small-group decision-making carries an immediate social cost to human team members, reshaping communication patterns and diminishing felt belonging and status. The authors call for a research agenda extending these findings to voice-based interactions and longitudinal settings to better understand and mitigate these effects.

title: Voice Memory for Agentic Speech Recognition
comment: Preprint. Technical report and open source: https://huggingface.co/huckiyang/voice-memory
summary: We present Voice Memory, a inference-only scheme for agentic speech recognition: at stream time, a frozen corrector reads a single per-domain memory.md and decides per utterance whether to act on the hypothesis or abstain and keep the 1-best. Asynchronously, a score-gated optimizer revises that file through bounded edits, accepting an edit only when it strictly improves a held-out score. Extended from classical ASR-LM framework, we refer this split the listener-thinker architecture; the two roles are coupled only through the memory, so no weights change and the learned skill stays auditable and portable. Restraint turns out to be the operative skill this loop discovers: unconstrained generative error correction (GER) over-corrects, breaking correct tokens on up to 64% of its edits on financial news, and Voice Memory, reduces this rate to 35%. Across ten HyPoradise domains with an open corrector, Voice Memory, lowers weighted word error rate from 8.36% to 7.52% (7.47% with three added in-context examples) without regressing any dataset below its 1-best baseline; gains concentrate where recoverable headroom is largest, including air-travel commands (8.40% to 3.40%) and noisy far-field speech (CHiME-4, 12.69% to 10.46%). The memory transfers across corrector families and adds zero parameters to the inference path. A demo and example code are provided for future studies.

AI.tldr: Voice Memory is an inference-only scheme for speech recognition that uses a frozen corrector and a per-domain memory file to selectively correct ASR hypotheses. A score-gated optimizer asynchronously updates the memory only when edits strictly improve a held-out score, reducing over-correction and improving WER across multiple domains without changing model weights.
AI.motivation: Generative error correction (GER) in ASR tends to over-correct, breaking correct tokens on up to 64% of edits. The authors aim to mitigate this by introducing a restrained, auditable, and portable correction mechanism that improves ASR without any weight changes or regressions.
AI.method: A listener-thinker architecture where a frozen corrector (thinker) consults a per-domain memory file at inference time to decide whether to correct each utterance or keep the 1-best hypothesis. An asynchronous, score-gated optimizer revises the memory via bounded edits that are accepted only when they strictly improve a held-out score. In-context examples can optionally augment the memory.
AI.result: Voice Memory reduces over-correction from 64% to 35%. Across 10 HyPoradise domains, weighted WER drops from 8.36% to 7.52% (7.47% with three in-context examples), with no dataset regressing below its 1-best baseline. Gains are largest in air-travel commands (8.40%→3.40%) and CHiME-4 (12.69%→10.46%). The memory transfers across corrector families and adds zero parameters to inference.
AI.conclusion: Voice Memory demonstrates that restraint—selective, memory-gated correction—is an effective, auditable strategy for improving ASR via GER without model retraining, weight changes, or inference-time parameter overhead.

title: RAG-HAR+: Towards Cost-Efficient LLM-Based Human Activity Recognition for Edge Deployment
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Mobile Computing. Extended version of the IEEE PerCom 2026 paper "RAG-HAR: Retrieval Augmented Generation-based Human Activity Recognition." (https://doi.org/10.1109/PerCom67906.2026.11524560)
summary: Human Activity Recognition (HAR) from wearable sensors supports applications in healthcare, rehabilitation, fitness tracking, and smart environments. Yet, existing deep learning approaches require dataset-specific training, large labeled corpora, and repeated adaptation to new sensor settings or activity taxonomies. Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Human Activity Recognition (RAG-HAR) addresses this by framing HAR as a training-free, retrieval-augmented task, in which statistical descriptions of sensor windows are used to retrieve similar labeled examples that guide LLM-based classification. We introduce RAG-HAR+, a retrieval-first and cost-optimized extension that strengthens retrieval while reducing dependence on LLM-based inference. RAG-HAR+ uses an offline Retrieval Designer Agent to design dataset-specific feature groups from a diverse pool of motion descriptors, enabling sensor windows to be compared using features better aligned with dataset-specific activity patterns. During inference, RAG-HAR+ uses majority voting over retrieved neighbors for samples with strong retrieval evidence and defers only uncertain cases to an LLM-based Ambiguity Resolver Agent. Across six HAR benchmarks, RAG-HAR+ maintains competitive or improved performance while reducing LLM usage, token consumption, and inference time. We further extend the RAG-HAR mobile prototype to demonstrate the practical feasibility of retrieval-first, LLM-assisted HAR in mobile sensing scenarios.

AI.tldr: RAG-HAR+ extends retrieval-augmented generation for human activity recognition by introducing an offline Retrieval Designer Agent for dataset-specific feature optimization and a majority-voting mechanism that defers only ambiguous cases to an LLM, achieving competitive performance with reduced LLM usage, token consumption, and inference time across six HAR benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning HAR methods require dataset-specific training, large labeled corpora, and repeated adaptation to new sensor configurations or activity taxonomies. RAG-HAR+ aims to further reduce dependence on costly LLM inference while preserving recognition accuracy in training-free HAR.
AI.method: RAG-HAR+ operates in two stages: (1) an offline Retrieval Designer Agent automatically selects dataset-specific feature groups from a diverse pool of motion descriptors to optimize retrieval alignment with activity patterns; (2) during inference, majority voting over retrieved neighbors handles samples with strong retrieval evidence, while only uncertain cases are deferred to an LLM-based Ambiguity Resolver Agent for final classification.
AI.result: Across six HAR benchmarks, RAG-HAR+ maintains competitive or improved classification performance compared to prior approaches while significantly reducing LLM usage, token consumption, and inference latency. A mobile prototype further validates practical feasibility in real-world sensing scenarios.
AI.conclusion: A retrieval-first, cost-optimized strategy with selective LLM assistance is both effective and practical for HAR, enabling training-free activity recognition that generalizes across datasets while minimizing computational overhead.

title: Property-driven Causal Abstractions for Markov Decision Processes
summary: Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) are widely used as decision-making models, commonly specified over factored state spaces through state variables and their valuations. The exponential blowup in the number of states renders many reasoning tasks in MDPs challenging. Abstractions are promising techniques to reduce MDPs and thus mitigate scalability issues. In this work, we introduce a notion of causality on factored MDPs and a novel property-driven causal abstraction technique that retains many characteristics of the original MDP model. For this, we rely on causal relations over state variable predicates and identify those states that share the same reasons for fulfilling or violating a given abstraction property. We theoretically and empirically compare various causal MDP abstractions using different model types such as MDPs, interval MDPs, or stochastic games. Our evaluation demonstrates the potential of our approach: For several standard benchmarks, we obtain small abstractions that allow us to compute near-optimal policies for the original MDP. Furthermore, our causal abstractions often generalize to related large-scale MDP models.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a property-driven causal abstraction technique for factored MDPs, using causal relations over state variable predicates to identify states sharing the same reasons for satisfying or violating a given property. The approach yields compact abstractions that enable near-optimal policy computation and generalize across related large-scale models.
AI.motivation: Factored MDPs suffer from exponential state-space blowup, making reasoning tasks intractable. Existing abstraction methods mitigate scalability but often lose crucial structural characteristics. The authors aim to leverage causality to produce property-preserving abstractions that retain meaningful MDP semantics while drastically reducing model size.
AI.method: The authors define a notion of causality over factored MDPs based on causal relations among state variable predicates. They identify equivalence classes of states that share identical causal reasons for fulfilling or violating a target property. These classes form the basis of a property-driven causal abstraction. The approach is instantiated across multiple model types — standard MDPs, interval MDPs, and stochastic games — and evaluated theoretically and empirically against standard benchmarks.
AI.result: On several standard benchmarks, the causal abstraction technique produces small abstract models from which near-optimal policies for the original MDP can be computed. The abstractions also demonstrate strong generalization, transferring effectively to related large-scale MDP instances.
AI.conclusion: Property-driven causal abstraction is a promising direction for scaling MDP reasoning, offering compact, semantically meaningful abstractions that preserve near-optimal decision quality and generalize beyond the original instance. The approach bridges causality and abstraction in a principled manner, with applicability across diverse probabilistic models.

title: ToxScreen: Detecting Whether an LLM Has Been Poisoned
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed in high-stakes domains, adversaries may poison training data to implant backdoors: hidden triggers that covertly manipulate model behavior at inference time. We ask whether a defender can recover such a trigger under realistic affordances, namely white-box access to the weights and knowledge of the behavior of concern, but no training data, no trusted reference model, no knowledge of the trigger, and no certainty that the model is poisoned. To evaluate whether a defender can recover such a trigger under realistic settings, we release ToxScreen, a benchmark of roughly 800 backdoored models spanning attack objectives, trigger mechanisms, poisoning rates, model scales, and backdoor training mechanisms. We also assert that the backdoors are high-quality: they achieve high attack success rates, generalize to unseen harmful inputs, and preserve clean-task performance. Scoring recovery of the planted trigger, we find that gradient-based prompt optimization fails in recovery, whereas a token look-up that ranks candidates by attack-success rate recovers the trigger wherever the backdoor is effective. To understand this more, we study the relationship between attack behaviors and the weights of an LLM. We find a phenomenon whereby backdoors operate via different mechanistic strategies than jailbreaks, allowing defenders to filter jailbreaks. Finally, no method reliably surfaces every backdoor, but a broadly jailbreakable model is itself anomalous, a useful signal even when the exact trigger is not recovered. We release all models and evaluation code

AI.tldr: ToxScreen provides a benchmark of ~800 backdoored LLMs and finds that simple token look-up via attack-success rate outperforms gradient-based prompt optimization for trigger recovery, while revealing that backdoors operate via distinct mechanistic strategies from jailbreaks.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are deployed in high-stakes domains, training data poisoning attacks that implant hidden backdoor triggers pose a serious threat. Existing defenses often assume unrealistic affordances (access to training data, trusted reference models, or knowledge of the trigger). The authors aim to investigate whether a defender can recover backdoor triggers under realistic constraints: white-box weight access, knowledge of the concerning behavior, but no training data, no trusted reference model, no trigger knowledge, and no certainty of poisoning.
AI.method: The authors release ToxScreen, a benchmark of approximately 800 backdoored models varying across attack objectives, trigger mechanisms, poisoning rates, model scales, and backdoor training methods. All backdoors are verified to be high-quality (high attack success rate, generalization to unseen harmful inputs, preserved clean-task performance). They then evaluate trigger recovery via two approaches: (1) gradient-based prompt optimization, and (2) a token look-up method that ranks candidate tokens by their attack-success rate. They further analyze the mechanistic differences between backdoor and jailbreak behaviors through weight-level investigation.
AI.result: Gradient-based prompt optimization fails to recover planted triggers. In contrast, token look-up via attack-success rate ranking successfully recovers triggers wherever the backdoor is effective. Backdoors operate through different mechanistic strategies than jailbreaks, enabling defenders to filter out jailbreaks. No method reliably surfaces every backdoor, but a broadly jailbreakable model is itself an anomalous signal useful for detection even when the exact trigger is not recovered.
AI.conclusion: Trigger recovery under realistic assumptions is partially feasible: simple attack-success rate ranking outperforms gradient optimization. The mechanistic distinction between backdoors and jailbreaks provides a practical filtering strategy, and general jailbreakability serves as a useful anomaly signal for identifying potentially poisoned models.

title: Examining the Efficacy of Graph Neural Network Message-Passing in Regression Contexts
summary:
Graph Neural Networks (GNN) facilitate effective prediction on graph data such as molecules, media networks and neural network blueprints. GNNs facilitate prediction through message passing techniques which define how information flows from a node to its neighbors. Due to the ubiquity of the graph data type, the development of newer and better GNNs has garnered much interest in the machine learning community.
  However, GNN evaluation and benchmarking is primarily driven by classification tasks. Thus, prospective GNN message passing layers are evaluated on their ability to outperform prior work in classification contexts. In contrast, GNNs are equally capable of performing scalar regression prediction, yet this class of problem is often overlooked when proposing new GNNs while the best classification GNNs are utilized in an a priori or off-the-shelf manner for regression problems. In response, this paper studies the efficacy of GNN layers in a slew of regression contexts from rank ordering, error minimization and insight extraction. Results show that deep convolutional GNNs, particularly GEN, are more effective at these tasks than attention-based GNNs, while other classical, theoretically-inspired GNNs remain competitive and efficient.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the classification-centric evaluation of GNNs by systematically benchmarking message-passing layers on scalar regression tasks, revealing that deep convolutional architectures (especially GEN) outperform attention-based GNNs in rank ordering, error minimization, and insight extraction.
AI.motivation: GNN evaluation is overwhelmingly driven by classification benchmarks, causing regression capabilities to be neglected. New GNN layers are designed and validated for classification, then applied off-the-shelf to regression without rigorous assessment. This paper addresses the gap by systematically studying GNN layer efficacy specifically in regression contexts.
AI.method: The authors benchmark a diverse set of GNN message-passing layers — including attention-based, deep convolutional, and classical theoretically-inspired architectures — across multiple regression scenarios: rank ordering, error minimization, and insight extraction. Performance is compared to determine which architectures generalize best beyond classification.
AI.result: Deep convolutional GNNs, particularly GEN (Graph Enhancement Network), consistently outperform attention-based GNNs across regression tasks. Classical, theoretically-motivated GNNs remain competitive and computationally efficient alternatives.
AI.conclusion: The GNN community should not default to classification-optimized architectures for regression problems. Deep convolutional GNNs like GEN offer superior regression performance, and the evaluation protocol for new GNN layers should include regression benchmarks to ensure broader applicability.

title: VITAL-RAG: Invariance Race for Context Allocation in Coding Agents
summary: Coding agents often retrieve code from an entire repository, but only limited evidence can fit into the final model input. Conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for coding agents treats fragments from the same code object as separate results, so redundant views can occupy multiple context positions and crowd out useful code. Grouping fragments by code object reduces this redundancy, but can discard local information needed for the task. We describe this tension as an invariance race: allocation should stay stable under redundant renderings but change when a fragment adds task-relevant semantics. To address this race, we introduce VITAL-RAG, which organizes evidence by canonical code object, keeps one query-relevant companion only when it adds semantics not already represented, and renders selected evidence under per-object and global token budgets. On RepoBench, VITALRAG improves Recall@4K from 39.59% to 63.67% while reducing evidence tokens by 35.63%. Across three model backends, it matches or outperforms recent baselines on RepoClassBench and achieves the highest raw Pass@1 on RepoExec.

AI.tldr: VITAL-RAG addresses the redundancy-vs-information trade-off in code retrieval by grouping fragments by code object, retaining only one semantically additive companion fragment, and applying token budgets, achieving significant improvements in recall and task performance while reducing token usage.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG for coding agents treats code fragments independently, causing redundant views of the same code object to occupy limited context windows and crowd out useful evidence. Conversely, naive grouping by object can discard task-relevant local semantics. The authors frame this as an "invariance race": retrieval allocation should be stable under redundant renderings but sensitive to semantically meaningful variations.
AI.method: VITAL-RAG organizes retrieved evidence by canonical code object. For each object, it keeps one query-relevant companion fragment only if that fragment adds semantics not already captured by the canonical representation. Evidence selection operates under both per-object and global token budgets, balancing local and overall context allocation.
AI.result: On RepoBench, VITAL-RAG improves Recall@4K from 39.59% to 63.67% while reducing evidence tokens by 35.63%. Across three model backends, it matches or outperforms recent baselines on RepoClassBench and achieves the highest raw Pass@1 on RepoExec.
AI.conclusion: The invariance-race formulation provides a principled lens for code retrieval, and VITAL-RAG demonstrates that object-aware, semantics-driven evidence selection can simultaneously boost retrieval quality and reduce context footprint, with consistent gains across multiple benchmarks and model backends.

title: GraphQAG: A Knowledge-Graph-Guided Visual Analytics Framework for Question-Answer Pairs Generation
summary: Question-answer (QA) pairs are widely used in knowledge base construction, question-answering systems, and the post-training of large language models (LLMs). However, important knowledge in long documents is often distributed across multiple paragraphs and connected through complex entity relationships. Such fragmented and relational knowledge poses substantial challenges for existing QA generation methods, which often fail to adequately cover core document content, cross-paragraph semantic connections, and multi-entity relationships. We present GraphQAG, a knowledge graph-guided visual analytics framework for generating high-quality QA pairs from long documents. GraphQAG follows a three-stage workflow. First, it constructs a document knowledge graph by segmenting the document into paragraphs and extracting salient entities and relations. Second, it builds a graph-based generation space from entities, relations, and multi-hop paths to constrain and guide LLM-based QA generation. Third, it uses the knowledge graph as an interactive visual representation, enabling users to explore document knowledge structures, inspect the coverage and evidence provenance of generated QA pairs, and iteratively refine the QA pair set through graph-based interactions. We evaluated GraphQAG through a user study with 16 participants, two case studies, and expert interviews. The results indicate that GraphQAG effectively supports users in identifying knowledge coverage gaps, examining generated QA pairs, and refining the QA pair set. These findings demonstrate the usefulness of combining knowledge graphs, LLM-based generation, and visual analytics for producing more comprehensive and trustworthy QA pairs from long documents.

AI.tldr: GraphQAG is a visual analytics framework that combines knowledge graphs, LLMs, and interactive visualizations to generate high-quality QA pairs from long documents, addressing challenges of fragmented and relational knowledge.
AI.motivation: Long documents contain knowledge distributed across multiple paragraphs with complex entity relationships. Existing QA generation methods fail to adequately capture core content, cross-paragraph semantic connections, and multi-entity relationships, necessitating a more structured and interactive approach.
AI.method: GraphQAG employs a three-stage workflow: (1) constructing a document knowledge graph via paragraph segmentation and entity/relation extraction; (2) building a graph-based generation space from entities, relations, and multi-hop paths to guide LLM-based QA generation; (3) providing an interactive visual representation of the knowledge graph for users to explore document structure, inspect QA coverage and evidence provenance, and iteratively refine QA pairs through graph-based interactions.
AI.result: A user study with 16 participants, two case studies, and expert interviews demonstrated that GraphQAG effectively helps users identify knowledge coverage gaps, examine generated QA pairs, and refine the QA pair set.
AI.conclusion: Combining knowledge graphs, LLM-based generation, and visual analytics proves useful for producing more comprehensive and trustworthy QA pairs from long documents.

title: Mergeable Model-Side Aggregation States for Long-Context Language Models
summary: A known limitation of long-context language models is their increasingly unreliable performance in non-additive, set-based aggregation as context length grows. Examples include cardinality estimation, set relationships, and grouped statistics, which widely exist in logs, program outputs, tables, and multi-turn conversations. To provide the aggregation state required by these tasks, we introduce a model-side aggregation interface that maintains compact Hash-based HyperLogLog (HLL) sketch states alongside a frozen language model. While the model processes the context, an extractor maps each relevant record to a canonical identity. The identity is then hashed and updates the HLL state. These states can be merged across context segments and/or read out directly for downstream reasoning, avoiding an additional generate-execute-return cycle. We validate the proposed approach by setting the HLL state size as 2 KiB (2,048 registers), which does not increase with context length or set cardinality. In a distinct-count experiment involving one million records, the mean relative error was 1.6%. In a separate merge test, states built from as many as 256 segments produced exactly the same readout as a single pass over the same stream. On 3,969 aggregate-then-reason tasks from 174 source windows, the fixed-budget interface reached 99.2% accuracy on Gemma 4 (31B, BF16), compared with 100.0% under exact aggregation; the paired gap was 0.8 percentage points (95% window-cluster CI: 0.5-1.3 points). On a matched set of 174 items, our method improved over direct full-context reasoning by 63.2 points on Qwen and 56.3 points on Gemma. The corresponding gains over chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning were 60.9 and 63.2 points, respectively. On a fixed 1,200-task Oolong-Synth subset, our method reached 91.1% on Qwen and 99.3% on Gemma. Code is available at https://github.com/songdc98/sketchops.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a model-side aggregation interface using compact Hash-based HyperLogLog (HLL) sketches (2 KiB fixed size) to solve long-context LMs' unreliability on set-based aggregation tasks. It achieves 99.2% accuracy on Gemma 4 (vs. 100% exact), and improves over direct reasoning by 56–63 points across models, without the overhead of generate-execute-return cycles.
AI.motivation: Long-context language models exhibit increasingly unreliable performance on non-additive, set-based aggregation tasks (cardinality estimation, set relationships, grouped statistics) as context length grows. These tasks are ubiquitous in logs, program outputs, tables, and multi-turn conversations, yet LMs lack a native mechanism to maintain compact, mergeable aggregation state across arbitrarily long contexts.
AI.method: The authors introduce a model-side aggregation interface that co-locates compact Hash-based HyperLogLog (HLL) sketch states alongside a frozen language model. An extractor maps each relevant record to a canonical identity, which is hashed to update the HLL state. These states are mergeable across context segments and directly readable for downstream reasoning, eliminating the need for an additional generate-execute-return cycle. The HLL state is fixed at 2 KiB (2,048 registers), independent of context length or set cardinality.
AI.result: (1) Distinct-count experiment over 1M records: 1.6% mean relative error. (2) Merge test: states built from up to 256 segments produced identical readout to a single pass. (3) On 3,969 aggregate-then-reason tasks from 174 source windows: 99.2% accuracy on Gemma 4 (31B, BF16) vs. 100.0% exact aggregation (gap: 0.8 pp, 95% CI: 0.5–1.3). (4) Improvement over direct full-context reasoning: +63.2 points (Qwen), +56.3 points (Gemma). (5) Improvement over CoT: +60.9 (Qwen), +63.2 (Gemma). (6) On Oolong-Synth 1,200-task subset: 91.1% (Qwen), 99.3% (Gemma).
AI.conclusion: The fixed-budget HLL sketch interface effectively addresses the aggregation reliability problem in long-context LMs without fine-tuning, achieving near-exact accuracy on aggregate-then-reason tasks while maintaining a constant memory footprint and supporting efficient state merging across segments.

title: Kairos: Numerically Robust News Recommendation under Item Cold-Start via Cholesky-based LinUCB
comment: English preprint. The German version was peer-reviewed and accepted at SKILL 2026 (Gesellschaft für Informatik)
summary: Algorithmic news personalization in regional markets often fails because modern deep learning models require massive interaction data while real-world news has a short Time-to-Live (TTL < 48 h) and shallow article pools. This structural item cold-start deprives collaborative filtering of the data needed for robust modeling. This paper presents Project Kairos, a framework that bridges this data scarcity through a contextual online learning approach (LinUCB). To ensure numerical integrity for continuous operation, Kairos replaces error-prone Sherman-Morrison inversions with direct rank-1 updates of Cholesky factors. This preserves the positive definiteness of the covariance matrix even under ill-conditioned data scenarios. Simultaneously, Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) integration addresses inference latency. Empirical evaluations based on the Tagesschau API demonstrate that exploiting semantic redundancy in the feature space achieves a 4.85-fold efficiency gain without significantly compromising ranking precision. Kairos thus provides a blueprint for high-performance recommendation systems in resource- and data-constrained environments.

AI.tldr: Project Kairos addresses data-scarce news personalization using contextual bandits (LinUCB) with numerically stable Cholesky updates and Matryoshka Representation Learning for latency reduction, achieving 4.85× efficiency gains on Tagesschau data.
AI.motivation: Deep learning recommenders fail in regional news markets due to structural item cold-start: short Time-to-Live (<48h), shallow article pools, and insufficient interaction data for collaborative filtering.
AI.method: A contextual online learning framework (LinUCB) with two key innovations: (1) rank-1 Cholesky factor updates instead of Sherman-Morrison inversions to maintain covariance matrix positive definiteness under ill-conditioned data; (2) Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) integration to reduce inference latency by exploiting semantic redundancy in the feature space.
AI.result: A 4.85-fold efficiency gain in inference latency without significant ranking precision degradation, validated through empirical evaluations using the Tagesschau API.
AI.conclusion: Kairos provides a viable blueprint for high-performance recommendation systems operating under resource and data constraints characteristic of regional news markets.

title: From Passive Video to Editable Experience: Physically Grounded Experience Synthesis for Embodied Intelligence
summary: The key bottleneck in embodied AI is not model architecture but data. Although billions of human manipulation videos exist online, robots cannot directly learn from them due to the embodiment gap between human morphology and robot hardware. We introduce Pegasus, a low-resource framework that bridges this gap by translating human demonstrations into robot-learnable data through structured knowledge transfer. Instead of relying on raw video prompts, Pegasus constructs a graph-based intermediate representation: a Task Graph extracted from human videos is transformed through Affordance and Constraint Graphs into a Robot Planning Graph for robot-conditioned video generation. A hierarchical affordance latent space models the relationship between object states, affordances, and tasks, enabling generalization beyond object identities. A closed-loop physics verifier further filters invalid generations using kinematic feasibility, collision constraints, and joint limits. We evaluate Pegasus across a range of egocentric manipulation benchmarks, including GTEA Gaze+ and EPIC-KITCHENS-100, and diverse robot embodiments, assessing Task Correctness, Executability, State Consistency, and Learnability. Results demonstrate reliable cross-embodiment translation and show that robot data generation can be reframed from a hardware collection problem into a scalable, low-resource knowledge transfer problem.

AI.tldr: Pegasus bridges the embodiment gap between human manipulation videos and robot learning by translating human demonstrations into robot-learnable data via structured knowledge transfer using graph-based intermediate representations, a hierarchical affordance latent space, and a physics verifier — reframing robot data generation as a scalable knowledge transfer problem.
AI.motivation: The key bottleneck in embodied AI is data scarcity for robots, not model architecture. Billions of human manipulation videos exist online but cannot be directly used due to the embodiment gap — differences in human morphology and robot hardware. Existing approaches fail because raw video prompts alone cannot bridge this gap.
AI.method: Pegasus employs a multi-stage structured knowledge transfer pipeline: (1) A Task Graph is extracted from human demonstration videos; (2) This is transformed through Affordance and Constraint Graphs into a Robot Planning Graph; (3) A hierarchical affordance latent space models relationships between object states, affordances, and tasks for generalization beyond specific object identities; (4) A closed-loop physics verifier filters invalid generations using kinematic feasibility, collision constraints, and joint limits; (5) The final output enables robot-conditioned video generation for downstream policy learning.
AI.result: Evaluated on egocentric manipulation benchmarks (GTEA Gaze+, EPIC-KITCHENS-100) across diverse robot embodiments, Pegasus demonstrates reliable cross-embodiment translation measured by Task Correctness, Executability, State Consistency, and Learnability metrics.
AI.conclusion: Robot data generation can be reframed from a hardware-dependent collection problem into a scalable, low-resource knowledge transfer problem, enabling robots to effectively learn from the vast corpus of existing human manipulation videos.

title: Defending Against Backdoor Attacks via Alignment Checking in Model-Contrastive Federated Learning
summary:
Federated Learning (FL) is vulnerable to backdoor attacks because of its distributed nature in edge computing scenarios. Existing defense methods show limited efficacy as they overlook the deviations among benign local updates caused by statistical heterogeneity and the stealthiness of backdoor attacks. To tackle these issues, we propose FedDAB, a two-phase method that combines local contrastive regularization with alignment checking, to defend against backdoor attacks. In the first phase, FedDAB introduces a novel model-contrastive term into the local objective to enhance direction and magnitude consistency among benign updates. In the second phase, FedDAB employs an alignment checking strategy to evaluate each local update in terms of overall-direction alignment and parameter-level alignment with historical information, excluding updates that exhibit abnormal alignment patterns from global aggregation. We theoretically prove FedDAB's robustness with a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$.
  Extensive experiments show that FedDAB outperforms existing defense methods against backdoor attacks.

AI.tldr: FedDAB is a two-phase federated learning defense against backdoor attacks, combining local contrastive regularization to align benign updates with global direction/magnitude, and alignment checking (overall-direction + parameter-level) against historical info to filter malicious updates. It achieves O(1/T) convergence and SOTA defense performance.
AI.motivation: Existing FL backdoor defenses are ineffective because they fail to address two key challenges: (1) deviations among benign local updates caused by statistical heterogeneity (non-IID data), and (2) the stealthiness of backdoor attacks that make malicious updates hard to distinguish from benign ones.
AI.method: FedDAB operates in two phases. Phase 1 introduces a model-contrastive regularization term into the local training objective to promote direction and magnitude consistency among benign client updates. Phase 2 employs an alignment checking strategy that evaluates each local update on two dimensions: overall-direction alignment and parameter-level alignment with historical update information. Updates exhibiting abnormal alignment patterns are excluded from global aggregation.
AI.result: The authors theoretically prove FedDAB's robustness with a convergence rate of O(1/T). Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedDAB outperforms existing defense methods against backdoor attacks in federated learning settings.
AI.conclusion: FedDAB effectively mitigates backdoor attacks in heterogeneous FL environments by enforcing update consistency through contrastive regularization and detecting anomalies via alignment checking, achieving both theoretical convergence guarantees and state-of-the-art empirical defense performance.

title: SCOUT: Per-Context Reset Curricula for Sparse-Reward Reinforcement Learning
summary: Sparse-reward reinforcement learning often fails because rollouts from the unassisted evaluation start rarely reach later task stages. Reset curricula address this by starting some training rollouts from easier intermediate states, called scaffolds. Such a curriculum faces two decisions: scaffold access, obtaining informative starts, and scaffold allocation, deciding how quickly that assistance is removed. Most prior curricula pace removal on one shared schedule, which can fail when task instances, or contexts, learn at different rates. We introduce SCOUT, an online, learner-agnostic reset controller that gives every context its own curriculum. Using only binary rollout success, SCOUT removes assistance after sustained success, restores it after failure, and cautiously tests a harder start when progress stalls, without changing the reward, optimizer, or learner. A counting construction shows that synchronized global pacing can be insufficient when contexts need conflicting amounts of assisted practice. Across six navigation and manipulation settings, scaffold access improves learning and enables success in three where unassisted training fails within the reported budget. In a constructed pacing conflict, each tested global schedule leaves one group unsolved, while SCOUT solves both. Average success can conceal this failure, so we also report the least successful group. Group-level pacing works when learning differences follow known groups but can fail when they occur within one group. SCOUT needs no group labels and remains consistently strong in both cases. A reset curriculum should remove assistance at the scale where learning progress differs.

AI.tldr: SCOUT is an online, learner-agnostic reset controller that gives each task context its own curriculum pace—removing assistance after sustained success, restoring it after failure, and testing harder starts when progress stalls—outperforming global pacing schedules, especially when contexts learn at different rates.
AI.motivation: Sparse-reward RL often fails because evaluation rollouts rarely reach later task stages. Reset curricula address this by starting training from intermediate "scaffold" states, but most prior work uses a single shared pacing schedule. This fails when different task instances (contexts) learn at different rates—some need more assisted practice than others. A single global schedule can leave slower-learning contexts unsolved, and average success can conceal this failure mode.
AI.method: SCOUT is an online, learner-agnostic reset controller that maintains a per-context curriculum using only binary rollout success signals. It removes assistance (advances to harder starts) after sustained success, restores assistance after failure, and cautiously tests a harder start when progress stalls. Crucially, it requires no changes to the reward, optimizer, or learner. The paper also provides a counting construction to formally demonstrate that synchronized global pacing is insufficient when contexts have conflicting assisted-practice needs.
AI.result: Across six navigation and manipulation settings, scaffold access improves learning and enables success in three tasks where unassisted training fails within the budget. In a constructed pacing-conflict scenario, every tested global schedule leaves at least one group unsolved, while SCOUT solves both. The paper also shows that group-level pacing works when learning differences follow known groups but fails when differences occur within a group; SCOUT needs no group labels and remains strong in both cases.
AI.conclusion: A reset curriculum should remove assistance at the scale where learning progress differs. SCOUT demonstrates that per-context pacing, driven only by binary success signals and without group labels, learner modification, or reward shaping, reliably outperforms global schedules—particularly when contexts exhibit heterogeneous learning dynamics. Reporting the least successful group, not just average success, is essential to detect pacing failures.

title: How Developers Experience Debugging Unfamiliar Codebases with Code Tours Generated and Evaluated by Local LLMs
summary: Code tours are interactive, onboarding documentation to guide developers through a codebase. Large Language Models (LLMs) can automatically synthesize code tours. Prior work on code tour generation has not studied developer experience or trust calibration when debugging unfamiliar codebases with code tours generated and evaluated by open-weight LLMs. This study surveys how the properties of components in open-weight LLM-authored code tours influence developers' experiences when debugging unfamiliar codebases. We built a pipeline that generated and evaluated code tours from real reproducible bugs. 26 developers with varying backgrounds participated in a user study. In total, 26 code tours were authored from real Java bugs mined from 2025 GitHub commits, with each tour independently judged by two different LLMs, resulting in 52 evaluated configurations. Participants thought aloud as they explored each tour. Three authors qualitatively coded the interviews to identify recurring themes. Developers generally preferred tours that scaled detail with the code length, avoided merely restating code, were easily scannable, and adopted a guiding tone. However, some preferences were mutually exclusive, such as the use of imperative mood. Stack traces were often insufficient to identify all steps developers found relevant. Developers also trusted descriptions they perceived as human-written more than those they believed were AI-generated. Finally, LLM-generated annotations of tour quality were unreliable: sycophancy, confabulation, and incoherence were pervasive. This work lays a basis for future research on fine-tuning open-weight models for code tour generation, personalizing generation to accommodate diverging preferences, selecting relevant steps beyond stack traces, calibrating users' trust to avoid both disuse and misuse, and improving open-weight LLMs' ability to be more trustworthy evaluators

AI.tldr: A user study with 26 developers investigated how properties of open-weight LLM-generated code tours affect debugging of unfamiliar codebases. Developers preferred tours with scaled detail, scannability, guiding tone, and no mere code restatement. Trust varied based on perceived authorship (human vs. AI). LLM evaluators of tour quality were unreliable due to sycophancy, confabulation, and incoherence.
AI.motivation: Prior work on LLM-generated code tours has not examined developer experience or trust calibration when debugging unfamiliar codebases, particularly using open-weight LLMs. Understanding how tour properties influence developer experience is essential for improving automated onboarding documentation.
AI.method: The authors built a pipeline to generate and evaluate code tours from real reproducible Java bugs mined from 2025 GitHub commits. 26 developers participated in a think-aloud user study, exploring 26 code tours, each independently judged by two different LLMs (52 evaluated configurations). Three authors qualitatively coded the interview transcripts to identify recurring themes.
AI.result: Developers preferred tours that: (1) scaled detail with code length, (2) avoided restating code, (3) were scannable, and (4) used a guiding tone. Some preferences were mutually exclusive (e.g., imperative mood). Stack traces proved insufficient for identifying all relevant steps. Trust was higher for descriptions perceived as human-written. LLM-generated quality annotations exhibited pervasive sycophancy, confabulation, and incoherence.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a foundation for future research on fine-tuning open-weight models for code tour generation, personalizing tours for diverging preferences, improving step selection beyond stack traces, calibrating user trust to mitigate disuse and misuse, and developing more trustworthy LLM evaluators.

title: ForgetBench: Benchmarking Forgetting Dynamics of Long-Term Parametric Memory in Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in knowledge acquisition and reasoning, yet their ability to retain previously acquired knowledge under repeated updates remains insufficiently understood. Existing evaluation paradigms primarily focus on single-step reasoning or static knowledge editing, which fail to capture the temporal dynamics of knowledge retention and degradation during continual model modification. In this work, we propose ForgetBench, a benchmark designed to systematically characterize forgetting behavior in LLMs under continual knowledge editing. ForgetBench introduces two complementary evaluation paradigms, namely concept-based QA and scenario-based QA, to disentangle isolated factual retention from structured relational knowledge preservation. Building upon a sequential editing framework, we construct temporally ordered knowledge streams and evaluate model behavior across multiple editing stages. To quantitatively analyze long-term retention dynamics, we further introduce a unified evaluation framework that models knowledge evolution over time, enabling the measurement of temporal decay, retention strength, and cross-instance stability. Extensive experiments across diverse models and editing methods demonstrate that existing approaches fail to strike a balance between long-term retention and generalization quality. Our findings highlight the need for more robust memory mechanisms that can effectively acquire, update, and preserve knowledge over time in future LLMs. Code will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: ForgetBench is a benchmark for measuring knowledge forgetting in LLMs under continual editing, using concept-based and scenario-based QA to assess isolated facts and relational knowledge retention over time, revealing that current methods fail to balance long-term retention with generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM evaluation paradigms focus on single-step reasoning or static knowledge editing, failing to capture temporal dynamics of knowledge retention and degradation during continual model modification. The gap is understanding how LLMs forget previously acquired knowledge under repeated updates.
AI.method: Proposes ForgetBench with two complementary evaluation paradigms: concept-based QA (isolated factual retention) and scenario-based QA (structured relational knowledge preservation). Uses a sequential editing framework with temporally ordered knowledge streams and evaluates across multiple editing stages. Introduces a unified evaluation framework modeling knowledge evolution over time, measuring temporal decay, retention strength, and cross-instance stability.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse models and editing methods show that existing approaches fail to balance long-term retention and generalization quality.
AI.conclusion: There is a need for more robust memory mechanisms in future LLMs that can effectively acquire, update, and preserve knowledge over time.

title: DenseOn with the LateOn: Fully Open Dense and Late-Interaction Models for Multilingual, Long-Context, and Code Search
summary: State-of-the-art retrieval models increasingly rely on closed training data, creating a reproducibility gap. We present an open end-to-end recipe for training retrieval models and study how English supervision transfers to multilingual retrieval through translate-train. We first reconstruct and curate 665M English contrastive pre-training pairs from 1.4B pairs across 34 public sources and build 1.88M supervised fine-tuning pairs with mined hard negatives. Training yields two 149M-parameter models: DenseOn, a single-vector dense model, and LateOn, a ColBERT-style late-interaction model. They achieve 56.20 and 57.22 average nDCG@10 on BEIR, respectively, setting new state-of-the-art results for this size class. We then translate the validated English data into eight languages, yielding 2.8B pairs with cross-lingual samples, and train mDenseOn and mLateOn, two 307M-parameter models built on mmBERT-base. Despite sharing their backbone, data, and objectives, their representations behave differently: the dense model is strong on English and translated languages but degrades outside translate-train support, whereas the late-interaction model generalizes better to unseen languages and scripts. This suggests that token-level matching turns translate-train from a target-language expansion strategy into a multilingual generalization recipe. We publicly release the models, datasets, and training code.

AI.tldr: Open-source end-to-end recipe for training retrieval models; English models set SOTA for 149M-parameter class on BEIR; multilingual translate-train on 8 languages reveals late-interaction (ColBERT-style) generalizes better to unseen languages than dense single-vector models.
AI.motivation: Address the reproducibility gap in state-of-the-art retrieval caused by closed training data, and investigate how English supervision transfers to multilingual retrieval via translate-train, comparing dense vs. late-interaction architectures.
AI.method: Reconstruct 665M English contrastive pre-training pairs from 1.4B pairs across 34 public sources; build 1.88M supervised fine-tuning pairs with mined hard negatives; train DenseOn (single-vector dense) and LateOn (ColBERT-style late-interaction), both 149M parameters. Translate validated English data into 8 languages to create 2.8B cross-lingual pairs; train mDenseOn and mLateOn (307M parameters, mmBERT-base backbone). Evaluate on BEIR and analyze cross-lingual generalization.
AI.result: DenseOn and LateOn achieve 56.20 and 57.22 average nDCG@10 on BEIR, setting new SOTA for the 149M-parameter size class. Multilingual models show divergent behavior: the dense model performs well on English and translated languages but degrades outside translate-train support; the late-interaction model generalizes better to unseen languages and scripts, suggesting token-level matching converts translate-train into a multilingual generalization strategy.
AI.conclusion: An open, reproducible retrieval training pipeline can match or exceed closed models. Translate-train with late-interaction architectures yields broader multilingual generalization beyond the translated languages, while dense models remain more confined to the training language distribution.

title: What Does It Take to Detect an AI Agent? Minimal Feature Sets for Behavioral Detection under Browser Automation
comment: 17 pages (11 main + appendices), 7 figures. Accepted at the North East AI Agents Day 2026 workshop, Jane Street, New York City. Workshop: https://ne-agents-day.github.io/
summary: Bot detectors deployed at scale treat traffic as binary: human or bot. This assumption breaks when AI agents browse the web through browser automation, a traffic class that is neither and that binary classifiers structurally cannot represent. We present a three-class detection framework distinguishing humans, bots, and AI agents, and show that the binary-vs-agent confusion is architectural: a binary human-vs-bot detector misroutes agent sessions because its label space lacks an agent class. On our controlled benchmark, an MLP binary classifier misclassifies 39.1% of real AI agents as human and a SAINT binary transformer misclassifies 34.5%; adding an explicit agent class yields per-class agent F1 = 1.000 in all 30 runs (3 model families $\times$ 10 seeds). To measure evasion resistance, we construct a five-level evasion ladder spanning passive observation, GAN-generated trajectories, and replay of real human cursor data ($n = 2299$ evasion sessions). Across 10 seeds and 3 model families we observe zero agent misses in 22990 per-seed predictions. The discriminative signal is a browser-automation artifact, not evidence of agent reasoning: Playwright does not emit the raw pointer-move and wheel-delta streams a physical input device produces, and this absence signature survives trajectory manipulation. Exhaustive search over all feature subsets of size 1-5 (9401 GBMs) shows that two behavioral features (mouse_event_rate, teleport_click_ratio) give 100% observed agent recall at every evasion level with agent precision 0.994; five features lift macro-F1 to 0.991. The signal is redundantly encoded: removing teleport_click_ratio leaves agent detection at 100%. The single-feature regime is degenerate, flagging every agent only by collapsing the classifier to always predict "agent". Two features robustly isolate agents; five separate all three traffic classes at macro-F1 $\geq 0.99$.

AI.tldr: Binary bot detectors fail against AI agents that use browser automation because such agents are neither human nor bot. The paper proposes a three-class framework (human/bot/AI agent), demonstrates that binary classifiers structurally misclassify agents, and shows that browser-automation artifacts (missing raw pointer/wheel events) provide a robust, evasion-resistant signal achieving near-perfect three-class separation with just 2–5 behavioral features.
AI.motivation: Current bot detection systems operate on a binary assumption (human vs. bot), but the emergence of AI agents using browser automation tools like Playwright creates a third traffic class that falls outside this taxonomy. Binary classifiers cannot structurally represent this class, leading to misrouting of agent sessions. The work aims to quantify this failure mode and provide a detection framework that explicitly models AI agents as a distinct class while remaining resistant to evasion.
AI.method: The authors (1) construct a controlled benchmark with three traffic classes; (2) evaluate binary classifiers (MLP, SAINT transformer) to quantify agent misclassification rates; (3) extend to a three-class framework across three model families × 10 seeds; (4) build a five-level evasion ladder (passive observation, GAN-generated trajectories, replay of real human cursor data, with 2299 evasion sessions) to test robustness; (5) perform exhaustive feature-subset search over 9401 GBMs to identify minimal discriminative features; and (6) analyze the root cause: Playwright's failure to emit raw pointer-move and wheel-delta streams that physical input devices produce.
AI.result: Binary classifiers misclassify 34.5%–39.1% of AI agents (as human). The three-class framework achieves per-class agent F1 = 1.000 across all 30 runs. Under evasion testing, zero agent misses occur across 22,990 per-seed predictions. Exhaustive feature search reveals two behavioral features (mouse_event_rate, teleport_click_ratio) yield 100% agent recall at every evasion level with 0.994 precision; five features achieve macro-F1 = 0.991.
