The signal is redundantly encoded and survives trajectory manipulation because it stems from an automation artifact, not agent reasoning.
AI.conclusion: The binary human-vs-bot paradigm is architecturally insufficient for the era of AI agents. Browser automation leaves a distinctive, low-level artifact signature (absent pointer-move and wheel-delta event streams) that is not easily masked by trajectory-level evasion and enables robust, computationally lightweight three-class discrimination with as few as two features. The finding has immediate implications for bot detection infrastructure deployed at scale.

title: InkShield: Writing Style Protection Against Unauthorized Handwriting Mimicry
summary: Recent handwritten text generators can reproduce a writer's style from publicly available references, posing risks of document forgery and identity misuse. An attacker may use a publicly available handwritten note or signature sample to generate forged recommendation letters or authorization forms, leading to document fraud, identity misuse, and misleading decisions. However, existing protections against unauthorized image editing or synthesis transfer poorly to handwriting style mimicry. Designed for natural images with complex backgrounds, they often optimize perturbations over the whole image. For sparse handwriting images, such global perturbations become conspicuous in blank background regions and largely degrade the visual quality. In this work, we propose InkShield, a proactive writing-style defense that protects reference images before release. InkShield selects a decoy writer to define a style-displacement direction, optimizes perturbations with a frozen handwriting-generation surrogate, and confines them to ink-stroke edges to avoid conspicuous background artifacts. On IAM, the average Top-1/Top-5 rates at which generated samples are retrieved as the target writer by two independent writer evaluators decrease from 11.94%/36.52% to 2.03%/8.79%. Meanwhile, the protected references remain visually close to the originals (LPIPS 0.0078), and the generated text remains readable. InkShield also exhibits transferability to other handwriting generators. Overall, InkShield provides practical protection against unauthorized handwriting style mimicry.

AI.tldr: InkShield is a proactive defense that protects handwritten reference images from style mimicry by applying imperceptible perturbations confined to ink-stroke edges, using a decoy writer to define a style-displacement direction. It significantly reduces writer identification rates while preserving visual quality and readability.
AI.motivation: Recent handwriting text generators can reproduce a writer's style from public samples, enabling document forgery and identity misuse. Existing protections (designed for natural images) apply global perturbations that are conspicuous on sparse handwriting images due to blank backgrounds, degrading visual quality. A handwriting-specific defense is needed.
AI.method: InkShield operates proactively by: (1) selecting a decoy writer to define a style-displacement direction, (2) optimizing perturbations using a frozen handwriting-generation surrogate model, and (3) confining perturbations exclusively to ink-stroke edges to avoid conspicuous background artifacts.
AI.result: On the IAM dataset, InkShield reduces the Top-1 writer retrieval rate from 11.94% to 2.03% and Top-5 from 36.52% to 8.79% across two independent writer evaluators. Protected references maintain high visual fidelity (LPIPS 0.0078) and generated text remains readable. The method also transfers to other handwriting generators.
AI.conclusion: InkShield provides practical, effective protection against unauthorized handwriting style mimicry, balancing strong defense with minimal visual degradation by spatially confining perturbations to stroke edges.

title: Existence-Field Diffusion Model for Spatial Point Processes with Variable Cardinality
summary: We study generative modeling of spatial point processes (SPP), where both the number of points and their spatial configuration are governed by a joint distribution. While diffusion models have achieved strong performance in modeling complex distributions, extending them to variable-cardinality SPP remains challenging. Existing approaches either decouple the modeling of cardinality and spatial structure, or rely on discrete trans-dimensional operations to modify the number of points, resulting in inflexible and asymmetric generative dynamics. We propose the existence-field diffusion model (EFDM) for spatial point processes modeling, where each potential point is associated with an existence variable representing its degree of presence. This enables a unified diffusion process that jointly models both spatial locations and cardinality without requiring explicit discrete transitions. We demonstrate that our approach provides a flexible and general framework for generative modeling of spatial point processes, achieving improved modeling capability on datasets with varying cardinality.

AI.tldr: EFDM introduces existence variables for each potential point in spatial point processes, enabling a unified diffusion framework that jointly models point locations and cardinality without discrete trans-dimensional operations.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion models for spatial point processes either decouple cardinality and spatial modeling or rely on discrete trans-dimensional operations to change point counts, leading to inflexible and asymmetric generative dynamics. A unified, flexible approach is needed.
AI.method: Proposes Existence-Field Diffusion Model (EFDM), where each potential point is assigned an existence variable representing its degree of presence, allowing a single continuous diffusion process to jointly model spatial locations and cardinality without explicit discrete transitions.
AI.result: EFDM provides a flexible and general generative modeling framework for SPP, achieving improved modeling capability on datasets with varying cardinality.
AI.conclusion: The existence-field formulation offers a principled way to unify spatial and cardinality modeling in diffusion-based SPP generation, overcoming limitations of prior decoupled or trans-dimensional approaches.

title: MindForge: Teaching Small Language Models Whole-Life-Cycle Software Engineering via Source-Free Program Synthesis
summary: Coding agents have made substantial progress on software engineering tasks that modify existing codebases, including bug fixing and feature implementation. However, constructing a complete program from scratch remains a major challenge: even the frontier models evaluated on ProgramBench fully resolve fewer than 1% of tasks. One obstacle is the lack of scalable training environments for this from-scratch setting, spanning the whole software engineering life cycle, as existing environment-construction frameworks focus only on a single phase in software development. To address this gap, we introduce MindForge, an automated pipeline that converts open-source command-line programs into source-free environments that expose only a compiled reference executable and its documentation. Using MindForge, we construct training environments from repositories disjoint from those in ProgramBench, and curate a high-quality data recipe consisting of program synthesis trajectories using GLM-5.2 as the teacher agent. Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-27B on these trajectories increases its ProgramBench average test pass rate from 37.98% to 49.51%, achieving performance comparable to substantially larger frontier models. Moreover, the fine-tuned model consistently improves over the base model across all seven unseen software engineering benchmarks, spanning long-horizon repository generation and translation, bug fixing, feature implementation, and cross-language issue resolution, with absolute gains of 31.00 points on RepoZero-C2Rust, 14.16 on DeepSWE, 10.70/4.56 on NL2Repo-Bench (with/without tests), 5.04 on SWE-bench Verified, 5.93 on SWE-bench Pro, 5.22 on SWE-bench Multilingual, and 4.94 on FeatBench.

AI.tldr: MindForge is an automated pipeline that converts open-source CLI programs into source-free training environments for program synthesis from scratch. Fine-tuning Qwen3.6-27B on trajectories from these environments boosts ProgramBench pass rate from 37.98% to 49.51% and yields consistent gains across seven unseen SE benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Coding agents struggle with constructing complete programs from scratch (frontier models resolve <1% of ProgramBench tasks). A key bottleneck is the absence of scalable training environments covering the full software engineering lifecycle — existing frameworks only address single development phases.
AI.method: The authors propose MindForge, an automated pipeline that converts open-source command-line programs into source-free training environments exposing only a compiled executable and documentation. They use GLM-5.2 as a teacher to generate program synthesis trajectories on MindForge-built environments (from repositories disjoint from ProgramBench), then fine-tune Qwen3.6-27B on this curated data recipe.
AI.result: Fine-tuning lifts ProgramBench average test pass rate from 37.98% to 49.51%, rivaling much larger frontier models. Gains generalize across seven unseen benchmarks: RepoZero-C2Rust (+31.00), DeepSWE (+14.16), NL2Repo-Bench (+10.70/+4.56 with/without tests), SWE-bench Verified (+5.04), SWE-bench Pro (+5.93), SWE-bench Multilingual (+5.22), and FeatBench (+4.94).
AI.conclusion: MindForge enables scalable, full-lifecycle training environments for from-scratch program synthesis. Fine-tuning on teacher-generated trajectories yields substantial and broadly generalizable improvements, demonstrating that environment quality and data curation can close the gap between mid-sized and frontier coding models.

title: Belief-Guided Decision Making with Uncertainty Gating in the Game of Go
summary: Recent advancements in Computer Go, driven by AlphaZero and MuZero, rely heavily on Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to correct the errors of the neural network policy. While effective on massive computational clusters, this dependence creates a critical bottleneck on consumer-grade hardware, where the computational cost of tree management severely limits inference rates. Furthermore, without deep search, these models suffer from hallucination, proposing moves with high confidence that are strategically fatal. This paper introduces a novel Belief-Guided architecture that disentangles the Policy head from a distinct Belief head. Unlike traditional value functions, the Belief head acts as an internal simulator and independent critic, modeling epistemic uncertainty and strategic stability. By integrating memory mechanisms (Transformer/GRU) to handle long-term dependencies and the Ko rule, and utilizing a gating mechanism to filter overconfident policy errors, our model shifts the burden of intelligence from runtime search to parametric "intuition." Experimental results demonstrate that this approach significantly improves search-free win rates and reduces hallucination, enabling professional-level play on limited hardware where massive MCTS is infeasible.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Belief-Guided architecture for Computer Go that separates the policy head from a novel Belief head, which models epistemic uncertainty and strategic stability. By integrating memory mechanisms (Transformer/GRU) and a gating mechanism to filter overconfident errors, the model reduces reliance on MCTS, enabling professional-level play on consumer-grade hardware without deep search.
AI.motivation: The heavy dependence of AlphaZero/MuZero-style models on MCTS creates a computational bottleneck on consumer hardware, severely limiting inference rates. Without deep search, these models hallucinate—proposing strategically fatal moves with high confidence. The authors aim to shift intelligence from runtime search to parametric "intuition," making professional-level Go feasible on limited hardware.
AI.method: The proposed Belief-Guided architecture disentangles the Policy head from a distinct Belief head. The Belief head functions as an internal simulator and independent critic, modeling epistemic uncertainty and strategic stability (unlike traditional value functions). Memory mechanisms (Transformer or GRU) handle long-term dependencies and the Ko rule. A gating mechanism filters overconfident policy errors by leveraging the Belief head's uncertainty estimates to suppress unreliable move proposals.
AI.result: Experimental results show significant improvement in search-free win rates and a reduction in hallucination. The approach enables professional-level play on limited hardware where massive MCTS is infeasible.
AI.conclusion: Shifting the burden of intelligence from runtime MCTS to parametric "intuition" via the Belief-Guided architecture is a viable path toward strong, efficient Computer Go on consumer-grade hardware, overcoming the hallucination and computational limitations of search-dependent models.

title: AgentSnare: Learning to Delay, Divert, and Defuse Autonomous Penetration Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents automate penetration testing through an observation-action loop, selecting actions based on observations returned by tools. This dependence allows defenders to inject deceptive observations that can mislead the agent's decision-making process. However, existing defenses rely heavily on static, isolated artifacts planted in the environment prior to an attack. Advanced agents can progressively recognize and bypass these artifacts, ultimately refocusing their exploitation attempts on the real target. To address this issue, we introduce AgentSnare, a trajectory-adaptive deception system that dynamically unfolds a decoy environment to continually steer the penetration agent away from the real target. Specifically, AgentSnare employs an artifact-construction policy model that constructs candidate artifacts conditioned on the agent's interaction history and decoy state. AgentSnare then validates these candidates and incrementally incorporates valid artifacts into a factually consistent decoy environment, thereby delaying the attack by absorbing its tool calls, diverting its post-entry trajectory within the decoy, and defusing it by inducing completion reports grounded in decoy evidence. Across 15 CVE-Bench web applications and three attacker models, AgentSnare absorbs 46.8% of the agent's tool calls in the decoy and retains 55.9% of post-entry actions there, while 90.0% of completion attempts are grounded in decoy evidence; across all 45 attacker-CVE pairs, no real target is successfully exploited at pass@3.

AI.tldr: AgentSnare is a dynamic decoy system that adapts to LLM-based penetration testing agents by constructing trajectory-aware deceptive artifacts, effectively absorbing tool calls, diverting post-entry actions, and preventing real target exploitation.
AI.motivation: Existing defenses against LLM penetration testing agents rely on static, pre-planted decoy artifacts that advanced agents can progressively recognize and bypass. A more adaptive defense is needed that dynamically responds to agent behavior.
AI.method: AgentSnare uses an artifact-construction policy model that generates candidate decoy artifacts conditioned on the agent's interaction history and decoy state. Candidates are validated and incrementally integrated into a factually consistent decoy environment. This dynamically unfolding decoy absorbs tool calls, diverts the agent's trajectory, and induces false completion reports grounded in decoy evidence.
AI.result: Evaluated across 15 CVE-Bench web applications and three attacker models: 46.8% of agent tool calls absorbed in the decoy, 55.9% of post-entry actions retained, and 90.0% of completion attempts grounded in decoy evidence. Across all 45 attacker-CVE pairs, no real target was successfully exploited at pass@3.
AI.conclusion: AgentSnare demonstrates that trajectory-adaptive, dynamically constructed decoy environments can effectively neutralize LLM-based penetration agents, outperforming static defenses by continuously adapting to agent behavior.

title: DHRCL:Training Code LLMs with Dense Hierarchical Rewards and Curriculum Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning is a natural post-training paradigm for code-oriented large language models because generated programs can be evaluated through parsing, execution, unit tests, and structural analysis.However, existing methods often rely on sparse outcome rewards or statically combine heterogeneous dense signals, even though syntax validity, executability, functional correctness, and structural organization describe different and progressively dependent programming capabilities. We propose DHRCL, a reinforcement learning framework with Dense Hierarchical Rewards and Curriculum Learning. DHRCL decomposes feedback into syntax validation, execution success, unit-test pass rate, and AST-based structural similarity, and organizes these signals through a three-stage Syntax, Execution, Pass & Structural curriculum. Stage duration is determined automatically from recent validation trends rather than manually specified capability thresholds. We further introduce stage-aware probability-based token credit redistribution. The mechanism follows a consolidation-to-refinement principle: it emphasizes established token patterns during syntax-oriented optimization, applies uniform propagation for non-local execution feedback, and allocates more credit or blame to less-established token decisions during final functional optimization. Under a unified Qwen3-8B and KodCode protocol, the experiments compare DHRCL with binary, pass-rate, reward-model-based, and verifiable dense-reward baselines. We further evaluate DHRCL across Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen3-14B backbones, showing that its advantage remains consistent as model capacity increases.

AI.tldr: DHRCL proposes a reinforcement learning framework for code LLMs that uses dense hierarchical rewards (syntax, execution, unit tests, AST similarity) organized through an adaptive three-stage curriculum, combined with stage-aware probability-based token credit redistribution. It outperforms sparse and static dense-reward baselines across multiple model sizes.
AI.motivation: Existing RL methods for code LLMs either use sparse outcome rewards or statically combine heterogeneous dense signals, failing to account for the progressive dependency among syntax validity, executability, functional correctness, and structural organization. There is a need for a framework that hierarchically organizes these capabilities in a developmentally appropriate sequence.
AI.method: DHRCL has two core components: (1) Dense Hierarchical Rewards — feedback decomposed into syntax validation, execution success, unit-test pass rate, and AST-based structural similarity, organized through a three-stage curriculum (Syntax → Execution → Pass & Structural) where stage duration is automatically determined from validation trends; (2) Stage-Aware Probability-Based Token Credit Redistribution — follows a consolidation-to-refinement principle, emphasizing established token patterns during syntax optimization, applying uniform propagation for execution feedback, and allocating more credit/blame to less-established tokens during final functional optimization.
AI.result: Under a unified Qwen3-8B and KodCode protocol, DHRCL outperforms binary, pass-rate, reward-model-based, and verifiable dense-reward baselines. The advantage remains consistent across Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Qwen3-14B backbones, demonstrating scalability with model capacity.
AI.conclusion: DHRCL demonstrates that hierarchically decomposing code-quality signals and organizing them through an adaptive curriculum with stage-aware credit assignment yields consistent and scalable improvements over existing RL fine-tuning approaches for code-oriented LLMs.

title: SpecFirst: Behavioral Specification Elicitation as a First-Class Step in Agent-Based Program Synthesis from Scratch
summary: LLM-based agents excel at software engineering tasks where an existing codebase provides context, but constructing a program from scratch remains fundamentally harder. Recent benchmarks such as ProgramBench quantify this gap: given only natural-language documentation and an execute-only binary as a behavioral oracle, even frontier models solve fewer than 1% of instances. Existing frameworks conflate documentation reading, behavioral exploration, and code synthesis into a single pass, causing agents to probe insufficiently, lose behavioral intent as context drifts, and propagate early misinterpretations into the final implementation. Inspired by classical requirements engineering, we argue that behavioral specification elicitation should be a first-class phase that precedes implementation. We present SpecFirst, a two-stage framework that forces the specification elicitation before code synthesis. A dedicated spec agent first probes the binary and combines observations with documentation into a structured specification. Next, a code synthesis agent then uses this specification to drive implementation. This decomposition resolves documentation ambiguities before coding begins and provides a stable behavioral reference throughout synthesis. We evaluate SpecFirst on all 200 ProgramBench instances across four models spanning two families and an order of magnitude of capability. SpecFirst consistently outperforms the single-loop baseline, improving test pass rates by 6.9%-21.3% and binary exploration coverage by 9.4%-18.5%, all statistically significant. Behavioral analysis on code synthesis further shows that a prior specification enables earlier and more sustained code construction. Our results demonstrate that an explicit requirements-engineering phase is an effective paradigm for from-scratch program construction.

AI.tldr: SpecFirst introduces a two-stage framework for program synthesis from scratch: a spec agent first elicits a structured behavioral specification by probing a binary oracle and reading documentation, then a code synthesis agent uses that specification to implement the program. Evaluated on ProgramBench, SpecFirst improves test pass rates by 6.9–21.3% and binary exploration coverage by 9.4–18.5% over single-loop baselines across four models.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents perform well on software engineering tasks within existing codebases but struggle with constructing programs from scratch — frontier models solve fewer than 1% of ProgramBench instances. Existing approaches conflate documentation reading, behavioral exploration, and code synthesis into a single pass, causing insufficient probing, loss of behavioral intent due to context drift, and propagation of early misinterpretations. The authors argue that behavioral specification elicitation should be a distinct, first-class phase preceding implementation, analogous to classical requirements engineering.
AI.method: SpecFirst is a two-stage framework. Stage 1: a dedicated spec agent probes the execute-only binary oracle and combines its observations with natural-language documentation to produce a structured behavioral specification. Stage 2: a separate code synthesis agent uses this specification as a stable reference to drive implementation. This decomposition resolves documentation ambiguities before coding begins. Evaluation is conducted on all 200 ProgramBench instances using four models from two families, with statistical significance testing.
AI.result: SpecFirst consistently outperforms the single-loop baseline across all four models tested. It achieves improvements of 6.9%–21.3% in test pass rates and 9.4%–18.5% in binary exploration coverage, all statistically significant. Behavioral analysis reveals that having a prior specification enables earlier initiation and more sustained code construction during the synthesis phase.
AI.conclusion: An explicit requirements-engineering phase — where behavioral specification is elicited before code synthesis — is an effective paradigm for improving LLM-based from-scratch program construction. The two-stage decomposition mitigates context drift and misinterpretation, yielding statistically significant gains over single-loop approaches.

title: Which RAG Paradigm Wins at Scale? A Scaling Study of Retrieval-Augmented Generation Paradigms
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods range from lexical and dense retrieval to graph-based indexing and agentic search. They are usually evaluated on different benchmarks at one corpus size, leaving their accuracy-cost scaling unclear. To bridge this gap, we present a controlled corpus-scaling study of these four paradigms. A ladder of 28 strictly nested tiers grows from roughly 1,000 to 512,000 documents while questions and a fixed bedrock of relevant and adversarial documents remain unchanged. Under one reader and judging protocol, we measure official accuracy, construction and query tokens, and latency. Our experimental results show that BM25 scales best in this controlled setting: it defines the low-cost end of the Pareto frontier at every measured tier and leads accuracy from mid-scale onward, without LLM-based construction. The File-System Agent matches or slightly exceeds BM25 at the smallest tiers but uses 39 times more query tokens per answer at the bedrock and falls nearly 20 points behind at full scale. A matched retrieval swap reverses this failure: Agent+BM25 scores 69.4 at full scale, versus 36.9 for raw-file agency and 54.8 for native BM25 on the same 150 questions. Graph-based RAG hits a construction wall: its heaviest builders use up to 24.6 generative LLM tokens per indexed corpus token yet stop within the first 2% of the full corpus, while scalable variants remain less accurate than BM25 at shared tiers.

AI.tldr: A controlled corpus-scaling study comparing four RAG paradigms (lexical, dense, graph-based, agentic) across 28 tiers from 1K to 512K documents reveals BM25 dominates the accuracy-cost Pareto frontier at all scales, while graph-based methods hit construction scalability walls and agentic methods degrade at larger corpora despite high query costs.
AI.motivation: RAG methods are typically evaluated on different benchmarks at a single corpus size, obscuring how accuracy and cost scale with corpus growth. The authors aim to fill this gap with a controlled, head-to-head comparison under uniform conditions.
AI.method: The authors construct a ladder of 28 strictly nested document tiers (≈1K to 512K documents) with fixed question sets and a bedrock of relevant and adversarial documents held constant. Four RAG paradigms — lexical (BM25), dense retrieval, graph-based indexing, and agentic (File-System Agent) — are evaluated under a single reader model and unified judging protocol. Metrics include official accuracy, construction tokens, query tokens, and latency.
AI.result: BM25 defines the low-cost end of the Pareto frontier at every tier and leads accuracy from mid-scale onward. The File-System Agent matches BM25 only at the smallest tiers while using 39× more query tokens; at full scale it falls ~20 points behind BM25. A hybrid Agent+BM25 swap recovers performance to 69.4 vs. 36.9 (raw agent) and 54.8 (native BM25). Graph-based RAG's heaviest builders consume up to 24.6 generative LLM tokens per indexed corpus token yet fail to scale beyond 2% of the full corpus; scalable graph variants underperform BM25 at shared tiers.
AI.conclusion: In controlled, like-for-like conditions, simple lexical retrieval (BM25) remains the most cost-effective and scalable RAG paradigm. Apparent advantages of more complex methods in prior work may stem from inconsistent evaluation setups rather than genuine superiority.

title: Setoka: A Benchmark for Hierarchical User Understanding in Personalized Agents over Heterogeneous Data
summary: Personalized agents are increasingly applied to assist users across a wide range of tasks. Effective personalized assistance requires not only retrieving explicit facts from past interactions stored in agent memory, but also inferring abstract personal characteristics. However, existing memory benchmarks primarily evaluate whether an agent can retrieve information explicitly stated in conversational histories, failing to provide an effective assessment of deeper user understanding. In this work, we propose Setoka, a benchmark for evaluating memory-augmented personalized agents with hierarchical user understanding from heterogeneous data. Grounded in theories from cognitive and personality psychology, Setoka defines four levels of user understanding, i.e., semantic memory, episodic memory, behavior pattern, and personality trait. Moreover, to enable realistic yet privacy-preserving evaluation, we design a psychometrics-based pipeline that synthesizes diverse, coherent heterogeneous user data and queries at scale. Finally, we leverage Setoka to evaluate 3 language models combined with 5 memory systems for 10 synthetic users. Our comprehensive evaluation reveals that while existing systems perform well on semantic memory retrieval, their performance declines on episodic memory. Moreover, when dealing with behavior pattern and personality trait understanding tasks that require integrating heterogeneous and fragmented information dispersed over time, performance declines even further. These findings demonstrate that user understanding cannot be handled by simple fact retrieval, motivating the design of memory mechanisms for cross-source integration and abstraction over long-term user behavior.

AI.tldr: Setoka is a benchmark for evaluating personalized agents across four hierarchical levels of user understanding (semantic memory, episodic memory, behavior patterns, personality traits). Using psychometrics-based synthetic data, the benchmark reveals that while existing systems handle semantic retrieval well, they struggle significantly with higher-level inference requiring cross-source integration and temporal abstraction.
AI.motivation: Existing memory benchmarks only assess explicit fact retrieval from conversation histories, failing to evaluate deeper user understanding such as inferring abstract personal traits. This gap motivates a benchmark grounded in cognitive/personality psychology that can measure hierarchical user understanding from heterogeneous data.
AI.method: Setoka defines four levels of user understanding (semantic memory, episodic memory, behavior pattern, personality trait) grounded in cognitive and personality psychology. A psychometrics-based pipeline synthesizes diverse, coherent heterogeneous user data and corresponding queries at scale. The benchmark evaluates 3 language models combined with 5 memory systems across 10 synthetic users.
AI.result: Existing systems perform well on semantic memory retrieval but show degraded performance on episodic memory. Performance declines sharply on behavior pattern and personality trait tasks requiring integration of fragmented, temporally-dispersed heterogeneous information. Simple fact retrieval is insufficient for higher-level user understanding.
AI.conclusion: User understanding demands more than fact retrieval; it requires memory mechanisms capable of cross-source integration and abstraction over long-term behavior. Setoka provides a foundation for developing and evaluating such mechanisms in personalized agents.

title: HoF-Bench: Rediscovering Real AI-Discovered CVEs Without Frontier Models
summary: LLM-based analyzers have begun finding real vulnerabilities in mature open-source projects: AISLE's analyzer is credited with more than 280 CVEs across 78 projects, including OpenSSL, curl, and GnuTLS. We introduce HoF-Bench (named after AISLE's public Hall of Fame), a benchmark built from 95 of these public AI-discovered CVEs across eight repositories pinned at vulnerable commits. Analyzers receive source and target-file scope but not CVE identifiers, descriptions, fixes, or expected mechanisms; a detector-blinded frontier-model judge credits only findings that identify the same code path, root cause, attack condition, and impact. A deliberately minimal LLM-based analyzer rediscovers up to 65 of the 95 CVEs (68%) under this strict protocol. No frontier model performs detection anywhere in the study. The ten detector backbones are five open-weight models (21B--284B total parameters, 3--13B active) and five proprietary small or "flash"-tier models. All of them run in the fixed scaffold with four repeated passes, an optional generated-context stage, and a replayable multi-round triage stage (7,600 model--CVE pass records). Difficulty is strongly structured by language; the CVEs missed by every model concentrate in C infrastructure code. HoF-Bench provides a compact test bed for comparing vulnerability scanners, their reliability across repeated runs, and the candidate volume they create. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/aisleinc/HoF-Bench.

AI.tldr: HoF-Bench is a benchmark of 95 AI-discovered CVEs across 8 repositories. Under a strict blinded protocol, a minimal LLM-based analyzer rediscovers up to 68% of CVEs. No frontier model performs detection; backbone models (both open-weight and proprietary flash-tier) are tested in a fixed scaffold with repeated passes. Difficulty clusters by language, with misses concentrated in C infrastructure code.
AI.motivation: LLM-based vulnerability analyzers (e.g., AISLE's) are finding real-world CVEs in critical projects like OpenSSL and curl, but rigorous, reproducible evaluation of such tools is lacking. The authors aim to provide a compact, standardized benchmark for comparing vulnerability scanners, measuring reliability across repeated runs, and assessing candidate volume.
AI.method: HoF-Bench is constructed from 95 public AI-discovered CVEs across 8 repositories pinned at vulnerable commits. Analyzers receive only source code and target-file scope—no CVE identifiers, descriptions, fixes, or expected mechanisms. A detector-blinded frontier-model judge credits findings only when they match the code path, root cause, attack condition, and impact. Ten detector backbones (5 open-weight models at 21B–284B total / 3–13B active parameters; 5 proprietary small/flash-tier models) run in a fixed scaffold with four repeated passes, an optional generated-context stage, and a replayable multi-round triage stage, yielding 7,600 model–CVE pass records.
AI.result: A deliberately minimal LLM-based analyzer rediscovers up to 65 of the 95 CVEs (68%) under the strict protocol. No frontier model performs detection anywhere in the study. Difficulty is strongly structured by language: CVEs missed by every model concentrate in C infrastructure code.
AI.conclusion: HoF-Bench offers a compact, reproducible test bed for vulnerability scanners, revealing that even minimal LLM-based analyzers can recover a substantial fraction of known AI-discovered CVEs, while highlighting that C infrastructure code remains a persistent challenge across all tested models.

title: Neural Architecture Search for Traffic Prediction: A Survey of Methods, Challenges, and Future Directions
comment: 8 pages, 3 tables. Accepted at UrbCom 2026, the 8th International Workshop on Urban Computing, co-located with IEEE DCOSS-IoT 2026
summary: Traffic prediction is a core task in intelligent transportation systems, supporting applications such as adaptive signal control, route guidance, and ride-hailing dispatch. Deep learning models, including graph convolutional networks, recurrent networks, and Transformers, achieve strong results on standard benchmarks, but their architectures are designed by hand, requiring significant expert effort and producing models that often generalize poorly across cities and datasets. Neural Architecture Search (NAS) offers a systematic alternative to manual design. It automates the search over candidate architectures of deep learning models, finding designs that match the spatial-temporal structure of traffic data without manual trial and error. This survey reviews NAS methods applied to traffic prediction, organized by search strategy: gradient-based methods, evolutionary methods, and one-shot weight-sharing methods. For each category, we analyze how the search space is designed to cover spatial and temporal traffic operators, and how the search strategy balances cost against architecture quality. We also discuss open challenges, computational scalability to large road networks, manual search space design, cross-city generalization, dynamic graph structure, and the open question of NAS for spatial-temporal foundation models, and identify directions for future research.

AI.tldr: This survey systematically reviews Neural Architecture Search (NAS) methods for traffic prediction, categorizing approaches into gradient-based, evolutionary, and one-shot weight-sharing methods, analyzing search space design and cost-quality trade-offs, and identifying open challenges including scalability, cross-city generalization, dynamic graphs, and spatial-temporal foundation models.
AI.motivation: Hand-designed deep learning architectures (GCNs, RNNs, Transformers) for traffic prediction require substantial expert effort and generalize poorly across different cities and datasets. NAS offers a systematic alternative by automating architecture discovery tailored to the spatial-temporal structure of traffic data, yet the fragmented literature demands a structured survey.
AI.method: This is a survey paper that reviews and taxonomizes existing NAS approaches for traffic prediction along three search strategy axes: (1) gradient-based methods, (2) evolutionary methods, and (3) one-shot weight-sharing methods. For each category, the authors analyze search space design (covering spatial and temporal traffic operators) and the trade-off between search cost and resulting architecture quality.
AI.result: The survey identifies that NAS can discover architectures competitive with or superior to hand-crafted models for traffic prediction. Key findings include: gradient-based methods offer faster search but may converge to sharp minima; evolutionary methods explore more diverse architectures at higher computational cost; one-shot methods amortize training cost via weight-sharing but suffer from ranking instability. Open challenges remain around scaling to large road networks, reducing reliance on manual search space design, cross-city generalization, handling dynamic graph structures, and extending NAS to spatial-temporal foundation models.
AI.conclusion: NAS is a promising direction for automating traffic prediction model design, but several open problems remain: improving computational scalability, automating search space construction, enabling cross-city transfer, incorporating dynamic graph structures, and exploring NAS for large-scale spatial-temporal foundation models. These represent key directions for future research.

title: Trusting-Trust Attack against an Entire Linux Distribution through Binary Manipulation
summary: Ken Thompson's trusting-trust attack, in which a compromised compiler backdoors the programs it builds and reproduces the backdoor in subsequent rebuilds of itself, is widely regarded as a threat specific to compilers. We show that it is not. We construct a complete trusting-trust attack around GNU strip, an ordinary build utility that neither inspects nor generates source code, using only manipulations of finished ELF files. In the bootstrap of the NixOS Linux distribution, a single tampered strip in the binary seed implants a payload that propagates from one generation of strip to the next and survives into the final standard environment after the seed leaves the dependency closure. On a real nixpkgs revision, the attack builds a complete graphical installer without failures and backdoors almost every one of its binaries, enabling arbitrary malicious behavior of the subverted packages.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that Ken Thompson's "Trusting Trust" attack is not exclusive to compilers. The authors construct a complete trusting-trust attack using GNU strip—an ordinary ELF binary manipulation utility—within the NixOS bootstrap chain, showing that a single compromised strip binary can propagate a backdoor across generations and into the final system without any source-code inspection or modification.
AI.motivation: To challenge the widely held assumption that Thompson's trusting-trust attack is a compiler-specific threat, and to demonstrate that the attack vector generalizes to ordinary build utilities that neither parse nor generate source code, thereby exposing a broader class of supply-chain vulnerabilities in bootstrappable build systems.
AI.method: The authors craft a trusting-trust attack around GNU strip by manipulating finished ELF binaries. A single tampered strip binary in the NixOS bootstrap seed is engineered to: (1) implant a payload into binaries it processes, and (2) propagate the backdoor into subsequent generations of strip itself. This is achieved purely through binary rewriting techniques on ELF headers and sections, without touching source code. The attack targets the nixpkgs ecosystem, building a complete graphical installer while remaining undetected through the bootstrap and into the final standard environment.
AI.result: The attack succeeded on a real nixpkgs revision: a single compromised strip binary in the bootstrap seed propagated its payload through successive generations of strip, survived the entire bootstrap process after the seed left the dependency closure, and produced a complete graphical installer with nearly all binaries backdoored. The compromised packages were capable of arbitrary malicious behavior.
AI.conclusion: The trusting-trust attack is a general binary-level threat, not confined to compilers. Any tool involved in producing or modifying binaries within a bootstrap chain is a potential vector. This has significant implications for the design and verification of bootstrappable build systems and reproducible builds, suggesting that defenses must address binary-level integrity throughout the entire dependency closure.

title: Where Detectors Fail: Closing the Tail-Domain Gap with Expert-Guided Mutual Distillation
summary: Multimodal fake news detectors often generalize poorly across domains because they learn to trust unreliable evidence: domain-specific shortcuts amplified by imbalanced data and semantically inconsistent text-image pairs that make cross-modal evidence unreliable. We propose Expert-Guided Mutual Distillation (EGMD), which learns what evidence to trust across the prediction pipeline. At the input level, input-level calibration encodes pair-level coherence as a shared gain before fusion. At the representation level, an expert-guided teacher aligns domain statistics and encourages domain-specific patterns to concentrate in specialized experts. At the decision level, prototype-anchored domain-specific students use mutual learning and dual-channel distillation to inherit the teacher's feature geometry and calibrated predictions while discouraging local domain priors. We further construct Weibo_Balanced, a domain-balanced benchmark that isolates the effect of imbalance on generalization. Across four datasets in two languages, EGMD achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while reducing domain bias by up to 57.3%.

AI.tldr: EGMD proposes a three-level (input, representation, decision) mutual distillation framework that calibrates cross-modal evidence to combat domain-specific shortcuts and semantic inconsistency in multimodal fake news detection, achieving SOTA accuracy with up to 57.3% domain bias reduction.
AI.motivation: Multimodal fake news detectors suffer from poor cross-domain generalization due to two issues: (1) imbalanced data amplifying domain-specific shortcuts, and (2) semantically inconsistent text-image pairs making cross-modal evidence unreliable. Models learn to trust spurious, domain-bound correlations rather than generalizable signals.
AI.method: EGMD operates at three levels: (1) Input-level calibration encodes text-image pair coherence as a shared gain before fusion. (2) Representation-level uses an expert-guided teacher that aligns domain statistics and concentrates domain-specific patterns into specialized experts. (3) Decision-level employs prototype-anchored domain-specific students with mutual learning and dual-channel distillation to inherit the teacher's feature geometry and calibrated predictions while suppressing local domain priors. Authors also introduce Weibo_Balanced, a domain-balanced benchmark isolating imbalance effects on generalization.
AI.result: EGMD achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across four datasets spanning two languages (Chinese and English). Critically, it reduces domain bias by up to 57.3%, demonstrating substantially improved cross-domain generalization.
AI.conclusion: Learning what cross-modal evidence to trust — via calibrated input fusion, expert-guided representation alignment, and prototype-anchored mutual distillation — effectively mitigates domain-specific shortcuts and semantic inconsistency, yielding robust multimodal fake news detection that generalizes across domains.

title: On-Policy Distillation for LLM Safety: A Routing Approach to Template-Robust Realignment
summary: Fine-tuning is the dominant paradigm for specializing large language models (LLMs), yet it exposes a critical vulnerability: malicious data providers can embed harmful behaviors into downstream corpora, creating models that retain professional skills while violating human values on demand. Existing safety-realignment defenses often fail in practice due to three key limitations: they frequently cause catastrophic forgetting of specialized skills; their effectiveness collapses when the defender cannot observe the attacker's prompt template; and successfully realigned models remain susceptible to re-jailbreaking via simple system prompt switches. To address these challenges, we propose Routing-based On-Policy Distillation (ROPD), a novel realignment framework that models the divergence between aligned and compromised output probability distributions rather than fitting specific prompt templates. We conduct extensive experiments comparing ROPD against four state-of-the-art baselines across three datasets and three base models with varying alignment strengths. Our results demonstrate that when baseline defenses face template mismatches, often accompanied by severe degradation in downstream task performance. In contrast, ROPD substantially mitigates template-mismatch risks, maintaining superior robustness in both defense effectiveness and capability preservation. While our analysis indicates ROPD is not entirely immune to template shifts, its performance degradation is negligible compared to existing methods, establishing a new standard for robust LLM realignment.

AI.tldr: ROPD is a novel fine-tuning realignment framework that uses routing-based on-policy distillation to defend against maliciously embedded behaviors in LLMs, maintaining robustness against prompt template mismatches while preserving downstream task performance—an area where existing defenses fail.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuned LLMs are vulnerable to malicious data providers embedding harmful behaviors. Existing safety-realignment defenses suffer from three critical failures: (1) catastrophic forgetting of specialized skills, (2) collapse when the defender cannot observe the attacker's prompt template, and (3) susceptibility to re-jailbreaking via simple system prompt switches.
AI.method: ROPD (Routing-based On-Policy Distillation) models the divergence between aligned and compromised output probability distributions rather than fitting specific prompt templates. It uses on-policy distillation with a routing mechanism that selectively activates safety-aligned vs. compromised behavioral pathways, decoupling safety realignment from template-specific patterns.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across three datasets and three base models with varying alignment strengths show that ROPD substantially mitigates template-mismatch risks. While baseline defenses suffer severe downstream task degradation under template mismatches, ROPD maintains superior robustness in both defense effectiveness and capability preservation, with negligible performance degradation compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: ROPD establishes a new standard for robust LLM realignment by decoupling safety from template-specific patterns. Although not entirely immune to template shifts, its degradation is negligible relative to baselines, demonstrating that probability-distribution-based divergence modeling is a more resilient defense paradigm than template-fitting approaches.

title: MemSecBench: Tracking Agent Memory Poisoning from Persistence to Consequence and Repair
summary: Memory systems allow agents to retain and reuse information from past interactions, but they can also let malicious content persist. A malicious instruction crafted by an attacker may be stored in long-term memory, recalled much later, and quietly shape a real action. Recent benchmarks increasingly examine agent memory security, yet few trace the same malicious semantics across persistence, downstream consequences, and selective repair under diverse memory-backend comparisons. To address this gap, we introduce MemSecBench, a task-grounded benchmark for the lifecycle security of agent memory systems. It contains 310 cases drawn from 48 realistic contexts across code and science, daily life, and office work. Each case follows a controlled Write--Execute--Forget protocol in an isolated runtime under an exact agent configuration, defined by an agent harness, a memory backend, and an LLM backend. Evidence-based adjudication combines a deterministic write check, checkpoint-specific judge-model evaluations, and programmatic gates across seven lifecycle checkpoints. The experimental design spans a 24-configuration matrix of two agent harnesses, four memory backends, and three LLM backends. Across all 24 configurations, malicious memory persists in 84.2% of all cases, and the full Write--Execute chain succeeds in 50.3%. Among successfully poisoned cases, 59.6% complete the full Execute chain, while 56.1% achieve selective repair.Compared with matched Native configurations, the largest absolute differences are 16.1 percentage points for end-to-end attack success and 41.3 percentage points for selective repair. These descriptive contrasts indicate that the evaluated memory system stacks differ in lifecycle security, both in the propagation of malicious memory and in selective repair after successful memory poisoning.

AI.tldr: MemSecBench is a benchmark for evaluating agent memory system security across its lifecycle. It comprises 310 cases across 48 contexts, testing 24 configurations (agent harness × memory backend × LLM backend). Results show malicious memory persists in 84.2% of cases, with full attack chains succeeding in 50.3%. Selective repair succeeds in 56.1% of poisoned cases, revealing significant security disparities across memory system stacks.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks examine agent memory security but fail to trace the same malicious semantics across persistence, downstream consequences, and selective repair under diverse memory-backend comparisons. This gap motivates a systematic, lifecycle-oriented benchmark.
AI.method: MemSecBench introduces a Write--Execute--Forget protocol in isolated runtimes. Each of the 310 cases (drawn from code/science, daily life, and office work) is evaluated via evidence-based adjudication combining deterministic write checks, checkpoint-specific judge-model evaluations, and programmatic gates across seven lifecycle checkpoints. The experimental design forms a 24-configuration matrix: 2 agent harnesses × 4 memory backends × 3 LLM backends.
AI.result: Malicious memory persists in 84.2% of all cases (all 24 configurations). The full Write--Execute chain succeeds in 50.3% of cases. Among successfully poisoned cases, 59.6% complete the full Execute chain and 56.1% achieve selective repair. Compared with matched Native configurations, the largest absolute differences are 16.1 pp for end-to-end attack success and 41.3 pp for selective repair.
AI.conclusion: The evaluated memory system stacks exhibit substantial differences in lifecycle security, both in malicious memory propagation and in selective repair capability after successful poisoning. These descriptive contrasts underscore the need for memory-backend-aware security hardening in agent systems.

title: Learning Dynamic User Personas from Implicit Interaction Streams via Iterative Refinement
summary: Personalizing large language models (LLMs) to individual users is essential for improving user experience, yet existing approaches typically rely on explicit preference supervision such as pairwise comparisons or demographic attributes, limiting their applicability in natural interaction settings. We propose IRIS, a framework that learns dynamic user personas directly from implicit interaction streams by extracting behavioral signals from everyday conversations and iteratively refining persona representations through a prediction-driven closed loop without requiring explicit feedback. We introduce an evaluation protocol based on behavior prediction, persona stability, and decision prediction. A proof-of-concept study on a synthetic interaction stream derived from public-domain autobiographical text shows that IRIS produces stable personas and distinguishes individual users while revealing limitations of memory-only approaches on recall-oriented metrics. We then validate IRIS on anonymized real-world Reddit r/AmItheAsshole (AITA) data, with personas built solely from each author's historical interactions. Across 100 authors, IRIS achieves the highest decision prediction accuracy among all evaluated methods (61.0%), outperforming static personas, memory-only retrieval, and no-personalization baselines. These results suggest that implicit behavioral modeling provides a scalable alternative to explicit preference learning for personalized LLMs and offers a practical foundation for adaptive conversational systems and embodied agents that require continuously evolving models of their users.

AI.tldr: IRIS is a framework that learns dynamic user personas from implicit conversation streams (without explicit feedback), achieving 61% decision prediction accuracy on Reddit AITA data, outperforming static persona, memory-only, and no-personalization baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM personalization methods require explicit preference supervision (pairwise comparisons, demographic attributes), which is impractical in natural interaction settings. A method is needed that can infer user personas passively from everyday conversational behavior.
AI.method: IRIS extracts behavioral signals from implicit interaction streams and iteratively refines persona representations through a prediction-driven closed loop. Evaluation uses a novel protocol measuring behavior prediction, persona stability, and decision prediction. Validated on synthetic autobiographical data and real Reddit AITA data (100 authors).
AI.result: On synthetic data, IRIS produces stable, user-distinguishing personas and exposes limitations of memory-only approaches on recall metrics. On Reddit AITA, IRIS achieves 61.0% decision prediction accuracy, outperforming all baselines (static personas, memory-only retrieval, no personalization).
AI.conclusion: Implicit behavioral modeling offers a scalable alternative to explicit preference learning for LLM personalization, providing a practical foundation for adaptive conversational systems and embodied agents requiring continuously evolving user models.

title: WikiLoop: Jointly Learning to Build and Navigate Agent-Native Wikis with Downstream Feedback
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures, 12 tables. Includes supplementary material
summary: Knowledge-base construction and querying are typically optimized in isolation: retrieval-augmented agents operate over a fixed, externally maintained index, whereas construction receives no signal from downstream use. We present WikiLoop, a feedback-coupled framework that jointly learns to build and navigate an agent-native Wiki, a persistent linked-page knowledge base designed for machine navigation. A role-conditioned shared policy supports two interfaces: a Navigator retrieves evidence from the Wiki to answer queries, and a Builder proposes structured edits evaluated through downstream navigation. The Navigator follows a sufficiency-before-efficiency objective that applies retrieval-cost penalties only after full evidence has been collected. The Builder learns from utility differences: a frozen Navigator scores each candidate edit by its change in downstream performance, while a guard penalty discourages regressions on unrelated queries. Training combines sequential role-specific optimization with a final joint stage over role-homogeneous batches. With Qwen3.5-9B as the common backbone, WikiLoop reaches 62.6 aggregate Answer Correctness on AuthTrace, 6.3 points above LLM-Wiki, base, with the largest gains on multi-document queries. Controlled comparisons support the intended effects of both objectives, and the learned edits remain useful to a held-out Navigator. Paired comparisons indicate that the final shared policy largely retains both role-specific capabilities, improves Navigator and end-to-end Answer Correctness by 0.4 points relative to the corresponding specialist references, and consolidates both interfaces into one model. Without dataset-specific training, WikiLoop also improves over the same-backbone LLM-Wiki, base on HotpotQA and MuSiQue.

AI.tldr: WikiLoop jointly optimizes knowledge base construction and retrieval by training a shared policy to both build and navigate an agent-native Wiki, using feedback from downstream task performance to guide edits, achieving strong improvements on multi-document QA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional retrieval-augmented systems treat knowledge base construction and querying as separate, isolated processes — the KB is built once without signals from how it will be used, and retrieval agents operate over a fixed index. This decoupling prevents the KB from adapting to the needs of downstream retrieval, leaving potential performance gains unrealized.
AI.method: WikiLoop introduces a role-conditioned shared policy with two interfaces: (1) Navigator — retrieves evidence from the Wiki to answer queries, using a sufficiency-before-efficiency objective that penalizes retrieval cost only after collecting complete evidence; (2) Builder — proposes structured edits to Wiki pages, evaluated by a frozen Navigator based on the utility difference (improvement in downstream answer correctness), with a guard penalty to prevent regressions on unrelated queries. Training proceeds in sequential role-specific phases followed by a final joint optimization over role-homogeneous batches. The backbone model is Qwen3.5-9B.
AI.result: WikiLoop achieves 62.6 aggregate Answer Correctness on AuthTrace, outperforming LLM-Wiki base by 6.3 points, with the largest gains on multi-document queries. Learned edits remain useful to a held-out Navigator. The final shared policy retains both role-specific capabilities, improving Navigator and end-to-end Answer Correctness by 0.4 points over specialist references, while consolidating two interfaces into one model. Without dataset-specific training, WikiLoop also improves over the same-backbone LLM-Wiki on HotpotQA and MuSiQue.
AI.conclusion: Co-training KB construction and retrieval through feedback coupling yields significant improvements, particularly for complex multi-document queries. The shared policy approach successfully consolidates Builder and Navigator capabilities into a single model without sacrificing performance, demonstrating the value of closing the loop between knowledge curation and downstream use.

title: AgentMap: Joint Equivalence and Subsumption Discovery for Ontology Matching
summary: Ontology matching (OM) has traditionally been formulated as either equivalence discovery or subsumption matching. The existing OM systems identify only one type of semantic correspondence and cannot simultaneously discover equivalence and subsumption mappings. In this paper, we introduce Hybrid Ontology Matching (HOM), a new OM task that unifies equivalence and subsumption discovery, and accordingly propose a Large Language Model (LLM)-based multi-agent OM framework AgentMap that is implemented by a series of interdependent semantic decisions. Given a concept in the source ontology, AgentMap integrates semantic retrieval, hierarchical search, and collaborative multi-agent LLM reasoning to progressively explore the target ontology, identifying either the equivalent concept, if one exists, or the most fine-grained subsumer. We further extend four OM datasets for a HOM benchmark and evaluate AgentMap under hybrid, equivalence-only, and subsumption-only settings. Experimental results show that AgentMap achieves promising performance on the hybrid setting, and at the same time outperforms equivalence matching and subsumption matching baselines on the equivalence-only and subsumption-only settings, respectively.

AI.tldr: Introduces Hybrid Ontology Matching (HOM) unifying equivalence and subsumption matching, and proposes AgentMap, an LLM-based multi-agent framework that progressively discovers either equivalent concepts or most fine-grained subsumers, outperforming baselines across all matching settings.
AI.motivation: Traditional ontology matching systems handle equivalence and subsumption matching in isolation, lacking a unified approach that can simultaneously discover both types of semantic correspondences.
AI.method: AgentMap employs a multi-agent LLM framework combining semantic retrieval, hierarchical search, and collaborative reasoning. Given a source concept, it progressively explores the target ontology to find either the equivalent concept or the finest-grained subsumer, framing matching as a series of interdependent semantic decisions.
AI.result: AgentMap achieves promising performance on the hybrid setting and outperforms equivalence-only and subsumption-only baselines on their respective settings across four extended OM benchmark datasets.
AI.conclusion: The HOM formulation and AgentMap framework demonstrate that unifying equivalence and subsumption matching with LLM-based multi-agent reasoning is effective, advancing the state of ontology matching.

title: Function Privatization in the Local Model
summary:
We study the problem of privately releasing functions, with a particular focus on curves, which are images of continuous functions on some finite interval. Many types of data exist naturally as curves, such as trajectory data or $1$D density curves. We shall primarily be interested in the local model setting, where the function to be privatized captures data belonging to one individual, which is the more challenging setting with limited prior work.
  Under the standard notion of local differential privacy (DP), any two arbitrarily different functions are required to be made indistinguishable by privatization, which is too strong to allow meaningful utility; we thus work with a generalized notion of DP known as Geo-Privacy (GP), which allows functions far apart to be distinguished more easily while providing strong protection for near functions. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework, we provide experimental evaluation on several datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses privately releasing function data (specifically curves) in the local model using Geo-Privacy (GP), a relaxed variant of differential privacy that allows distance-based distinguishability, since standard local DP is too stringent for meaningful utility on functional data.
AI.motivation: Many real-world data types (trajectories, density curves) are naturally represented as functions/curves. Privatizing such data in the local model — where one individual's function must be protected — is challenging. Standard local DP requires arbitrarily different functions to be indistinguishable, which destroys utility. A more practical privacy notion is needed that protects nearby functions strongly while allowing distant functions to be distinguished.
AI.method: The authors adopt Geo-Privacy (GP), a generalized differential privacy framework where distinguishability between outputs scales with the distance between underlying functions, rather than enforcing uniform indistinguishability. They design privatization mechanisms for releasing functions/curves under this GP framework in the local model setting.
AI.result: The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through experimental evaluation on several real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: Geo-Privacy provides a viable and effective privacy framework for releasing curve/function data in the challenging local model, overcoming the utility limitations of standard local differential privacy by allowing distance-dependent privacy guarantees.

title: Conformal Changepoint Localization and Root Cause Analysis with Corrupted Observations
summary: Detecting when the statistical behavior of an engineered system changes, and identifying which component is responsible, are core problems in the monitoring of telecommunication networks, robotic platforms, security infrastructure, and multi-agent systems. In safety- and mission-critical deployments, such decisions must be accompanied by statistical reliability guarantees rather than by point estimates alone. Conformal changepoint localization (CONCH) and conformal root cause analysis (CROC) meet this need by returning confidence sets that contain the true changepoint, or the true root-cause stream, with a user-specified probability, without parametric assumptions on the data-generating process. In practice, however, observations are frequently corrupted, e.g., by outliers, sensor faults, or adversarial perturbations. While the finite-sample coverage of these procedures is preserved under contamination, the resulting confidence sets can become uninformatively large. Adopting a Huber-type contamination model, this paper proposes weighted CONCH (W-CONCH) and weighted CROC (W-CROC), which downweight observations that are likely to be corrupted with the goal of reducing confidence set size when data may be corrupted. The weighting mechanism, derived from a formal bound on the unknown corrupted data densities, leverages pre-existing second-order classifier-based uncertainty signals, such as those produced by evidential deep learning or Bayesian learning. W-CONCH and W-CROC are further generalized by introducing a meta-learning procedure for the weights that optimizes a differentiable surrogate of the confidence set size. Experiments on image-based and real-world changepoint and root-cause benchmarks show that uncertainty-based weighting substantially reduces confidence set size while maintaining the target coverage.

AI.tldr: W-CONCH and W-CROC extend conformal changepoint localization and root cause analysis by incorporating uncertainty-based weighting to reduce confidence set sizes under data corruption, while maintaining finite-sample coverage guarantees. A meta-learning procedure further optimizes weights via a differentiable surrogate of set size.
AI.motivation: Conformal methods like CONCH and CROC provide finite-sample coverage guarantees for changepoint detection and root cause analysis without parametric assumptions, but under Huber-type contamination (outliers, sensor faults, adversarial perturbations), their confidence sets can become uninformatively large despite preserved coverage. The goal is to reduce set size while retaining statistical validity.
AI.method: The authors propose W-CONCH and W-CROC, which downweight likely-corrupted observations using a weighting mechanism derived from a formal bound on unknown corrupted data densities. The weights leverage second-order classifier-based uncertainty signals (e.g., from evidential deep learning or Bayesian learning). A meta-learning extension optimizes weights by minimizing a differentiable surrogate of confidence set size.
AI.result: Experiments on image-based and real-world changepoint and root-cause benchmarks demonstrate that uncertainty-based weighting substantially reduces confidence set size while maintaining target coverage.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-based weighting effectively mitigates the inflation of conformal confidence sets under data corruption, preserving both statistical validity and practical informativeness. The meta-learning generalization offers further optimization potential.

title: Revisiting Lossy Verification in Speculative Decoding: Mechanisms, Trade-offs, and Failure Modes
summary: Speculative Decoding (SD) accelerates large language model inference by allowing a lightweight draft model to propose tokens that are subsequently verified in parallel by a larger target model. Recent approaches introduce lossy verification schemes to further improve efficiency by relaxing strict distributional matching. Yet such relaxation silently rewrites the decoding distribution, and the resulting acceleration can come at the cost of unstable, sometimes severely degraded generation quality. In this work, we present a principled analysis of the distributions induced by lossy verification methods. We show that many seemingly distinct approaches differ only superficially and can be classified into two categories: truncation-based verification and collaborative verification. We further construct a diagnostic evaluation framework across curated benchmarks. For truncation-based methods, we identify a fundamental pitfall: performance can degrade significantly compared to the true truncation sampling baseline due to distributional distortion. For collaborative verification, we uncover a key principles: controlling the overshoot of draft probabilities relative to target probabilities is essential to prevent low-quality outputs. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZhouYuxuanYX/Fast-HSD.

AI.tldr: The paper provides a principled analysis of lossy speculative decoding methods, classifying them into truncation-based and collaborative verification categories. It identifies fundamental pitfalls in truncation-based methods (distributional distortion degrading quality) and key principles for collaborative methods (controlling probability overshoot), supported by a diagnostic evaluation framework.
AI.motivation: Lossy speculative decoding methods sacrifice strict distributional matching for speed, but the resulting acceleration can cause unstable and severely degraded generation quality. The relationship among these seemingly diverse methods and their failure modes were not well understood.
AI.method: The authors conduct a principled theoretical analysis of the distributions induced by lossy verification, revealing that existing methods fall into two categories: truncation-based verification and collaborative verification. They construct a diagnostic evaluation framework with curated benchmarks to systematically assess generation quality degradation.
AI.result: Truncation-based methods suffer from significant performance degradation relative to true truncation sampling baselines due to distributional distortion. For collaborative verification, controlling the overshoot of draft probabilities relative to target probabilities is identified as essential for preventing low-quality outputs.
AI.conclusion: Lossy speculative decoding methods must carefully manage the trade-off between speed and generation quality. The proposed taxonomy and diagnostic framework enable better understanding and design of future methods, with probability overshoot control being critical for collaborative verification approaches.

title: Linguistic Monoculture in LLM-Assisted Language Use
summary: Writing and communication are increasingly mediated by large language models (LLMs) that are being used to draft, revise and polish text. Although such assistance can improve clarity and help authors meet institutional expectations, widespread reliance on shared models may reduce population-level variation in linguistic form, a phenomenon we refer to as linguistic monoculture. We develop a mathematical framework in which authors and LLMs are represented as distributions over linguistic features and coevolve through repeated interaction. We analyze three interaction mechanisms: a shared model with a fixed linguistic distribution, a shared model recursively updated from author outputs, and personalized models updated through author-specific and population-level feedback. We characterize the resulting equilibria and convergence rates, showing that, shared models can drive authors toward a common norm, recursive feedback relocates the shared norm without altering pairwise spread under common conformity, and personalization can preserve a family of distinct author-model equilibria with nonzero linguistic diversity. We then endogenize conformity as a strategic choice trading off private benefits from clarity, legibility, and perceived fluency against distinctive style. Within this utility model, individually rational authors may conform more than is socially optimal because they do not internalize the value their distinctiveness provides to others, creating a negative externality and a price of monoculture that is finite for each fixed instance but can grow without bound when distinctiveness dominates authenticity. Synthetic simulations illustrate how fixed shared assistance, recursive feedback, and personalization produce different long-run diversity outcomes.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the concept of "linguistic monoculture" — the reduction in population-level linguistic diversity caused by widespread reliance on shared LLMs for writing assistance. Using a mathematical coevolution framework, it analyzes how fixed shared models, recursively updated shared models, and personalized models affect linguistic diversity, showing that personalization can preserve diversity while shared models drive convergence. The authors also model conformity as a strategic choice and demonstrate that individually rational authors over-conform relative to the social optimum, creating a negative externality.
AI.motivation: As LLMs become ubiquitous tools for drafting, revising, and polishing text, there is growing concern that shared reliance on these models will homogenize linguistic expression across populations. The authors aim to formalize this concern mathematically, distinguishing "linguistic monoculture" from mere conformity, and to analyze which interaction mechanisms preserve or erode diversity.
AI.method: The authors construct a mathematical framework where authors and LLMs are represented as probability distributions over linguistic feature spaces. They analyze three coevolution mechanisms: (1) a shared model with a fixed distribution (authors conform via exponential-family gradient updates), (2) a shared model recursively updated from author outputs, and (3) personalized models updated through both author-specific and population-level feedback. Equilibria and convergence rates are characterized analytically. They then embed conformity as a strategic choice within a utility model where authors trade off private benefits (clarity, legibility, fluency) against stylistic distinctiveness, analyzing the resulting Nash equilibrium versus social optimum.
AI.result: Under a fixed shared model, all authors converge exponentially to the model's distribution, eliminating diversity. Recursive feedback relocates the shared norm but does not alter pairwise spread when authors share the same conformity parameter. Personalization preserves a family of distinct author-model equilibria with nonzero diversity, determined by the weight on population-level feedback. In the utility model, authors over-conform because they fail to internalize the value their distinctiveness provides to others, resulting in a "price of monoculture" that can grow unboundedly when distinctiveness dominates authenticity in the social welfare function.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a rigorous formalization of linguistic monoculture as an emergent phenomenon from repeated human-LLM interaction. The findings suggest that personalization mechanisms can mitigate diversity loss, and that the negative externality from individually rational conformity implies a need for coordination or intervention to achieve socially optimal linguistic diversity. The framework opens avenues for empirical measurement and mechanism design to balance the benefits of LLM assistance against the value of linguistic variation.

title: From Conceptual Hydrologic Models to Conceptually Interpretable Neural Networks: A Snow-Water Mass-Conserving-Perceptron Framework for Discovering Catchment-Scale Precipitation-Storage-Runoff Representations
comment: 125 pages; Main text: 7 tables, 18 figures; Supplementary Materials: 3 texts, 10 tables, 32 figures
summary: The Mass-Conserving Perceptron (MCP) establishes a modeling paradigm in which conceptual hydrologic models can be reformulated as physically constrained, conceptually interpretable neural networks. Here, we develop a snow-water MCP network framework and evaluate it across 513 CAMELS-US basins. We first recast a coupled two-state SOIL-MCP and SNOWMCP conceptual model as a mass-conserving neural network and show that the hydrologic-model and neural-network formulations achieve comparable predictive performance. We then examine cross-node state-information sharing within two-state HYDROMCP architectures and evaluate broader single-layer networks constructed from three types of interpretable MCP units with one to five states. Across CONUS, the median KGEss increases from 0.82 for one-state networks to 0.89 for two-state networks and 0.90 for five-state networks, suggesting diminishing aggregate gains beyond two states. Basin-specific MCP and LSTM selection yields the same median KGEss of 0.90, while the selected MCP networks use fewer parameters on average. Complementary AIC- and KGE-based selection identifies compact, basin-specific directed-graph representations that balance predictive accuracy and model complexity. These analyses provide an empirical basis for identifying the numbers, types, and interactions of states needed for hydrologic representation. Future studies should test joint training against multiple hydrologic responses, such as streamflow, snow water equivalent, and groundwater storage.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the Mass-Conserving Perceptron (MCP) framework to snow-influenced hydrology by developing a coupled SOIL-MCP and SNOW-MCP neural network, demonstrating that two-state architectures yield substantial predictive gains (KGE from 0.82 to 0.89) over one-state models, with diminishing returns beyond two states, and showing that basin-specific MCP selection matches LSTM performance (median KGE 0.90) with fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: To investigate how the Mass-Conserving Perceptron paradigm can incorporate snow processes, determine the optimal number and type of interpretable hydrologic states for streamflow prediction across diverse CONUS basins, and compare MCP networks against LSTMs in terms of predictive accuracy and parameter efficiency.
