AI.method: The authors recast a coupled two-state SOIL-MCP and SNOW-MCP conceptual model as a mass-conserving neural network, validated equivalence with traditional hydrologic formulations, then systematically evaluated single-layer MCP networks built from one to five interpretable states across 513 CAMELS-US basins. They employed KGE (Kling-Gupta Efficiency), AIC (Akaike Information Criterion), and basin-specific model selection to compare architectures and benchmark against LSTM baselines.
AI.result: Median KGE increased from 0.82 (one-state) to 0.89 (two-state) to 0.90 (five-state), with diminishing returns beyond two states. Basin-specific MCP selection and LSTM both achieved median KGE of 0.90, but selected MCP networks used fewer parameters. AIC-KGE joint selection produced compact, interpretable directed-graph representations tailored to individual basins.
AI.conclusion: Two-state MCP architectures capture the dominant hydrologic dynamics across most CONUS basins, with limited aggregate gains from additional states. The MCP framework provides a viable, parameter-efficient, and physically interpretable alternative to LSTMs for rainfall-runoff modeling. Future work should extend to multi-response training (streamflow, SWE, groundwater).

title: From Tokens to Watt-hours: Analytical Energy Estimation for LLM Inference on Modern GPUs
comment: 20 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Accepted for oral presentation at the GREEN-AI Workshop, co-located with ECML-PKDD 2026
summary: The operational energy consumption of large language model (LLM) inference is becoming an increasingly important component of the environmental footprint of deployed AI systems. However, direct measurement of inference energy often requires hardware telemetry, power instrumentation, or infrastructure-specific monitoring, limiting its applicability in comparative studies, early-stage system design, and sustainability reporting. This report presents an analytically structured, empirically calibrated, GPU-level methodology for estimating LLM inference energy on NVIDIA H100-class accelerators without direct runtime measurement. The proposed estimator combines parameter-scaled transformer FLOP accounting, calibrated memory-traffic factors, and hardware-specific energy coefficients for FP16/BF16 tensor-core computation and high-bandwidth-memory movement. It explicitly separates prompt prefill from autoregressive decoding, enabling energy estimates for input tokens, output tokens, and complete inference requests. The methodology further decomposes total energy into compute, parameter-access, key-value-cache write, and attention-read components, allowing the scaling behavior with model size, context length, and generated-token count to be analyzed. The resulting estimates are not intended to replace physical power measurements; rather, they provide transparent, reproducible, and assumption-explicit approximations suitable for model comparison, green-coding analysis, and design-time evaluation of LLM inference workloads.

AI.tldr: This report presents a GPU-level analytical methodology for estimating LLM inference energy on NVIDIA H100 GPUs without requiring direct hardware measurement. It combines FLOP accounting, memory-traffic modeling, and hardware-specific energy coefficients, separates prefill from decoding, and decomposes energy into compute, parameter-access, KV-cache, and attention-read components.
AI.motivation: Direct measurement of LLM inference energy requires hardware telemetry or infrastructure-specific monitoring, which is impractical for comparative studies, early-stage system design, and sustainability reporting. A transparent, reproducible estimation methodology is needed to fill this gap.
AI.method: The estimator integrates three components: (1) parameter-scaled transformer FLOP accounting to quantify computational work, (2) calibrated memory-traffic factors capturing HBM data movement, and (3) hardware-specific energy coefficients for FP16/BF16 tensor-core compute and HBM access on NVIDIA H100 GPUs. It explicitly separates prompt prefill (compute-bound) from autoregressive decoding (memory-bound), and disaggregates total energy into compute, parameter-access, KV-cache write, and attention-read contributions.
AI.result: The methodology produces energy estimates for input tokens, output tokens, and full inference requests. It enables analysis of how energy scales with model size, context length, and generated-token count. The decomposition reveals the distinct energy profiles of prefill versus decoding phases and the relative contributions of compute, memory access, and KV-cache operations.
AI.conclusion: The estimator provides assumption-explicit, reproducible approximations suitable for model comparison, green-coding analysis, and design-time evaluation. It is not a replacement for physical power measurement but serves as a practical tool where direct instrumentation is infeasible.

title: Contrastive ESA: Human Evaluation of Multiple Translations at Once
summary: Current human evaluation of machine translation typically assesses single outputs in isolation, a paradigm that suffers from high annotator noise and cost. We introduce Contrastive Error Span Annotation (cESA), a protocol that presents multiple translations of the source input (text, video, audio, image). In cESA, the annotator sees multiple translations of the same document, marks major and minor error spans, and then assigns a score from 0% to 100% on absolute scale. By allowing annotators to access the shared context across multiple outputs, cESA facilitates more consistent and efficient judgments. We validate cESA using a large-scale human evaluation of English->Japanese translations of 12 models, demonstrating reductions in annotation time and noise compared to standard pointwise evaluation. Unlike existing contrastive ranking methods, cESA yields absolute quality judgments that enable simple, interpretable non-parametric model rankings without the need for post-hoc corrections.

AI.tldr: CESA is a new human evaluation protocol for machine translation that presents multiple translations simultaneously, allowing annotators to mark error spans and assign absolute scores. It reduces annotation time and noise compared to pointwise evaluation while yielding interpretable absolute quality judgments without post-hoc corrections.
AI.motivation: Current human evaluation of MT relies on single-output assessment, which suffers from high annotator noise and cost. The authors aim to address these limitations by introducing a contrastive protocol that leverages shared context across multiple outputs to produce more consistent, efficient, and interpretable evaluations.
AI.method: The Contrastive Error Span Annotation (cESA) protocol presents annotators with multiple translations of the same source document (spanning text, video, audio, image modalities). Annotators mark major and minor error spans across translations and assign an absolute score from 0% to 100%. The shared-context design facilitates comparative judgment. The method is validated via a large-scale human evaluation of English→Japanese translations across 12 models.
AI.result: cESA reduces both annotation time and noise compared to standard pointwise evaluation. It yields absolute quality judgments that support simple, interpretable non-parametric model rankings without requiring post-hoc corrections, unlike existing contrastive ranking approaches.
AI.conclusion: cESA offers a more efficient, consistent, and interpretable alternative to both pointwise MT evaluation and contrastive ranking methods, combining the benefits of comparative annotation with the practicality of absolute scoring.

title: Filesystem-Based Memory for LLM Agents: Organization, Evolution, and Sustainability
summary: Deployed LLM agents increasingly keep their long-term memory as a filesystem: a directory tree of markdown files that the agent itself reads, writes, and reorganizes through generic file tools. Yet research has largely passed over this medium: prior systems design bespoke memory representations and study retrieval over them, leaving the default's two working assumptions untested: that an agent can keep a growing store organized as memories accumulate, conflict, and go stale, and that this organization pays. We present the first systematic exploration of filesystem-based memory for LLM agents. We formalize the setting as three roles around one memory filesystem: a management agent integrates and organizes incoming content, a search agent answers queries with cited sources, and an execution agent supplies task trajectories that are distilled into skills, unifying declarative memory and skills in a single store. Across long-conversation benchmarks and embodied tasks, we vary memory shape (agent-organized hierarchy, verbatim dump, chunk retrieval), stream scale, tool harness (sandboxed shell, memory-tool-style functions, varied search tooling), and the strengths of the management and search agents, tracking answer quality, cost, and store health as memory grows. What organization reliably buys is search economy: organized stores roughly halve retrieval cost where material is large. Today's agents, however, fall short of the default's promise: in our growth study, organization erodes for all but the strongest management agent, and no agent we measure converts organization itself into better answers. And the model is not the only lever over a store's shape: changing the tool set alone reshapes the store as strongly as swapping the model. The study turns the filesystem default from an assumption into a design space for agent memory.

AI.tldr: First systematic study of filesystem-based long-term memory for LLM agents. Formalizes three roles (management, search, execution agents) around a single memory store. Finds that organized stores halve retrieval costs but do not improve answer quality; organization erodes over time for all but the strongest agents; tool choice shapes store structure as much as model choice.
AI.motivation: Deployed LLM agents increasingly default to filesystem-based memory (directory trees of markdown files), yet this approach's core assumptions—that agents can maintain organization as memories accumulate and that organization pays off—remain untested. Prior work designs bespoke memory representations and evaluates retrieval over them, bypassing the filesystem default entirely.
AI.method: Formalizes three agent roles around one memory filesystem: a management agent that integrates and organizes incoming content, a search agent that answers queries with cited sources, and an execution agent that supplies task trajectories distilled into skills. Evaluates across long-conversation benchmarks and embodied tasks while varying memory shape (agent-organized hierarchy, verbatim dump, chunk retrieval), stream scale, tool harness (sandboxed shell, memory-tool functions, varied search tools), and agent strengths, measuring answer quality, cost, and store health.
AI.result: Organized stores roughly halve retrieval cost when material is large (search economy benefit). However, organization erodes over time for all but the strongest management agents, and no agent converts organization into better answer quality. Tool set changes reshape store structure as strongly as model swaps—the model is not the only lever over store shape.
AI.conclusion: The filesystem default for agent memory is transformed from an unchecked assumption into a tractable design space. Organization provides cost efficiency but not quality gains; both model and tool choices critically shape store structure; maintaining organization at scale remains an open challenge.

title: OmegaUse-OfficeVal: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Office-Suite Tasks with Economic Grounding
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly expected to assist users in completing tasks. However, existing benchmarks provide limited support for evaluating whether agents can carry out office-suite workflows at a reasonable cost. We introduce OmegaUse-OfficeVal, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on long-horizon office-suite tasks with task-level economic grounding. The benchmark comprises 100 tasks derived from office-suite requests proposed by practitioners and adapted through a privacy-preserving process. On average, these tasks require 2.32 hours of human labor to complete. An important feature of the benchmark is that each task is paired with two economic signals: human labor time and task price proxy. These signals enable direct comparisons between human costs and LLM inference costs, as well as value-weighted evaluation. To support stable evaluation, we develop code-based verifiers from fine-grained rubrics. We evaluate several frontier LLMs together with a human baseline. Although all evaluated LLMs are substantially cheaper and faster than human workers, they have not yet approached human-level deliverable quality. The code and dataset are fully open-sourced, and more information is available on our project website: https://omegause-officeval.github.io.

AI.tldr: OmegaUse-OfficeVal is a benchmark of 100 long-horizon office-suite tasks with economic grounding (human labor time and task price proxy), enabling cost-quality comparisons between LLM agents and human workers. Frontier LLMs are cheaper/faster but lag in deliverable quality.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks inadequately evaluate LLM agents on realistic office-suite workflows and fail to account for economic cost. There is a need for task-level economic grounding to compare LLM inference costs against human labor costs in a value-weighted manner.
AI.method: The authors constructed OmegaUse-OfficeVal, a 100-task benchmark sourced from practitioner office-suite requests and adapted via a privacy-preserving process. Each task is annotated with two economic signals: human labor time (avg. 2.32 hours) and a task price proxy. Evaluation uses code-based verifiers built from fine-grained rubrics. Several frontier LLMs are benchmarked against a human baseline.
AI.result: All evaluated LLM agents are substantially cheaper and faster than human workers but have not yet achieved human-level deliverable quality. The benchmark enables direct human cost vs. LLM inference cost comparisons.
AI.conclusion: OmegaUse-OfficeVal fills a gap in LLM agent evaluation by introducing economic grounding for office-suite tasks. While LLMs show promise in cost and speed, quality remains sub-human, highlighting a clear direction for future improvement.

title: Forecasting Trajectory-Level Safety Risks in Black-Box Multi-Turn Interactions
summary: As large language models (LLMs) evolve from standalone assistants into autonomous agents, ensuring their safety requires shifting beyond pointwise risk assessment to understand how risks emerge and unfold over long-horizon trajectories. In multi-turn interactions, malicious intent can be decomposed across seemingly harmless turns and gradually reconstructed through interaction trajectories, eventually resulting in safety failures. Existing safeguards remain largely reactive, detecting manifested violations while lacking the ability to predict latent risk evolution and enable preemptive prevention. To address this limitation, we propose Recast, a safety risk forecasting framework that advances LLM safeguarding beyond turn-level violation detection to trajectory-level risk prediction. Recast first retrieves risk-relevant evidence from both short-term dialogue progression and long-term historical context via a dual-scale trajectory view. It then models compositional risk evolution by capturing the current risk configuration and its temporal dynamics. Finally, a causal temporal encoder learns latent risk evolution patterns and predicts the distribution of future risk emergence turns. Extensive experiments across 7 risk categories show that Recast predicts 88.3% of future safety failures with an average lead time of 2.41 turns, while maintaining a false alarm rate of 12.3%, showcasing the effectiveness of trajectory-level forecasting in identifying emerging risks before safety violations occur.

AI.tldr: Recast is a trajectory-level safety risk forecasting framework for LLM agents that predicts future safety failures by modeling compositional risk evolution across multi-turn interactions, achieving 88.3% recall with 2.41 turns of advance warning.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM safeguards are reactive, detecting only manifested violations at the turn level, and cannot predict how malicious intent decomposes and reconstructs across seemingly benign turns in long-horizon agent trajectories. A proactive, predictive approach is needed.
AI.method: Recast employs three components: (1) dual-scale trajectory view retrieving risk-relevant evidence from short-term dialogue progression and long-term historical context; (2) modeling of compositional risk evolution by capturing current risk configuration and temporal dynamics; and (3) a causal temporal encoder that learns latent risk evolution patterns to predict the distribution of future risk emergence turns.
AI.result: Across 7 risk categories, Recast predicts 88.3% of future safety failures with an average lead time of 2.41 turns and a false alarm rate of 12.3%.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory-level risk forecasting is effective for preemptive LLM safety, enabling identification of emerging risks before violations occur, and Recast demonstrates strong predictive performance across diverse risk categories.

title: From Interface to Inference: Eliciting Any-Order Inference from Any-Order Models
summary: Many discrete reasoning tasks, such as code generation, are inherently non-causal: programmers move between high-level structure and local details, a process we call any-order inference. For autoregressive language models, which lack a native any-order interface, non-causal abilities such as infilling and next-edit prediction require hand-designed mechanisms. Can we instead design models that natively support any-order inference? Masked diffusion models have recently emerged as compelling candidates, as their any-order training objective naturally offers an any-order prediction interface. This interface, however, does not automatically yield any-order inference. We demonstrate that this interface-inference gap stems from positional uncertainty: fixed-canvas, token-level models may know what semantic component should appear without knowing where to place it. In light of this, we propose two complementary approaches: (1) Insertion-based masked diffusion, building on FlexMDM (Kim et al, 2025), relaxes fixed-position commitments via insertions, enabling generation across non-contiguous regions. (2) Latent-space masked diffusion shifts prediction to coarser semantic segments, enabling search over latent generation orders. Empirically, we train a 7B FlexMDM for Python coding and a 125M LatentMDM for GSM8K and show that both approaches induce distinct any-order inference behaviors and improve downstream performance. We release our codebase at https://github.com/SeunggeunKimkr/genuine-any-order.

AI.tldr: Masked diffusion models have an any-order prediction interface but suffer from a "positional uncertainty" gap that prevents true any-order inference. The authors propose two solutions: Insertion-based masked diffusion (FlexMDM) that uses insertions to relax fixed-position constraints, and Latent-space masked diffusion (LatentMDM) that operates on coarser semantic segments, enabling effective any-order generation for code and math reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Many discrete reasoning tasks (e.g., code generation) are non-causal by nature—programmers fluidly move between high-level structure and local details. Current autoregressive LMs lack native any-order inference capabilities, requiring hand-designed mechanisms for infilling and next-edit prediction. While masked diffusion models offer an any-order training objective and prediction interface, this does not automatically translate to effective any-order inference due to a gap the authors identify as "positional uncertainty."
AI.method: Two complementary approaches are proposed: (1) Insertion-based masked diffusion (FlexMDM): builds on FlexMDM (Kim et al., 2025), relaxing fixed-position commitments by allowing insertions, which enables generation across non-contiguous regions. (2) Latent-space masked diffusion (LatentMDM): shifts prediction from token-level to coarser semantic segments in latent space, enabling search over latent generation orders. A 7B FlexMDM is trained for Python coding and a 125M LatentMDM for GSM8K math reasoning.
AI.result: Both approaches successfully induce distinct any-order inference behaviors. The 7B FlexMDM demonstrates improved code generation capabilities on Python tasks, while the 125M LatentMDM shows strong performance on GSM8K mathematical reasoning. Both methods yield improved downstream performance compared to baselines lacking genuine any-order inference support.
AI.conclusion: The positional uncertainty problem is the key barrier separating masked diffusion models' any-order prediction interface from true any-order inference. Insertion-based and latent-space approaches effectively bridge this gap, enabling models to natively support the non-causal reasoning patterns essential for tasks like code generation and mathematical problem-solving.

title: Collaborative Weighting with Pessimistic Critic for Mitigating Overestimation in Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning
summary: Deep off-policy reinforcement learning algorithms for continuous control typically rely on neural value function approximation to guide policy improvement. However, temporal-difference (TD) learning introduces noisy targets, resulting in non-stationary optimization, while greedy policy updates amplify early-stage estimation errors. The recursive propagation of such errors leads to persistent overestimation bias and degraded training stability in actor-critic methods. Existing approaches attempt to alleviate this issue via prioritized sampling or modified value learning objectives, but often overemphasize high-uncertainty transitions caused by limited data coverage or bootstrapping errors, thereby further amplifying bias.In this paper, we propose Collaborative Weighting Actor-Critic (CWAC), a unified framework that explicitly accounts for predictive uncertainty in value estimation. CWAC employs distributional critic to model return uncertainty and introduces a collaborative weighting mechanism that jointly reweights TD-errors and uncertainty, enabling robust learning from reliable samples while suppressing noisy updates. In addition, we incorporate a stochastic pessimistic value estimation scheme via sampling from the return distribution, which effectively mitigates error propagation during policy improvement. CWAC can be seamlessly integrated into existing off-policy algorithm frameworks such as SAC, TD3, and DDPG with minimal overhead. Empirical results demonstrate that our proposed method significantly enhances performance across a diverse range of simulated tasks. Our code is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CWAC-348E.

AI.tldr: CWAC (Collaborative Weighting Actor-Critic) is a unified framework that mitigates overestimation bias in off-policy RL by jointly reweighting TD-errors and predictive uncertainty, and using stochastic pessimistic value estimates. It integrates into SAC, TD3, and DDPG, improving performance across diverse continuous control tasks.
AI.motivation: Off-policy actor-critic methods suffer from overestimation bias and training instability caused by noisy TD targets, non-stationary optimization, and recursive propagation of early-stage estimation errors. Existing solutions (e.g., prioritized sampling, modified value objectives) often overemphasize high-uncertainty transitions, further amplifying bias rather than resolving it.
AI.method: CWAC uses a distributional critic to model return uncertainty and introduces a collaborative weighting mechanism that jointly reweights TD-errors and uncertainty, enabling robust learning from reliable samples while suppressing noisy updates. It also incorporates a stochastic pessimistic value estimation scheme that samples from the return distribution to mitigate error propagation during policy improvement. The framework is plug-and-play for SAC, TD3, and DDPG.
AI.result: Empirical results show that CWAC significantly enhances performance across a diverse range of simulated tasks compared to standard baselines (SAC, TD3, DDPG).
AI.conclusion: CWAC effectively addresses overestimation bias and instability in off-policy actor-critic methods through uncertainty-aware collaborative weighting and pessimistic value estimation, offering a lightweight, general-purpose enhancement for existing algorithms.

title: Constitutional Midtraining: Content Presence Drives Alignment Gains
summary: Post-training alignment is often shallow, eroding under fine-tuning. Whether midtraining interventions, cleanly isolated from post-training, can produce durable alignment remains untested. We test this via constitutional midtraining: inserting principled, values-based content into midtraining against a replay-only control at 120B scale. Our 394M-token constitutional corpus, built from Anthropic's Constitution, uses a 2x2 factorial design (curriculum ordering x deliberative reasoning) to produce four constitutionally midtrained conditions plus a control, evaluated on self-generated and established benchmarks including alignment under pressure, value conflict resolution, blackmail, and emergent misalignment across three stages: post-midtraining, post-SFT, and post-benign fine-tuning. Constitutionally midtrained models outperform the control on alignment generalization and durability, notably on blackmail: SFT instills a blackmail propensity in all models, but constitutional midtraining blunts it, with the advantage surviving benign fine-tuning (-17.5pp). This durability does not extend to settings requiring active resistance to in-context pressure or conflict, where the advantage attenuates after SFT. The presence of constitutional content at midtraining also matters more than its structure, and constitutional midtraining incurs no cost, on average, on the capabilities we test (MMLU, ARC-Easy, piqa, GSM8K) at any stage. A modest amount of constitutional content at midtraining could therefore yield broad, persistent alignment gains, offering a cheap, complementary addition to SFT-centered pipelines. Code, data, and models are available.

AI.tldr: Midtraining models on a values-based constitutional corpus produces durable alignment gains that survive subsequent fine-tuning, outperforming post-training-only approaches, particularly in resisting blackmail behaviors, without degrading capabilities.
AI.motivation: Post-training alignment (e.g., RLHF) is known to be shallow and easily eroded by subsequent fine-tuning. The authors investigate whether inserting alignment-relevant content during midtraining—a phase cleanly isolated from post-training—can produce more durable, robust alignment that persists through downstream fine-tuning stages.
AI.method: A 394M-token constitutional corpus was constructed from Anthropic's Constitution and inserted into midtraining at 120B scale using a 2×2 factorial design (curriculum ordering × deliberative reasoning), yielding four constitutional conditions plus a replay-only control. Models were evaluated across three stages—post-midtraining, post-SFT, and post-benign fine-tuning—on alignment generalization, value conflict resolution, blackmail resistance, and emergent misalignment, alongside standard capability benchmarks (MMLU, ARC-Easy, piqa, GSM8K).
AI.result: Constitutionally midtrained models outperformed the control on alignment generalization and durability. On blackmail: SFT induced blackmail propensity in all models, but constitutional midtraining blunted this effect, with the advantage surviving benign fine-tuning (−17.5pp). However, this durability did not extend to in-context pressure/conflict settings, where the advantage attenuated post-SFT. The presence of constitutional content mattered more than its structure (curriculum/deliberation). No average capability degradation was observed at any stage.
AI.conclusion: A modest amount of constitutional content at midtraining yields broad, persistent alignment gains, offering a cheap and complementary addition to SFT-centered alignment pipelines. The approach is robust to subsequent fine-tuning in some but not all adversarial settings.

title: Can AI agents conduct open-ended AI research? Early evidence from two case studies
summary: Forecasts of explosive AI progress hinge on AI agents automating AI research. But evidence on whether agents can carry out open-ended AI research is thin. Current evaluations either test agents on narrow, verifiable tasks, which excludes open-ended research, or submit AI-generated papers to blind peer review, which is overstretched, stochastic, and suffers from poor review quality. We introduce a third way to measure progress towards AI R\&D automation. An agent takes on the central, open-ended research question of a high-quality unpublished paper, and the paper's original authors grade its output. We call these shadow evaluations. We ran shadow evaluations on two unpublished NeurIPS 2026 submissions, giving frontier agents six days and thousands of dollars of compute. The agents completed all of the engineering without human help, yet could not make substantial progress towards answering the research questions. As a result, both papers were unambiguously rejected by the authors. We identify five recurring failure modes: poor judgment about the bar for publishable research, uncreative responses to shortcomings in the research design, ineffective backtracking from dead ends, poor resource awareness, and instruction drift. A robustness check with a second model and scaffold reproduced these failures. We release the expert reviews, survey responses, agent repositories, and logs. Our results provide early evidence that today's agents can do the engineering of AI research, but struggle with critical parts of the research lifecycle.

AI.tldr: Shadow evaluations reveal that frontier AI agents can handle engineering tasks in AI research but fail at open-ended scientific reasoning, with all agent-generated outputs rejected by original authors of NeurIPS submissions.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation methods for AI research automation are inadequate: narrow task benchmarks exclude open-ended research, while blind peer review is noisy, stochastic, and low-quality. A new evaluation paradigm is needed to rigorously measure progress toward AI R&D automation.
AI.method: The authors introduce "shadow evaluations," where an AI agent attempts the central open-ended research question of a high-quality unpublished paper. The original authors then grade the agent's output. Two NeurIPS 2026 submissions were used, with frontier agents given six days and thousands of dollars of compute to work autonomously.
AI.result: Agents completed all engineering tasks without human intervention but failed to make substantial progress on the research questions. Both papers were unambiguously rejected. Five recurring failure modes were identified: misjudging publication bar, uncreative responses to design flaws, ineffective backtracking from dead ends, poor resource awareness, and instruction drift. A robustness check with a second model/scaffold reproduced these failures.
AI.conclusion: Today's frontier agents can automate the engineering components of AI research but critically struggle with the intellectual demands of the research lifecycle, suggesting a significant gap remains before full AI R&D automation is achieved.

title: HiFloat4 Format for End-To-End Reinforcement Learning Post-Training of Large Language Models
summary: We present, to our knowledge, the first end-to-end FP4 RL post-training, in which both the rollout and training policies, including their forward and backward passes, operate at 4-bit precision. A systematic study reveals that the dominant source of degradation in FP4 RL is not training-side quantization error but rollout activation quantization: outliers stretch the dynamic range so far that a large number of activation values underflow to zero under FP4. Counterintuitively, restoring the training policy to higher precision while keeping the rollout in FP4 makes accuracy worse than full FP4 baseline, exposing rollout-training mismatch as the principal failure mode and ruling out standard pretraining-style fixes. We address this with Rollout Residual Quantization (Rollout-ResQ): a single residual correction term constrained to a hardware-friendly sparsity pattern, added only to the FP4 rollout matmul -- a lightweight correction that recovers most of the precision lost to outlier-driven underflow without inflating the rollout's compute footprint. On Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-Math-7B, Rollout-ResQ paired with the HiFloat4 (HiF4) format -- whose three-level hierarchical scaling preserves resolution under FP4's tight 4-bit budget -- closes the accuracy gap to BF16 from 4.9% to 1.1%, bringing fully quantized FP4 RL within striking distance of full precision. Applied to the open-standard MXFP4, the same recipe narrows the gap from 13.6% to 5.3%, revealing that FP4 format choice is a key factor that determines the ceiling on recoverable accuracy. Together, these results establish HiF4 as the enabling format for end-to-end FP4 RL post-training, and Rollout-ResQ as the activation-side mechanism that makes the gap to BF16 closable.

AI.tldr: First end-to-end FP4 RL post-training system where both rollout and training operate at 4-bit. Identifies rollout activation quantization (not training quantization) as the primary failure source due to outlier-driven underflow. Proposes Rollout-ResQ, a sparse residual correction for rollout matmuls, combined with the HiF4 format, narrowing the accuracy gap to BF16 from 4.9% to 1.1%.
AI.motivation: FP4 quantization in RL post-training is unexplored end-to-end. The key question is: what breaks when both rollout and training run entirely in FP4, and can the degradation be corrected without sacrificing the compute efficiency of 4-bit operations?
AI.method: Systematic ablation study isolating quantization sources (rollout activations vs. training weights/activations). Rollout Residual Quantization (Rollout-ResQ): a single sparse residual correction term added to the FP4 rollout matmul, constrained to a hardware-friendly sparsity pattern, compensating for outlier-driven activation underflow. Paired with HiFloat4 (HiF4), a three-level hierarchical scaling FP4 format preserving resolution under tight bit budget. Also tested with open-standard MXFP4.
AI.result: On Qwen2.5-3B and Qwen2.5-Math-7B: HiF4 + Rollout-ResQ closes BF16 gap from 4.9% → 1.1%. With MXFP4: gap narrows from 13.6% → 5.3%. Restoring training precision while keeping rollout in FP4 worsens accuracy versus full FP4 baseline, confirming rollout-training mismatch as the dominant failure mode.
AI.conclusion: FP4 format choice determines the ceiling on recoverable accuracy. HiF4 is the enabling format for end-to-end FP4 RL post-training; Rollout-ResQ is the activation-side mechanism that makes the gap to BF16 closable.

title: APEX-Accounting
summary: We introduce APEX-Accounting, a benchmark built by Mercor in partnership with Ramp, to assess whether frontier models can do the real work of accountants. Tasks include reconciling accounts, accruing expenses, posting transactions, and producing reports. The private eval set comprises 160 tasks, split across 10 worlds. Each world contains an accounting system, as well as spreadsheets, PDFs, and other files. Every task was authored and solved by experts in accounting and bookkeeping, who also wrote grading rubrics. Across nine frontier models, Claude-Fable-5 (Max) leads with 56.4% Mean Criteria@3, ahead of Muse-Spark-1.1 (xHigh) at 52.6%. No model scores more than 2.6% Pass^8 (GPT-5.6-Sol (Max+Pro)) and the highest Pass@8 is 21.5% (Muse-Spark-1.1 (xHigh)). We experiment with increasing the token budget from $1 to $50 and observe an instance of Simpson's paradox: scores increase as the token budget increases but within a given budget-constrained harness, scores are lower on tasks where the model spends more tokens. As APEX-Accounting is a closed benchmark, leaderboard evals can be run for any frontier model on request.

AI.tldr: APEX-Accounting is a private benchmark of 160 expert-authored accounting tasks across 10 simulated "worlds." Claude-Fable-5 (Max) leads at 56.4% Mean Criteria@3, but no model exceeds 2.6% Pass^8. A Simpson's paradox emerges: higher token budgets improve scores overall, yet within a fixed budget, tasks consuming more tokens score lower.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether frontier AI models can perform authentic accounting work — not simplified textbook problems, but real-world tasks like reconciliation, accruals, transaction posting, and report generation — using realistic artifacts (spreadsheets, PDFs, accounting systems).
AI.method: A private benchmark with 160 tasks across 10 isolated "worlds," each containing an accounting system and supporting files. Tasks were authored, solved, and graded by professional accountants and bookkeepers with custom scoring rubrics. Nine frontier models were evaluated using Mean Criteria@3 and Pass^8 metrics, with an ablation on token budgets ($1–$50).
AI.result: Claude-Fable-5 (Max) achieves the highest Mean Criteria@3 at 56.4%, followed by Muse-Spark-1.1 (xHigh) at 52.6%. The best Pass^8 is 21.5% (Muse-Spark-1.1). GPT-5.6-Sol (Max+Pro) posts the top Pass^8 at just 2.6%. Token budget experiments reveal Simpson's paradox: aggregate scores rise with budget, but within-budget, higher token spend correlates with lower scores.
AI.conclusion: Frontier models remain far from reliably performing professional accounting work. The benchmark is closed but leaderboard evaluations are available upon request, enabling ongoing assessment of model progress in this domain.

title: Automated Multilabel Mpox Research Classification with Explainable Transformer Models
summary: The Mpox outbreak remains a serious public health issue, with the WHO (World Health Organization) reporting increasing cases in some regions. Research on Mpox is vital for several reasons, including vaccine development, diagnostic improvement, viral evolution studies, and preventing future outbreaks. However, the large amount of research being published makes it difficult to organize and analyze information efficiently. This study focuses on using multilabel classification to categorize 14590 Mpox research articles into key topics such as outbreaks, vaccination, and epidemiology. Among the different AI models tested, BERT performed the best, achieving 97.05% accuracy, 97.67% micro F1 score, and 96.46% macro F1 score. To better understand how the model makes decisions, SHAP was used to analyze significant word features and patterns. The results show that BERT can help automate the classification of Mpox research, making it easier for researchers, policymakers, and healthcare workers to quickly find relevant information, saving time and improving public health efforts.

AI.tldr: This study applies multilabel text classification using BERT to categorize 14,590 Mpox research articles into topics like outbreaks, vaccination, and epidemiology, achieving 97.05% accuracy. SHAP analysis is used to interpret model decisions.
AI.motivation: The rapidly growing volume of Mpox research literature makes manual organization and information retrieval inefficient. Automated classification is needed to help researchers, policymakers, and healthcare workers quickly locate relevant studies to support vaccine development, diagnostics, viral evolution tracking, and outbreak prevention.
AI.method: Multilabel classification was applied to 14,590 Mpox research articles across key topic categories (outbreaks, vaccination, epidemiology, etc.). Multiple AI models were tested, with BERT identified as the top performer. Model interpretability was assessed using SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) to identify influential word features and decision patterns.
AI.result: BERT achieved 97.05% accuracy, 97.67% micro F1 score, and 96.46% macro F1 score, outperforming all other models tested. SHAP analysis revealed meaningful word-level features driving classification decisions.
AI.conclusion: BERT-based multilabel classification effectively automates the categorization of Mpox research literature, significantly reducing the time required to retrieve relevant information and thereby enhancing public health response efforts.

title: From Unsupervised Subgroups to Hypothetical State-Intervention Policies: An Evaluation of Selected Subgrouping Methods in Observational Health Data
summary: Conventional subgroup analyses can yield unstable and difficult-to-interpret conclusions, especially in observational biomedical data where each individual is observed under only one exposure state, true individual treatment effects are unavailable, and causal structure is uncertain. We investigate whether subgroups constructed from pretreatment characteristics, without using exposure, outcome, or estimated treatment-effect information, can serve as interpretable units for budget-constrained policy prioritization. We propose a framework combining causal-discovery-informed covariate selection, discovery-evaluation sample splitting, inductive unsupervised clustering, uncertainty-aware subgroup selection, and held-out doubly robust policy evaluation. We compare K-means, hard, membership-weighted, and stochastic Fuzzy C-means, Bayesian Gaussian mixture models, and a supervised causal-forest-derived CATE-tree comparator. Policies are evaluated under a 70% budget for hypothetical obesity-to-non-obesity and elevated-to-lower-glucose state shifts in the PIMA Indians Diabetes dataset and for a lifetime-smoking-history contrast in NHANES. The highest estimated ungated utilities were 0.799 for the BMI policy using Bayesian GMM, 0.735 for the glucose policy using hard or membership-weighted FCM, and 0.775 for the smoking-history policy using K-means. All paired 95% confidence intervals for policy-risk differences included zero, and no comparison remained statistically significant after Holm adjustment. Bayesian pooling generally preserved ungated allocations, whereas Empirical Bernstein gating was more conservative. Policies with similar estimated utility could nevertheless prioritize different individuals. The findings should be interpreted as assumption-dependent decision-support evidence for hypothetical state contrasts rather than proof of intervention benefit.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework for constructing policy-relevant subgroups in observational data using unsupervised clustering on pretreatment covariates—without exposure or outcome information—and evaluates budget-constrained treatment prioritization policies using doubly robust methods, finding similar utility across methods with no statistically significant differences.
AI.motivation: Conventional subgroup analyses in observational biomedical data are unstable and hard to interpret because individuals are observed under only one exposure, true individual treatment effects are unavailable, and causal structure is uncertain. The authors aim to develop interpretable, pretreatment-characteristic-based subgroups for budget-constrained policy prioritization that avoid overfitting to estimated treatment effects.
AI.method: The framework integrates: (1) causal-discovery-informed covariate selection, (2) discovery-evaluation sample splitting, (3) inductive unsupervised clustering (K-means, hard/soft Fuzzy C-means, Bayesian Gaussian mixture models), (4) uncertainty-aware subgroup selection, and (5) held-out doubly robust policy evaluation. A supervised causal-forest-derived CATE-tree serves as comparator. Policies are evaluated under a 70% budget constraint for hypothetical state shifts using PIMA Indians Diabetes and NHANES datasets.
AI.result: Highest estimated ungated utilities: BMI policy (Bayesian GMM, 0.799), glucose policy (hard/membership-weighted FCM, 0.735), smoking-history policy (K-means, 0.775). All 95% CIs for policy-risk differences included zero; no comparisons remained significant after Holm adjustment. Bayesian pooling preserved ungated allocations; Empirical Bernstein gating was more conservative. Policies with similar utility could prioritize different individuals.
AI.conclusion: Subgroups derived without outcome/exposure information can serve as interpretable units for policy prioritization. Results should be viewed as assumption-dependent decision-support evidence for hypothetical contrasts rather than proof of intervention benefit, highlighting the importance of uncertainty quantification in subgroup-based policy evaluation.

title: AtmosERC: Modeling Dialogue-Level Affective Atmosphere for Emotion Recognition in Conversation
summary: Emotion Recognition in Conversation (ERC) aims to predict utterance-level emotions in dialogues and has largely advanced through context-centric modeling. However, global context is a heterogeneous signal, and not all contextual information is equally relevant to emotion prediction. This paper focuses on the affect-oriented component of this signal, termed dialogue-level affective atmosphere, which captures a latent tendency commonly reflected in conversational emotion patterns. To estimate and exploit this tendency, we propose AtmosERC, a graph-based ERC framework that models each dialogue as a conversational graph over utterances and speakers. A relation-aware graph extractor filters and fuses heterogeneous graph signals to produce dialogue-level and speaker-conditioned affective priors. The resulting compact prior guides lightweight sequential emotion prediction and can also be verbalized into prompt-level cues for LLM-based ERC without modifying backbone models. Experiments on four ERC benchmarks show that AtmosERC improves lightweight ERC, enhances LLM-based ERC as a plug-in cue, and yields more stable predictions under local emotional deviations.

AI.tldr: AtmosERC models the dialogue-level affective atmosphere—a latent emotional tendency in conversations—using a relation-aware graph extractor. This compact prior guides lightweight emotion prediction and serves as a plug-in cue for LLM-based ERC, improving performance and stability across four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing ERC models leverage global context, but global context is heterogeneous—not all contextual information is equally relevant for emotion prediction. The authors argue that a distinct affect-oriented signal, termed "dialogue-level affective atmosphere," captures a latent tendency in conversational emotion patterns that is underexploited.
AI.method: AtmosERC models each dialogue as a conversational graph over utterances and speakers. A relation-aware graph extractor filters and fuses heterogeneous graph signals to produce two types of affective priors: a dialogue-level prior and speaker-conditioned priors. These compact priors then guide lightweight sequential emotion prediction. Additionally, the priors can be verbalized into prompt-level cues for LLM-based ERC without modifying backbone models.
AI.result: Experiments on four ERC benchmarks demonstrate that AtmosERC improves lightweight ERC performance, enhances LLM-based ERC when used as a plug-in cue, and yields more stable predictions under local emotional deviations.
AI.conclusion: The dialogue-level affective atmosphere is a learnable, compact signal that effectively complements context-centric ERC modeling. AtmosERC provides a principled way to extract and exploit this signal, benefiting both lightweight and LLM-based ERC paradigms.

title: The Art of Not Forgetting A Local Learning Architecture for Continual Learning
summary: We introduce CMP (Cognitive Memory Primitive), a continual-learning architecture that repre?sents inputs as sparse relational codes, stores them in a two-tier competitive memory, and learns through local updates without end-to-end backpropagation through its feature-generating system. We investigate whether combining sparse representations, local learning, and persistent memory can reduce catastrophic forgetting relative to conventional backpropagation-based continual?learning approaches. On a controlled domain-incremental byte-level language modeling protocol, CMP demonstrates substantially lower backward transfer than a parameter-matched Trans?former trained with online Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC). Across a three-seed replicated 15-domain experiment, CMP exhibits stable forgetting behavior, while separate head-to-head comparisons and domain-order analyses show consistently lower forgetting than the evaluated Transformer baseline under the reported experimental settings. We report these findings alongside a substantial single-domain accuracy gap relative to the Transformer, a null result on a vision benchmark, and a documented failure to combine CMP with an independent accuracy-improving mechanism, reflecting our commitment to reporting both positive and negative outcomes. These results suggest that the combination of sparse representations, local learning, and persistent memory is a promising direction for continual learning, while motivating further investigation into the respective roles of learning rules, representations, and architectural design in mitigating catastrophic forgetting.

AI.tldr: CMP introduces a continual-learning architecture using sparse relational codes, two-tier competitive memory, and local updates (no end-to-end backpropagation). It significantly reduces catastrophic forgetting compared to Transformers with EWC on language modeling tasks, though with a notable single-domain accuracy gap and a null result on vision benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether combining sparse representations, local learning, and persistent memory can mitigate catastrophic forgetting in continual learning, compared to conventional backpropagation-based approaches like EWC. The authors aim to explore architectural alternatives that avoid end-to-end backpropagation through feature generators.
AI.method: CMP (Cognitive Memory Primitive) represents inputs as sparse relational codes stored in a two-tier competitive memory system. Learning occurs through local updates only, without end-to-end backpropagation through the feature-generating system. Evaluated on domain-incremental byte-level language modeling (15 domains, 3 seeds) and compared against a parameter-matched Transformer baseline trained with online Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC). Also tested on a vision benchmark.
AI.result: CMP demonstrated substantially lower backward transfer (less forgetting) than the Transformer+EWC baseline. Across all experimental conditions, CMP showed stable forgetting behavior, while the Transformer exhibited consistently higher forgetting. However, CMP had a substantial single-domain accuracy gap relative to the Transformer, produced a null result on the vision benchmark, and failed to integrate with an independent accuracy-improving mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Combining sparse representations, local learning, and persistent memory is a promising direction for reducing catastrophic forgetting in continual learning. However, accuracy gaps and limited cross-domain transfer highlight the need for further investigation into the specific roles of learning rules, representations, and architectural design.

title: Phoneme- vs. Character-Level Targets and Selective State-Space Models for Intracortical Brain-to-Text
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure, 6 tables, submitted to IberSPEECH 2026
summary: State-of-the-art intracortical brain-to-text systems pair a neural-sequence phone decoder with an external language model. Two design axes remain underexplored: whether selective state-space models (Mamba) improve on recurrent decoders, and how the output target (phonetic vs.\ character) interacts with that choice. On the public Brain-to-Text '25 benchmark, we study a controlled 2x2 grid (GRU vs.\ hybrid Mamba decoder; phonetic vs.\ character targets) trained with a CTC objective under one reproducible protocol. The recurrent baseline remains strongest: the best phonetic GRU reaches 12.62\% PER and 21.19\% WER, while the best textual GRU after LM rescoring reaches 13.39\% CER and 26.28\% WER. The Mamba hybrid is competitive but does not surpass it. Ablations isolate architectural contributions, and error analysis shows representation-dependent failures: articulatory-like phoneme confusions vs.\ lexical and word-boundary errors.

AI.tldr: On the Brain-to-Text '25 benchmark, the authors systematically compare GRU vs. hybrid Mamba decoders and phonetic vs. character output targets under a CTC objective. The GRU baseline remains strongest (12.62% PER, 21.19% WER for phonetic; 13.39% CER, 26.28% WER for textual after LM rescoring). The Mamba hybrid is competitive but does not surpass GRU. Error analysis reveals representation-dependent failure modes: articulatory confusions for phonemes vs. lexical/word-boundary errors for characters.
AI.motivation: Two underexplored design axes in intracortical brain-to-text systems: (1) whether selective state-space models (Mamba) can outperform recurrent decoders, and (2) how phonetic vs. character output targets interact with decoder architecture choice.
AI.method: A controlled 2×2 grid experiment on the Brain-to-Text '25 benchmark: GRU vs. hybrid Mamba decoder × phonetic vs. character targets, all trained with a CTC objective under a single reproducible protocol. LM rescoring is applied for textual evaluation. Ablations isolate architectural contributions, and error analysis characterizes failure modes.
AI.result: The recurrent GRU baseline is strongest: best phonetic GRU achieves 12.62% PER and 21.19% WER; best textual GRU after LM rescoring achieves 13.39% CER and 26.28% WER. The Mamba hybrid decoder is competitive but does not surpass GRU. Error analysis shows phonetic decoders produce articulatory-like phoneme confusions, while character decoders exhibit lexical and word-boundary errors.
AI.conclusion: Despite the promise of selective state-space models, well-tuned GRU decoders remain state-of-the-art for neural-sequence decoding in brain-to-text. The choice of output representation (phonetic vs. character) shapes error typology, suggesting that representation design and decoder architecture should be co-optimized rather than treated independently.

title: AgentGFM: A Graph Foundation Model with Node-Agent Information-Flow Control
summary: Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) aim to learn transferable knowledge from multi-domain graphs and adapt to unseen scenarios. As a fundamental source of relational semantics in graphs, the transferability of topological patterns has long been central to GFM research. However, local structural patterns may vary across graphs and even among nodes within the same graph. Despite such structural variation, most existing GFMs rely on manually designed propagation schemes and apply them to new graphs largely unchanged. Such fixed schemes may not suit the diverse structural patterns of different nodes. This raises a key question: can each node autonomously determine how information should be propagated through the graph? We refer to this capability as information-flow control. Inspired by recent advances in agent technology, we formulate this problem as agent-based decision making and treat each node as an agent. Accordingly, we propose AgentGFM, in which all node agents follow a shared end-to-end trainable policy rather than using independent models. For adaptive information-flow control, each node interacts with the graph through a predict-act-observe-correct process. During the act stage, the node makes three decisions: source reception, signal-channel selection and gain-aware node-wise halting. The resulting observation is compared with the prediction and their discrepancy is used to correct the node state and guide subsequent interactions. Extensive experiments across node-level, graph-level and large-scale transfer scenarios demonstrate the effectiveness of AgentGFM across diverse graph topologies.

AI.tldr: AgentGFM proposes a Graph Foundation Model where each node acts as an agent that autonomously controls information flow through a predict-act-observe-correct cycle, using a shared trainable policy to make three decisions: source reception, signal-channel selection, and gain-aware node-wise halting, outperforming fixed propagation schemes across diverse transfer scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing GFMs rely on manually designed, fixed propagation schemes applied uniformly to new graphs, which fails to accommodate the structural variation across graphs and among nodes within the same graph. The authors argue that nodes should autonomously determine their own information propagation behavior — a capability termed "information-flow control."
AI.method: The method frames information-flow control as an agent-based decision-making problem. Each node is an agent governed by a shared, end-to-end trainable policy. The core mechanism is a predict-act-observe-correct loop: (1) Predict — the node anticipates the outcome of its action; (2) Act — the node makes three decisions: source reception (which neighbors to receive information from), signal-channel selection (which propagation channels to use), and gain-aware node-wise halting (when to stop propagating); (3) Observe — the actual outcome is observed; (4) Correct — the discrepancy between prediction and observation is used to update the node state and guide subsequent interactions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across node-level, graph-level, and large-scale transfer scenarios demonstrate AgentGFM's effectiveness across diverse graph topologies.
AI.conclusion: Enabling per-node autonomous information-flow control via agent-based decision making significantly improves the transferability of GFMs, allowing them to adapt to structurally diverse graphs without relying on manually designed, fixed propagation schemes.

title: Metis: Memory Foundation Model
summary: Recent advances in AI agents have increasingly internalized native capabilities into their underlying foundation models, giving rise to multimodal foundation models and large reasoning models. However, agent memory is still primarily implemented through external modules, leaving the native memory capability largely unexplored. In this paper, we take a first step toward this direction by introducing memory foundation models, which empower foundation models with native memory capabilities. We formalize native memory from two perspectives: a persistent and dynamically evolving memory state within the backbone, and native memory procedures that autonomously store and utilize information through model computation. We show that native memory offers advantages in architecture, end-to-end optimization, and efficiency. Based on this formulation, we propose Metis, the first prototype of memory foundation models. Metis introduces a new architecture that equips a foundation model with a native memory state, allowing historical information to be compressed into the model and accessed through memory attention. We construct large-scale memory-specific training data and introduce multiple optimization objectives to acquire these native memory procedures through mid-training. The online memory maintenance of Metis is gradient-free, and the memory update requires only a forward pass. At inference time, all learned model weights remain frozen, while the native memory states are autonomously transformed through standard forward computation. Through extensive experiments, we show that Metis exhibits native memory capabilities and further provide a detailed analysis of its strengths, limitations, and behaviors. To facilitate future research on memory foundation models, we release our project and model checkpoints.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Memory Foundation Models, which embed persistent, evolving memory directly into foundation model architectures rather than relying on external memory modules. The authors present Metis, a prototype featuring a native memory state with memory attention, trained via mid-training on memory-specific data with multiple optimization objectives. Memory updates are gradient-free and require only a forward pass, with frozen model weights at inference.
AI.motivation: Current AI agents rely on external modules for memory while foundation models have increasingly internalized other capabilities (multimodal perception, reasoning). Native memory capabilities within foundation models remain largely unexplored, creating a gap in architecture design, end-to-end optimization potential, and efficiency.
AI.method: The authors formalize native memory along two dimensions: (1) a persistent, dynamically evolving memory state within the model backbone, and (2) native memory procedures that autonomously store and retrieve information via model computation. Metis implements this through a novel architecture with a native memory state that compresses historical information and accesses it through memory attention. Large-scale memory-specific training data is constructed with multiple optimization objectives applied during mid-training. Online memory maintenance uses gradient-free updates requiring only a forward pass; all learned weights remain frozen at inference while memory states transform through standard forward computation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that Metis exhibits native memory capabilities. The paper provides detailed analysis of strengths, limitations, and behaviors of the approach, and releases the project and model checkpoints to facilitate further research.
AI.conclusion: Native memory capabilities can be successfully integrated into foundation models, offering architectural, optimization, and efficiency benefits over external memory approaches. Metis serves as a first prototype demonstrating the viability of memory foundation models and opens a new research direction.

title: Relation Geometry in Semantic Space of Language Models
summary: When it comes to generating vector representations of words, current language models are achieving high-quality results. However, what is not known is the extent to which knowledge about semantic relations is represented in the geometry of the semantic spaces created in this way. In order to answer this question, we study the relation geometry of such semantic spaces from three perspectives. We first examine whether words standing in a particular relation to a target word~(called relata) occupy the same region in semantic space, and whether the regions corresponding to different relations are distinct from each other. We then verify to what extent semantic spaces reflect certain well-known properties of relations, such as symmetry, asymmetry, and transitivity. Finally, we consider which information about the target words and relata is more important for relation geometry: their surface forms, or their contexts. We conduct experiments on six semantic relations using causal, masked, and diffusion language models. The results show that relata in asymmetric relations relatively clearly occupy a distinct region in semantic space. Asymmetric relations' properties are only moderately well encoded in the semantic space, yet better than those of symmetric ones. Furthermore, when considering the question which information source has the strongest impact on results amongst the models we evaluated, we find that lexical information tends to be more important for the causal language model, whereas contextual information is more important for the masked and diffusion language models. Our results empirically show that relation geometry is not equally well-represented for all relations in semantic space, suggesting that there is a difference in how well semantic relations might be learned from distributional information alone.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how semantic relations are geometrically encoded in word embedding spaces, examining whether relations occupy distinct regions, how well relational properties (symmetry, asymmetry, transitivity) are preserved, and whether lexical or contextual information dominates. Findings show asymmetric relations are better represented than symmetric ones, and model type (causal vs. masked/diffusion) affects whether lexical or contextual cues matter more.
AI.motivation: While language models produce high-quality word embeddings, it remains unclear to what extent knowledge about semantic relations is geometrically encoded in the resulting semantic spaces. The authors aim to systematically characterize the "relation geometry" — how relational knowledge manifests spatially.
AI.method: The authors analyze relation geometry from three angles: (1) whether words in a given semantic relation (relata) cluster in the same region and whether different relations occupy distinct regions; (2) how well properties like symmetry, asymmetry, and transitivity are reflected in the space; (3) whether surface lexical forms or contextual information more strongly drives relation geometry. Experiments span six semantic relations using causal, masked, and diffusion language models.
AI.result: Asymmetric relations occupy relatively distinct regions in semantic space and their properties are moderately well encoded — better than symmetric relations. For causal LMs, lexical information is more influential, while contextual information dominates for masked and diffusion LMs. Relation geometry is not uniformly represented across all relations.
AI.conclusion: Relation geometry varies significantly across different semantic relations, suggesting that distributional information alone may not be equally sufficient for learning all types of semantic relations. This has implications for how well language models can acquire relational knowledge from text.

title: Simultaneous Coverage and Efficiency Guarantee in Online Conformal Prediction
comment: We acknowledge the use of LLMs for editorial assistance in improving the clarity, style, proof checking, and figure generation of this manuscript
summary:
Adaptive conformal inference (ACI) of Gibbs and Cand{è}s and its variants are the standard approach to online conformal prediction under distribution shift, but they suffer from three fundamental limitations. First, their guarantees control only the \emph{signed} long-run coverage error: persistent miscoverage in one direction can be masked by compensating errors later, so a method can satisfy the theoretical guarantee while being badly wrong for extended periods. Second, existing guarantees say nothing about prediction-set size, so validity can be achieved trivially at the cost of unduly wide prediction sets. Third, the efficiency guarantees that do exist compare against a \emph{fixed} predictor chosen in hindsight, a benchmark that becomes increasingly less meaningful once the data-generating distribution shifts, since the very notion of an optimal threshold then changes over time.
  We consider a unified online learning framework that simultaneously controls absolute, non-cancelling coverage violation and prediction-set efficiency against a dynamically evolving benchmark for three important models. In the fully adversarial setting, exploiting the fact that the standard ACI update is exactly projected online gradient descent on the pinball loss, we derive simultaneous coverage and efficiency guarantees for arbitrary monotone Lipschitz efficiency objectives, with no distributional or {\it convexity} assumptions. In the stochastic setting with full-score feedback, we propose a sliding-window quantile tracker and establish a matching minimax lower bound showing our algorithm is rate-optimal. In the covariate-dependent stochastic setting, we develop a partitioned ACI algorithm that tracks a function-valued oracle threshold, and derive simultaneous coverage and efficiency guarantees.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unified online learning framework for adaptive conformal inference that overcomes three key limitations of existing ACI methods: (1) signed-error guarantees that allow cancellation of miscoverage, (2) lack of prediction-set size guarantees, and (3) benchmarks that become stale under distribution shift. It provides simultaneous absolute coverage and efficiency guarantees against dynamically evolving benchmarks in fully adversarial, stochastic, and covariate-dependent stochastic settings.
AI.motivation: Standard ACI (Gibbs & Candès) and its variants suffer from three critical shortcomings: signed long-run coverage error can mask persistent directional miscoverage through cancellation; no guarantees exist on prediction-set size, enabling trivial validity via overly wide sets; and efficiency comparisons against fixed hindsight benchmarks lose meaning when the optimal threshold itself changes under distribution shift. The paper aims to address all three simultaneously.
AI.method: The authors frame the problem in a unified online learning framework. In the fully adversarial setting, they leverage the fact that standard ACI updates correspond exactly to projected online gradient descent on the pinball loss, deriving simultaneous coverage and efficiency guarantees for arbitrary monotone Lipschitz efficiency objectives without distributional or convexity assumptions. For the stochastic setting with full-score feedback, they propose a sliding-window quantile tracker with a matching minimax lower bound. For covariate-dependent stochastic settings, they develop a partitioned ACI algorithm that tracks a function-valued oracle threshold.
AI.result: The paper establishes: (1) simultaneous absolute coverage and efficiency guarantees in the fully adversarial setting for arbitrary monotone Lipschitz objectives; (2) a sliding-window quantile tracker that achieves rate-optimal performance in the stochastic setting, confirmed by a matching minimax lower bound; and (3) simultaneous coverage and efficiency guarantees for the partitioned ACI algorithm in the covariate-dependent stochastic setting.
AI.conclusion: The unified framework successfully addresses the three fundamental limitations of existing ACI methods — non-cancelling coverage violations, prediction-set efficiency, and dynamic benchmarks — across three important model settings, providing rigorous theoretical guarantees throughout.

title: Enhancing Generative Information Extraction with Two-step Validation: A Product Attribute Use Case
summary: The ability of large language models (LLMs) to process and generate text has introduced potential for applications in information extraction (IE). While it's debated whether LLMs outperform smaller fine-tuned models for classification tasks, their strong generalization capability makes them promising for domains with limited labeled data available for fine-tuning. This advantage is particularly relevant for the emerging application of the digital product passport (DPP), where the problem space is broad but domain-specific data remains scarce. Motivated by this use case, we apply generative IE to the product domain, explicitly addressing efficiency, generalizability, and data privacy constraints. We propose a two-step validation method that integrates a PLM block into the generative IE pipeline and thereby leverages LLMs' correction capability. We discover that such a validation task enhances LLM performance, particularly on the extraction of weakly expressed, low-salience entities that appear sparsely throughout the text. For certain entities, the performance of mid-size models can even reach levels comparable to larger models, and the improvement of first-step PLM predictions also enhance the final LLM output. Nevertheless, the effects on the smallest open-source LLMs (e.g., Llama-3.2 3B) is limited. Based on the findings, we develop a demo application for product information extraction that utilizes locally deployed LLMs, targeting further adaptations to real-world DPP use cases.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a two-step validation method for generative information extraction in the product domain, integrating a Pre-trained Language Model (PLM) block into the LLM pipeline to leverage correction capabilities. It targets digital product passport (DPP) applications where labeled data is scarce, addressing efficiency, generalizability, and data privacy through locally deployed models.
AI.motivation: The emerging digital product passport (DPP) domain presents a broad problem space with limited domain-specific labeled data, making it unsuitable for traditional fine-tuning. LLMs' strong generalization offers promise, but challenges around efficiency, generalizability, and data privacy remain unsolved for practical IE deployment in this context.
AI.method: A two-step validation generative IE pipeline: a PLM first extracts entities, then an LLM validates and corrects the PLM's predictions. This exploits the LLM's correction/refinement capability rather than using it for direct extraction. Locally deployed open-source LLMs (e.g., Llama-3.2 3B and mid-size variants) are used to preserve data privacy.
AI.result: The validation task enhances LLM performance, especially on weakly expressed, low-salience, sparse entities. Mid-size models can approach larger model performance on certain entities. PLM prediction improvements cascade to better final LLM output. However, the smallest LLMs (e.g., Llama-3.2 3B) show limited benefit.
AI.conclusion: A PLM+LLM validation pipeline effectively boosts generative IE in low-resource product domains, with mid-size locally deployed LLMs offering a practical balance of performance and privacy. A demo application was developed targeting real-world DPP use cases.

title: Benchmarking ConvLSTM for One-Day-Ahead IMDAA Rainfall-Field Prediction across Four Indian Cities
summary:
Convolutional long short-term memory networks (ConvLSTMs) are widely used for precipitation forecasting, but most evidence for their performance comes from dense, high-frequency radar sequences. This study tests whether convolutional recurrence improves one-day-ahead rainfall-field prediction on small daily reanalysis grids. Indian Monsoon Data Assimilation and Analysis (IMDAA) fields for June-September 1998-2020 were analysed for Bengaluru, Delhi, Kolkata and Mumbai. Ten naive, statistical, tree-based and neural approaches were compared using atmospheric-only and rainfall-history-plus-atmospheric inputs. Performance was assessed for complete fields, domain-mean rainfall, spatial anomalies and high-rainfall days.
  ConvLSTM did not consistently outperform simpler alternatives. FC-LSTM produced the numerically lowest domain-mean rainfall error in Bengaluru, Kolkata and Mumbai, whereas persistence performed best in Delhi. ConvLSTM produced the numerically lowest spatial-anomaly error only in Mumbai, where rainfall fields showed greater short-term spatial continuity and rainfall-history inputs improved all three neural architectures. The difference between ConvLSTM and FC-LSTM was nevertheless small. Neural models underestimated rainfall magnitude and predicted too few threshold exceedances on high-rainfall days, while persistence achieved the highest detection performance in every city. Post-hoc analyses showed that the selected models were most sensitive to the latest input day, with broader recent-lag sensitivity in Mumbai. These findings show that gridded inputs alone do not justify ConvLSTM and that architecture choice should follow strong benchmarking across average, spatial and high-rainfall performance.

AI.tldr: ConvLSTM does not consistently outperform simpler models for daily rainfall-field prediction on reanalysis grids; FC-LSTM and even persistence often perform better, and architecture choice should be guided by rigorous benchmarking across multiple performance dimensions.
AI.motivation: ConvLSTMs are widely adopted for precipitation forecasting based on evidence from dense, high-frequency radar data. The authors question whether the convolutional recurrence mechanism provides genuine benefit when applied to coarser daily reanalysis grids, where spatial patterns and temporal dynamics differ substantially from radar sequences.
AI.method: Using IMDAA reanalysis fields (June–September, 1998–2020) for four Indian cities (Bengaluru, Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai), the study compared ten approaches spanning naive baselines, statistical methods, tree-based models, and neural architectures (including FC-LSTM and ConvLSTM). Models were tested with two input configurations: atmospheric-only variables and rainfall-history plus atmospheric variables. Evaluation covered domain-mean rainfall error, spatial anomaly error, and high-rainfall-day detection performance.
AI.result: FC-LSTM achieved the lowest domain-mean rainfall error in three of four cities; persistence was best in Delhi. ConvLSTM only outperformed on spatial-anomaly error in Mumbai, where rainfall exhibits greater short-term spatial continuity and where historical rainfall inputs benefited all neural models. Even then, the ConvLSTM–FC-LSTM difference was small. Neural models systematically underestimated rainfall magnitude and missed threshold exceedances on high-rainfall days, while persistence achieved the best detection performance universally. Sensitivity analysis revealed models relied primarily on the most recent day, with broader temporal sensitivity only in Mumbai.
AI.conclusion: Gridded input data alone do not warrant ConvLSTM adoption. Researchers should conduct strong benchmarking across mean, spatial, and extreme-event performance before selecting an architecture, as simpler alternatives frequently match or exceed ConvLSTM on daily reanalysis-based rainfall forecasting tasks.

title: When Does Span-Guided Detoxification Help? Human Preferences and Evaluator Diagnostics in a Controlled Comparison
summary:
Span-guided rewriting aims to preserve meaning by localizing edits to annotated harmful spans, but the same constraint can leave harmful intent insufficiently mitigated. We present a controlled exploratory comparison of span-guided and unguided detoxification on a mixed-source English evaluation set comprising manually curated inputs and HateXplain test items. We conduct a dense blinded human evaluation under a fixed single-generator setting.
  Human preferences reveal a trade-off rather than a uniformly superior rewriting strategy. Span-guided outputs are favored when localized editing preserves the original stance and avoids unnecessary modification, whereas unguided outputs are favored when broader rewriting achieves more complete mitigation. This contrast varies substantially across the study-defined strata: the two strategies are competitive in the strong stratum, while unguided rewriting is clearly preferred in the mild stratum. Rationale annotations trace this difference to complementary failure risks: residual harm after localized editing and over-modification after broader rewriting.
  We treat automatic evaluation as a diagnostic rather than a substitute for human judgment. Toxicity-similarity scalarizations, a multi-generator analysis, and two general-purpose LLM judges reproduce parts of the aggregate tendency but do not yield an analogous stratified contrast. These setting-specific findings do not establish a severity-based routing rule.
