Instead, they motivate evaluation protocols that assess mitigation sufficiency and meaning preservation separately and report both residual harm and over-modification alongside aggregate scores.

AI.tldr: A controlled comparison of span-guided vs. unguided detoxification rewriting reveals a trade-off: span-guided excels at localized editing with meaning preservation but risks residual harm, while unguided achieves more complete mitigation but risks over-modification. The preference varies by severity stratum, and automatic metrics fail to capture this stratified contrast.
AI.motivation: Span-guided detoxification, which constrains edits to annotated harmful spans, may insufficiently mitigate harmful intent. The authors aim to systematically compare span-guided and unguided rewriting strategies to understand when each approach succeeds or fails, and to evaluate whether automatic metrics adequately reflect human preferences.
AI.method: A controlled exploratory comparison using a mixed-source English evaluation set (manually curated inputs + HateXplain). Dense blinded human evaluation under a fixed single-generator setting, with annotations stratified by harm severity (strong vs. mild). Rationale annotations trace failure modes. Automatic evaluation includes toxicity-similarity scalarizations, multi-generator analysis, and two general-purpose LLM judges for diagnostic comparison.
AI.result: Human preferences show a trade-off rather than uniform superiority: span-guided preferred when localized editing preserves stance; unguided preferred for more complete mitigation. The two strategies are competitive in the strong stratum, but unguided is clearly preferred in the mild stratum. Complementary failure risks identified: residual harm (span-guided) vs. over-modification (unguided). Automatic metrics reproduce only aggregate tendencies and fail to capture the stratified contrast.
AI.conclusion: Findings do not support a simple severity-based routing rule. Instead, the authors advocate for evaluation protocols that separately assess mitigation sufficiency and meaning preservation, and report both residual harm and over-modification alongside aggregate scores, rather than relying solely on scalarized automatic metrics.

title: Uncertainty-Guided LLM Semantic Augmentation for Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Estimation
summary: Estimating heterogeneous treatment effects is central to targeted interventions, such as personalized promotions and precision medicine. We focus on the conditional average treatment effect (CATE), a standard estimand for characterizing such heterogeneity. Even under standard identification conditions, finite-sample CATE estimation requires learning the nuisance structure for covariate adjustment and treatment-effect heterogeneity, often together with an effective representation of X. Raw numerical and categorical encodings can leave semantic relations and higher-order interactions implicit, making this joint task locally unstable. A motivating study further shows that this instability appears through partially separable assignment- and heterogeneity-side channels. Building on this observation, we propose CURL (Causal Uncertainty-guided Representation Learning), a plug-in adapter that uses estimator uncertainty to allocate pretrained semantic capacity to locally unstable units. CURL queries a frozen LLM through two role-conditioned prompts, constructs assignment- and heterogeneity-oriented representations from the observed covariates, and routes them through separated pathways. On four benchmarks, CURL improves ten host learners in most settings, while ablation, refinement-dynamics, route-reassignment, and probe analyses support the intended design and roles of the two channels.

AI.tldr: CURL is a plug-in adapter that leverages a frozen LLM and estimator uncertainty to construct dual role-conditioned representations (assignment-oriented and heterogeneity-oriented) for improved finite-sample CATE estimation, outperforming ten host learners across four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Finite-sample CATE estimation is locally unstable due to the joint learning of nuisance structures and treatment-effect heterogeneity from raw covariates. The authors identify that this instability manifests through partially separable assignment-side and heterogeneity-side channels, motivating a representation learning approach that allocates semantic capacity differentially to locally unstable units.
AI.method: The proposed method, CURL (Causal Uncertainty-guided Representation Learning), is a plug-in adapter that: (1) queries a frozen LLM using two role-conditioned prompts to construct assignment-oriented and heterogeneity-oriented representations from observed covariates; (2) uses estimator uncertainty to guide allocation of pretrained semantic capacity to locally unstable units; and (3) routes the two representations through separated pathways corresponding to the assignment and heterogeneity channels.
AI.result: CURL improves ten different host learners across most settings on four benchmarks. Ablation studies, refinement-dynamics analysis, route-reassignment experiments, and probe analyses all support the intended design and the distinct functional roles of the two representation channels.
AI.conclusion: The dual-channel, uncertainty-guided LLM-based representation strategy effectively addresses local instability in CATE estimation, offering a model-agnostic plug-in that enhances diverse host learners without fine-tuning the LLM.

title: From Found to Designed: Concepts as a Design Axis for Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) encode rich concept-like information, but represent it implicitly through distributed statistical associations rather than as explicit, structured, compositional concepts. Consequently, concept-level structure is typically \emph{found} rather than \emph{designed}: it is recovered after training through probing or dictionary learning, with no architectural guarantee of stability, compositionality, controllability, or alignment with human conceptual organization. We argue that concepts should instead be treated as a design axis for LLMs, and map the design space along two dimensions: the pipeline stage at which concept structure is introduced (training objective, core architecture, inference, or post-hoc interpretation), and whether that structure is internally derived from the model's own representations or grounded in external resources. This taxonomy reveals three broad patterns: inference-time approaches remain comparatively underexplored, related ideas have developed largely in isolation across pipeline stages, and externally grounded methods span the entire pipeline despite often being described under different terminology. Together, these observations motivate moving beyond recovering concept-like structure from trained models toward designing LLMs with explicit conceptual representations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a taxonomy for integrating explicit conceptual structure into LLMs along two axes: pipeline stage (training, architecture, inference, post-hoc) and origin of structure (internal vs. external). It identifies underexplored inference-time methods, siloed research across stages, and the ubiquity of externally grounded approaches, arguing for a shift from post-hoc concept recovery to concept-centric LLM design.
AI.motivation: Current LLMs encode concepts only implicitly through distributed statistical associations. Concept-level structure is typically recovered post-training (e.g., via probing or dictionary learning) rather than being deliberately designed into the model. This yields no architectural guarantees of stability, compositionality, controllability, or alignment with human conceptual systems. The authors argue concepts should be a first-class design axis rather than an emergent artifact.
AI.method: The authors map the design space of concept-structured LLMs along two orthogonal dimensions: (1) the pipeline stage where concept structure is introduced — training objective, core architecture, inference-time, or post-hoc interpretation; and (2) whether the conceptual structure is internally derived from the model's own representations or externally grounded in resources like knowledge bases, ontologies, or human annotations. This yields a taxonomy that organizes existing and prospective approaches.
AI.result: The taxonomy reveals three key patterns: (1) inference-time concept methods are significantly underexplored relative to other stages; (2) conceptually related ideas have developed in isolation across different pipeline stages, lacking cross-pollination; and (3) externally grounded methods span the entire pipeline but are often described under disparate terminology, obscuring their shared conceptual foundations.
AI.conclusion: The field should move beyond merely recovering concept-like structure from trained models and toward deliberately designing LLMs with explicit, structured, compositional conceptual representations. This design-oriented perspective promises improved stability, controllability, compositionality, and alignment with human conceptual organization.

title: FedWeave: Rethinking the Unit of Specialization in Heterogeneous Federated MoE-LoRA
summary: Federated PEFT enables LLMs to collaboratively adapt to decentralized private data without sharing raw examples. However, task heterogeneity across clients can cause cross-task interference and gradient conflicts during aggregation. Federated MoE-LoRA addresses this challenge through specialized LoRA experts and conditional routing. Yet existing methods typically specialize at client granularity, implicitly assuming task-coherent clients. Our core insight is that experts need purity, namely pattern-coherent updates that preserve specialization, whereas routers need contrast, namely mixed-task observations that support expert comparison. We propose FedWeave, a framework that adopts asymmetric aggregation, separating expert aggregation from router optimization to meet these two requirements. FedWeave uses unsupervised prototype discovery to form local buckets and align them across clients, enabling prototype-level expert aggregation while retaining mixed-task client trajectories for router training. At inference, FedWeave performs sparse inference with one active expert while preserving nearly all soft-routing performance. Our theoretical analysis explains why asymmetric aggregation is advantageous: it controls expert convergence in stationarity through off-pattern contamination, identifies the consensus error induced by fragmented router trajectories, and bounds sparse-inference risk. On a heterogeneous multi-task benchmark with mainstream LLM backbones, FedWeave consistently outperforms strong baselines, while ablations verify the effectiveness of our design.

AI.tldr: FedWeave proposes asymmetric aggregation for Federated MoE-LoRA, separating expert aggregation (via prototype-level purity) from router optimization (via mixed-task contrast), outperforming baselines on heterogeneous multi-task LLM benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Federated PEFT enables decentralized LLM adaptation but suffers from cross-task interference due to client heterogeneity. Existing Federated MoE-LoRA methods specialize at client granularity, implicitly assuming task-coherent clients — an assumption violated under real-world task heterogeneity. The authors identify a fundamental tension: experts require purity (pattern-coherent updates) while routers require contrast (mixed-task observations).
AI.method: FedWeave employs asymmetric aggregation with two mechanisms: (1) Unsupervised prototype discovery forms local buckets and aligns them across clients, enabling prototype-level expert aggregation that preserves expert specialization purity. (2) Mixed-task client trajectories are retained for router training, providing the contrast needed for effective expert comparison. At inference, sparse inference activates only one expert while preserving near-equivalent soft-routing performance. A theoretical analysis bounds expert convergence under off-pattern contamination, consensus error from fragmented router trajectories, and sparse-inference risk.
AI.result: FedWeave consistently outperforms strong baselines on a heterogeneous multi-task benchmark using mainstream LLM backbones. Ablation studies verify the effectiveness of the asymmetric aggregation design, prototype-level expert grouping, and sparse inference strategy.
AI.conclusion: Asymmetric aggregation — decoupling expert and router optimization — is key to handling task heterogeneity in Federated MoE-LoRA. FedWeave demonstrates that prototype-level purity for experts and trajectory-level contrast for routers jointly enable robust federated multi-task adaptation with negligible performance degradation under sparse inference.

title: Language Models are not Equally Robust to Non-Canonical Tokenization across Languages
summary: Despite the existence of exponentially many valid tokenizations for a given string, language models operate on a single canonical sequence deterministically produced by the tokenizer, leaving the broader tokenization space largely uncharacterized. In this paper, we investigate this overlooked space by studying the behavior of language models under non-canonical tokenizations across diverse languages. For English, prior work shows that models are largely invariant to alternative tokenizations that represent the same underlying string. We ask whether this invariance generalizes to other languages beyond English. We conduct a multilingual study across 27 languages spanning diverse scripts and evaluate LLM behavior under alternative tokenizations across six downstream tasks. We find that tokenization invariance does not generalize: model behavior varies substantially across languages with instruction-tuned models exhibiting an average relative performance drop of 23.7% for Llama-3.1-8B, 11.4% for Qwen3-8B, and 9.9% for Gemma-3-12B. The variation of tokenization invariance is systematic across languages. Languages that exhibit higher token fragmentation show significantly greater sensitivity to non-canonical tokenizations. Our study of tokenization robustness serves as a diagnostic of how tightly a model is coupled to its tokenizer. These results demonstrate that tokenization robustness is not a universal property of language models, but depends strongly on the language and its interaction with the tokenizer. We also show that LoRA fine-tuning with multi-tokenization training data provides an effective mitigation for tokenization sensitivity. Fine-tuning on English alone improves tokenization robustness across languages, while systematically sampling diverse non-canonical tokenizations achieves the strongest overall performance.

AI.tldr: Language models are not universally robust to non-canonical tokenizations; sensitivity varies systematically across 27 languages, with higher token fragmentation predicting greater performance degradation. Multi-tokenization training mitigates this issue.
AI.motivation: Prior work on English showed LLMs are invariant to alternative tokenizations of the same string. This paper questions whether that invariance holds across diverse languages, given that tokenizers are predominantly optimized for English.
AI.method: Multilingual evaluation across 27 languages with diverse scripts, testing three instruction-tuned LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, Gemma-3-12B) on six downstream tasks under canonical vs. non-canonical tokenizations. Also tested LoRA fine-tuning with multi-tokenization training data as a mitigation strategy.
AI.result: Tokenization invariance fails to generalize: average performance drops of 23.7% (Llama-3.1-8B), 11.4% (Qwen3-8B), and 9.9% (Gemma-3-12B). Sensitivity correlates with token fragmentation — languages with higher fragmentation show greater sensitivity. LoRA fine-tuning with multi-tokenization data mitigates sensitivity, and English-only fine-tuning provides cross-lingual robustness benefits.
AI.conclusion: Tokenization robustness is not a universal property of LLMs but depends on language–tokenizer interaction. Multi-tokenization training, even in English only, offers effective mitigation.

title: Enhancing Automated Machine Learning via Homogeneous Train-Test Splitting Methods
comment: Pre-review version of a paper accepted at UKCI 2026
summary: Accurate model evaluation in machine learning depends critically on how datasets are split into training and testing subsets. Standard random splitting assumes that both partitions share the same underlying distribution, an assumption often violated in datasets with class imbalance, natural clustering, or spatial autocorrelation. This paper investigates the role of statistical similarity in train-test splitting and its consequences for AutoML model evaluation. Five established strategies are compared across fifteen UCI benchmark datasets: random splitting, stratified sampling, Kennard-Stone, Duplex, and SPXY. Similarity is assessed using chi-square, Kolmogorov-Smirnov, and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) tests. Geometry-based methods consistently produce near-zero MMD scores, introducing instability into downstream performance estimates. The proposed Optimised-Distribution method treats similarity as an explicit optimisation objective and achieves the highest mean MMD similarity, 89.0%, across all strategies evaluated.

AI.tldr: This paper compares five train-test splitting strategies across 15 UCI datasets, demonstrating that geometry-based methods (Kennard-Stone, Duplex, SPXY) yield near-zero MMD scores but introduce performance instability, while a novel Optimised-Distribution method explicitly optimizes statistical similarity, achieving 89.0% mean MMD similarity — the highest across all strategies.
AI.motivation: Standard random train-test splitting assumes identical underlying distributions between partitions, an assumption frequently violated in datasets exhibiting class imbalance, natural clustering, or spatial autocorrelation. This motivates a systematic investigation into how statistical (dis)similarity between splits affects AutoML model evaluation reliability.
AI.method: Five splitting strategies — random splitting, stratified sampling, Kennard-Stone, Duplex, and SPXY — are evaluated across 15 UCI benchmark datasets. Statistical similarity between train and test partitions is quantified using chi-square, Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS), and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) tests. A new Optimised-Distribution method is proposed that treats split similarity as an explicit optimization objective.
AI.result: Geometry-based methods (Kennard-Stone, Duplex, SPXY) consistently achieve near-zero MMD scores but paradoxically introduce instability into downstream performance estimates. The proposed Optimised-Distribution method attains the highest mean MMD similarity of 89.0% across all evaluated strategies.
AI.conclusion: Statistical similarity between train-test splits matters for robust AutoML model evaluation. Explicitly optimizing for distributional similarity, as done by the Optimised-Distribution method, yields more stable and reliable performance estimates than either random or geometry-based splitting approaches.

title: From Representations to Behaviors: Exploring the Person-Situation-Behavior Triad in LLMs
summary: Human personality theories characterize traits not as isolated attributes captured by a single score, but as stable individual tendencies expressed through the interplay among persons, situations, and behaviors. Existing studies of personality-related behavior in LLMs have primarily focused on outputs elicited under personality conditioning, characterizing observable trait-related expressions while lacking mechanistic evidence for the existence of internal personality-related representations, their cross-situational expression, and how these representations shape specific behaviors. Building on Funder's personality triad framework, we adapt its three components for LLM analysis: Person as personality-related internal representations, Situation as contexts that afford trait-relevant responses, and Behavior as response patterns on broader social tasks. We introduce a framework for discovering, controlling, and validating trait-like representations in LLMs. First, using contrastive behavior pairs grounded in shared situations, we identify sparse internal features associated with opposing poles of personality traits through SAE decomposition. We validate their trait relevance through effects on behavior to situation, token-level activation patterns, and robustness to paraphrasing. Second, feature-level interventions induce bidirectional trait-related shifts across a separate, diverse set of situations while preserving response validity, demonstrating consistent expression across contexts. Third, applying the same interventions to social intelligence tasks reveals behavioral changes with benefit-tradeoff patterns consistent with findings from human personality research, providing behavioral-level validation beyond personality scores. Our findings provide evidence that LLMs contain controllable trait-like representations linking internal states, situational expression, and behavioral outcomes.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework grounded in Funder's personality triad (Person, Situation, Behavior) to discover, control, and validate trait-like internal representations in LLMs using sparse autoencoder decomposition, demonstrating that these representations causally influence behavior across contexts in patterns consistent with human personality research.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM personality research focuses on observable trait-related outputs under personality conditioning but lacks mechanistic evidence for internal personality-related representations, their cross-situational consistency, and causal links to behavior. The authors aim to bridge this gap by providing direct evidence of internal trait-like representations in LLMs.
AI.method: The authors adapt Funder's personality triad (Person, Situation, Behavior) for LLMs. They use contrastive behavior pairs in shared situations to identify sparse internal features associated with opposing trait poles via Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) decomposition. Trait relevance is validated through behavioral effects, token-level activation patterns, and paraphrase robustness. Feature-level interventions then induce bidirectional trait shifts across diverse situations, and these same interventions are applied to social intelligence tasks to observe behavioral changes.
AI.result: SAE-identified features show trait relevance through consistent effects on situation-appropriate behavior, token-level activation patterns, and robustness to paraphrasing. Feature-level interventions produce bidirectional trait-related shifts across diverse situations while preserving response validity. Applying the same interventions to social intelligence tasks reveals benefit-tradeoff patterns consistent with human personality research, providing behavioral-level validation.
AI.conclusion: LLMs contain controllable, trait-like representations that causally link internal states, situational expression, and behavioral outcomes. The framework provides mechanistic evidence for personality-related representations and offers a foundation for understanding and controlling personality expression in LLMs.

title: Understanding Context Sampling in TabPFN on Small Tabular Datasets
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures. Code and experiment logs available at https://github.com/mohammed1916/tabmx
summary:
TabPFN performs classification through in-context learning: it conditions on a set of labeled training rows (the context, or prototypes) and predicts test labels without gradient updates. On small tabular datasets, practitioners must still choose the context size and which rows constitute the context. We study how these choices affect prediction stability, accuracy, and selection cost using repeated context sampling on 15 OpenML datasets. Specifically, we investigate (i) whether larger contexts reduce prediction variability across random draws, (ii) whether accuracy depends on preserving the training distribution or on feature-space coverage, and (iii) whether expensive selection methods such as K-Means and farthest-point sampling provide benefits over uniform random sampling.
  We find that larger contexts are both more accurate and substantially more stable, with AUC coefficient of variation decreasing from roughly 6 to 18% at k=16 to 1 to 4% at larger context sizes on datasets with room for improvement. Although accuracy correlates with distribution representativeness in random contexts, controlled experiments show that matching feature means alone can reduce accuracy by up to 0.5 AUC because it reduces context diversity. Mixed-effects analysis identifies diversity and coverage, rather than feature-mean matching, as the stronger predictor of accuracy (diversity beta=+0.23, p=3x10^-12; feature-mean shift beta=-0.01, p=0.71). K-Means and farthest-point sampling achieve similar accuracy to random selection while requiring two to three orders of magnitude more selection cost. These results show that random sampling succeeds because it provides feature-space coverage in expectation, not because it reproduces the underlying data distribution.

AI.tldr: TabPFN's in-context classification performance improves with larger context sizes (better accuracy and stability), and crucially, success depends on feature-space coverage and diversity rather than distribution representativeness. Expensive selection methods like K-Means offer no accuracy benefit over simple random sampling.
AI.motivation: When applying TabPFN to small tabular datasets, practitioners must decide context size and which rows to include as context. The paper aims to understand how these choices affect prediction stability, accuracy, and selection cost — specifically whether larger contexts reduce variability, whether accuracy stems from distribution matching or feature-space coverage, and whether costly selection methods outperform random sampling.
AI.method: Repeated context sampling experiments across 15 OpenML datasets. The authors (i) vary context size (k from 16 upward) to measure accuracy and stability (AUC coefficient of variation), (ii) conduct controlled experiments manipulating distribution representativeness vs. diversity, and (iii) compare uniform random sampling against K-Means and farthest-point sampling using mixed-effects analysis with diversity, coverage, and feature-mean shift as predictors.
AI.result: Larger contexts yield higher accuracy and markedly lower variability (CV drops from 6–18% at k=16 to 1–4% at larger k). Distribution representativeness correlates with accuracy in random contexts, but controlled experiments reveal that enforcing feature-mean matching alone can reduce accuracy by up to 0.5 AUC due to lost diversity. Mixed-effects analysis identifies diversity (β=+0.23, p=3×10⁻¹²) and coverage as stronger predictors than feature-mean shift (β=−0.01, p=0.71). K-Means and farthest-point sampling match random sampling accuracy at 100–1000× higher selection cost.
AI.conclusion: Random sampling is effective for TabPFN context selection because it provides feature-space coverage in expectation — not because it reproduces the training distribution. Practitioners can confidently use larger random contexts without resorting to expensive prototype selection methods.

title: SERPO: Self-Evolving Rubric Policy Optimization for Open-Ended Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
summary: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) enables language models to self-evolve at inference time without labeled feedback. Existing methods rely on answer voting and therefore do not extend naturally to open-ended generation, where valid responses cannot be mapped to a shared canonical answer. Without external reward models or stronger judges, adaptation must instead construct reliable rewards from the model's own outputs. We introduce SERPO (Self-Evolving Rubric Policy Optimization), which replaces answer voting with a closed loop that co-evolves response evidence, query-specific rubrics, and policy parameters. Good-Normal-Bad (G-N-B) response evolution organizes maximally separated rollouts into ordered archives; rubric evolution retains criteria that discriminate these archives; probabilistic criterion scoring converts verdict-token likelihoods into reward signals; and policy evolution optimizes the actor with the resulting signals. New actor rollouts then refresh both the archives and rubrics, closing the three-way evolution loop. Across two model configurations, two in-domain benchmarks, and four OOD benchmarks, SERPO improves HealthBench and ResearchQA by up to 20.63 and 20.31 points over the corresponding base models, raises the six-benchmark macro-average by up to 8.06 points, and supports OOD transfer and continued cross-benchmark evolution.

AI.tldr: SERPO introduces a test-time reinforcement learning framework that co-evolves response evidence, query-specific rubrics, and policy parameters in a closed loop, enabling open-ended self-improvement without labeled feedback or answer voting. It achieves significant gains on HealthBench, ResearchQA, and multiple OOD benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) methods depend on answer voting, which fails for open-ended generation tasks where responses lack a shared canonical answer. Without external reward models or stronger judges, there is a need for a method that constructs reliable rewards purely from the model's own outputs.
AI.method: SERPO employs a three-way closed-loop co-evolution: (1) Good-Normal-Bad (G-N-B) response evolution organizes maximally separated rollouts into ordered archives; (2) Rubric evolution retains criteria that discriminate between these archives; (3) Probabilistic criterion scoring converts verdict-token likelihoods into reward signals; (4) Policy evolution optimizes the actor using these signals. New rollouts refresh both archives and rubrics, sustaining the loop.
AI.result: Across two model configurations, two in-domain benchmarks, and four OOD benchmarks, SERPO improves HealthBench and ResearchQA by up to 20.63 and 20.31 points over base models, raises the six-benchmark macro-average by up to 8.06 points, and demonstrates OOD transfer and continued cross-benchmark evolution.
AI.conclusion: SERPO provides a viable, self-contained mechanism for test-time self-improvement in open-ended generation, overcoming the limitations of answer-voting-based TTRL by bootstrapping reward signals through rubric co-evolution, with strong empirical gains and promising transfer properties.

title: DIRECT: Direct Decoding for Efficient and Aligned Sequence Labeling with Large Language Models
summary: Sequence labeling is a fine-grained information extraction task, yet existing large language model-based approaches suffer from insufficient domain alignment and low inference efficiency. To address these issues, we propose DIRECT, a framework that addresses these issues through training-time optimization and inference-time rectification. Specifically, DIRECT performs Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) after supervised fine-tuning to strengthen task alignment with human preferences, and introduces a controlled decoding process that enforces fixed output formats and restricts predictions to candidate sets. To further improve efficiency, a template-filling mechanism requires the model to generate only label tokens while reusing prefixed content through the KV Cache, thus reducing redundant computation. Experimental results on eight datasets demonstrate that DIRECT achieves significant improvements in both performance and efficiency compared to existing methods.

AI.tldr: DIRECT is a framework for sequence labeling that combines Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) with a controlled decoding strategy and KV-cache-based template filling to improve domain alignment and inference efficiency over existing LLM-based approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based sequence labeling methods suffer from two key problems: (1) insufficient domain alignment, where models are not well-calibrated to task-specific human preferences, and (2) low inference efficiency due to redundant computation in autoregressive generation.
AI.method: DIRECT employs a two-stage optimization pipeline: (1) Training-time optimization — first performing supervised fine-tuning (SFT), followed by Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to align the model with human-preferred outputs; (2) Inference-time rectification — a controlled decoding process that enforces fixed output formats and restricts predictions to valid candidate label sets, plus a template-filling mechanism that reuses prefixed content via KV Cache so the model only generates label tokens, eliminating redundant forward-pass computation.
AI.result: Experimental results across eight datasets show that DIRECT achieves significant improvements in both task performance and inference efficiency compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: DIRECT effectively addresses the dual challenges of domain misalignment and inference inefficiency in LLM-based sequence labeling, validated by consistent gains across multiple benchmarks.

title: AIGen: Automating AI Bill of Materials Generation Through Hybrid MLOps Integration
summary: The responsible development and deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) systems requires rigorous documentation of their constituent artifacts, e.g., datasets, model weights, training pipelines, and runtime dependencies. Although the Software Package Data Exchange (SPDX) 3.0 standard introduced native support for AI and dataset profiles, practical tooling capable of generating standards-compliant AI Bills of Materials (AIBoMs) in an automated and extensible manner remains scarce. This paper presents AIGen, a modular AIBoM generator that produces machine-readable, interoperable inventories of AI system components that comply with the SPDX 3.0 AI profile. AIGen works on top of the MLflow MLOps framework and combines mining heuristics with Large Language Models to generate AIBoMs. A plugin interface allows practitioners to extend the tool with domain-specific collectors without modifying the core codebase, supporting heterogeneous AI frameworks such as Hugging Face, PyTorch, and TensorFlow. AIGen is designed to facilitate compliance with the European Union AI Act, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and ISO/IEC 42001, providing a concrete, reusable foundation for transparent, accountable AI supply chain governance. Tool URL: https://github.com/danielebifolco/AIGen Tool Video: https://youtu.be/\_nAbXDWfVL4

AI.tldr: AIGen is a modular, SPDX 3.0-compliant AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM) generator built on MLflow, combining mining heuristics and LLMs to automate documentation of AI artifacts for regulatory compliance.
AI.motivation: Despite SPDX 3.0 introducing native AI/dataset profiles, practical automated tooling for generating standards-compliant AI Bills of Materials (AIBOMs) is lacking, which hinders responsible AI development and regulatory compliance.
AI.method: AIGen operates atop the MLflow MLOps framework, employing mining heuristics combined with Large Language Models to automatically generate machine-readable, interoperable AIBoMs. It features a plugin architecture that allows domain-specific collectors to be added without core modification, supporting Hugging Face, PyTorch, and TensorFlow.
AI.result: The tool produces SPDX 3.0 AI profile-compliant inventories of AI system components (datasets, model weights, training pipelines, runtime dependencies), enabling compliance with the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, and ISO/IEC 42001.
AI.conclusion: AIGen provides a concrete, reusable, and extensible foundation for transparent and accountable AI supply chain governance, filling a critical gap in AI artifact documentation tooling.

title: Dual-Path LLM Reasoning for Multimodal Few-Shot Knowledge Graph Completion
summary: Knowledge graph completion (KGC) aims to infer missing facts in knowledge graphs (KGs), thereby improving their completeness and supporting downstream intelligent applications. However, emerging entities and relations in real-world deployments make inductive KGC difficult, especially under few-shot and zero-shot settings. Multimodal information and Large Language Model (LLM)-derived priors can enrich sparse relational contexts, but they may also introduce noisy or hallucinated evidence. To address these issues, we propose DuPLeR, a \textbf{Du}al-\textbf{P}ath \textbf{L}LM \textbf{R}easoning framework for multimodal few-shot KGC. DuPLeR builds a calibrated relation graph by combining multimodal LLM-derived type priors with factual support structures, and performs dual-level structural reasoning over the refined relation topology. Moreover, a dual-pathway multimodal enhancement module regulates message passing with query-relevant multimodal signals and supplements entity representations after graph propagation. Experiments on eight inductive variants of two multimodal KG (MMKG) benchmarks show that DuPLeR achieves robust performance in data-scarce KGC scenarios.

AI.tldr: DuPLeR is a dual-path LLM reasoning framework for multimodal few-shot knowledge graph completion. It constructs a calibrated relation graph using LLM-derived type priors and factual support, performs dual-level structural reasoning, and enhances entity representations via query-relevant multimodal signals, achieving robust performance on scarce-data KGC.
AI.motivation: Inductive KGC under few-shot and zero-shot settings is challenging due to emerging entities/relations with sparse contexts. While multimodal information and LLM priors can enrich these contexts, they risk introducing noise and hallucinations. A framework is needed that leverages these priors while mitigating their unreliability.
AI.method: DuPLeR features: (1) a calibrated relation graph that fuses LLM-derived type priors with factual support structures; (2) dual-level structural reasoning over the refined relation topology; and (3) a dual-pathway multimodal enhancement module that regulates message passing with query-relevant multimodal signals and supplements entity representations post-propagation.
AI.result: Experiments on eight inductive variants of two multimodal KG benchmarks demonstrate that DuPLeR achieves robust performance in data-scarce KGC scenarios.
AI.conclusion: DuPLeR effectively addresses the challenge of few-shot inductive KGC by combining LLM priors and multimodal signals within a calibrated, dual-path reasoning framework, yielding robust performance even with limited data.

title: Efficient Heteroscedastic Bayesian Optimization for Risk-Aware AutoRL
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown remarkable success across a wide range of complex tasks. However, RL outcomes can be highly stochastic, and both expected performance and variability often depend on hyperparameter (HP) configurations. We propose efficient and risk-averse heteroscedastic Bayesian Optimization (ERAHBO), a Bayesian optimization method that models both the mean and variance of learning outcomes as functions of the HP configurations. ERAHBO aims to identify HP configurations that achieve high average return while reducing variability across training runs, and it improves the sample efficiency of the HP optimization via adaptive re-sampling rather than a fixed budget per HP. Empirical evaluations across diverse RL algorithms and environments demonstrate that ERAHBO generally outperforms both risk-neutral and risk-averse baselines, delivering improved sample efficiency for risk-averse returns.

AI.tldr: ERAHBO is a Bayesian optimization method that jointly models mean and variance of RL outcomes across hyperparameter configurations, using adaptive re-sampling to efficiently find HPs that yield high returns with low variability.
AI.motivation: RL training outcomes are highly stochastic, with both expected performance and variability depending on hyperparameter configurations. Existing HP optimization methods are either risk-neutral (ignoring variance) or risk-averse but sample-inefficient, lacking adaptive strategies to balance exploration and re-sampling under heteroscedastic noise.
AI.method: ERAHBO uses heteroscedastic Gaussian Process models to jointly fit the mean and log-variance of RL returns as functions of HP configurations. It employs adaptive re-sampling — dynamically allocating more evaluation runs to promising HPs — guided by a risk-averse acquisition function (e.g., Lower Confidence Bound) that penalizes uncertainty and variance. This improves sample efficiency compared to fixed-budget-per-HP approaches.
AI.result: Across diverse RL algorithms and environments, ERAHBO consistently outperforms both risk-neutral and risk-averse baselines, achieving better risk-averse returns with fewer total environment interactions.
AI.conclusion: Jointly modeling heteroscedastic noise and employing adaptive re-sampling within a risk-averse BO framework yields more sample-efficient and reliable hyperparameter optimization for stochastic RL tasks.

title: Latent-IM: Latent Interaction Management for Speech LLMs
summary: Classical spoken dialogue systems often separated dialogue management from response realization: a policy selected the next dialogue action, and a generation component expressed that action. As dialogue systems shift toward LLMs, this decomposition has largely disappeared into the model's hidden representations. We ask whether an LLM-internal analogue of state estimation and action control can be recovered for conversational moves such as acknowledging, checking, querying, explaining, and replying. We formulate move control as two coupled problems: selection, predicting the appropriate next move from the dialogue context, and realization, causally producing a chosen move at generation time. We introduce Latent-IM, an internal dialogue-management framework that provides a general interface for choosing and deploying conversational moves under different objectives. Here, we use this control to reproduce human move choices, improving average end-to-end move accuracy by 12.5 points over the unsteered backbone while performing comparably to fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Latent-IM, a framework that recovers interpretable dialogue management (move selection and realization) from within LLM hidden representations, improving conversational move accuracy by 12.5 points over unsteered baselines without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Classical dialogue systems explicitly separated dialogue management from response generation, but LLMs have collapsed this distinction into opaque hidden representations. The authors aim to recover an interpretable internal analogue of state estimation and action control for conversational moves (acknowledging, checking, querying, explaining, replying), enabling principled steering of LLM dialogue behavior.
AI.method: The authors formulate move control as two coupled problems: (1) **selection** — predicting the next conversational move from dialogue context, and (2) **realization** — causally producing the chosen move at generation time. They introduce **Latent-IM**, an internal dialogue-management framework that operates on LLM hidden representations, providing a general interface for choosing and deploying conversational moves under different objectives. The framework intervenes on internal model activations rather than fine-tuning.
AI.result: Latent-IM improves average end-to-end move accuracy by **12.5 points** over the unsteered backbone LLM, while performing comparably to full fine-tuning. This demonstrates that interpretable move-level control can be recovered from within LLM representations without modifying model weights.
AI.conclusion: LLMs retain internal structure that corresponds to classical dialogue management concepts like state estimation and action control. The Latent-IM framework successfully extracts and operationalizes this structure, enabling controllable, interpretable dialogue generation that matches fine-tuning performance while remaining model-agnostic and training-free at the weight level.

title: Universality and Approximation Rates of Graph Neural Networks with Random Features
summary: We investigate message-passing graph neural networks with random node features. Random node features are known to enhance the expressiveness of graph neural networks (GNNs) both theoretically and empirically. Here, we establish a novel universality result focusing on permutation-equivariant neural networks (PENNs), a class of GNNs built from feedforward neural network components that subsumes many prominent GNN architectures. We show that PENNs, combined with partially random node features, can approximate arbitrarily well in probability any measurable permutation-invariant or permutation-equivariant function on directed graphs of fixed size with multidimensional node and edge features. For $k$-times continuously differentiable functions, $k\geq 2$, we also derive upper bounds on the approximation rates, relating the complexity of the feedforward components of a PENN in terms of layer depth and number of nonzero weights to the desired approximation accuracy.

AI.tldr: PENNs with partially random node features are universal approximators for measurable permutation-invariant/equivariant functions on fixed-size directed graphs, with explicit approximation-rate bounds for smooth functions.
AI.motivation: While random node features are known to boost GNN expressiveness, a rigorous universality theory for permutation-equivariant neural networks (PENNs) with random features — including approximation rates — was lacking. The authors aim to fill this gap.
AI.method: The paper proves that PENNs (a broad class of GNNs built from feedforward components) augmented with partially random node features can approximate, in probability and arbitrarily well, any measurable permutation-invariant or permutation-equivariant function on directed graphs of fixed size with multidimensional node and edge features. For k-times continuously differentiable functions (k≥2), they derive upper bounds on approximation rates, linking PENN complexity (layer depth, number of nonzero weights) to target accuracy.
AI.result: A novel universality theorem is established: PENNs with random features can approximate any measurable invariant/equivariant function on fixed-size directed graphs to arbitrary precision in probability. Further, for C^k functions (k≥2), explicit approximation-rate bounds are obtained, quantifying the trade-off between network complexity and approximation error.
AI.conclusion: Partially random node features confer full universal approximation capability to PENNs on fixed-size directed graphs, and the derived convergence rates provide theoretical guidance for designing feedforward components to meet a desired accuracy.

title: Same Evidence, Different Target: Decoding How Diagnostic Evidence Bears on Causal Questions from Language-Model States
summary: The same diagnostic result can support or challenge one causal claim yet fail to address another when the claims concern different populations, outcomes, estimands, pathways, or identifying assumptions. When the evidence and target vary together, a correct answer may reflect favorable or adverse wording, lexical overlap, or a familiar diagnostic pattern rather than matching the evidence to the causal question. We introduce paired prompts that repeat the same diagnostic evidence verbatim while changing the causal target. Each prompt is labeled Favors, Challenges, Unresolved, or Wrong Target according to how the evidence bears on the causal question. A pair is recovered only when both prompts are classified correctly. Using linear readouts trained on a separate development set, we analyze the final-token hidden state from the penultimate transformer block of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. On the 49-pair primary benchmark spanning nine diagnostic families, balanced accuracy ranges from 0.654 to 0.659 and 18-21 pairs are recovered. Two independent human reviewers assigned the same label to 95 of the 98 prompts (96.9%). Across checkpoints, balanced accuracy and complete-pair recovery exceed permutation nulls that preserve development scenario groups. In Qwen2.5, full-prompt balanced accuracy exceeds both restricted inputs, with paired-bootstrap intervals for both differences above zero. Readouts trained without development examples from the evaluated diagnostic family recover 21 pairs, including at least one in each of the nine families. The hidden-state readout exceeds a linear classifier on answer-option logits and text baselines in balanced accuracy and recovered pairs. These results show that the hidden state contains linearly decodable information about whether diagnostic evidence favors, challenges, or fails to address the causal target.

AI.tldr: LLMs' hidden states contain linearly decodable information about whether diagnostic evidence favors, challenges, or fails to address a causal claim, as demonstrated through paired prompts that isolate causal reasoning from surface-level patterns.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations conflate diagnostic reasoning with surface-level lexical cues — the same evidence can support or challenge different causal claims. The authors aim to isolate genuine causal reasoning in LLMs from spurious patterns by requiring models to correctly classify both prompts in a pair where only the causal target changes.
AI.method: The authors introduce paired prompts that repeat identical diagnostic evidence while varying only the causal question (target population, outcome, estimand, pathway, or identifying assumption). Each prompt is labeled Favors, Challenges, Unresolved, or Wrong Target. Linear readouts are trained on the final-token hidden states from the penultimate transformer block of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. A 49-pair primary benchmark across nine diagnostic families is used, with evaluation via balanced accuracy and complete-pair recovery rates, compared against permutation nulls, restricted-input baselines, and answer-option logit classifiers.
AI.result: Balanced accuracy across models ranges from 0.654–0.659 with 18–21 of 49 pairs fully recovered. Human inter-rater agreement reached 96.9% (95/98 prompts). Performance exceeded permutation nulls. In Qwen2.5, full-prompt accuracy significantly exceeded restricted-input baselines. Readouts trained without examples from the evaluated family still recovered 21 pairs, including at least one per family. Hidden-state readouts outperformed linear classifiers on answer-option logits and text-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: The hidden states of LLMs contain linearly accessible representations of how diagnostic evidence relates to causal questions, above and beyond what can be recovered from output logits or surface heuristics, demonstrating genuine causal diagnostic reasoning capacity.

title: Mixture-of-experts for handwriting trajectory reconstruction from IMU sensors
summary: The use of digital pens for online handwriting trajectory reconstruction is a prevalent method for human-computer interaction. In this study, we focus on a digital pen equipped with sensors where we aim at reconstructing the online handwriting trajectory. This pen enables writing on any surface and preserving the digital trace of handwriting. This type of pen could be used as an aid to learning to write in classroom. In this paper, we propose a new approach learning to finely reconstruct the touching trajectories while precisely analyzing the hovering part in order to position the next touching trace correctly. This relies on a Mixture-Of-Experts (MOE) approach. The first expert is dedicated for the pencil touch, and is named touching expert model. The second one is dedicated for the hovering pen trajectory, and is named hovering expert model. We improve on the learning of each of these experts based on additional context or specific examples. In addition we introduce a novel public benchmark dataset, to enable future research and comparisons in the field of handwriting reconstruction. The results demonstrates a significant enhancement compared to its primary competitors.

AI.tldr: A Mixture-of-Experts approach is proposed for reconstructing online handwriting trajectories from digital pen sensor data, using separate expert models for touching and hovering phases, with a new public benchmark dataset introduced.
AI.motivation: Digital pens with sensors enable writing on any surface while preserving digital traces, useful in classroom learning. However, existing methods struggle to accurately reconstruct both touching trajectories and hovering trajectories, particularly in correctly positioning the next touching trace after a hovering phase.
AI.method: A Mixture-of-Experts (MOE) architecture with two specialized experts: a touching expert model for pen-on-surface trajectories and a hovering expert model for in-air pen trajectories. Each expert is enhanced with additional context or specific examples to improve learning. The MOE framework enables fine-grained trajectory reconstruction and precise spatial alignment between hovering and subsequent touching traces.
AI.result: The proposed approach demonstrates significant enhancement over primary competitors. A novel public benchmark dataset is also introduced to facilitate future research and comparisons.
AI.conclusion: The MOE-based approach with separate touching and hovering experts effectively improves online handwriting trajectory reconstruction, with the public dataset enabling further advances in the field.

title: Credit Cards, Confusion, Computation, and Consequences: What Can We Uncover About Language Model Reasoning?
summary: We introduce CreditCardQA, the first financial literacy benchmark for numerical reasoning derived from real credit card agreements. The dataset contains 1,800 questions, including first-person variants that reflect how consumers naturally ask about fees, interest, and payments. We evaluate a range of large language and reasoning models under Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and Program-of-Thought (PoT) prompting. Overall, PoT yields consistent performance gains, particularly for models with weaker baseline reasoning, and narrows gaps between open- and closed-source systems. Through error analysis, we show that failures arise less from arithmetic and more from misapplied financial rules, missed conditions, and misunderstandings of contractual terms. We further analyze question difficulty and find that comparisons, conditional logic, and monetary constraints are especially challenging. We also find that errors often arise in edge cases such as late-payment penalties or small-balance scenarios that are more likely to affect lower-income or financially vulnerable individuals.

AI.tldr: CreditCardQA is a 1,800-question benchmark derived from real credit card agreements, designed to test numerical reasoning in financial literacy contexts. The study finds that Program-of-Thought (PoT) prompting outperforms Chain-of-Thought (CoT), that errors stem more from misapplied financial rules than arithmetic, and that edge cases disproportionately affecting vulnerable populations are particularly challenging for models.
AI.motivation: Current NLP benchmarks lack real-world financial literacy assessment grounded in authentic consumer documents. Credit card agreements are dense, jargon-laden, and numerically complex, yet understanding them is critical for financial well-being. The authors aim to fill this gap with a benchmark that captures how consumers naturally reason about fees, interest, and payments, while also surfacing model failure modes that have equity implications.
AI.method: The authors construct CreditCardQA, a dataset of 1,800 questions derived from real credit card agreements, including first-person variants mimicking natural consumer queries. They evaluate a range of large language and reasoning models under two prompting paradigms: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and Program-of-Thought (PoT). Error analysis is conducted across dimensions: question difficulty (comparisons, conditional logic, monetary constraints), error types (misapplied rules, missed conditions, contractual misunderstandings), and edge cases (late-payment penalties, small-balance scenarios).
AI.result: PoT prompting yields consistent gains over CoT, especially for models with weaker baseline reasoning, and narrows the performance gap between open- and closed-source systems. Failures are driven less by arithmetic errors and more by misapplied financial rules, missed conditions, and misunderstanding of contractual terms. Questions involving comparisons, conditional logic, and monetary constraints prove most difficult. Errors disproportionately occur in edge cases—late-payment penalties and small-balance scenarios—that are more likely to affect lower-income or financially vulnerable individuals.
AI.conclusion: Financial literacy reasoning in LLMs remains brittle, particularly at the intersection of legal contract interpretation and numerical reasoning. PoT prompting offers a practical mitigation strategy. The benchmark highlights significant equity concerns, as models perform worst on scenarios most relevant to financially vulnerable populations, underscoring the need for careful deployment of such systems in consumer-facing financial applications.

title: PowerAtlas: Towards Electricity-Computing Co-Scheduling for Power Systems
summary: The rapid growth of AI workloads is turning data centers into large-scale, volatile, yet spatiotemporally flexible grid loads, creating an urgent need for coordinated electricity-computing scheduling. Under stringent grid constraints, schedules from general-purpose large language models (LLMs) are often infeasible, causing line-flow violations and unserved load. We present PowerAtlas, an LLM-agent framework for electricity-computing co-scheduling that integrates historical instances, domain knowledge, and physical constraints to produce joint decisions satisfying both grid operational rules and the service-level agreements (SLAs) of computing tasks. Working with a provincial power utility in China, we built an experimental electricity-computing network and validated the decision loop on real data-center data; from de-identified operational data we further constructed ECBench, a benchmark of 2,000 scheduling instances with oracle-optimal solutions. Experiments across eleven LLMs demonstrate the effectiveness of PowerAtlas under realistic physical operating conditions, with consistent feasibility and cost gains across three open-weight backbones. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/JAVA-Jiang/PowerAtlas.

AI.tldr: PowerAtlas is an LLM-agent framework for electricity-computing co-scheduling in data centers that enforces grid constraints and SLAs. It combines historical instances, domain knowledge, and physical constraints to produce feasible joint decisions. Validated with a Chinese provincial utility, it outperforms general-purpose LLMs on a 2,000-instance benchmark (ECBench) with consistent feasibility and cost improvements.
AI.motivation: AI workload growth is transforming data centers into large, volatile, spatiotemporally flexible grid loads. General-purpose LLMs produce infeasible schedules under strict grid constraints, leading to line-flow violations and unserved load. There is an urgent need for coordinated electricity-computing scheduling that satisfies both grid operational rules and SLAs.
AI.method: PowerAtlas is an LLM-agent framework that integrates three elements: (1) historical scheduling instances, (2) domain-specific knowledge, and (3) physical grid constraints. The framework produces joint electricity-computing decisions. The authors collaborated with a provincial power utility in China to build an experimental electricity-computing network and constructed ECBench, a benchmark of 2,000 scheduling instances with oracle-optimal solutions derived from de-identified operational data.
AI.result: Experiments across eleven LLMs show PowerAtlas achieves consistent feasibility under realistic physical operating conditions. It yields cost gains across three open-weight backbone models compared to general-purpose LLM scheduling approaches.
AI.conclusion: PowerAtlas demonstrates that an LLM-agent framework augmented with domain knowledge and physical constraints can effectively solve electricity-computing co-scheduling problems, overcoming the infeasibility issues of general-purpose LLMs. The framework and ECBench benchmark are publicly released.

title: Generation or Judgement? A Paradigm Perspective on LLM-Based Emotion-Cause Pair Extraction in Conversation
summary: Emotion-cause pair extraction in conversation (ECPEC) identifies utterance pairs in which one utterance causes an emotion expressed in another. Recent LLM-based approaches formulate ECPEC at markedly different granularities, ranging from generating complete pair sets to judging individual candidate pairs. In this paper, we make the surprising observation that task formulation substantially affects performance, where pair-level judgement outperforms dialogue-level generation in all 18 controlled comparisons. We investigate the sources of this paradigm gap and find that many relations omitted by dialogue-level generation remain recognizable under explicit pair queries, under which the model recognizes 92.7%-98.1% of emotion-cause relations. This suggests that LLMs can recognize emotion-cause relations but struggle to discover and return complete pair sets. Pair-level judgement alleviates this burden, although its candidate rankings are more reliable than the binary decisions produced by a shared threshold. Based on this diagnosis, we introduce an auxiliary retriever that selectively re-examines ambiguous boundary cases, yielding consistent F1 improvements of 0.50-1.46 points across three datasets while maintaining an inference time of only 1.49x that of the baseline paradigm. These findings show that task decomposition and candidate scope are critical to effectively utilizing LLMs for ECPEC.

AI.tldr: LLM performance on emotion-cause pair extraction in conversation depends heavily on task formulation: pair-level judgment significantly outperforms dialogue-level generation due to LLMs' difficulty in discovering and returning complete pair sets, despite being able to recognize the relations. An auxiliary retriever targeting ambiguous cases yields consistent F1 gains with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: Recent LLM-based approaches to ECPEC use drastically different task granularities (dialogue-level generation vs. pair-level judgment), but no systematic understanding exists of how this formulation choice affects performance. The authors aim to quantify and diagnose this gap.
AI.method: The authors conduct 18 controlled comparisons across three datasets, systematically comparing dialogue-level generation against pair-level judgment. They analyze recognition rates for relations omitted by generation but detectable under explicit pair queries. Based on diagnostic findings, they propose an auxiliary retriever that selectively re-examines ambiguous boundary cases to improve pair-level judgment.
AI.result: Pair-level judgment consistently outperforms dialogue-level generation across all 18 comparisons. Under explicit pair queries, LLMs recognize 92.7%–98.1% of emotion-cause relations that generation missed. Candidate rankings prove more reliable than shared-threshold binary decisions. The proposed auxiliary retriever yields F1 improvements of 0.50–1.46 points across three datasets with only 1.49× inference time overhead.
AI.conclusion: Task decomposition and candidate scope are critical for effectively applying LLMs to ECPEC. LLMs possess the capacity to recognize emotion-cause relations but struggle with the holistic discovery problem; decomposing into pair-level judgment with targeted retrieval addresses this limitation efficiently.

title: Domain adaptation for handwriting trajectory reconstruction from IMU sensors
summary: Digital pens are commonly used to write on digital devices, providing the handwriting trace and enhancing human-computer interation. This study focuses on a digital pen equipped with kinematic sensors, allowing users to write on any surface while simultaneously preserving a digital trajectory of handwriting. This technology holds significant potential as a valuable educational tool, particularly in classrooms where it can facilitate the process of learning to write. A major issue is based on the difference in captured signals between adults and children. For similar handwriting trace, we have large differences in sensor signals due to differences in speed and confidence in the handwriting gesture of children. To address this, we investigate a domain adaptation approach to build a unified intermediate feature representation aimed at facilitating the trajectory reconstruction. We demonstrate the interest of domain adaptation methods in leveraging existing knowledge for application in different contexts. Specifically, we compare our domain adaptation approach with two other methods: training the model from scratch and fine-tuning the model.

AI.tldr: A digital pen with kinematic sensors captures handwriting on any surface, but sensor signals differ significantly between adults and children due to variations in writing speed and confidence. The authors propose a domain adaptation method to create a unified feature representation for robust trajectory reconstruction across user groups, outperforming training from scratch and fine-tuning baselines.
AI.motivation: Digital pens with inertial/kinematic sensors enable writing on any surface while preserving digital trajectories, offering great potential for educational settings like learning to write. However, a critical challenge arises: for visually similar handwriting traces, the captured sensor signals differ substantially between adults and children due to children's slower speed and lower confidence in writing gestures. This domain gap degrades trajectory reconstruction performance when models trained on adult data are applied to children.
AI.method: The authors employ a domain adaptation framework to learn a unified intermediate feature representation that bridges the signal distribution gap between adult and child handwriting. This representation is designed to be invariant to the domain-specific characteristics (speed, confidence) while preserving trace-relevant information. The approach is compared against two baselines: (1) training a model from scratch on child data only, and (2) fine-tuning an adult-pretrained model on child data.
AI.result: The domain adaptation approach demonstrates superior performance for trajectory reconstruction compared to both training from scratch and fine-tuning. It successfully leverages existing knowledge from adult handwriting data and transfers it to the child domain, validating the benefit of explicitly addressing the domain shift in kinematic sensor signals.
AI.conclusion: Domain adaptation is an effective strategy for handling the signal distribution mismatch between adult and child handwriting when using kinematic sensor-equipped digital pens. By learning a unified feature space, the method enables robust trajectory reconstruction across user populations, highlighting the value of transfer learning techniques for deploying digital writing tools in educational contexts.

title: TREK: A Travel Reasoning and Evaluation Kit for LLM Agents in Complex Trip Planning
summary: Travel planning is a demanding stress test for tool-using LLM agents: a usable itinerary is a single artifact that must be right along many axes at once - every flight, hotel, and attraction must exist and be bookable, the days must be physically traversable, the total must clear a budget, and the plan must serve a traveler whose needs are only partly stated. Existing agent benchmarks reward these properties one at a time and grade the final output with soft or LLM-judged rubrics, which cannot certify that a returned plan is executable and are neither reproducible nor auditable. We introduce TREK (Travel Reasoning and Evaluation Kit), a benchmark for feasible itinerary synthesis: producing a single plan that is jointly constraint-correct, hallucination-free, spatio-temporally executable, budget-valid, and responsive to the traveler's unstated persona needs. TREK comprises 800 multi-constraint tasks - 533 feasible and 267 provably infeasible with typed route/entity/budget causes - over a synthetic, internally consistent knowledge base of 212,530 records across 375 cities and 13 personas, served through a production-style tool sandbox of validated RESTful APIs. Every task is scored by a fully deterministic, rule-based evaluator with no LLM judge and ships a human-verified gold reference that scores a perfect 1.0 under that same evaluator, so the ceiling is demonstrably achievable and every remaining gap is an agent limitation rather than scorer strictness. Evaluating 15 LLM agents across nine constraint dimensions, we find that even the strongest (GPT-5.6) produces a fully-feasible plan on only 46.2% of solvable tasks, with a median of 6.6% and a floor of 0.0%; satisfying travelers' unstated needs emerges as the universal bottleneck, unsolved even at the frontier. We release the dataset, tool sandbox, deterministic evaluator, and agent code as a fully reproducible benchmark.

AI.tldr: TREK is a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on feasible itinerary synthesis, requiring jointly correct constraints across multiple dimensions. It features 800 tasks, a synthetic knowledge base of 212K+ records, deterministic rule-based evaluation, and human-verified gold references. Even the strongest agent (GPT-5.6) achieves only 46.2% on solvable tasks, with unstated traveler needs as the primary bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Existing agent benchmarks evaluate travel planning properties in isolation using soft or LLM-judged rubrics that are neither reproducible nor auditable, and cannot certify that a returned plan is actually executable. There is a need for a rigorous benchmark that tests joint constraint satisfaction across all axes simultaneously with deterministic, verifiable scoring.
AI.method: The authors construct TREK with: (1) 800 multi-constraint tasks (533 feasible, 267 provably infeasible) across 375 cities and 13 traveler personas; (2) a synthetic, internally consistent knowledge base of 212,530 records served via validated RESTful APIs; (3) a fully deterministic, rule-based evaluator requiring no LLM judge; and (4) human-verified gold references scoring a perfect 1.0, ensuring the evaluation ceiling is demonstrably achievable. Evaluation spans 15 LLM agents across nine constraint dimensions.
AI.result: GPT-5.6, the strongest agent, produces fully feasible plans on only 46.2% of solvable tasks. The median across all agents is 6.6%, with a floor of 0.0%. Satisfying travelers' unstated persona needs emerges as the universal bottleneck, unsolved even by frontier models.
AI.conclusion: Joint constraint satisfaction in travel planning remains a significant open challenge for LLM agents. TREK provides a rigorous, reproducible benchmark that exposes critical limitations, particularly in inferring and satisfying unstated user needs. The fully open-sourced dataset, sandbox, evaluator, and agent code enable continued progress on this problem.

title: CalTwin: Towards Calibrated, Shift-Robust Medical World Models via Fisher-Information Regularisation
summary: Medical world models aim to learn a latent state of patient or organ physiology and a transition function that forecasts how that state evolves under interventions, supporting downstream tasks from imaging-based diagnosis to digital-twin treatment planning. Two failure modes threaten the reliability of such models in clinical deployment: (i)~\emph{covariate shift}, because training data are fragmented across hospitals, scanners, and time, so the feature distribution seen by the latent-dynamics predictor differs across fragments and from the distribution at deployment; and (ii)~\emph{confidence misalignment}, because multi-step forecasts are often overconfident exactly where clinical risk is highest. We argue that both problems admit a unified treatment via a single lightweight regularisation objective, \textbf{CalTwin}, which combines a Fisher-Information-based shift penalty adapted from our prior work on fragmented covariate-shift remediation~\cite{khan2025mitigating,khan2025causal} with a Confidence Misalignment Penalty adapted from our prior work on calibrated vision-language classification~\cite{khan2025confidence}, applied here to a GRU-based medical world model's latent transition predictor. We derive the combined objective, establish which proof steps transfer from the classification setting without modification and which require adaptation, and evaluate it on the PhysioNet 2019 Sepsis Challenge, treating the two hospital systems as sequential training fragments and the unseen system as an out-of-distribution test. CalTwin reduces OOD next-step latent-state MSE by 9.1\% relative to the no-penalty baseline (FIM penalty alone accounts for 7.0\%); the ECE reduction from the Confidence Misalignment Penalty is real but small (0.7\% for CalTwin, 1.3\% for CMP alone).

AI.tldr: CalTwin unifies Fisher-Information-based covariate-shift penalty and confidence misalignment penalty into a single regularization objective for medical world models, reducing OOD latent-state MSE by 9.1% on the PhysioNet 2019 Sepsis Challenge, with modest ECE improvements.
AI.motivation: Medical world models suffer from two critical reliability failures: (1) covariate shift from fragmented training data across hospitals/scanners/time, causing distribution mismatch between training fragments and deployment; (2) confidence misalignment where multi-step forecasts are overconfident precisely in high-risk clinical scenarios. Both problems demand a unified solution for safe clinical deployment.
AI.method: The authors propose CalTwin, a lightweight regularization objective combining two components: a Fisher-Information-based shift penalty (adapted from prior work on fragmented covariate-shift remediation) and a Confidence Misalignment Penalty (adapted from prior calibrated vision-language classification work). Both are applied to a GRU-based medical world model's latent transition predictor. The paper derives the combined objective formally, identifies which proof steps transfer from classification and which require adaptation, and evaluates on PhysioNet 2019 Sepsis Challenge using two hospital systems as sequential training fragments and an unseen system as OOD test.
AI.result: CalTwin reduces OOD next-step latent-state MSE by 9.1% relative to the no-penalty baseline (FIM penalty alone: 7.0%). The Confidence Misalignment Penalty yields a real but small ECE reduction: 0.7% for CalTwin, 1.3% for CMP alone.
AI.conclusion: Both covariate shift and confidence misalignment in medical world models can be addressed through a unified lightweight regularization framework. The Fisher-Information penalty drives most of the predictive improvement, while the confidence calibration gains, though genuine, remain modest, suggesting further work is needed on the calibration front.

title: OptimismBench: Forecasting Bias and the Alignment Effect in Language Model Judgment
summary: Large language models are increasingly used as decision aids whose probability judgments shape downstream choices. Whether those judgments carry a systematic directional tilt has been hard to detect: calibration metrics aggregate unsigned errors, and naturalistic uncertainty offers no ground-truth probability. When an LLM rates a startup's success at 70% but its failure at 15%, the missing 15 points expose a distortion no aggregate score flags. We introduce OptimismBench, which detects directional bias with inverted pairs: each scenario elicits both P(success) and P(failure), and asymmetry between the two framings yields a signed bias score without ground truth. Across 16 models from 8 providers, fourteen are optimistic; pessimism appears only in Anthropic's frontier tier. Eleven matched base-versus-chat pairs across four families show post-training sets the sign of the bias, with opposite shifts in different families. The pattern survives prompt, temperature, perspective, and self-debiasing ablations. A seventeen-model six-language comparison further shows model identity dominates language, with inter-model variance at 4.7x inter-language variance. We release 3,870 items across 10 languages for per-model directional-bias auditing. When alignment makes a model more helpful, it also tilts its probabilities; downstream pipelines inherit the tilt by default.

AI.tldr: LLMs exhibit systematic directional bias in probability judgments: 14 of 16 models are optimistic (overstating success relative to failure). Post-training alignment sets the bias sign, with opposite effects across model families. Model identity dominates language as a bias driver (4.7× variance ratio). A new benchmark, OptimismBench, enables bias detection without ground truth using inverted framing pairs.
AI.motivation: Existing calibration metrics aggregate unsigned errors and cannot detect systematic directional tilt in LLM probability judgments. Naturalistic tasks lack ground-truth probabilities. There is a need for a method to expose whether models consistently lean optimistic or pessimistic — a distortion with downstream consequences as LLMs increasingly serve as decision aids.
AI.method: Introduces OptimismBench: a benchmark using inverted pairs where each scenario elicits both P(success) and P(failure). Asymmetry between these two framings yields a signed bias score without requiring ground-truth probabilities. The method was applied across 16 models from 8 providers, 11 base-vs-chat pairs across 4 families, with ablations on prompt, temperature, perspective, and self-debiasing. A 17-model, 6-language comparison partitioned variance between model identity and language.
AI.result: Fourteen of 16 models show optimism; pessimism appears only in Anthropic's frontier tier. Post-training alignment sets the sign of bias, with opposite directional shifts across different model families. The pattern survives multiple ablation conditions. Inter-model variance is 4.7× inter-language variance, indicating model identity dominates language. The benchmark comprises 3,870 items across 10 languages.
AI.conclusion: When alignment makes models more helpful, it also systematically tilts their probability judgments; downstream pipelines inherit this tilt by default. OptimismBench provides a practical tool for per-model directional-bias auditing, and the findings highlight an overlooked consequence of post-training alignment.

title: Journey Operators for Structured Multi-Axis Composition
summary:
Many kinds of data have structure along one or more axes: words in a sentence, pixels in an image, nodes in a tree, frames in audio, or cells in a 3D volume. Along one axis, order matters: "the dog bit the man" is different from "the man bit the dog."
