Across independent axes, however, neither composition nor movement should depend on the order of axes: in an image, composing right then down should give the same result as composing down then right, and moving right then down should describe the same relative position as moving down then right.
  We develop a framework for modeling this kind of multi-axis structure. Each data item carries its content together with a small transformation for each axis. A path connecting two positions defines a journey; the journey operator is the product of per-axis transformations along that path, governing both how data composes along the path and how relative position is described. When the transformations are fixed, our framework recovers Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) and its multi-dimensional variants. When they depend on the data, the model gains a content-adaptive positional inductive bias.
  We show exactly when these paths are well-defined: both composition and movement across axes are path-independent precisely when the axis transformations commute. We also prove that, under the stated toral-frame symmetry, cocycle, bilinearity, and norm-preservation assumptions, the resulting pairwise scoring rule must take the form of block-wise rotations, explaining why RoPE-like methods arise naturally.
  Finally, we use this theory to design JoFormer, a model for value aggregation, and relate it to attention and state-space models (SSMs).
  Initial experiments across vision, language, and length generalization suggest that these inductive biases can have observable consequences in
  practice.

AI.tldr: Proposes a framework for multi-axis structured data where path independence requires commuting axis transformations. Derives RoPE-like block-wise rotations from symmetry principles, and introduces JoFormer for value aggregation with connections to attention and SSMs.
AI.motivation: Many data modalities (text, images, audio, 3D volumes) possess multi-axis structure where order matters along each axis but not across independent axes. Existing methods like RoPE handle single-axis position well, but a principled framework for ensuring path-independent composition and movement across multiple axes is lacking.
AI.method: The authors develop a framework where each data item carries content plus a per-axis transformation. A path between two positions defines a journey operator as the product of per-axis transformations along that path. They prove path independence holds iff axis transformations commute. Under toral-frame symmetry, cocycle, bilinearity, and norm-preservation assumptions, they derive that pairwise scoring must take the form of block-wise rotations (generalizing RoPE). They then design JoFormer, a value aggregation model, and connect it to attention and SSM architectures.
AI.result: The framework recovers RoPE and its multi-dimensional variants as a special case when transformations are fixed. With data-dependent transformations, it yields a content-adaptive positional inductive bias. Initial experiments across vision, language, and length generalization tasks show observable consequences of these inductive biases in practice.
AI.conclusion: Path-independent multi-axis structure emerges naturally from commuting axis transformations and leads to block-wise rotation-based scoring rules. This theoretical foundation unifies RoPE-like methods and enables new architectures like JoFormer, demonstrating practical benefits across modalities.

title: Evaluating Regional Bias in LLMs From Abstract Stereotype to Concrete Social Decision-Making
summary: Regional bias in large language models (LLMs) may shape both perceptions of regional groups and decisions about individuals from different regions. Yet existing studies often examine these manifestations separately, leaving their structure and consequences unclear. We introduce Stereotypes-to-Decisions (S2D), a systematic framework evaluating regional bias from abstract stereotypes to concrete social decisions. Covering all 34 provincial-level administrative regions of China, S2D evaluates six LLMs using stereotype ratings of Warmth (perceived friendliness and trustworthiness) and Competence (perceived capability and intelligence), along with paired-choice tasks across Education, Occupation, and Social Interaction. Results reveal substantial regional differences in regional scores, with considerable agreement across models, especially for Competence and Occupation decisions. Furthermore, these patterns are associated with regional economic and digital development indicators and display mixed human-like stereotypes, with some regions rated highly on one dimension but poorly on the other. They also remain largely stable across Chinese and English prompts. Overall, our findings show that regional bias in LLMs is prevalent, systematic, and consequential, motivating more regionally aware evaluation and mitigation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces S2D (Stereotypes-to-Decisions), a framework that systematically evaluates regional bias in LLMs across all 34 provincial-level regions of China, assessing stereotype ratings (Warmth and Competence) and downstream decisions in Education, Occupation, and Social Interaction. Six LLMs show substantial, systematic regional bias that correlates with economic/digital indicators, exhibits mixed stereotypes, and remains stable across languages.
AI.motivation: Existing studies examine regional bias in LLMs in fragmented ways—either looking at abstract stereotype perceptions or concrete social decisions separately—leaving the structure and real-world consequences of such biases unclear. The authors aim to unify these perspectives and provide a comprehensive, systematic account of how regional stereotypes in LLMs translate into consequential social decisions.
AI.method: The authors propose the Stereotypes-to-Decisions (S2D) framework, covering all 34 provincial-level administrative regions of China. They evaluate six LLMs using two stereotype dimensions from the Stereotype Content Model: Warmth (friendliness, trustworthiness) and Competence (capability, intelligence). These stereotype ratings are then linked to paired-choice decision tasks across three domains: Education, Occupation, and Social Interaction. The study also examines associations with regional economic and digital development indicators and tests stability across Chinese and English prompts.
AI.result: Results reveal substantial regional differences in stereotype scores, with high inter-model agreement—particularly for Competence and Occupation decisions. These bias patterns correlate with regional economic and digital development indicators. The stereotypes are mixed (regions may score high on Warmth but low on Competence, or vice versa) and remain largely stable across Chinese and English prompts.
AI.conclusion: Regional bias in LLMs is prevalent, systematic, and consequential—shaping both perceptions of regional groups and concrete decisions about individuals. The findings motivate the need for more regionally aware evaluation and mitigation strategies in LLM development.

title: SkillRise: Agentic Reinforcement Learning for Cross-Task Skill Evolution
summary: Large language model agents often encounter related yet distinct tasks that share reusable solution patterns. Yet standard agentic reinforcement learning treats tasks as independent episodes, while existing approaches to skill learning either focus on repeated attempts of one task or use pipelines with multiple stages that entangle extraction, retrieval, and execution. We introduce SkillRise, a unified reinforcement learning framework for learning skills across tasks. SkillRise organizes related instances into progressively challenging sequences and uses a single policy to alternate between task solving and curating an evolving skill document passed directly to the next task. Decoupled credit assignment across tasks supervises solving with the current task outcome and curation with discounted downstream outcomes. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld show that SkillRise achieves the strongest Pass@1 performance among the compared methods, with gains over the strongest baseline ranging from 2.3 to 8.5 percentage points. Although trained across distinct tasks, its learned curation policy remains effective for repeated attempts on the same task. Further analysis reveals scaling at test time across tasks: performance improves with longer sequences of related tasks even when each task is attempted only once. This trend suggests that SkillRise reuses transferable skills across tasks rather than benefiting from repeated sampling of the same task. SkillRise further retains strong performance while substantially reducing the runtime overhead of skill learning pipelines with multiple stages. Together, these results provide a simple and efficient training paradigm for LLM agents to extract, refine, and reuse transferable skills across tasks.

AI.tldr: SkillRise is a unified RL framework that trains LLM agents to concurrently solve tasks and curate a reusable skill document across progressively challenging task sequences, achieving superior Pass@1 performance with efficient runtime compared to multi-stage pipelines.
AI.motivation: Standard agentic RL treats tasks as independent episodes, ignoring reusable solution patterns across related tasks. Existing skill-learning approaches either focus on repeated single-task attempts or use cumbersome multi-stage pipelines that entangle extraction, retrieval, and execution. There is a need for a unified framework that learns transferable skills across distinct tasks in a simple, efficient manner.
AI.method: SkillRise organizes related task instances into progressively challenging sequences. A single policy alternates between (1) solving the current task and (2) curating an evolving skill document that is passed directly to the next task. Decoupled credit assignment is used: the solving action is supervised by the current task outcome, while the curation action is supervised by discounted downstream task outcomes. This enables end-to-end RL training of both capabilities without multi-stage pipelines.
AI.result: On ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld, SkillRise achieves the strongest Pass@1 performance, outperforming the best baseline by 2.3–8.5 percentage points. The learned curation policy remains effective even for repeated attempts on the same task. Test-time scaling shows that performance improves with longer sequences of related tasks (each attempted only once), indicating cross-task skill transfer. SkillRise also substantially reduces runtime overhead compared to multi-stage skill-learning pipelines.
AI.conclusion: SkillRise provides a simple, efficient training paradigm enabling LLM agents to extract, refine, and reuse transferable skills across tasks. The results demonstrate that a unified RL approach with decoupled credit assignment and progressive task sequencing effectively captures reusable patterns, yielding strong performance and test-time scaling benefits.

title: FedTopo: Relation-Level Topology Sharing for Model-Heterogeneous Federated Learning
comment: 13 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to ICDE 2027 (first submission round)
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative learning over decentralized data silos without centralizing raw data. However, heterogeneous local architectures often induce non-aligned representation spaces, making it difficult to transfer global knowledge across silos. Existing paradigms share this knowledge as model parameters, distilled predictions, or class prototypes, yet all encode it in an absolute space that must be aligned across clients. Heterogeneous backbones break this alignment, so the shared knowledge becomes unreliable and misleads local training. We propose FedTopo, a relation-level framework that encodes global knowledge as class relation topology, capturing how classes relate within each client rather than where they lie in feature space. Each client builds its relation topology from local prototypes and uploads it with class statistics. The server then aggregates these relations in a reliability-aware manner that down-weights weakly supported ones, and broadcasts the global topology to clients. The global topology guides local training by emphasizing topology-similar negative classes. Experiments on three datasets under eight heterogeneous backbones show that FedTopo consistently outperforms parameter-, distillation-, and prototype-sharing baselines, with low communication and no inference overhead. Our code is available at https://github.com/Zhaoyang-Ma/FedTopo.

AI.tldr: FedTopo proposes a federated learning framework that encodes global knowledge as class relation topology rather than absolute feature-space representations, enabling robust collaboration across heterogeneous model architectures.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous local architectures in federated learning produce non-aligned representation spaces, making absolute-space knowledge transfer (parameters, logits, prototypes) unreliable and potentially misleading for local training.
AI.method: Each client builds a class relation topology from local prototypes and uploads it with class statistics. The server aggregates these topologies using reliability-aware weighting (down-weighting weakly supported relations) and broadcasts the global topology. Local training is guided by emphasizing topology-similar negative classes.
AI.result: FedTopo consistently outperforms parameter-sharing, distillation-based, and prototype-sharing baselines across three datasets and eight heterogeneous backbones, while maintaining low communication cost and no inference overhead.
AI.conclusion: Encoding global knowledge at the relational level (class relation topology) effectively circumvents the representation alignment problem in heterogeneous FL, offering a practical and communication-efficient solution.

title: Pangram 4 Technical Report
summary: We present Pangram 4, the latest deep-learning-based AI-text classification model from Pangram Labs. We achieve an AUROC of 0.9916 with a false positive rate of 0.0041% and a false negative rate of 0.3396%. In addition to its increased overall accuracy compared with Pangram 3, Pangram 4 exhibits superior out-of-distribution generalization and robustness to adversarial attacks. Another novel contribution of Pangram 4 is its improved ability to distinguish fine-grained edits and mixed AI-human co-authored text. We demonstrate improvements to both boundary detection tasks and the detection of interleaved AI assistance. Finally, we report metrics on standard AI detection benchmarks showing that Pangram 4 achieves state-of-the-art performance on the AI text detection task across a wide variety of settings and domains.

AI.tldr: Pangram 4 is a new deep-learning AI-text classifier from Pangram Labs achieving 0.9916 AUROC, with strong out-of-distribution generalization, adversarial robustness, and improved detection of mixed AI-human text, attaining SOTA on standard benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To advance AI-generated text detection beyond prior work (Pangram 3) by improving overall accuracy, generalization to unseen domains, robustness against adversarial attacks, and the ability to detect subtle forms of AI involvement such as fine-grained edits and interleaved AI-human co-authored content.
AI.method: Deep-learning-based classification model (architectural and training details not specified in the abstract) designed to detect AI-generated text, with enhancements over Pangram 3 focused on boundary detection, mixed-authorship segmentation, and adversarial robustness.
AI.result: AUROC of 0.9916; false positive rate of 0.0041%; false negative rate of 0.3396%. Superior out-of-distribution generalization and adversarial robustness vs. Pangram 3. Improved detection of fine-grained edits, interleaved AI assistance, and boundary detection in mixed human-AI text. State-of-the-art performance on standard AI detection benchmarks across diverse settings and domains.
AI.conclusion: Pangram 4 represents a significant advance in AI-text detection, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy with exceptionally low false positive rates, while demonstrating practical capabilities for real-world scenarios involving mixed and partially AI-authored content.

title: Budget-Aware LLM Discovery via Cost-Calibrated Frontier Utility
summary: Large language models increasingly support scientific and algorithmic discovery through inference-time search over evaluated candidates. Existing adaptive discovery controllers assign credit based only on score progress, even though prompt length, retries, and guidance calls cause search actions to incur different token costs. We prove that cost-blind credit can forfeit all but a vanishing fraction of attainable quality as frontiers multiply and costs diverge. Under a fixed search-side token budget, the controller must decide which frontier is improving and whether its gain justifies the realized cost before the budget is exhausted. We introduce \textbf{CostAda}, a cost-calibrated adaptive controller built around \emph{cost-calibrated frontier utility}. The utility values frontier progress relative to realized action cost and conditions that credit on the remaining budget. CostAda uses this signal to control local exploration intensity, frontier allocation, and budgeted tactic intervention. Cost and remaining budget therefore shape the search rather than serving only as accounting variables or a stopping rule. CostAda reaches the strongest baseline's full-budget quality with at most half the budget on twelve of sixteen benchmark--backbone pairs while achieving the strongest mean final quality on all eight benchmarks under GLM-5 and GPT-5.4.

AI.tldr: CostAda is a cost-calibrated adaptive controller for inference-time search that incorporates token costs and remaining budget into credit assignment, achieving superior quality at significantly lower budgets compared to cost-blind baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing adaptive discovery controllers for LLM inference-time search assign credit based solely on score progress, ignoring that different search actions incur different token costs. The authors prove that cost-blind credit can forfeit nearly all attainable quality as search frontiers multiply and costs diverge, motivating a cost-aware approach.
AI.method: CostAda introduces cost-calibrated frontier utility, which values frontier progress relative to realized action cost and conditions credit on the remaining budget. This signal controls local exploration intensity, frontier allocation, and budgeted tactic intervention, making cost and remaining budget integral to search dynamics rather than mere accounting variables.
AI.result: CostAda reaches the strongest baseline's full-budget quality with at most half the budget on 12 of 16 benchmark–backbone pairs and achieves the strongest mean final quality on all 8 benchmarks under both GLM-5 and GPT-5.4 backbones.
AI.conclusion: Cost-calibrated credit assignment is essential for efficient inference-time search, and CostAda demonstrates that integrating cost awareness into adaptive control yields substantial budget savings without sacrificing—and often improving—final output quality.

title: Mental World Modeling
summary: World models enable a predictive substrate for planning and action, yet existing formulations merely answer a physical question: what/where it is, and how will it evolve. Human behavior, however, is driven by hidden mental state (what a person believes, wants, intends, feels, and considers socially permissible), so a model that tracks the physical scene but not what each agent knows and believes about it predicts the wrong action for the right-looking scene. We formulate Mental World Modeling (MWM), a generic theoretical framework that makes mental variables core components of a world model rather than posthoc rationales: MWM aintains a coupled physical-mental world state, renders a target-specific partial observation, and simulates how candidate actions jointly update both components. We instantiate the framework in MENTIS, a training-free and fully inspectable baseline that decomposes the process into state parsing, target-observation generation, action decomposition, coupled physical and mental transition, and branch-level value evaluation. On a manually constructed, quality-controlled dataset of situated decision scenarios spanning text, image, and sounding-video stories, experiments with 8 modern LLM-based world models demonstrate that explicitly modeling the mental state is essential for predicting human decisions. Deeper analyses further expose the bottlenecks of current mental world modeling. We expect MWM as a next stage of world modeling, from simulating physical scenes to simulating the minds that act in them.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Mental World Modeling (MWM), a framework that integrates hidden mental states (beliefs, desires, intentions) into world models alongside physical states. The authors implement MENTIS, a training-free baseline, and show across text, image, and video scenarios that modeling mental states is essential for predicting human decisions, while also revealing current limitations in mental world modeling.
AI.motivation: Existing world models only answer physical questions (what/where something is, how it evolves), but human behavior is driven by hidden mental states—beliefs, wants, intentions, feelings, and social norms. A model tracking only physical scenes will predict wrong actions for scenarios that look physically correct, because it misses what each agent knows and believes.
AI.method: The authors propose MWM, a generic framework maintaining a coupled physical-mental world state, rendering target-specific partial observations, and simulating joint updates. They instantiate it via MENTIS, a training-free, inspectable baseline decomposing the process into: state parsing, target-observation generation, action decomposition, coupled physical-mental transition, and branch-level value evaluation. Experiments use 8 LLM-based world models on a manually curated, quality-controlled dataset of decision scenarios across text, image, and sounding-video stories.
AI.result: Explicitly modeling mental state significantly improves prediction of human decisions across all modalities. Ablation and deeper analyses expose bottlenecks in current mental world modeling capabilities of LLM-based systems.
AI.conclusion: MWM represents a next stage for world modeling—moving from simulating physical scenes to simulating the minds that act within them. The framework and findings highlight both the necessity and current limitations of mental state modeling for human-aligned decision prediction.

title: Tight Generalization Bound for AdaBoost
summary: In this paper we show that the generalization error of AdaBoost is $Θ\big(\tfrac{d\ln(nγ^{2}/d)}{nγ^2}+\tfrac{\ln(1/δ)}{n}\big)$, where $γ$ is the advantage guaranteed by the weak learner, $d$ is the VC-dimension of the class containing the weak hypotheses, $n$ is the sample size, and $δ$ is the confidence parameter. The contribution of this paper is the upper bound; the matching lower bound follows from prior work. The upper bound proof follows by combining the known fact that AdaBoost outputs a voting classifier whose voting function has zero empirical $γ/2$-margin loss with what is, to the best of our knowledge, a new margin-based generalization bound for voting classifiers.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a tight generalization error bound for AdaBoost of Θ(d ln(nγ²/d)/(nγ²) + ln(1/δ)/n), where the upper bound is the novel contribution and the lower bound follows from prior work. The proof combines AdaBoost's zero empirical γ/2-margin loss property with a new margin-based generalization bound for voting classifiers.
AI.motivation: To characterize the exact generalization error rate of AdaBoost, providing both upper and lower bounds that match, thereby resolving the sample complexity of the algorithm in terms of VC-dimension d, margin γ, sample size n, and confidence δ.
AI.method: The upper bound is derived by (1) leveraging the established fact that AdaBoost produces a voting classifier with zero empirical γ/2-margin loss on the training set, and (2) applying a novel margin-based generalization bound for voting classifiers. The matching lower bound is cited from existing literature.
AI.result: A tight Θ-bound on AdaBoost's generalization error: Θ(d ln(nγ²/d)/(nγ²) + ln(1/δ)/n). This captures the exact dependence on all key parameters.
AI.conclusion: The generalization error of AdaBoost is fully characterized by the derived bound. The work fills a gap by providing the upper bound, which together with the prior lower bound yields a tight characterization.

title: Thinking Under Uncertainty: Evidence Use and Information-Seeking in Language Models
summary: Inference-time thinking improves the performance of large language models, but aggregate outcomes do not reveal whether models use available evidence more effectively or seek information that could improve future decisions. We distinguish these responses by measuring action preference, thinking length, and reported confidence under matched uncertainty. Ten open-weight models completed matched horizon-style two-armed bandit trials in thinking and non-thinking modes. A cognitive model separated value-guided action and uncertainty-independent choice noise from two behavioral signatures of exploration: a UCB-like preference for the less-known arm and Thompson-like choice variability that increases with total uncertainty. On average, thinking strengthened value-guided action and reduced uncertainty-independent choice noise, without producing UCB-like exploration or strengthening Thompson-like exploration. Outside action, the information-imbalanced history condition, which also displayed more observations than the matched balanced condition, was associated with greater thinking length. Reported confidence became more sensitive to decision difficulty and more strongly associated with chosen task evidence. We interpret these thinking-length and reported-confidence patterns as consistent with metacognitive control and metacognitive monitoring, respectively, without establishing either process. Decoder sweeps, especially temperature, altered choice noise and thinking length but did not reproduce the joint cross-output pattern. In this controlled decision setting, thinking improved how models acted on current evidence, while neither measured signature supported a shift toward a more information-seeking policy.

AI.tldr: In controlled two-armed bandit tasks, inference-time thinking in LLMs improved value-guided action selection and reduced choice noise, but showed no evidence of increased information-seeking exploration (UCB or Thompson-like). Thinking length and confidence reporting patterns suggested metacognitive processes, with decoder sweeps failing to reproduce the joint behavioral pattern.
AI.motivation: Aggregate performance improvements from inference-time thinking do not reveal the underlying mechanism — whether models use current evidence more effectively or shift toward information-seeking policies. The authors aimed to disambiguate these accounts using behavioral signatures from reinforcement learning and cognitive science.
AI.method: Ten open-weight LLMs completed matched horizon-style two-armed bandit trials in both thinking and non-thinking modes. A cognitive model decomposed behavior into value-guided action, uncertainty-independent choice noise, UCB-like exploration (preference for less-known arms), and Thompson-like exploration (choice variability increasing with total uncertainty). The design included an information-imbalanced condition (more observations) matched with a balanced condition. Thinking length and reported confidence were also analyzed, with decoder sweeps (temperature etc.) used as a control.
AI.result: Thinking strengthened value-guided action and reduced uncertainty-independent choice noise, with no evidence of UCB-like or enhanced Thompson-like exploration. Thinking length was greater in the information-imbalanced condition. Reported confidence showed increased sensitivity to decision difficulty and stronger association with chosen-task evidence. Decoder sweeps altered choice noise and thinking length but did not reproduce the joint cross-output pattern observed under thinking.
AI.conclusion: In this controlled decision setting, inference-time thinking improved how models acted on current evidence rather than shifting them toward information-seeking policies. The thinking-length and confidence patterns are consistent with metacognitive control and monitoring, respectively, though neither process was definitively established.

title: TREA-Net: A Transferable Residual Epidemiological Adaptation Network for Dengue Incidence Forecasting
summary: Accurate multi-week dengue forecasting supports timely vector-control interventions, outbreak preparedness, and healthcare resource allocation. However, newly established surveillance systems often lack the historical data needed to train reliable neural forecasting models. Although pretrained time-series models offer promising zero-shot forecasts, their cross-domain training may not capture local epidemiological dynamics. We propose TREA-Net, a Transferable Residual Epidemiological Adaptation Network for dengue forecasting under limited data. TREA-Net augments neural forecasting backbones with projections from an Environmental Time-Series Susceptible-Infected-Recovered model and learns a lightweight gated residual correction transferable from data-rich to data-scarce regions. Its node-invariant design accommodates surveillance systems with different numbers of locations, while target adaptation requires learning only two global parameters. We transfer knowledge from long-running dengue surveillance in Colombia and Nicaragua to 8-week-ahead forecasting in Mexico and Malaysia using only 78 or 104 weeks of target data. Across five neural backbones and ten transfer settings, TREA-Net improves the corresponding backbone in 9 out of 10 settings, with statistically significant gains. When integrated with TiRex, a foundation model for forecasting, it achieves the lowest mean absolute error across all target datasets. Conformal prediction further maintains empirical coverage while reducing 8-week prediction-interval width by 29.6% in Mexico. These results demonstrate TREA-Net's potential as a lightweight and portable early-warning framework for health agencies with limited surveillance data.

AI.tldr: TREA-Net is a lightweight transfer learning framework that augments neural forecasting models with epidemiological compartmental projections and a gated residual correction, enabling accurate multi-week dengue forecasts for regions with limited surveillance data by transferring knowledge from data-rich to data-scarce settings.
AI.motivation: Newly established dengue surveillance systems lack the historical data needed to train reliable neural forecasting models. While pretrained time-series models offer zero-shot forecasts, their cross-domain training often fails to capture local epidemiological dynamics. There is a need for a method that enables accurate forecasting under severe data scarcity by leveraging knowledge from data-rich regions.
AI.method: TREA-Net integrates three components: (1) an Environmental Time-Series Susceptible-Infected-Recovered (SIR) model that provides mechanistic projections capturing local transmission dynamics; (2) a lightweight gated residual correction module that learns to combine and adjust neural backbone forecasts with SIR projections; and (3) a node-invariant architecture that enables transfer across surveillance systems with different numbers of locations, requiring only two global parameters for target adaptation. Knowledge is transferred from Colombia and Nicaragua (source) to Mexico and Malaysia (target) using only 78–104 weeks of target data for 8-week-ahead forecasting.
AI.result: TREA-Net improved the corresponding backbone in 9 out of 10 transfer settings across five neural backbones, with statistically significant gains. When integrated with TiRex (a foundation forecasting model), it achieved the lowest mean absolute error across all target datasets. Conformal prediction maintained empirical coverage while reducing 8-week prediction-interval width by 29.6% in Mexico.
AI.conclusion: TREA-Net demonstrates strong potential as a lightweight, portable early-warning framework for health agencies operating surveillance systems with limited historical data, effectively bridging data-rich and data-scarce regions through transferable epidemiological adaptation.

title: Amortized Moment Matching for Visual Generation
summary: We propose amortized moment matching, utilizing neural networks to learn data moments as distributional training signals. By casting diffusion denoisers through polynomial projections, we establish a general framework for moment amortization, revealing that an $n$-th degree projection explicitly identifies data moments up to order $n+1$. Derived from the tractable affine case, we instantiate the Amortized Fréchet Distance (AMFD) loss. Unlike FD-loss which relies on explicit marginal moment calculations, AMFD is able to dynamically learn conditional moments via an alternating, matrix-free optimization pipeline that effortlessly scales to high-dimensional data. When operating on global representation features, AMFD serves as a powerful post-training objective; empirically, its neural formulation yields more robust training dynamics than exact statistical matching, substantially surpassing the FD baseline on the FDr$^6$ metric and achieving superior one-step generation on ImageNet. Furthermore, it unlocks direct exploration within native generative spaces, suggesting that the first two moments can identify target distributions only in spaces with strong semantics. Finally, when scaled to text-to-image generation, the condition-aware nature of AMFD unlocks massive gains in instruction-following capabilities, enabling our one-step models to outperform their multi-step FLUX.2 [klein] 4B teachers on the GenEval benchmark while achieving on-par performance on PickScore. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/poppuppy/amfd.

AI.tldr: Proposes Amortized Moment Matching (AMFD), a neural network-based framework that learns data moments as distributional training signals. It generalizes diffusion denoisers via polynomial projections, enabling scalable, matrix-free optimization that surpasses existing Fréchet Distance methods, achieves state-of-the-art one-step generation on ImageNet, and significantly improves instruction-following in text-to-image generation.
AI.motivation: Existing Fréchet Distance (FD) loss relies on explicit marginal moment calculations, which scale poorly to high-dimensional data and suffer from unstable training dynamics. The authors aim to replace exact statistical matching with a learned, amortized neural formulation that dynamically captures conditional moments and scales gracefully to high dimensions.
AI.method: The core idea is amortized moment matching: casting diffusion denoisers through polynomial projections, where an n-th degree projection identifies data moments up to order n+1. From the tractable affine case, they derive the Amortized Fréchet Distance (AMFD) loss, which uses neural networks to learn moments and employs an alternating, matrix-free optimization pipeline. The framework operates on global representation features as a post-training objective.
AI.result: AMFD yields more robust training dynamics than exact statistical matching, substantially surpasses the FD baseline on the FDr⁶ metric, achieves superior one-step generation on ImageNet, and demonstrates that first two moments identify target distributions only in semantically strong spaces. In text-to-image generation, condition-aware AMFD enables one-step models to outperform the multi-step FLUX.2 4B teacher on GenEval while matching PickScore performance.
AI.conclusion: Amortized moment matching provides a scalable, robust, and high-performing alternative to exact moment-based distribution matching. Its neural formulation improves training stability, unlocks efficient one-step generation, and excels in conditional settings like text-to-image synthesis, with strong practical implications for generative model distillation.

title: ReCo: Reweighting GRPO Against Distributional Concentration
summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has become a standard reinforcement learning method for post-training language models. Recent work shows that GRPO can reduce the base model's reasoning capacity and underperform it in Pass@k when k is large, indicating reduced coverage of reasoning paths. We find that this reduction is associated with GRPO concentrating on responses that the base model already generates with high probability. We trace this concentration to two mechanisms in the GRPO update. At the response level, high-probability responses dominate the group gradient through repeated occurrence. At the token level, GRPO's importance ratio scales gradients, further reinforcing tokens that become more likely under the current policy. We propose ReCo, a reweighting method that addresses both effects. Response contributions are normalized by their expected occurrence within the rollout group, and the token-level importance ratio is replaced with a variance-based ratio that gives larger update scale to non-saturated decision points where alternative token choices remain plausible. Across Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B/7B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, ReCo improves Pass@k for large values of k and is comparable to GRPO for small values of k.

AI.tldr: GRPO concentrates on high-probability responses from the base model, reducing reasoning path coverage (lower Pass@k for large k). The authors identify two mechanisms causing this — response-level dominance by repeated high-probability samples and token-level gradient scaling via importance ratios — and propose ReCo, which normalizes response contributions and uses variance-based token ratios, improving Pass@k for large k on math reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: GRPO, while standard for RL-based post-training of language models, reduces the base model's reasoning capacity and underperforms in Pass@k when k is large, indicating diminished coverage of diverse reasoning paths. The authors aim to diagnose and mitigate this failure mode.
AI.method: The authors first analyze GRPO, identifying two concentration mechanisms: (1) response-level: high-probability responses dominate group gradients via repeated occurrence in rollouts; (2) token-level: the importance ratio scales gradients, reinforcing already-likely tokens. They then propose ReCo, which reweights by: (a) normalizing response contributions by their expected occurrence within the rollout group, and (b) replacing the importance ratio with a variance-based ratio that gives larger updates to non-saturated decision points where alternative token choices remain plausible.
AI.result: Across Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B/7B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, ReCo improves Pass@k for large k while remaining comparable to GRPO for small k.
AI.conclusion: GRPO's concentration on high-probability responses reduces reasoning diversity, and ReCo effectively counters both response-level and token-level concentration mechanisms, restoring coverage of reasoning paths and improving Pass@k at large k without sacrificing small-k performance.

title: Actions Have Consequences: Detecting Outcome Performativity using Intervention Testing
comment: 25 pages, 18 Figures. Accepted to the 29th International Conference on Discovery Science, 2026
summary: In many domains such as Palliative Care, Credit Assignment and Recommender Systems, predictions may causally influence the outcomes they predict. This phenomena is known as Outcome Performativity. This paper formalises an approach for detecting Outcome Performativity using prediction intervention called Outcome Performativity A/B Detection (OPAB). OPAB enables the detection of Outcome Performativity by assessing the dissimilarity in outcome distributions produced by different predictions groups (interventions). If that dissimilarity is significant, Outcome Performativity is detected. We derive sample complexity bounds for OPAB under various Outcome Performative assumption classes which we empirically validate. Results show that detecting Outcome Performativity using OPAB is achievable in numerous cases. Results also show the presence of regions of indistinguishability which describe settings where the allotted number of interventions are insufficient for detecting Outcome Performativity. The results of which have broader practical implications for the detectability of Outcome Performativity in settings where samples are scarce, cost-prohibitive or potentially unethical to obtain. The paper concludes with a case study on the efficacy of OPAB on the Open Bandits dataset, and provides directions for future work.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces OPAB (Outcome Performativity A/B Detection), a prediction intervention method for detecting outcome performativity by comparing outcome distributions across different prediction groups. It derives and validates sample complexity bounds, identifies regions of indistinguishability where detection fails due to insufficient interventions, and demonstrates practical efficacy on the Open Bandits dataset.
AI.motivation: In domains like palliative care, credit assignment, and recommender systems, predictions can causally influence the outcomes they aim to predict — a phenomenon termed Outcome Performativity. Detecting whether such performativity exists is critical, yet no formal detection framework with theoretical guarantees existed prior to this work.
AI.method: The authors propose OPAB, which operates by partitioning predictions into distinct intervention groups (A/B style) and statistically testing the dissimilarity between their resulting outcome distributions. They derive sample complexity bounds under several classes of outcome performative assumptions and empirically validate these bounds. They also characterize regions of indistinguishability — settings where limited intervention samples render performativity undetectable.
AI.result: OPAB successfully detects outcome performativity across numerous simulated scenarios. The derived sample complexity bounds hold empirically. The analysis reveals regions of indistinguishability with practical implications: when samples are scarce, cost-prohibitive, or unethical to collect, performativity may be fundamentally undetectable. A case study on the Open Bandits dataset further demonstrates OPAB's real-world efficacy.
AI.conclusion: Outcome performativity detection via OPAB is feasible under realistic conditions, but the existence of indistinguishability regions imposes fundamental limits on detectability in resource-constrained or ethically constrained settings. The work opens avenues for future research into more sample-efficient detection methods and broader empirical validation.

title: Two Calls Beat Five Agents: Evaluating Multi-Agent Pipelines Against Self-Refinement for Local Language Models
summary: Multi-agent LLM pipeline systems break down the task among multiple roles for better reasoning, but are benchmarked mainly with large-scale commercial models. In this study, we investigate Parishad, a structured multi-agent system involving five roles, by deploying it on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, a local model, on two datasets: GSM8K (500 questions) and HumanEval (164 questions), compared with prompting directly and two-call self-refinement. The multi-agent system drops GSM8K accuracy from 75.0\% to 45.0\% with JSON data format due to the error accumulation problem. With plaintext format, the accuracy is restored to 82.0\%. A two-call self-refinement strategy (V1) can achieve 86.2\% accuracy on GSM8K, with 7.4$\times$ lower token usage. However, the same V1 implementation on HumanEval---where direct accuracy is already 96.3\%---actively destroys performance (66.5\%). A task-aware gated redesign (V2) applied to HumanEval preserves accuracy at 95.1\%. Our results demonstrate that communication format and implementation details determine outcomes more than architectural complexity, and that simpler approaches match or outperform multi-agent pipelines for local 7B model deployment. All code and data are released.

AI.tldr: Investigates a 5-role multi-agent LLM system (Parishad) on a local 7B model, finding that communication format and implementation details matter more than architectural complexity, and that simpler strategies often outperform complex multi-agent pipelines.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM pipelines are predominantly benchmarked on large-scale commercial models. The authors aim to assess whether such structured multi-agent systems provide genuine benefits when deployed on smaller, locally-run open-source models (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), and to isolate what factors drive performance changes.
AI.method: The authors implement Parishad, a structured 5-role multi-agent system, on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and evaluate it on GSM8K (math reasoning, 500 questions) and HumanEval (code generation, 164 questions). They compare against direct prompting and a two-call self-refinement baseline (V1). They ablate JSON vs. plaintext communication formats and introduce a task-aware gated refinement design (V2) for HumanEval.
AI.result: On GSM8K: direct accuracy 75.0%; Parishad with JSON format drops to 45.0% (error accumulation); plaintext format restores to 82.0%; two-call self-refinement V1 reaches 86.2% with 7.4× lower token usage. On HumanEval: direct accuracy 96.3%; V1 self-refinement destroys performance (66.5%); task-aware gated V2 preserves accuracy at 95.1%.
AI.conclusion: Communication format (JSON vs. plaintext) and implementation details dominate outcomes over architectural complexity. Simpler approaches (direct prompting, self-refinement) can match or exceed multi-agent pipelines for local 7B model deployment. Task-aware gating mechanisms can mitigate the destructive effects of unnecessary refinement on already-solved tasks.

title: Temporally Centered SIGReg Improves Multi-Task LeWorldModel Learning: From Analysis to Method
summary: Recent work on LeWorldModel (LeWM) has shown that the Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularizer (SIGReg) enables stable end-to-end world-model learning from pixels by regularizing the latent marginal distribution toward an isotropic Gaussian, thereby preventing representation collapse. While effective and elegant in single-task settings, this recipe does not extend reliably to multi-task training, leading to substantially worse downstream behavior-cloning performance. In this paper, we show that marginal Gaussianization compresses the separation between task-dependent latent clusters relative to within-cluster variation. This compression introduces representation aliasing across tasks and states, and makes the learned representations highly sensitive to small visual perturbations. To address this problem, we apply SIGReg to temporally centered residuals rather than to the latent marginal distribution. This surrogate target places no direct regularization pressure on the separation among cluster centers, removes the requirement that the full latent follow a single isotropic Gaussian, and retains the anti-collapse effect of SIGReg. On the LIBERO benchmark, our method improves downstream success on the long-horizon suite by 1.7x and raises the average success rate across four suites from 53.2% to 73.6%. Without external pretraining, it slightly outperforms Diffusion Policy trained from scratch and approaches the performance of large-scale pretrained policy baselines. These results reveal a structural incompatibility between marginal Gaussian priors and multi-task latent structure, and provide a simple route toward stable and scalable end-to-end multi-task world-model learning.

AI.tldr: Marginal Gaussianization in world models causes representation aliasing across tasks; applying SIGReg to temporally centered residuals instead preserves cluster separation and yields significant multi-task performance gains.
AI.motivation: LeWM with SIGReg works well for single-task world-model learning but fails in multi-task settings. The authors identify that marginal Gaussianization compresses inter-cluster separation relative to intra-cluster variation, causing representation aliasing and sensitivity to visual perturbations across tasks.
AI.method: Instead of applying SIGReg to the latent marginal distribution, the authors apply it to temporally centered residuals. This surrogate target removes direct regularization pressure on cluster-center separation, eliminates the requirement that the full latent follow a single isotropic Gaussian, while preserving the anti-collapse benefits of SIGReg.
AI.result: On LIBERO, the method improves long-horizon suite success by 1.7× and raises average success across four suites from 53.2% to 73.6%. It slightly outperforms scratch-trained Diffusion Policy and approaches large-scale pretrained policy baselines, all without external pretraining.
AI.conclusion: There is a structural incompatibility between marginal Gaussian priors and multi-task latent structure. Applying SIGReg to temporally centered residuals provides a simple, stable, and scalable solution for end-to-end multi-task world-model learning.

title: Surrogate assisted diversity estimation in neural ensemble search
comment: The paper was presented at the "Artificial Intelligence Applications and Innovations 2026" conference. The final publication is available at https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-032-30612-8_12
summary: Ensembles are a standard way to improve the performance and robustness of deep neural networks, but their effectiveness crucially depends on both the quality and the diversity of individual models. Most neural architecture search (NAS) methods are computationally expensive. Extending them to neural ensemble search (NES), which requires joint optimization of individual architectures and their ensemble composition, leads to an exponential growth of the search space and makes the problem computationally intractable. To address this, we introduce a dual-objective surrogate-guided ensemble search: candidate architectures are represented as directed acyclic graphs, and two surrogate models are trained independently to estimate predictive accuracy and diversity potential. Their combined estimates guide an NES framework that efficiently identifies architectures that are both individually strong and collectively diverse. Our final ensemble achieves competitive or superior performance compared to standard baselines such as Deep Ensembles and Random Search on FashionMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a dual-objective surrogate-guided neural ensemble search (NES) method that efficiently finds architectures that are both individually accurate and collectively diverse, achieving competitive performance against Deep Ensembles and Random Search on standard benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Ensembles improve DNN performance and robustness, but their effectiveness depends on both individual model quality and diversity. Extending NAS to NES causes exponential search space growth, making joint optimization of individual architectures and ensemble composition computationally intractable.
AI.method: Candidate architectures are represented as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Two independent surrogate models are trained to estimate (1) predictive accuracy and (2) diversity potential. Their combined estimates guide an NES framework to efficiently identify architectures that are both individually strong and collectively diverse.
AI.result: The final ensemble achieves competitive or superior performance compared to Deep Ensembles and Random Search baselines on FashionMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100.
AI.conclusion: Dual-objective surrogate guidance effectively addresses the computational intractability of NES, enabling the discovery of ensembles that balance individual accuracy with collective diversity.

title: Foundation Models for Face Presentation Attack Detection: A Unified Linear-Probing Benchmark
summary: Face presentation attack detection (PAD) remains challenging under cross-dataset evaluation, where domain shift degrades models trained on a single dataset. The scarcity of large-scale labeled data motivates adapting pretrained vision models rather than training task-specific architectures from scratch, raising a fundamental question: do general-purpose vision foundation models encode PAD-relevant information accessible with minimal task-specific training? To investigate, we systematically evaluate 24 frozen encoders, including self-supervised vision transformers, vision-language encoders, and supervised CNNs, using a unified linear-probing protocol on the MCIO benchmark (MSU-MFSD, CASIA-FASD, Replay-Attack, OULU-NPU). The backbone remains fixed, and only a lightweight linear head is trained to isolate the PAD information already present in the pretrained representation. %We report intra- and cross-dataset performance, along with accuracy-compute trade-offs, relative to two specialist PAD baselines. Results show that frozen foundation-model representations can support strong intra-dataset PAD performance with only a linear classifier, but this performance does not reliably transfer across datasets. Model scale is beneficial within several families, although the effect is not monotonic and is strongly mediated by architecture and pretraining. InternViT-6B achieves the lowest mean intra-dataset error, whereas CLIP ViT-B/32 offers the most favorable cross-dataset transfer-compute trade-off among the evaluated probes. These findings suggest that while pretrained representations contain PAD-relevant information, explicit adaptation remains necessary to address domain shift.

AI.tldr: Evaluates 24 frozen pretrained vision encoders for face PAD via linear probing, finding strong intra-dataset but weak cross-dataset performance, with InternViT-6B best intra-dataset and CLIP ViT-B/32 best transfer-compute trade-off.
AI.motivation: Face PAD suffers from domain shift in cross-dataset settings, and large-scale labeled PAD data is scarce. The authors investigate whether general-purpose vision foundation models already encode PAD-relevant information that can be extracted with minimal training, avoiding the need for task-specific architectures trained from scratch.
AI.method: Systematic linear-probing evaluation of 24 frozen encoders (self-supervised ViTs, vision-language encoders, supervised CNNs) on the MCIO benchmark (MSU-MFSD, CASIA-FASD, Replay-Attack, OULU-NPU). Only a lightweight linear head is trained on frozen backbone features to isolate pre-existing PAD-relevant information.
AI.result: Frozen foundation models achieve strong intra-dataset PAD performance with linear classifiers but fail to transfer reliably across datasets. Scale helps within model families but is non-monotonic and mediated by architecture/pretraining. InternViT-6B achieves lowest mean intra-dataset error; CLIP ViT-B/32 offers best cross-dataset transfer-compute trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained representations contain PAD-relevant information accessible via linear probing, but explicit adaptation beyond frozen representations is necessary to address domain shift in cross-dataset face PAD.

title: What Can Latent World Models Know? Physical Parameter Identifiability in Multimodal Predictive Representations
summary: A central premise of latent world models is that predicting the future forces a representation to internalize the physics of its environment. Which physical quantities does a trained latent actually contain, and what decides this? We answer with controlled interventions in POKEWORLD, an interactive environment whose visually identical objects hide mass, drag, and contact stiffness. A certificate-gated protocol first certifies each parameter as recoverable from raw observations, then measures whether it enters the latent, so a null result can be attributed to the objective rather than to the environment. The resulting identifiability map has two organizing mechanisms and one frontier. Inputs limit what can be known, while prediction targets decide what is retained. Stiffness enters the latent only when touch is forecast ($R^2=0.50$, compared with $-0.02$ when the same signal is merely fused into the input), and under single-step prediction a vision-only latent discards even perfectly visible object state. Drag marks the frontier. It carries a recoverability certificate of 0.89 yet plateaus near 0.13 under every deterministic prediction objective we test, while a supervised head on the same trunk reaches 0.45. Parameters whose readout is slow and ratio-type under the sensed coordinates fall outside what these objectives acquire. On RH20T, an input-target factorial across scaling curves reproduces both mechanisms across two robots and 4,258 episodes. Every arm missing information or prediction pressure stays flat over a fivefold data range, and only the full multimodal objective forecasts force beyond a persistence baseline, with held-out gains that grow with scale. Objective structure determines which physical parameters a latent acquires, and additional data improves only the parameters it already acquires.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates which physical parameters are learned by latent world models, using controlled interventions in a custom environment (POKEWORLD) and real-world robotic data (RH20T). It finds that prediction targets, not just input modality, determine which physics enter the latent representation, identifying a "frontier" of parameters (like drag) that are recoverable from observations but not acquired by standard prediction objectives.
AI.motivation: Latent world models are premised on the idea that predicting the future forces representations to internalize environmental physics, but it is unclear which physical quantities actually enter the latent and what governs this selection. The authors aim to disentangle whether failures to recover physical parameters stem from the objective function or from insufficient information in observations, requiring a rigorous causal framework with ground-truth access.
AI.method: The authors introduce POKEWORLD, an interactive environment with visually identical objects that vary in hidden physical parameters (mass, drag, contact stiffness). They employ a certificate-gated protocol: first, a certifier verifies that each parameter is recoverable from raw observations (establishing an upper bound); second, they measure whether the parameter enters the latent under various prediction objectives. They systematically vary inputs (vision-only, multimodal) and prediction targets (single-step, multi-step, with/without touch forecasting) to build an identifiability map. The findings are validated on RH20T, a real-world robot dataset, using a factorial design across input modalities, prediction targets, and data scales (4,258 episodes, two robots).
AI.result: Two organizing mechanisms emerge: (1) inputs limit what can be known, (2) prediction targets decide what is retained. Stiffness only enters the latent when touch is forecast (R²=0.50 vs. -0.02 when merely fused into input). Single-step vision-only prediction discards perfectly visible object state. Drag forms a "frontier": it has a recoverability certificate of 0.89 but plateaus at ~0.13 under all deterministic prediction objectives tested, while a supervised head on the same trunk reaches 0.45. Parameters with slow, ratio-type readout under sensed coordinates fall outside what prediction objectives acquire. On RH20T, scaling curves confirm both mechanisms: unimodal or single-task arms stay flat across a fivefold data range, while only the full multimodal objective forecasts force beyond a persistence baseline, with gains that grow with scale.
AI.conclusion: Objective structure — specifically what is being predicted — determines which physical parameters a latent representation acquires. Additional data improves only those parameters the objective already captures; it does not cause new physical quantities to emerge. This implies that designing prediction targets is more critical than scaling data for learning specific physical properties, and that some parameters (like drag) may require objectives beyond standard next-step or multi-step deterministic prediction.

title: BayesAME: Bayesian Active Model Evaluation
summary: Evaluating large generative models across benchmarks is time-consuming and computationally expensive. This drives the need for methods that can estimate full benchmark performance by evaluating models on only a subset of items, known as a coreset. Current literature mostly requires the practitioner to input a coreset size. However, when reliable performance estimation takes priority over efficiency, an evaluation method should also be capable of automatically determining a coreset size that reflects this priority. We introduce BayesAME, a sequential Bayesian framework specifically targeting automatic determination of the coreset size. BayesAME models performance as a random variable by defining a latent ability for each group of items sharing the same historical model performances, with a joint prior distribution encoding the belief that the target model behaves similarly to these historical models. The posterior distribution over these abilities is used to derive performance estimators, quantify performance uncertainty, and select items to add to the coreset via an information-gain criterion. The coreset is iteratively augmented until the performance estimate fluctuation and the performance uncertainty fall below their respective user-defined thresholds. We propose a multi-target extension that captures performance correlations across multiple target models to further reduce the coreset size. Through extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks, we demonstrate that BayesAME consistently outperforms sequential adaptations of existing methods. Crucially, our comprehensive analysis addresses recent skepticism in the literature, establishing that non-random coreset selection is advantageous over random selection. Finally, we highlight that leveraging continuous response log-likelihoods over traditional binary scores significantly enhances estimation accuracy.

AI.tldr: BayesAME is a sequential Bayesian framework that automatically determines coreset size for benchmark evaluation by modeling item-group latent abilities, using information-gain for item selection, and stopping when performance uncertainty drops below user-defined thresholds. It extends to multi-target settings and demonstrates superiority over existing methods.
AI.motivation: Evaluating large generative models on full benchmarks is computationally prohibitive. Existing coreset methods require users to manually specify coreset size, but when estimation reliability is paramount, an automatic stopping criterion is needed. The authors also seek to address skepticism about whether non-random coreset selection truly outperforms random selection.
AI.method: BayesAME models model performance as a random variable via latent abilities for item groups sharing historical performance patterns, with a joint prior encoding similarity to historical models. The posterior over abilities yields performance estimators and uncertainty quantification. Items are added to the coreset iteratively using an information-gain criterion. Stopping occurs when both performance estimate fluctuation and uncertainty fall below user-defined thresholds. A multi-target extension captures inter-model performance correlations to further reduce coreset size.
AI.result: BayesAME consistently outperforms sequential adaptations of existing methods across diverse benchmarks. Non-random coreset selection proves advantageous over random selection. Using continuous response log-likelihoods instead of binary scores significantly improves estimation accuracy.
AI.conclusion: BayesAME provides an effective, principled solution for automatic coreset sizing in benchmark evaluation, establishing that non-random, uncertainty-driven item selection with continuous likelihoods yields superior performance estimation compared to both random baselines and existing sequential methods.

title: TreeCCA: Canonical Correlation Analysis via Gradient-Boosted Trees
summary:
Gradient-boosted trees dominate tabular machine learning, yet canonical correlation analysis has always relied on linear or neural encoders. We propose \textbf{TreeCCA}, the first method to train gradient-boosted tree ensembles end-to-end as CCA encoders, inheriting their plug-and-play reliability: no architecture design, familiar hyperparameters, and strong performance with defaults. The technical enabler is the Eckart-Young (EY) loss, which supplies closed-form per-sample gradients that slot directly into any standard GBT library (XGBoost, LightGBM) as a custom objective.
  TreeCCA is the first CCA method to combine nonlinear accuracy with native interpretability: every tree split selects one feature, so gain importances reveal which inputs drive cross-view correlation at no extra cost. We demonstrate these properties on synthetic benchmarks, where TreeCCA matches or exceeds Deep CCA (2.61 vs.\ 2.43 on Signed Power; 2.93 vs.\ 2.89 on Hermite), and on a sparse benchmark with zero linear cross-view covariance, where TreeCCA recovers the true support with $\text{Precision@}S = 1.00$ at $p=50$ while PMD finds no signal. On the UCI HAR sensor-fusion benchmark, TreeCCA achieves comparable accuracy to Deep CCA at $5\times$ lower cost, while XGBoost gain importances directly validate a physics-motivated hypothesis about the data --- an interpretation not readily available with neural encoders. Across five popular tabular multi-view datasets, TreeMCCA consistently matches or exceeds linear CCA in both nonlinear correlation extraction and downstream classification accuracy.

AI.tldr: TreeCCA is the first method to train gradient-boosted tree ensembles end-to-end as CCA encoders using the Eckart-Young loss, enabling nonlinear accuracy with native interpretability via feature gain importances, matching or exceeding Deep CCA on benchmarks while being simpler and cheaper.
AI.motivation: Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) has historically relied on linear or neural encoders, while gradient-boosted trees (GBTs) dominate tabular ML with their plug-and-play reliability, strong defaults, and interpretability. There is a gap: no method existed to use GBTs as CCA encoders end-to-end.
AI.method: TreeCCA trains gradient-boosted tree ensembles (XGBoost, LightGBM) as CCA encoders using the Eckart-Young (EY) loss, which provides closed-form per-sample gradients compatible as a custom objective in any standard GBT library. The method extends to multi-view settings (TreeMCCA). Interpretability is native: tree split gain importances reveal which features drive cross-view correlation.
AI.result: TreeCCA matches/exceeds Deep CCA on synthetic benchmarks (2.61 vs 2.43 on Signed Power; 2.93 vs 2.89 on Hermite). On a sparse benchmark with zero linear cross-view covariance, TreeCCA achieves Precision@S = 1.00 at p=50 while PMD finds no signal. On UCI HAR sensor-fusion, TreeCCA matches Deep CCA at 5× lower cost while gain importances validate a physics-motivated hypothesis. TreeMCCA matches or exceeds linear CCA on five tabular multi-view datasets in both nonlinear correlation and downstream classification.
AI.conclusion: TreeCCA successfully bridges the gap between GBTs and CCA, offering the first method that combines nonlinear cross-view correlation extraction with native tree-based interpretability, plug-and-play simplicity, and strong empirical performance comparable to or better than deep neural alternatives.

title: Lottery Tickets Are Not Deployment Tickets
summary: Reports on how sparsification, compression, and lottery tickets change model behavior have been mixed in the prior literature, with beneficial effects observed in some studies and adverse effects in others. Moreover, prior work has not considered actual deployment conditions, where decision logic is already fixed for the incumbent. To assess these mixed findings from a practical standpoint, we study the production-replacement question at the deployment level, namely whether an accuracy-matched lottery ticket or another sparse challenger can replace an incumbent dense model without reconfiguring downstream decision logic. We therefore audit a broad, protocol-specific panel of deployment-relevant behaviors spanning calibration, OOD response, class-level reliability, representations, and downstream policy decisions, and summarize clean-accuracy-excluded deviations with a behavioral-compatibility distance. Across extensive experiments, sparse candidates repeatedly recover dense-reference accuracy yet remain behaviorally different; in several study-band-matched settings, LTs also show lower corruption accuracy. In small-gap settings with fixed-threshold policy diagnostics, lottery-ticket replacement changes 7% to 10% of accept--review decisions. This churn creates precisely the burden that drop-in replacement is meant to avoid: reconfiguring and revalidating downstream decision logic. These findings establish the limits of clean-accuracy certification: Establishing compatibility with a fixed incumbent is distinct from attributing churn uniquely to sparsity or treating every measured deviation as harmful. Our theory explains the routing result: Even exact pointwise top-1 agreement cannot bound fixed-threshold decision changes, and small confidence shifts near the operating boundary can generate first-order routing churn.

AI.tldr: Sparse models (lottery tickets) that match dense models on clean accuracy still exhibit significant behavioral deviations — including calibration, OOD robustness, and representation shifts. In deployment, these deviations cause 7–10% decision churn under fixed-threshold policies, undermining drop-in replacement. Theoretically, even exact top-1 agreement cannot bound decision changes when confidence scores shift near the operating threshold.
AI.motivation: Prior literature reports contradictory findings on whether sparsification helps or harms model behavior. Crucially, no prior work evaluates sparse models under real deployment conditions where downstream decision logic (thresholds, policies) is already fixed for an incumbent dense model. The paper asks: can a sparse challenger truly serve as a drop-in replacement without forcing costly reconfiguration of the production pipeline?
AI.method: The authors define a behavioral-compatibility distance that aggregates deviations across a protocol-specific panel: calibration error, OOD/corruption accuracy, class-level reliability, representational similarity, and fixed-threshold downstream policy decisions. They compare accuracy-matched lottery tickets (and other sparse variants) against dense incumbents, measuring churn — the fraction of accept/review decisions that flip under a fixed decision boundary. A theoretical result shows that even perfect pointwise top-1 agreement cannot bound fixed-threshold routing churn, because small confidence shifts near the threshold drive first-order decision changes.
AI.result: Across extensive experiments, sparse candidates consistently recover dense-reference clean accuracy yet remain behaviorally different on multiple axes. Lottery tickets show lower corruption accuracy in several settings. In small-gap regimes under fixed-threshold policies, lottery-ticket replacement changes 7–10% of accept/review decisions — substantial churn that necessitates revalidation. The theory confirms this is a structural phenomenon: exact top-1 agreement provides no safety guarantee against routing churn.
AI.conclusion: Clean-accuracy matching is insufficient to certify a sparse model as a safe drop-in replacement. Behavioral compatibility with a fixed incumbent requires a broader audit beyond accuracy. The paper establishes that attribution of churn uniquely to sparsity and treating every deviation as harmful are both distinct from the practical compatibility question, and it provides a theoretical explanation for why even pointwise agreement fails to prevent decision-level disruption.

title: CoCaRS: Correlation Calibration-Based Redundancy Suppression for Heterogeneous Knowledge Distillation
summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) enables a compact student model to learn from a powerful teacher and has become an effective paradigm for model compression. The emergence of diverse model architectures has extended KD from homogeneous to heterogeneous settings. However, differences in architectural inductive biases between the teacher and student models often result in substantial representation discrepancies, limiting the effectiveness of direct knowledge transfer. Recently, redundancy suppression has offered a new perspective on heterogeneous KD by preserving cross-architecture invariance and reducing feature redundancy through decorrelation of teacher-student feature correlations. Nevertheless, this formulation may weaken useful structural information through uniform decorrelation, while a fixed coefficient may make the effective contribution of redundancy suppression sensitive to teacher-student pairs and training stages. To address these problems, Correlation Calibration-based Redundancy Suppression (CoCaRS) is proposed to better retain structural information while suppressing redundancy and reduce sensitivity to coefficient settings across teacher-student pairs and training stages. Specifically, CoCaRS calibrates feature decorrelation through Confusion Evidence Estimation (CEE) and Strength Allocation Control (SAC), which respectively capture reliable semantic relations for correlation estimation and preserve discriminative structure during decorrelation. Adaptive Coefficient Regulation (ACR) further regulates the contribution of the calibrated redundancy suppression objective according to its relative loss scale, reducing sensitivity to coefficient settings. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K validate the effectiveness of CoCaRS in improving distillation performance and reducing sensitivity to coefficient settings. Code will be released soon.

AI.tldr: CoCaRS proposes a calibrated redundancy suppression method for heterogeneous knowledge distillation that better retains structural information and adaptively regulates the contribution of the decorrelation objective, improving performance and reducing sensitivity to coefficient settings.
AI.motivation: Existing redundancy suppression methods for heterogeneous KD use uniform decorrelation and fixed coefficients, which can weaken useful structural information and make the distillation process sensitive to teacher-student pairs and training stages.
AI.method: CoCaRS introduces three components: (1) Confusion Evidence Estimation (CEE) to capture reliable semantic relations for correlation estimation; (2) Strength Allocation Control (SAC) to preserve discriminative structure during decorrelation; and (3) Adaptive Coefficient Regulation (ACR) to dynamically adjust the redundancy suppression contribution based on relative loss scale.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K validate that CoCaRS improves distillation performance and reduces sensitivity to coefficient settings across different teacher-student pairs and training stages.
AI.conclusion: CoCaRS effectively addresses the limitations of uniform decorrelation and fixed coefficients in heterogeneous KD by calibrating feature decorrelation and adaptively regulating its contribution, achieving superior and more robust distillation outcomes.

title: Parameter-Free Dynamic Regret for Online Convex Optimization under Heavy-Tailed Noise
summary: We study online convex optimization (OCO) in non-stationary environments under heavy-tailed noise, where the stochastic gradient oracle admits only a finite $p$-th central moment for some $p \in (1, 2]$. While static regret is well-understood, achieving universal dynamic regret in a parameter-free manner remains an open challenge. We resolve this by proposing \textbf{HT-PAder}, a parameter-free algorithm combining restarted AdaGrad experts over a geometric pool of block lengths with a pathwise meta-algorithm, \textbf{AdaGrad-Hedge}, which requires no moment conditions on meta-losses. For a domain of diameter $D$, Lipschitz constant $G$, noise level $σ$, and comparator path length $P_T$, HT-PAder achieves an expected universal dynamic regret of \[ \widetilde O\left( GD\sqrt{T(1+P_T/D)} + σD T^{1/p}(1+P_T/D)^{(p-1)/p} \right). \] The algorithm does not require prior knowledge of any of these problem parameters. Even in the special case of finite variance ($p=2$), HT-PAder provides the first parameter-free minimax universal dynamic regret guarantee. We also prove a matching lower bound, establishing the optimality of the path-length exponent.

AI.tldr: HT-PAder is a parameter-free algorithm for non-stationary online convex optimization under heavy-tailed noise (finite p-th moment, p∈(1,2]), achieving optimal universal dynamic regret without requiring prior knowledge of any problem parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing OCO methods either require bounded variance (p=2) or need prior knowledge of problem parameters to achieve dynamic regret guarantees. The open challenge is parameter-free universal dynamic regret under heavy-tailed noise with only finite p-th moment (p∈(1,2]), where neither the noise level σ, path length P_T, nor moment bound p is known in advance.
AI.method: HT-PAder combines two components: (1) restarted AdaGrad experts operating over a geometric grid of block lengths to handle unknown path length, and (2) a pathwise meta-algorithm called AdaGrad-Hedge that requires no moment conditions on meta-losses, enabling the overall scheme to be fully parameter-free. The algorithm adapts to unknown D, G, σ, P_T, and p.
AI.result: HT-PAder achieves expected universal dynamic regret of Õ(G D √(T(1+P_T/D)) + σ D T^{1/p} (1+P_T/D)^{(p-1)/p}). A matching lower bound is proved, confirming optimality of the path-length exponent. For p=2 (finite variance), this provides the first parameter-free minimax universal dynamic regret guarantee.
AI.conclusion: The paper resolves the open problem of parameter-free universal dynamic regret in heavy-tailed OCO, establishing both an upper bound via HT-PAder and a matching lower bound, thus characterizing the minimax optimal rate.

title: Single-Beat Cuffless Blood Pressure Estimation Using Ear-PPG and ECG with a Lightweight Hybrid Learning Framework
summary: Continuous cuffless blood pressure (BP) monitoring remains challenging due to motion artifacts, physiological variability, and the limited robustness of conventional pulse transit time (PTT) models under dynamic conditions. Many prior approaches rely on multi-second windows to stabilize estimation, an assumption that is frequently violated during real-world monitoring with intermittent signal corruption. Here, we show that discriminative BP-related information is preserved at the single-beat level and present a lightweight multi-modal wearable framework for continuous BP estimation.
