The system integrates synchronized chest electrocardiography (ECG) and ear-clip reflectance photoplethysmography, each co-located with a 6-axis inertial measurement unit to provide motion context. We introduce a hybrid learning architecture in which a one-dimensional convolutional neural network extracts a 64-dimensional embedding from individual PPG beats and fuses it with 30 physiology-grounded features, including PTT statistics and heart rate variability, followed by LightGBM regression. The method was evaluated using a multi-phase stress protocol ($n=10$) and the PulseDB public dataset with subject-disjoint validation. Across 30 independent runs, the model achieved mean absolute errors of $4.02 \pm 0.21$~mmHg for systolic BP and $1.79 \pm 0.05$~mmHg for diastolic BP, corresponding to a 28.2\% reduction in combined MAE relative to baseline models. By enabling beat-wise estimation without long temporal context, this framework supports computationally efficient cuffless BP monitoring suitable for wearable deployment under practical resource constraints. The source code for this work is available at https://github.com/SYMBIOX-Lab/BP-wireless.

AI.tldr: A lightweight multi-modal wearable framework for beat-wise cuffless blood pressure estimation using ECG, PPG, and IMU signals, achieving MAE of 4.02 mmHg (SBP) and 1.79 mmHg (DBP) via a hybrid CNN + LightGBM architecture.
AI.motivation: Continuous cuffless BP monitoring suffers from motion artifacts and physiological variability; conventional PTT models require multi-second stable windows that are unrealistic during real-world intermittent signal corruption. The authors hypothesize that discriminative BP information exists at the single-beat level.
AI.method: A wearable system integrating chest ECG and ear-clip reflectance PPG, each with a 6-axis IMU for motion context. A hybrid architecture uses a 1D-CNN to extract 64-dim embeddings from individual PPG beats, fused with 30 physiology-grounded features (PTT statistics, HRV), followed by LightGBM regression. Evaluated via multi-phase stress protocol (n=10) and PulseDB with subject-disjoint validation over 30 independent runs.
AI.result: MAE of 4.02 ± 0.21 mmHg for SBP and 1.79 ± 0.05 mmHg for DBP, representing a 28.2% reduction in combined MAE compared to baseline models.
AI.conclusion: Beat-wise estimation without long temporal context enables computationally efficient cuffless BP monitoring suitable for wearable deployment under practical resource constraints.

title: Equilibrium Training of Energy-Based Models with Parallel Trajectory Tempering
summary: Energy-Based Models (EBMs) provide an interpretable framework for generative modeling of scientific data, but poor Markov Chain Monte Carlo mixing often limits their reliability. We introduce a training algorithm based on Parallel Trajectory Tempering (PTT), which exploits the continuity of the optimization path to maintain equilibrium sampling throughout learning. This enables stable and fast training on highly multimodal and data-scarce scientific datasets. Combined with reservoir sampling and adaptive optimization, PTT has a computational cost comparable to Persistent Contrastive Divergence, making it a practical replacement for standard training methods. It also provides direct estimates of thermalization times, equilibrium samples from trained models, and accurate log-likelihoods at essentially no additional cost. Experiments on Restricted Boltzmann Machines show that PTT consistently outperforms existing EBM training approaches. On discrete tabular data, it also surpasses state-of-the-art deep generative models, yielding higher-quality samples and greater robustness to overfitting and limited data. Our results make equilibrium maximum-likelihood training of EBMs practical and computationally efficient.

AI.tldr: PTT introduces a training algorithm for Energy-Based Models that leverages parallel trajectory tempering to maintain equilibrium sampling during learning, enabling stable, fast training on multimodal, data-scarce scientific datasets while outperforming existing EBM and deep generative approaches.
AI.motivation: EBMs offer interpretable generative modeling for scientific data but suffer from poor MCMC mixing, which undermines reliability. Existing training methods struggle with highly multimodal distributions and limited data, motivating the need for an approach that ensures equilibrium sampling throughout training.
AI.method: The authors propose Parallel Trajectory Tempering (PTT), which exploits continuity along the optimization path to maintain equilibrium sampling throughout learning. PTT is combined with reservoir sampling and adaptive optimization, achieving computational cost comparable to Persistent Contrastive Divergence. It simultaneously provides estimates of thermalization times, equilibrium samples, and accurate log-likelihoods at negligible additional cost.
AI.result: On Restricted Boltzmann Machines, PTT consistently outperforms existing EBM training methods. On discrete tabular data, it surpasses state-of-the-art deep generative models, yielding higher-quality samples and greater robustness to overfitting and limited data.
AI.conclusion: PTT makes equilibrium maximum-likelihood training of EBMs both practical and computationally efficient, serving as a viable replacement for standard methods like Persistent Contrastive Divergence.

title: Scores Are Not Decisions: Cost-Aware Stopping for Tool Acquisition in LLM Agents
summary: As LLM agents increasingly depend on diverse external services such as search engines, databases, and connectors, agent harnesses face a fundamental tool-selection challenge: acquiring too few tools leaves the task under-informed, while too many adds cost, context load, and privacy exposure. Routers and retrievers can rank candidate tools by relevance, but a ranking alone does not determine how many are worth selecting. Existing approaches leave acquisition under heterogeneous costs unaddressed. We formulate this decision as cost-aware marginal decision-focused stopping (CAM-DF) over ranked tool prefixes, with CAM-DF-lite as a compact interpretable variant. We train directly on the offline gap between stopping now and the best continuation: its sign labels the decision, its magnitude weights each error by the payoff at stake. We prove this objective is Bayes-aligned with the stopping target and that score-only rules are suboptimal under heterogeneous costs. We evaluate on 1,343 tasks across five tool-use domains. On $τ$-bench Retail, CAM-DF attains the highest payoff among deployable methods, with gains over a predict-then-threshold baseline across all five ranking sources and two cost regimes. Our approach is state-of-the-art under heterogeneous costs and high cost pressure, with larger gains under weaker rankings. In live execution, CAM-DF exposes the agent to 37\% fewer tools than full access while maintaining comparable task success. The CAM-DF family is a lightweight pre-execution plugin that turns existing tool rankings into lower-cost acquisition decisions without fine-tuning the underlying LLM.

AI.tldr: CAM-DF is a lightweight, cost-aware stopping rule that decides how many tools from a ranked list are worth acquiring for an LLM agent, optimizing the trade-off between tool informativeness and heterogeneous usage costs without fine-tuning the underlying model.
AI.motivation: LLM agents face a tool-selection problem: too few tools yield under-informed tasks, too many increase cost, context load, and privacy risk. Existing routers and retrievers only rank tools by relevance but do not determine the optimal number to select, especially under heterogeneous per-tool costs. This gap motivates a principled stopping framework.
AI.method: The authors formulate tool acquisition as Cost-Aware Marginal Decision-Focused stopping (CAM-DF) over ranked tool prefixes. They train directly on the offline gap between stopping now and the best continuation — using the sign for classification labels and the magnitude to weight errors by payoff at stake. A compact variant, CAM-DF-lite, offers interpretability. The method is a pre-execution plugin requiring no LLM fine-tuning.
AI.result: Evaluated on 1,343 tasks across five tool-use domains: CAM-DF achieves the highest payoff among deployable methods on τ-bench Retail, outperforming predict-then-threshold baselines across all five ranking sources and two cost regimes. Gains are largest under heterogeneous costs, high cost pressure, and weaker rankings. In live execution, CAM-DF reduces tool exposure by 37% while maintaining comparable task success.
AI.conclusion: CAM-DF provides a state-of-the-art, lightweight solution for cost-aware tool selection that turns existing tool rankings into optimal acquisition decisions. It is Bayes-aligned, theoretically grounded, and empirically validated as superior to score-only rules under heterogeneous costs.

title: Sky sphere representation in language models
summary:
We analyze whether language models of size ~100B have a representation of the night sky map that is decodable from their residual stream. We find that most of the considered open-source models do have such a representation, and it often even surfaces to the top principal components on prompts that ask questions like ``what is close to this object in the night sky''. In all but one model this representation showed significant scores in LOO testing, containing up to 65-85% of variance ($R^2$-score) and having median angular error down to $12^\circ-21^\circ$. We verify that our representation is not a simple leak from a correlated flat representation. To our knowledge, this representation is the first example of a curved high-dimensional irreducible feature manifold.
  Codes used in the paper are published at https://github.com/l3erdnik/Decodable-sky

AI.tldr: Large language models (~100B parameters) encode a decodable representation of the night sky map in their residual streams, with sky coordinates recoverable from principal components, achieving high explained variance (R² up to 65–85%) and median angular errors of 12°–21°.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether LLMs possess internal spatial world models — specifically, a structured representation of the night sky — that can be extracted and decoded from their residual stream activations, and whether such representations constitute genuinely curved, high-dimensional feature manifolds rather than artifacts of flat correlated representations.
AI.method: The authors probed the residual streams of open-source LLMs (~100B scale) on astronomy-related prompts (e.g., "what is close to this object in the night sky"). They applied dimensionality reduction (PCA) to extract sky coordinate representations, evaluated via leave-one-out (LOO) testing, R² scores for explained variance, and median angular error. They also conducted control analyses to rule out leakage from flat correlated representations.
AI.result: Most models exhibited significant, decodable night sky representations, often surfacing in top principal components. LOO testing showed significant scores, with R² capturing up to 65–85% of variance and median angular errors as low as 12°–21°. Controls confirmed the representation is not attributable to simple flat correlation leakage. The authors claim this is the first example of a curved high-dimensional irreducible feature manifold.
AI.conclusion: LLMs develop structured internal representations of the night sky that are decodable, spatially accurate, and geometrically non-trivial (curved manifold). This provides evidence that LLMs can internalize coherent world models beyond surface-level statistical patterns.

title: Hierarchical Spatio-Temporal Transformer for Coherent Emergency Department Forecasting
comment: Accepted at 11th Workshop on Data Science for Social Good - ECML PKDD 2026
summary: Emergency Departments (EDs) are critical access points in healthcare systems, yet they face persistent pressure from unpredictable patient demand, seasonal surges, and non-urgent visits. Effective ED planning requires forecasts at multiple decision-making levels: hospitals need local demand estimates for staffing and bed management, regions require forecasts to coordinate healthcare units, and national authorities need system-wide projections for capacity planning. However, most existing approaches forecast ED demand independently at a single level, ignoring the hierarchy linking hospitals, regions, and national systems. This can produce incoherent predictions, where hospital-level forecasts do not aggregate consistently to regional or national demand. We propose HierSTT, a hierarchical Transformer-based framework for coherent multi-level ED forecasting. HierSTT jointly predicts hospital, regional, and national level demand in a single end-to-end model. A Temporal Fusion Transformer captures national dynamics, while spatio-temporal Transformer encoder-decoder modules model regional and hospital demand conditioned on higher-level forecasts. A coherence-aware loss penalizes cross-level inconsistencies during training. We further introduce a nationwide Portuguese ED dataset covering 81 hospitals across 5 regional health administrations, with heterogeneous covariates at each level. Experiments show that HierSTT reduces average WAPE by 32\% relative to the best non-hierarchical deep learning baseline and outperforms all classical hierarchical reconciliation methods, while producing near-coherent predictions across levels. Additional resources associated with this work are available at https://github.com/FilipaLino/HierSTT.

AI.tldr: HierSTT is a hierarchical Transformer-based framework that jointly forecasts emergency department demand at hospital, regional, and national levels, ensuring cross-level coherence via a coherence-aware loss, and outperforms both non-hierarchical deep learning baselines and classical reconciliation methods on a new Portuguese ED dataset.
AI.motivation: ED demand forecasting is typically done independently at a single level (hospital, regional, or national), ignoring the hierarchical relationships among these levels. This leads to incoherent predictions where lower-level forecasts don't sum to higher-level totals, undermining coordinated planning.
AI.method: HierSTT uses a Temporal Fusion Transformer for national-level dynamics and spatio-temporal Transformer encoder-decoder modules for regional and hospital demand conditioned on higher-level forecasts, all trained end-to-end with a coherence-aware loss that penalizes cross-level inconsistencies. The framework is evaluated on a novel nationwide Portuguese ED dataset spanning 81 hospitals and 5 regional health administrations.
AI.result: HierSTT reduces average WAPE by 32% relative to the best non-hierarchical deep learning baseline and outperforms all classical hierarchical reconciliation methods, while producing near-coherent predictions across all levels.
AI.conclusion: Joint hierarchical forecasting with coherence constraints significantly improves multi-level ED demand prediction, enabling better coordinated resource planning across hospitals, regions, and national healthcare systems.

title: Voronoi Histograms for Adaptive Vectorization of Expected Persistence Diagrams
summary: Persistence Diagram (PD) is known to capture point cloud topology effectively, but its computation has high time complexity. Expected Persistence Diagram (EPD) has been developed to reduce the time cost by studying the topology of multiple subsets of a point cloud and it serves as a distribution of topological features. Existing EPD vectorizations often rely on predefined point transformations, such as Gaussian or landscape functions. We study an alternative discretization based on Voronoi histograms, which trades smooth functional approximation for adaptive partition-based counting. We propose to use Voronoi Diagram-based histogram as the vectorization of EPD, without imposing an explicit smooth point transformation model. Under stated separation and normalization conditions, we establish stability bounds and characterize when the histogram representation preserves Wasserstein-scale variation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed representation on real-world datasets which have significant topological features for classification and dimensionality reduction tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Voronoi Diagram-based histogram as a novel vectorization method for Expected Persistence Diagrams (EPD), replacing smooth functional approximations with adaptive partition-based counting. It establishes stability bounds under separation and normalization conditions, and demonstrates effectiveness on real-world classification and dimensionality reduction tasks.
AI.motivation: Persistence Diagrams (PD) are powerful for capturing point cloud topology but computationally expensive. EPD reduces this cost by aggregating topological features across subsets, yet existing EPD vectorization methods rely on predefined smooth transformations (e.g., Gaussian, landscape functions) that may not adapt well to the underlying data distribution. A more adaptive, partition-based alternative is needed.
AI.method: The authors propose using a Voronoi Diagram-based histogram to discretize the EPD. Rather than imposing an explicit smooth point transformation model, this method partitions the persistence diagram space adaptively using Voronoi cells and counts feature occurrences within each cell. Theoretical analysis establishes stability bounds and conditions under which the histogram preserves Wasserstein-scale variation, relying on stated separation and normalization conditions.
AI.result: The Voronoi histogram representation preserves Wasserstein-scale variation under the established separation and normalization conditions. Empirical validation on real-world datasets shows the method is effective for classification and dimensionality reduction tasks where topological features play a significant role.
AI.conclusion: The Voronoi Diagram-based histogram offers a viable and theoretically grounded alternative to smooth functional vectorizations of EPD, combining adaptivity with stability guarantees and strong empirical performance on topology-sensitive tasks.

title: Minimal Markovization via Stable Quotients in Holonomy-Cover Decision Processes
summary: An agent acting under partial observability must retain a recursively updateable statistic of history that restores the Markov property, but the smallest such statistic is generally unknown. We characterize this minimal Markov sufficient statistic for holonomy-cover decision processes, a structured POMDP class in which the visible dynamics are Markov and every realized visible transition applies a fixed permutation to a hidden mode. In particular, we construct the stable quotient, the coarsest observation-wise abstraction preserving one-step rewards and quotient successors, and prove that the pair of the current observation and stable class forms an exact finite Markov state. When the current class is correctly initialized, exact class tracking requires exactly the minimal memory symbols, in the sense that under reachability and pairwise decision separation at a maximizing observation, no arbitrary finite-memory controller can use fewer. Under resettable diagnostics, nearest-prototype class inference has exponentially decaying error, and a calibrate-then-restart reduction transfers finite-MDP guarantees to the recovered state. The results enable \emph{Holonomy Memory Reinforcement Learning}. It represents memory by the current stable class, updates it through ordered edge transports, identifies local class coordinates when diagnostics are available, and applies a standard finite-MDP RL backbone after synchronization. Experiments recover an exact compression from raw states to quotient states and achieve perfect paired-order accuracy with three decision-time memory states, matching the quotient oracle and outperforming the non-oracle baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs the minimal Markov sufficient statistic for holonomy-cover decision processes (a structured POMDP class). It proves that the stable quotient—the coarsest observation-wise abstraction preserving rewards and successors—paired with the current observation forms an exact finite Markov state requiring minimal memory. This enables Holonomy Memory Reinforcement Learning, which uses stable class tracking and achieves exact compression with minimal memory states in experiments.
AI.motivation: Agents under partial observability need a recursively updateable statistic of history to restore the Markov property, but the minimal such statistic is generally unknown. The authors aim to characterize this minimal Markov sufficient statistic for a structured POMDP class where visible dynamics are Markov and each visible transition applies a fixed permutation to a hidden mode.
AI.method: The authors construct the stable quotient—the coarsest observation-wise abstraction that preserves one-step rewards and quotient successors. They prove this forms an exact finite Markov state when paired with the current observation. Under reachability and pairwise decision separation conditions, they show minimal memory optimality. For inference, they provide nearest-prototype class inference with exponentially decaying error under resettable diagnostics and a calibrate-then-restart reduction to transfer finite-MDP guarantees.
AI.result: The stable quotient paired with current observation provably forms an exact finite Markov state requiring minimal memory symbols. Nearest-prototype class inference achieves exponentially decaying error. Experiments demonstrate exact compression from raw states to quotient states and perfect paired-order accuracy using only three decision-time memory states, matching the quotient oracle and outperforming non-oracle baselines.
AI.conclusion: The results establish Holonomy Memory Reinforcement Learning as a principled framework where memory is represented by the current stable class, updated via ordered edge transports, with local class coordinates identified when diagnostics are available. A standard finite-MDP RL backbone can be applied after synchronization, yielding provably minimal memory representations that empirically match oracle performance.

title: Cost-Sensitive Conformal Prediction and Human-in-the-Loop Abstention for Imbalanced High-Stakes Decision Support: A Multi-Domain Benchmark
summary: High-stakes decision systems in credit scoring, fraud detection, healthcare, and industrial safety require reliable uncertainty quantification under severe class imbalance and asymmetric error costs. Standard marginal conformal prediction (CP) provides valid overall coverage guarantees; however, we show that it severely under-covers rare, costly minority classes, with minority-class coverage dropping to as low as 0.5% on certain datasets. To characterize and address this limitation, we conduct a comprehensive benchmark comparing marginal CP, class-conditional (Mondrian) CP, and cost-controlled abstention mechanisms across 15 real-world imbalanced tabular datasets, 7 classification models, 3 probability calibration techniques, and 10 random seeds, resulting in 3,150 experimental runs. Our results show that Mondrian CP restores valid minority-class coverage, achieving an average minority-coverage improvement of 61.7 percentage points over marginal CP (p < 1e-80). Furthermore, combining Mondrian CP with cost-controlled abstention significantly reduces expected decision cost compared with standard decision boundaries, confidence-based rejectors, and risk-controlled rejectors under realistic human review budgets. We further quantify dataset-specific break-even thresholds at which deferring ambiguous instances to human experts becomes cost-effective. These findings provide practical guidance for deploying distribution-free, cost-aware uncertainty quantification in high-stakes decision support systems.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks uncertainty quantification methods under class imbalance, showing that standard conformal prediction drastically under-covers minority classes. Mondrian (class-conditional) conformal prediction restores valid minority-class coverage (+61.7 pp), and combining it with cost-controlled abstention minimizes expected decision cost in high-stakes applications.
AI.motivation: High-stakes decision systems (credit, fraud, healthcare, industrial safety) suffer from severe class imbalance and asymmetric misclassification costs. Standard marginal conformal prediction—while providing valid overall coverage—catastrophically fails on rare, costly minority classes (coverage as low as 0.5%), undermining trust in safety-critical deployments.
AI.method: A large-scale benchmark across 15 real-world imbalanced tabular datasets, 7 classification models, 3 calibration techniques, and 10 random seeds (3,150 total runs), comparing: (1) marginal conformal prediction, (2) Mondrian (class-conditional) conformal prediction, and (3) cost-controlled abstention mechanisms. They further derive dataset-specific break-even thresholds for cost-effective human deferral under review budgets.
AI.result: Mondrian CP restores valid minority-class coverage, yielding an average improvement of 61.7 percentage points over marginal CP (p < 1e-80). Combining Mondrian CP with cost-controlled abstention significantly reduces expected decision cost compared to standard decision boundaries, confidence-based rejectors, and risk-controlled rejectors under realistic human review constraints.
AI.conclusion: Mondrian conformal prediction with cost-controlled abstention is the recommended approach for distribution-free, cost-aware uncertainty quantification in class-imbalanced, high-stakes settings. Dataset-specific break-even thresholds provide actionable guidance for deciding when human expert review is economically justified.

title: Skillful forecasting of offshore winds from satellite scatterometer constellations
summary: Accurate intraday forecasts of offshore wind are becoming increasingly important for power system operation and the integration of growing shares of offshore wind energy. Operational forecasts rely predominantly on numerical weather prediction (NWP), which is not optimized for lead times of minutes to hours, where initial-condition accuracy dominates forecast skill. Although satellite scatterometer observations are routinely assimilated into NWP, they have not previously been used directly for forecasting. Here we present WindCastNet, the first satellite-based nowcasting framework for offshore wind speed and direction, introducing a new paradigm for intraday forecasting that learns from spatiotemporally irregular satellite observations. WindCastNet predicts offshore wind fields from observations acquired by satellite scatterometer constellations. WindCastNet employs a partial convolutional long short-term memory network that exploits microwave radar observations from the European, Chinese, and Indian scatterometers despite their irregular spatial coverage, asynchronous sampling, and variable revisit times. Spatial observation masks and inter-observation intervals are encoded, while a continuous temporal representation enables forecasts at arbitrary lead times. Evaluated over the North Sea, WindCastNet reduces the root-mean-square error by 23% and 7% relative to the HARMONIE MEPS model at lead times of 1 and 2 h, respectively, and outperforms persistence by 9-15% during the first three forecast hours. Forecast skill decreases under strong-wind conditions and spatially non-uniform flow. These results demonstrate that satellite scatterometer constellations can provide an independent and competitive source of short-term offshore wind forecasts, opening new opportunities for renewable energy forecasting but also broader marine weather applications, including tropical cyclone nowcasting.

AI.tldr: WindCastNet is the first satellite-based nowcasting framework for offshore wind, using partial convolutional LSTM networks to generate intraday forecasts of wind speed and direction from irregular scatterometer observations, outperforming NWP and persistence at 1-3 hour lead times over the North Sea.
AI.motivation: Operational offshore wind forecasts rely on NWP models that are suboptimal for intraday (minutes to hours) lead times where initial-condition accuracy is critical. Satellite scatterometer observations are routinely assimilated into NWP but have never been used directly for forecasting, representing an untapped, independent data source for short-term offshore wind prediction.
AI.method: WindCastNet employs a partial convolutional long short-term memory (LSTM) network that ingests microwave radar observations from European, Chinese, and Indian scatterometer constellations. The architecture handles irregular spatial coverage, asynchronous sampling, and variable revisit times by encoding spatial observation masks and inter-observation intervals, while a continuous temporal representation enables forecasts at arbitrary lead times.
AI.result: Evaluated over the North Sea, WindCastNet reduces RMSE by 23% and 7% relative to the HARMONIE MEPS NWP model at 1 h and 2 h lead times, respectively, and outperforms persistence by 9–15% during the first three forecast hours. Forecast skill degrades under strong-wind conditions and spatially non-uniform flow.
AI.conclusion: Satellite scatterometer constellations provide an independent, competitive source of short-term offshore wind forecasts, with potential applications extending beyond renewable energy to broader marine weather contexts including tropical cyclone nowcasting.

title: When Do Learned Diffusion Proposals Help Constraint Solving? A Controlled Study on Continuous Algebraic Systems
summary: Solving a continuous algebraic constraint system requires two decisions: which values satisfy the constraints, and which structural augmentation renders an unsolvable system solvable. Classical solvers answer the first well and the second only by enumeration. On that discrete decision, a candidate-conditioned repair ranker choosing among K augmentations reaches the exhaustive-search ceiling at a fraction of the calls, outperforming random (0.997 vs 0.236 balanced nonlinear menu accuracy; p < 10^-70; 0.982 +/- 0.006 across seeds) and beating a budget-matched per-candidate probe on accuracy and cost. MARC turns such a system into a factor graph, over which a graph-neural diffusion denoiser proposes assignments, descent on an exact computer-algebra energy polishes them, and an exact symbolic checker certifies solutions. Evaluations of diffusion-based proposals rarely include one control: random multi-start under the same refinement budget. Applied to our system, it sharply curtails what the learned proposal contributes on the value decision. Does it beat random multi-start at choosing satisfying assignments? Only narrowly, in a predictable regime. Across trapped low-dimensional families it ties with random restart, but dominates in high dimension, where random search fails. Once variables couple, the advantage is gone. Since all methods share one polish and one checker, best-of-K random multi-start succeeds with probability exactly 1 - (1 - q(n))^K, where q(n) is single-start reachability; one measured constant, with no free parameters, reproduces the entire curve (mean absolute error 0.012). The favorable regime is not specific to our synthetic families: across eight real-world systems in robotics, positioning, optimization, and algebra, classical multi-start solved all eight, none in the learning-favorable regime. We map the regimes in which learned proposals improve solvers.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates whether learned diffusion-based proposal methods genuinely improve solving continuous algebraic constraint systems compared to classical random multi-start baselines. It finds that learned proposals only narrowly beat random restart in high-dimensional, uncoupled regimes; once variables couple, the advantage vanishes. Classical multi-start solved all eight real-world systems tested, none in the learning-favorable regime.
AI.motivation: Existing work on diffusion-based neural solvers for continuous algebraic constraint systems lacks proper baselines. The authors aim to rigorously test whether learned proposals actually outperform random multi-start under identical refinement budgets, and to characterize precisely when (if ever) learned methods contribute beyond exhaustive search.
AI.method: The paper introduces MARC, a system combining a factor-graph representation with a graph-neural diffusion denoiser for proposing assignments, gradient descent on an exact computer-algebra energy for polishing, and an exact symbolic checker for certification. The key methodological contribution is the rigorous control comparison: random multi-start under the same refinement budget. The authors also derive an analytical model for best-of-K random success probability: 1 - (1 - q(n))^K, where q(n) is single-start reachability, and validate it against empirical curves (MAE 0.012). They evaluate across synthetic families and eight real-world systems (robotics, positioning, optimization, algebra).
AI.result: The repair ranker outperforms random (0.997 vs 0.236 balanced nonlinear menu accuracy, p < 10⁻⁷⁰). For value decisions, learned proposals beat random multi-start only in high-dimensional, uncoupled regimes; they tie with random restart in trapped low-dimensional families. Once variables couple, the advantage disappears. The analytical model reproduces the entire success curve with one measured constant and no free parameters. Classical multi-start solved all eight real-world systems, none operating in the learning-favorable regime.
AI.conclusion: Learned proposals offer marginal and regime-specific gains over classical random multi-start for continuous algebraic constraint solving. The paper provides a clear map of when learned methods help (high dimension, uncoupled) and when they do not (low dimension, coupled, real-world systems), arguing that rigorous baselines are essential for evaluating neural solvers in this domain.

title: Inverse Learning of Latent Risk-Neutral Densities from Irregular Option Quotes
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF 2026)
summary: Accurate option prices do not imply accurate recovery of the latent risk-neutral density. We study this distinction with two complementary benchmarks. A controlled benchmark exposes simulator-truth densities for latent evaluation, while a chronological NIFTY benchmark tests only held-out market prices. A two-component lognormal mixture has the lowest aggregate price, $L^1$, Wasserstein, and fixed-tail errors on the synthetic benchmark. Learned operators retain narrower strengths: DeepONet reduces 1% quantile and variance error by 39.0% and 34.6% relative to the mixture, and a quote transformer reduces $L^1$ by 16.4% on the structurally misspecified Merton family. A numerical conditioning analysis explains why these rankings can differ: after enforcing mass and forward constraints, 95 of 126 pricing directions are numerically null, and two densities separated by $L^1 = 0.061$ produce identical prices on the covered strikes. On 524 held-out NIFTY calls, validation-selected test-time adaptation reduces DeepONet RMSE by 28.3%, but per-expiry mixture and SVI fits remain much more accurate. The evidence supports target-dependent inductive bias, not a universal winner.

AI.tldr: Accurate option pricing does not guarantee accurate recovery of risk-neutral densities. Using synthetic and real-market benchmarks, the paper shows that while a two-component lognormal mixture performs best overall, neural operators like DeepONet and quote transformers excel in specific error metrics. A numerical conditioning analysis reveals that most pricing directions are numerically null due to constraints, explaining the price-density disconnect. Test-time adaptation helps neural methods but classical models remain more accurate on held-out NIFTY data.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by the critical distinction between fitting option prices accurately and recovering the true latent risk-neutral density (RND). In quantitative finance, RNDs are used for risk management, pricing exotic derivatives, and monetary policy analysis, yet practitioners often assume that accurate price calibration implies accurate density recovery. The authors challenge this assumption and seek to quantify the gap using rigorous benchmarks.
AI.method: The study employs two complementary benchmarks: (1) a controlled synthetic benchmark with simulator-truth densities for latent evaluation using metrics like L¹, Wasserstein distance, fixed-tail errors, and quantile/variance errors; and (2) a chronological NIFTY benchmark testing only held-out market prices. Methods compared include a two-component lognormal mixture, SVI parameterization, DeepONet, and a quote transformer. A numerical conditioning analysis examines the Jacobian of prices with respect to density parameters after imposing martingale and forward constraints, revealing that 95 of 126 pricing directions are numerically null.
AI.result: The two-component lognormal mixture achieves the lowest aggregate price, L¹, Wasserstein, and fixed-tail errors on synthetic data. DeepONet reduces 1% quantile error by 39.0% and variance error by 34.6% relative to the mixture. The quote transformer reduces L¹ by 16.4% on structurally misspecified Merton-family densities. Two densities separated by L¹ = 0.061 can produce identical prices on covered strikes. On 524 held-out NIFTY calls, validation-selected test-time adaptation reduces DeepONet RMSE by 28.3%, but per-expiry mixture and SVI fits remain substantially more accurate.
AI.conclusion: There is no universal winner across all metrics and settings. The evidence supports target-dependent inductive bias: classical mixtures excel in aggregate and tail metrics, while neural operators offer narrower advantages on specific error dimensions. The severe ill-conditioning of the price-to-density mapping structurally limits any method's ability to uniquely recover RNDs from prices alone, especially under no-arbitrage constraints.

title: From Classification to Regression: Using a Fruitfly to Solve Equations
summary: We present a novel approach to regression tasks using classification which is motivated by the mechanism used by fruitflies to sense their environment. Specifically, we formulate a general framework for learning nonlinear input-output relationships by replacing complex global surrogate models with a finite library of representative local patterns. Since scientific data often occupy limited and recurring regions of the input space, we generate predictions by measuring similarities between a query and stored patterns, then combining their associated responses through weighted reconstruction. We apply this approach to nonlinear dynamical systems, data-driven regression, and physics-informed learning using suitable embeddings and similarity measures. For dynamical systems, our offline-online workflow extracts patterns from data or governing equations during the offline phase, while online prediction requires only similarity evaluation and response aggregation. This structure helps us reduce computational and memory demands while providing explicit control over the trade-off among accuracy, storage, and inference cost.

AI.tldr: A fruitfly-inspired regression framework that replaces global surrogate models with a finite library of local patterns, using similarity-based weighted reconstruction for prediction. Applied to nonlinear dynamical systems, data-driven regression, and physics-informed learning with tunable accuracy-storage-cost trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Traditional regression relies on complex global surrogate models (e.g., neural networks) that are computationally and memory-intensive. The authors draw inspiration from the fruitfly olfactory system, which uses a library of local representative patterns for rapid, efficient sensing — motivating a shift from global approximation to pattern-matching-based regression that is both lighter and more interpretable.
AI.method: The proposed framework constructs a finite library of representative local input-output patterns. During inference, a query is compared against stored patterns using suitable similarity measures (with appropriate embeddings), and predictions are generated via weighted aggregation of the responses associated with the most similar patterns. For dynamical systems, an offline-online workflow is adopted: pattern extraction (from data or governing equations) occurs offline, while online prediction involves only similarity evaluation and response reconstruction, minimizing runtime cost.
AI.result: The approach reduces computational and memory demands compared to global surrogate models. It provides explicit, tunable control over the trade-off among prediction accuracy, storage footprint, and inference cost, making it adaptable to resource-constrained settings.
AI.conclusion: Local pattern-matching regression, inspired by biological sensing, offers a viable and efficient alternative to global surrogates for scientific computing tasks, particularly where data occupies limited, recurring regions of the input space. The framework is versatile across dynamical systems, data-driven, and physics-informed regression contexts.

title: Do You Really Need to Pretrain Q-Functions for Online RL Fine-Tuning?
summary: Pre-training followed by fine-tuning has become the dominant recipe for learning performant policies, and in value-based reinforcement learning (RL) this raises a natural question: given a pretrained policy, should the Q-function be pretrained on offline data too? Conventional wisdom suggests it should, but recent results show that online RL with a randomly-initialized Q-function can result in highly performant and reliable policies without needing to pretrain the Q-function. In this paper, we systematically study whether pretraining the Q-function actually helps when fine-tuning on top of a pretrained base policy. We find, surprisingly, that naive Q-function pretraining often provides little benefit over random initialization. We show this stems from a fundamental mismatch: the Q-function learned during pretraining targets the pretrained policy's Q-function, not the Q-function that online fine-tuning converges to, and this gap persists even after offline value maximization. Motivated by this finding, we propose Initialization via Policy Ensemble (IPE), a simple method that trains multiple diverse policies and uses their pooled rollouts to bootstrap the Q-function learning in online RL. Across a suite of challenging continuous control benchmarks, IPE yields an average 1.26x improvement in fine-tuning performance over naive Q-function pre-training.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically investigates whether Q-function pretraining helps when fine-tuning a pretrained policy in online RL. Surprisingly, naive Q-function pretraining often provides little benefit due to a mismatch: the pretrained Q-function targets the pretrained policy's behavior, not the optimal policy that online fine-tuning converges to. The authors propose IPE (Initialization via Policy Ensemble), which uses diverse policy rollouts to bootstrap Q-function learning, achieving 1.26x average improvement over naive pretraining.
AI.motivation: Pre-training followed by fine-tuning is standard in RL, but it's unclear whether the Q-function should also be pretrained alongside the policy. While conventional wisdom favors Q-function pretraining, recent empirical results suggest online RL with randomly-initialized Q-functions can still produce strong policies. This contradiction motivates a systematic study of whether Q-function pretraining actually provides benefits.
AI.method: The authors first conduct a systematic empirical analysis comparing naive Q-function pretraining (standard offline RL on the same dataset) against random initialization during online fine-tuning of a pretrained policy. They identify a fundamental distributional mismatch between the pretrained Q-function and the Q-function needed for online convergence. To address this, they propose IPE: training an ensemble of diverse policies offline, generating rollouts from all of them, and using this pooled data to initialize the Q-function, providing broader coverage of the state-action space relevant to online fine-tuning.
AI.result: Naive Q-function pretraining often yields negligible improvement over random initialization due to the identified mismatch. IPE consistently outperforms both random initialization and naive Q-function pretraining across challenging continuous control benchmarks, with an average 1.26x improvement in fine-tuning performance.
AI.conclusion: Q-function pretraining is not inherently beneficial — its utility depends critically on whether the pretrained Q-function aligns with the target of online fine-tuning. IPE addresses this mismatch by leveraging diverse policy rollouts, providing a simple yet effective initialization strategy that bridges the gap between offline pretraining and online fine-tuning.
